News.title: Airlines criticise air traffic control as second glitch causes more disruption
News.content:
Airlines have criticised the UK's air traffic control system after a second technical problem in two weeks caused major disruption to UK flights.

EasyJet said Monday's incident "once again calls into question the resilience" of the service, while Wizz Air said there was a "national confidence crisis" in National Air Traffic Services (Nats), which runs the UK's air traffic.

Nats said a "connectivity issue" at Prestwick was behind the disruption across Scotland, Northern Ireland and northern England - and had "nothing to do" with a separate software defect at Swanwick earlier this month.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said further issues today "cause even greater concern" about the UK's air traffic control.

When asked by reporters whether he would look to fire the head of Nats, Burnham said "these are clearly serious issues and they need to be fully investigated".

He added that the transport secretary was taking the issues "extremely seriously" and initially it's a matter for her "to get to the bottom of... and why there has been a recurrence."

The underlying issue causing Monday's disruption has since been resolved, with Nats saying it was running at "full capacity" although officials warned of knock-on effects.

A spokesperson said they were now "focused on working with our customers to recover their residual delays and help get their operations back to normal".

More than 150 flights were cancelled at UK airports on Monday - including 140 departures and 137 arrivals, according to aviation analytics company Cirium.

Easyjet was the worst affected airline, with 48 of its 670 scheduled departures cancelled, while British Airways has seen 13 cancellations from its 513 scheduled departures.

The UK Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) said passengers who had flights disrupted were "unlikely" to be entitled to compensation.

It said the technical issue is "likely to be considered the result of 'extraordinary circumstances' under passenger rights rules", meaning that "although passengers should be looked after by airlines, they are unlikely to be entitled to compensation for delays or cancellations that were directly caused by the incident".

An independent review by the CAA into the resilience of the UK's air traffic control system is under way and the results will be published "within six months", it said.

News.title: UK to provide Saudi Arabia with 'defensive' military support, says Burnham
News.content:
Defensive support is described by UK officials as that which aides Saudi air force jets shooting down incoming Houthi missiles and drones.

The singular Voyager aircraft is part of a core fleet of nine - eight military registered and another civilian registered - on the Royal Air Force (RAF)'s books.

The RAF also has five others available for military recall if needed.

Speaking to reporters travelling with him on the way to the United Nations General Assembly in New York, Burnham linked cost of living pressures to the decision.

"I go back to the point I made about cost-of-living pressures and acting to secure the interests of Britain and the wider region," he said.

"Because of course Saudi Arabia has been experiencing attacks, is looking at potential further disruption, and we need to keep those pathways open, and hence our agreement to the request."

Shipping routes through the Red Sea are a vital artery of the world economy.

The Houthis recently seized control of the strategic port city of Mokha and Perim Island, a gateway to the Red Sea - a key shipping route used by Saudi Arabia.

In a BBC interview last week, Nato Secretary-General Mark Rutte hinted that European support for Saudi Arabia was likely.

He said: "I would not be surprised if some phone calls were taking place between European allies, 'hey, how are we going to deal with this?'.

"Let's see what happens, and if Nato can help, we will always be helpful."

Energy Minister Martin McCluskey last week told MPs that the UK was "providing air defence support" to Saudi Arabia through the defence partnership that they have, although would not be drawn on questions of operational military activity.

In January 2024, the UK joined the US in launching air strikes against Houthi targets across Yemen.

Then-Prime Minister Rishi Sunak said the UK "acted in self-defence" following the Houthis' targeting of ships, including a Royal Navy warship.

He also said the strikes were "necessary, proportionate, and targeted" to protect lives and commercial shipping.

Further joint air strikes from the UK and US followed in 2024, external.

News.title: Flights at major US airports delayed after cable cut by construction workers
News.content:
Hundreds of flights have been delayed at major airports in the US after construction workers accidentally cut a cable needed for air traffic control.

Ground stops and delays were issued on Monday afternoon for airports in New York, Pennsylvania, New Jersey and Massachusetts.

Hours later, US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the cable had been repaired and airports would resume normal operations, though delays were still expected.

The major east coast disruption came ahead of the UN General Assembly (UNGA) in New York City on Tuesday, which is expected to be attended by scores of world leaders arriving into New York-area airports.

That includes UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who managed to board his flight before the delays began and was expected to arrive on time.

The delays happened after the damaged cable impacted the Terminal Radar Approach Control system, which is used to guide planes during takeoff and landing, transport officials said.

New Jersey public transportation agency NJ Transit told CBS News, the BBC's US partner, that its construction workers had accidentally severed the line and that markers had been wrongly placed at the digging site.

The BBC has reached out to NJ Transit for comment.

Duffy earlier said the damage was caused by workers from Amtrak, the US national operator of intercity railroad service, who were doing the construction work. This "caused a telecom outage" which forced the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to ground flights, Duffy posted on X.

An Amtrak spokesperson said in a statement, reported by US media, that the incident involved a NJ Transit contractor. Telecommunications company Verizon, which owns the cable, also said it was not responsible.

The severed cable was actually a backup network, and the error was only discovered after the primary circuit failed, according to the head of the FAA, Bryan Bedford.

Newark Liberty International Airport in New Jersey - one of the three major airports that services New York City - was the most heavily impacted by today's air traffic control disruptions, according to flight-tracking website FlightAware.

It reported that 267 departing flights were delayed today, while a further 257 flights destined for Newark were also delayed.

John F Kennedy International Airport and LaGuardia Airport, both in New York, were also affected, as was Philadelphia International Airport.

One passenger, Douglas Tewnion, said he boarded a flight to New York from Edinburgh and that his plane had been diverted to Boston, Massachusetts instead.

He told the BBC that, two hours after his flight was due into New York, he and the other passengers were still "sitting on the same plane, on the tarmac at Boston with no information".

Though "everyone is in good spirits", Tewnion said "it's just a pain" to see two more hours waiting added onto a lengthy flight.

Additional reporting by Ione Wells

News.title: Watch: Police raid organised crime targets in Teesside
News.content:
Cleveland Police have carried out one of their biggest raids on organised crime targets in years.

About 130 officers were involved in the operation which saw 17 people arrested in the Middlesbrough area.

The raids are part of a response to a crash on the nearby A66 last month, which resulted in the death of two officers in a police pursuit.

Five men also died when their Volkswagen Passat went the wrong way down the road and hit a Cleveland Police armed response vehicle heading in the opposite direction.

The BBC's Stuart Whincup was with the police as they carried out the arrests.

Read more about the raids in this story.

News.title: Infantino says he is open to Fifa reform
News.content:
Fifa president Gianni Infantino has proposed an external review of how world football's governing body operates, and says he is open to reform.

In a letter sent to members of the Fifa Council and all of its national associations, Infantino explains the independent process would "recommend potential improvements".

Before a meeting of the Council next month, Infantino says he is also suggesting a consultation on "how Fifa's decision-making can be further strengthened".

This would include proposals on the role of the president, as well as "practical ways to strengthen transparency, participation and accountability in major strategic initiatives".

Infantino has come under increasing pressure over his aborted Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal. That would have involved selling stakes in the World Cup and other competitions to private investors, and it sparked a major backlash.

In what appears to be a conciliatory gesture, Infantino writes: "Over recent weeks, I have taken time to listen before writing to you", and says the consultation will be with confederations, member associations and "relevant stakeholders".

He insists that the FFE plan "did not involve relinquishing Fifa's control or authority over sporting decisions. Obviously!"

His letter adds: "The proposal entered the public domain before Fifa's planned institutional process had been completed and before it could be presented in full to the Council and the member associations. I recognise that, without the full context, this caused concern and created the impression that decisions had already been taken. They had not."

Infantino also claims that "democratic processes, independence and sporting authority were never for sale. They are not for sale and never will be."

He states he remains "fully committed to leading Fifa and confident in what we can achieve together".

Infantino's letter comes after Uefa and Concacaf - the confederations for Europe and North America, Central America and the Caribbean - demanded Fifa pays $10m to all 211 members from its cash reserves.

FFE would have meant a new company being created to manage commercial and ticketing rights of all Fifa competitions, including World Cups, with 21% sold off to a private investment company.

Infantino claims that the collapse of FFE "does not diminish our ambition or our responsibility to invest more of Fifa's success back into football.

"We will continue to explore sustainable ways to grow Fifa's resources and expand development and solidarity support for every member association," he adds in the letter.

"What changes is not the ambition, but the strength of the process through which major ideas are developed, tested and decided.

"The progress we have made over the past decade gives us a strong foundation for the future. It also gives us the confidence to examine whether our governance remains suited to the scale and complexity of the decisions ahead."

Earlier this month, Football Association chair Debbie Hewitt, a Fifa vice-president, told Infantino to release all documents relating to his controversial plan.

The 56-year-old Swiss-Italian Fifa leader will stand for election for a fourth time in March 2027, with his opponents having until 18 November to find an alternative candidate.

Last month, European football's governing body Uefa began preparing criminal legal proceedings against Infantino at courts in the US over the FFE plan, demanding the release of all documents.

Fifa hit back and accused Uefa of a "smear campaign against it and its leadership" in a challenge to the litigation.

News.title: Death of Cindy Crawford's son Presley Gerber being investigated as suspected overdose
News.content:
He went on to model for brands including Burberry, Dolce & Gabbana, and Bottega Veneta.

His father Rande Gerber, a well-known businessman, co-founded the Casamigos tequila brand with George Clooney.

In recent years, Presley Gerber had spoken openly about his mental health challenges and drug use.

In 2023, he told the Studio 22 podcast: "Having struggled with mental health, depression and some other things that come along with that, I think that whether I help one person or a hundred people get out of that place that I was in at one point in my life, that's all I need to do."

And in this month's American Vogue, external, Kaia discussed her brother's struggles with addiction. She said: "When something like that happens in a family, it kind of levels everyone.

"I think that's also why I started to self-identify as the easy one and never wanted to ask for help."

She added: "My parents for most of our lives were very, very private and didn't share anything - and now we have this absolute teacher, my brother, who says, 'I'm gonna be very human for everyone.' There's only so much you can hide from the world. And trying to put a lid on something just makes the person feel like you're ashamed of them."

News.title: Man charged with causing death by dangerous driving over crash that killed 6
News.content:
A man has been charged with causing death by dangerous driving over a crash that killed six people, including two children.

Shannen Morgan and Shane Roller died along with two of their daughters, nine-year-old Rubie, and Lillie, four, when the family's car collided with a motorbike on the A61 between Barnsley and Wakefield on 21 July 2024.

Husband and wife Christopher and Janine Barton, from Barnsley, who were both travelling on the motorcycle, also died in the crash.

Christopher Cockell, 50, is due to appear at Leeds Magistrates' Court in October charged with six counts of causing death by dangerous driving.

An inquest previously heard that the silver Ford Focus being driven by Mr Roller, 33, collided head on with the BMW motorcycle being driven by Mr Barton, 56, at about 15:50 BST between Staincross and Newmillerdam.

Wakefield Coroner's Court heard the collision happened as the motorcycle was overtaking another vehicle on the single-carriageway road, which had a 50mph (80 km/h) speed limit.

Coroner's support officer Phil Marr told the hearing: "As a result of a head-on impact, the car was spun to the side of the road, where it caught fire.

"It was not possible to release any of the occupants and all four were pronounced dead by paramedics at the scene."

News.title: Watch: Timelapse shows typhoon barrelling towards Japan
News.content:
A powerful typhoon passing Japan's eastern coast is bringing major disruption and heavy rainfall in its wake.

The police are urging nearly two million people at risk in Tokyo and surrounding areas to leave their homes.

Satellite footage showed Typhoon Dujuan crossing the Pacific Ocean towards Japan.

Read more about the "imminent threat to life" caused by the typhoon.

News.title: Seventeen arrested in Teesside organised crime raids
News.content:
Police have carried out a series of early morning raids targeting those suspected of being involved in organised crime.

Cleveland Police said 17 people had been arrested during the operation - involving about 130 officers including some from the National Crime Agency - across South Bank, Grangetown and Eston, near Middlesbrough, on Monday.

It is part of a high-profile response to a crash on the nearby A66 last month which came at the end of a police pursuit and left two officers dead.

Five men also died when their Volkswagen Passat went the wrong way down the road and hit a Cleveland Police armed response vehicle heading in the opposite direction.

The force said Monday's raids had seen people arrested on suspicion of various offences including drugs and assault.

A convoy of about a dozen vans started the operation shortly after 08:00 BST, with roads temporarily blocked by patrol cars.

Officers used battering rams to force entry to several properties as parents walked past with their children on the school run.

News.title: Two pilot whales dead after mass stranding
News.content:
Two pilot whales have died after a distressed pod was spotted off the Northumberland coast.

British Divers Marine Life Rescue (BDMLR) said it had been alerted to a group of about 40 whales near to the shore at Amble at 15:00 BST on Sunday.

It said the whales had been "behaving in a distressed manner typically seen prior to a stranding event".

Due to the tides, attempts to refloat the animals had been unsuccessful, the charity said, and rescue teams were forced to withdraw.

Whales are highly social mammals and are well known for stranding in groups because they travel in large, close-knit communities which rely on constant communication.

There are a range of theories for why beachings occur. Some experts say the animals can become disorientated after following fish they hunt to the shore.

Others believe that one individual can mistakenly lead whole groups to shore.

News.title: Young people aren't snowflakes - mental distress is rising, says head of official review
News.content:
Accusations that the young are a snowflake generation are wrong, the head of an independent review into mental health, ADHD and autism has told the BBC.

Prof Peter Fonagy said in an exclusive interview that there had been a real rise in mental distress among children and young people, with anxiety, depression, self-harm and eating disorders the most common.

He said it was "harder to be young" now given the economic and employment uncertainty young people face, coupled with the challenges presented by social media.

His review was ordered nine months ago by Wes Streeting after the then-health secretary claimed in an interview that young people were over-diagnosed and "written off".

It is likely to feed into government policies on everything from NHS services and benefits to support for young people who are not in education, employment or training.

Fonagy said he chose to speak to the BBC ahead of the publication, which is expected later this week, because he was concerned the debate around ADHD and autism would "obscure" the wider issue of mental health.

More than 100 experts and families with experience of mental health problems have worked on the review with Fonagy, a clinical psychologist and adviser to NHS England.

He said it will conclude that the rise in mental health problems since the 1990s was real, with about one in four 16 to 24-year-olds now struggling.

The data on this is contested as some sources rely on self-reporting, while sceptics argue greater awareness and reduced stigma around mental health mean more people are coming forward.

Some have also questioned whether society was now over-medicalising distress in people's lives â giving people diagnoses when what they are facing is temporary stress that they should learn to cope with.

Last year, the BBC found that many GPs had concerns about over-diagnosis and felt normal life stresses were being over-medicalised.

NHS figures, external show the number of children and young people in contact with mental health services in England has risen by 50% in the past five years.

News.title: 'I see my abusers in the supermarket' - Oxford grooming gang survivors' ongoing torment
News.content:
Warning: This story contains details of sexual violence

Survivors of an Oxford grooming gang say they still see men who sexually abused them, and who have not been brought to justice, walking around the city.

"A shop, a petrol station, a restaurant - everywhere you can imagine - you'll see a man that's done something," one survivor, Sarah, tells BBC Panorama.

Sarah and two other survivors believe "hundreds" of perpetrators are still free. An ex-police detective who led the initial investigation into grooming gangs in Oxford agrees.

It is the first time that Sarah (whose name we have changed) and one of the other women have spoken out publicly about what they were subjected to.

Gangs of men were found to have sexually exploited and abused underage girls in several towns and cities - including Rotherham, Rochdale and Telford, as well as Oxford - between the 1990s and 2010s.

Oxford was one of the places where most of the perpetrators were identified as older men of Pakistani heritage. In some cases, such as in Rotherham, police were accused of hesitating to act out of fear of being seen as racist. But in Oxford a serious case review found no evidence that this had been a factor.

Now, the government has launched a national inquiry to address why vulnerable children were not protected in England and Wales - including whether attitudes to the girls or the ethnicity of the perpetrators contributed to the failings.

News.title: British Museum bans visitors from photographing Bayeux Tapestry
News.content:
The British Museum has banned visitors from taking photographs of the Bayeux Tapestry over concerns that they were taking too long to view the historic work.

Curators had initially allowed photos to be taken but reversed that decision after long queues delayed ticket-holders from accessing the exhibition.

The medieval embroidery, which is on display in Britain for the first time, depicts the events leading up to the Norman conquest of England and the Battle of Hastings in 1066.

Visitors are being allowed into the sold-out exhibit in groups every 40 minutes and told to keep moving along the 68m (230ft) work in one direction.

But people stopping to take photographs along the way was restricting that flow and delaying later visitors.

A British Museum spokeswoman said: "There has been enormous interest in viewing the tapestry, and our priority is to ensure that all visitors have the best experience possible.

"In order to do this, we have made the decision to restrict photography while people are moving along the length of the tapestry."

The 11th Century artwork - which is not a tapestry and was actually embroidered in England - is currently on loan from its home in Normandy, France, and will be displayed in London until July 2027.

British Museum bosses decided that the embroidery would be displayed in a single, straight line, unlike the horseshoe-shaped gallery in which it is displayed in Bayeux.

The loan was confirmed following a Franco-British summit in 2025, following years of planning between the two countries.

Under the agreement, the British Museum is funding the costs of move while insurance is provided by the UK government.

The artefact was carefully packed in a climate-controlled crate and was given a police escort along the unprecedented 350-mile (560km) journey from its home to central London.

Some would-be visitors have criticised the high price of tickets - as much as three times what it costs to see the Bayeux Tapestry in France - to cover the museum's expenses.

Tickets for the exhibition are sold out until 31 December but more are expected to go on sale in October.

Alternately, a full-scale replica of the Bayeux Tapestry is available to see for free in Tewkesbury Abbey in Gloucestershire and at Reading Museum.

News.title: Helen Jenner unveiled by Nigel Farage as new leader of Reform in Wales
News.content:
Nigel Farage has unveiled Helen Jenner as the newly-elected leader of Reform in Wales, replacing Dan Thomas after his arrest on suspicion of assault and controlling or coercive behaviour.

Speaking on the steps of the Senedd in Cardiff on Monday, Farage said: "I've known Helen for many, many years. She is a determined campaigner."

Farage said he felt sorry about former leader Thomas's "personal difficulties" and that it had been untenable for him to continue, adding: "We could have done without this bump in the road."

Jenner, who served as Thomas's deputy alongside her role as Senedd member for Bangor Conwy MÃ´n, said it was an honour to be elected to the top job.

A leadership vote was held by Reform's 33 Senedd members on Monday morning, and Jenner confirmed that her colleague Jason O'Connell had stood against her.

Figures were not published by the party on Monday but BBC Wales was told the vote was believed to be close.

O'Connell had not been expected to stand, and there had been no vote of the wider party membership.

Speaking to reporters outside the Senedd, Farage said there would be a vote for a new Welsh deputy leader to replace Jenner on Tuesday.

News.title: Specialist courts for rape cases to be rolled out in England and Wales
News.content:
Specialist courts to handle cases of rape and other sexual offences will be introduced across England and Wales over the next two years, the prime minister has announced.

Each crown court will have at least one courtroom set up to hear such cases, while alleged victims will be able to view proceedings remotely and give evidence from a separate room via video link.

They will also be provided with private entrances and waiting rooms to separate them from defendants, though this will be dependent on the architecture of each building.

Rape Crisis England and Wales said this was a "significant step forward" that would introduce several reforms it had been requesting for years.

"Taken together, they reflect the urgency of ensuring that courts are fit for purpose and properly meet the needs of victims and survivors, which is crucial to securing justice," the charity's chief executive, Ciara Bergman, said.

Charities have complained that low prosecution rates for sexual offences and delays to court proceedings had disuaded victims from coming forward or pursuing justice.

Just 2.8% of rape offences recorded by police led to prosecutions in the year ending March 2024 and were the crimes that took the longest to investigate.

A prior ONS study, using data from 2017-2020, suggested that only a sixth of the actual number of rape and attempted rape victims had reported their assault to the police, with more than a third saying this was because they felt the police could not help or that the process would be humiliating.

Victims minister Alex Davies-Jones said the new measures were part of efforts to bring down a backlog of Crown Court cases, which stood at 80,098 at the end of March.

Rape Crisis England and Wales said 15,373 of these cases - 19% - related to sexual offences.

Davies-Jones told BBC Breakfast that the introduction of specialist courtrooms "isn't enough on its own" to tackle the backlog and stressed the importance of the Courts and Tribunals Bill to improve "timeliness, effectiveness and also prevention".

The Conservatives say the "long overdue" move should not come with restricting the number of jury trials, which is another provision of the bill.

Under the new measures, expected to cost around Â£23m of the Ministry of Justice's budget, court staff will also be given "trauma-informed training" and a single person of contact will be assigned to each survivor.

From next month, trials will be given a fixed date rather than placed on floating lists in what Prime Minister Andy Burnham said was an effort to "rebalance the scales of justice and put victims first".

There are 84 crown court buildings across England and Wales, containing around 500 courtrooms, and Davies-Jones said the government was determined that every one of them would have at least one specialist rape and sexual offences courtroom by 2028.

Where architecture might prevent courtroom upgrades, Davies-Jones said staff would be expected to co-ordinate a "trauma informed approach" - for instance by scheduling different arrival times and rooms to give evidence from for victims and defendants.

The government said the changes follow Labour MP Charlotte Nichols showing "immense strength and bravery" in speaking publicly about being raped and calling for changes to the justice system.

Nichols waived her automatic right to anonymity in March when she made a Commons speech in which she described having to wait more than 1,000 days to go to court.

News.title: Two arrested over major fire at Folkestone hotel
News.content:
Two people have been arrested on suspicion of arson after a fire at a seaside hotel which led to hundreds of people being evacuated.

Kent Police said a 38-year-old man and 21-year-old woman were held after the blaze at the Grand Burstin Hotel in Folkestone on Saturday.

The fire broke out at the hotel in Marine Parade in the early hours and about 280 people were evacuated from the building.

A total of 90 people were relocated from neighbouring Pavilion Court in Marine Terrace following concerns raised by safety inspectors, Folkestone and Hythe District Council said.

The pair who were arrested have been released while inquiries continue, a police spokesperson said.

Scientists have identified the reasons why the bacterial strain that caused a fatal meningitis B outbreak in Kent was so dangerous.

New genetic analysis shows the virulent strain acquired characteristics from benign bacteria that typically reside harmlessly in human throats.

Traced back to a Canterbury venue in March 2026, the outbreak resulted in 21 diagnoses of invasive meningococcal disease (IMD) over seven days.

Two teenagers lost their lives as a result of the infection, with nine further patients needing intensive care treatment.

Specialists from the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) alongside Oxford University researchers conducted bacterial genome sequencing to determine why the strain proved so potent.

Their findings indicate the menB bacteria absorbed fragments of DNA from separate organisms via horizontal gene transfer, a mechanism allowing bacteria to borrow genetic traits without reproducing.

According to the analysis, these modifications altered how the bacteria interacts with human cells, making it particularly effective at causing severe illness and potentially impacting how it was recognised by the immune system.

According to the UKHSA these invasive strains can emerge suddenly and are unpredictable, meaning similar outbreaks are likely to occur again.

Students queuing to receive vaccines and antibiotics at the University of Kent campus in Canterbury back in March ( PA )

It may also explain why it did not continue to spread.

Dr Charlene Rodrigues, consultant in pathogen genomics at UKHSA, said: “This investigation shows just how quickly and dramatically these bacteria can change, sometimes acquiring new traits from harmless bacteria circulating nearby, that make them more likely to cause disease.

“The fact this outbreak variant was able to spread to so many young people was due to the social environment, a place where lots of close social mixing takes place.

“Through genomic surveillance and sequencing every cultured case of invasive meningococcal disease in England, we can spot when something unusual is emerging and understand what we’re dealing with in real-time.

“What’s particularly interesting about this research is that it suggests the very same genetic changes that made this strain so dangerous may also explain why it hasn’t continued to spread.

“But that is not something we could have predicted and these genetic events can happen again.

“That unpredictability is exactly why continued surveillance and rapid response systems are so important, as are vaccination and public awareness of the signs and symptoms of meningococcal disease.”

Following the Kent outbreak, a one-off menB vaccination programme was launched to protect young people heading to university this autumn.

In July, the Joint Committee on Vaccination and Immunisation (JCVI) also recommended that teenagers should be offered the jab on the NHS around the age of 15, with catch-up programmes for those who would otherwise miss out.

The findings will be presented at the UKHSA’s annual conference in Manchester.

A federal judge on Monday refused to block the Trump administration from giving SpaceX more than 700 acres (280 hectares) of wildlife refuge as part of a land swap in Texas, while environmental groups vowed to continue their legal challenge.

U.S. District Judge Fernando Rodriguez Jr. declined the plaintiffs' request for a preliminary injunction to prevent the parcel exchange, saying they failed to prove it would worsen ecological risks to a Gulf Coast region already transformed by billionaire Elon Musk’s rocket operations.

In June, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service approved moving forward with the deal with SpaceX, which would surrender 683 acres (276 hectares) the company owns in exchange for the federal land in the Lower Rio Grande Valley National Wildlife Refuge. The 103,000-acre (41,700-hectare) refuge spans four counties along the Texas border and is home to animal habitats and historical landmarks.

Maps show the land SpaceX would acquire would be closer to the company's launchpad near the U.S.-Mexico border.

The swap amounts to a gift of public lands to SpaceX, “clearing the way for bulldozers to tear into this wildlife refuge as soon as next week and turn a public treasure into a private payday,” said Laiken Jordahl, a spokesperson with the Center for Biological Diversity, which filed the lawsuit alongside other opponents including tribal groups. Jordahl said Monday that the litigation will continue even as the exchange goes forward.

“This court order is not the final word. These lands hold incredible spiritual, historical and conservation value for the people and wildlife of South Texas. We won’t stop fighting to keep this irreplaceable public wildlife refuge safe from SpaceX bulldozers,” Jordahl said in a statement.

The lawsuit asks the federal court to halt the exchange, which has worried SpaceX opponents in the area who have long criticized the company's expanding footprint over lost access to beaches and concerns over exploding rockets.

The Fish and Wildlife Service didn’t respond to a request for comment on Monday’s decision. Previously, a spokesperson had said the agency does not comment on ongoing litigation.

The agency issued a final environmental assessment report in June that determined the exchange would cause no significant impact to the area. The report said the federal government believed the acquisition would represent a “net conservation benefit” and provide “substantial long-term conservation value and improving landscape-scale habitat connectivity across refuges in South Texas.”

The judge said that the plaintiffs offered “relatively weak” evidence of environmental harm.

“While they rightfully argue that the preservation of wildlife and historical lands furthers the public interest, they present no evidence demonstrating that the Property will suffer aesthetic, environmental, cultural, or historical degradation during the pendency of this lawsuit,” Rodriguez wrote in his ruling.

In addition, the judge said a preliminary injunction would result in modifications to SpaceX’s development plans, “placing additional hardship on the company’s ability to meet milestones and contractual obligations.”

SpaceX did not return an email seeking comment on the judge's ruling.

The space exploration company first broke ground in Texas more than a decade ago and has expanded rapidly, so much that SpaceX employees last year voted to incorporate their own local government called Starbase.

News.title: Man charged with causing deaths of six people by dangerous driving
News.content:

A man has been charged with causing the deaths of six people more than two years after a crash.

Christopher Cockell, 50, of Gresford Close, Woolley Grange, has been charged with six counts of causing death by dangerous driving, West Yorkshire Police said

Four members of the same family, including two children, and a married couple on a motorcycle were killed in the crash on the A61, near the village of Mapplewell, Barnsley, in July 2024.

Shane Roller, 33, his partner Shannen Morgan, 30, and their daughters, Rubie and Lillie Morgan-Roller, aged nine and four, died when their Ford Focus car was in collision with the motorbike.

Mr Roller and Ms Morgan had a third daughter who was not in the car.

The married couple, Christopher Barton, 56, and Janine Barton, 48, who were on the BMW S100 XR motorbike, also died in the crash.

Cockell is due to appear at Leeds Magistrates’ Court on October 28.

More to follow...

Energy bills for British households could be reduced if the Government encouraged the widespread adoption of flexible, time-varying tariffs, a major new report has suggested.

Although generation costs fluctuate "a lot" depending on location and timing, the vast majority of domestic energy customers remain on flat rates that ignore these differences, according to research by the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) and LSE, funded by the Nuffield Foundation as part of the IFS Green Budget.

Due to frequent high winds, power generated in Scotland is often "effectively free", creating such an abundance of energy that the grid operator is regularly forced to pay wind farm operators to switch off turbines to prevent system overloading.

Conversely, during times of peak demand – particularly across the south of England – costly gas-fired generators are paid to step in and boost power supply.

open image in gallery Household electricity bills could fall if the Government promoted the take-up of time-varying prices, according to a report ( PA )

Despite the Government ruling out localised electricity markets or zonal pricing models, the study highlights alternative ways to align customer charges with generation costs, including shifting standard domestic tariffs onto a time-varying footing by default.

The authors also advocate offering relatively higher financial subsidies for electric heat pump installations in low-cost generation regions, alongside bigger solar panel subsidies in areas where demand is more likely to be met by gas generators.

Adjusting household bills to reflect market conditions would give consumers stronger financial incentives to shift power usage to off-peak hours—such as charging electric vehicles or running washing machines when it is cheapest—thereby driving down overall consumer bills, the report concluded.

On a broader scale, ministers could help relieve ongoing cost-of-living strains driven by elevated power costs by taking action to modernise and streamline the efficiency of the UK’s electricity system, it said.

Expenses associated with balancing power supply against national demand are forecast to double in real terms by the end of the decade to £7 billion, figures in the report show.

It also concluded that adopting a "more balanced" strategy towards net zero—relying less on the rapid decarbonisation of electricity over the rest of this decade than currently planned—would lower the total cost of achieving overall decarbonisation.

open image in gallery Households have been warned to expect higher energy bills this winter Yui Mok/PA) ( PA Archive )

Bobbie Upton, research economist at the IFS and a co-author of the report, said: "Encouraging greater take-up of time-varying electricity prices could lower electricity bills for consumers with minimal cost to the Government.

"The extent of savings would depend on how enthusiastically consumers adopted time-varying contracts and then adjusted when they consumed electricity.

"But evidence suggests savings are possible, with the potential savings increasing significantly as more households adopt electric vehicles and technology that automatically shifts consumption to times when prices are low.

"Looking ahead, high electricity prices look set to be with us for many years to come. Improving the efficiency of the electricity market would have a long-run pay-off."

Mark Franks, director of welfare at the Nuffield Foundation, said: "Electricity prices matter for all households, but they are particularly important for those on low incomes.

"Energy bills account for a much higher proportion of spending among poorer households, and uncertainty about possible future price rises creates anxiety within families already operating with very little financial headroom.

"Any credible options for reducing the costs faced by consumers, particularly the most vulnerable, should therefore be considered carefully by government."

Employees grieving a loss during early pregnancy or the death of a relative are set to gain statutory time off under expanded rules outlined by the government.

Beginning in April next year, the statutory bereavement right will cover staff who lose a spouse, partner, parent, adult child or sibling.

Step and half relatives will also be included, alongside foster, kinship care and adoptive relationships, which currently hold no statutory protection in terms of workplace leave.

Women and their partners who suffer a pregnancy loss prior to 24 weeks, including a miscarriage, a termination and an unsuccessful IVF embryo transfer, will be entitled to up to two weeks of unpaid leave.

There is an existing right to leave for parents who experience a stillbirth after 24 weeks of pregnancy, or the death of a child under 18.

The Employment Rights Act 2025 established this new statutory right to unpaid leave for employees who suffer the loss of a relative.

Monday’s announcement follows a consultation aimed at ensuring the new entitlement is “shaped with the needs of employees and employers”.

The move follows campaigning, including by grieving parents who had no formal recognition of their loss, to end “inconsistency and confusion”, the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade said.

Despite estimates that one in five women in the UK experience a miscarriage, there is no legal right to bereavement leave in these circumstances.

Work minister Kate Dearden said: “No-one should have to fight for time to grieve.

“These changes back people going through some of the hardest moments of life, whoever they are and wherever they work.

From April next year, the bereavement right will apply to workers who lose a spouse or partner, parent, adult child or sibling ( Getty Images )

“I want to thank the campaigners whose courage and testimonies have made this change happen.”

The department said that while the vast majority of affected workers have understanding employers, there needs to be a “safety net beyond this discretion”.

Regarding loss during pregnancy, the right to bereavement leave will apply to partners, the other biological parent, or intended parents in a surrogacy arrangement.

“This recognises in law that pregnancy loss affects the whole family and that all families across Great Britain have their grief acknowledged and are treated fairly at one of the hardest times in life,” the Department said.

Vicki Robinson, Miscarriage UK chief executive, said: “This is an important step in recognising pregnancy loss as a bereavement and the profound impact it can have, and we hope will provide a baseline for employers to go further.

“We still strongly believe bereavement leave should be paid, and we will continue to press for this through our leave for every loss campaign.

“We will continue work with government to ensure the detail and guidance provide meaningful and compassionate support for everyone affected by pregnancy loss.”

TUC general secretary Paul Nowak said: “No one experiencing the devastating loss of a loved one or a pregnancy should have to worry that they cannot take the time off to grieve.

“Most employers already provide workers with time off after bereavement. But these new protections will make sure all working families have the time and space they need during some of life’s toughest moments.

“They show that stronger workers’ rights are not just good for employees and employers, they are the foundation of a fairer and more decent society.”

The government is also conducting a wider review of parental leave and pay.

This covers issues such as the call for “Hugh’s Law” which would provide statutory paid leave for parents of seriously ill children, and the rights of parents with terminally ill children.

The consultation on the new measures showed more than eight in ten employers and nine in ten organisations representing business supported bereavement leave after the death of an immediate family member.

The NHS could avoid up to 20,600 deaths each year with its current funding if it were more productive, a new think tank report has said.

Analysis by the Health Foundation think tank found thousands of deaths could be avoided if the NHS were better at diagnosing conditions earlier, such as cancer, and could save lives without spending more money.

The think tank also found there is “substantial scope to improve outcomes within the funding already available to the NHS”, which could also result in an average of an extra 2.5 to 4.5 years of good health for people.

When asked where the NHS could make the most improvements to reduce avoidable deaths, researchers said diagnosing cancer earlier and finding people with high blood pressure or conditions such as diabetes. Overall, the study said improving NHS productivity could deliver £33 billion in annual savings.

open image in gallery The NHS could avoid 20,600 deaths each year with its current funding, according to a new report ( PA Wire )

Around one in five types of cancer are diagnosed through emergency routes like trips to A&E.

Anita Charlesworth, report author and senior economic adviser at the Health Foundation, said: “This is mission critical for the NHS, which cannot simply keep doing more of the same.

“We've got the goal, obviously, to improve five-year survival for cancer from currently around 60 per cent to 75 per cent by 2035. Early diagnosis will be critical to that.

“It's technically possible. Obviously, in a lot of areas we also know that we're still diagnosing far too many cancers in A&E as an emergency, rather than picking them up earlier. So that would be an example of a potentially preventable, early death.”

She also said for diseases such as cardiovascular disease there are too many people with undiagnosed and unmanaged hypertension, and also people with diabetes who are diagnosed late, when it is harder to manage.

“Early diagnosis and secondary prevention are really, really critical; we have parts of the country that are doing that really, really well, and other parts of the country, which are really struggling,” Dr Charlesworth added.

“We think leadership, the quality of leadership and management, good data to understand what those barriers are [to diagnosis], and the freedom to act and innovate, to think about why it is that we're not being able to reach people [and] not getting that early diagnosis. Those are all really critical factors. So it is possible that in many parts of the country, there are outstanding individual organisations existing side by side with large numbers of potentially avoidable deaths.”

open image in gallery Researchers said diagnosing cancer, blood pressure and diabetes earlier could help prevent avoidable deaths ( Getty )

The Health Foundation report calls for changes such as releasing the NHS from unnecessary regulation, reporting and compliance tasks, as well as establishing a national “test-and-learn” approach to scaling up things that could improve productivity, for example through the use of artificial intelligence (AI).

Researchers noted that increasing NHS productivity is “sometimes… seen as exhorting hard-working staff to work even harder, in a system already under considerable strain” and this must be challenged.

They added: “At its heart, productivity means achieving better health outcomes from the resources available.”

The government has set a target of 2 per cent annual productivity growth in the NHS following a slump during the pandemic, and hospitals are currently surpassing this at 3.5 per cent – though there is concern that is not sustainable.

The report said current issues threatening productivity include the “constant churn”, including too many targets, and not enough focus on health outcomes.

Researchers also heard from staff how “poor IT wastes clinical time, limited estate and equipment constrains activity, and gaps in administrative support shift additional work onto clinicians”.

“More than half the surgical workforce report theatre access is a major challenge,” they added.

Despite a 44 per cent increase in consultants, the number of inpatients going through the system and coming off the waiting list remained 5 per cent lower in 2025-2026 than in 2015-2016, the study added.

Furthermore, the bill for essential repairs to NHS buildings “is large and growing”, with ageing hospitals and “constrained diagnostic, theatre and bed capacity” affecting how patients move through to be treated and discharged.

While AI offers opportunities, the “NHS has repeatedly struggled to take advantage of the potential offered by technology” in the past, the report added.

A Department of Health and Social Care spokesperson said: “We are already making important progress to realise the productivity gains that are achievable within the NHS, and making sure that patients see the benefit through record numbers of appointments, tests and scans.

“These gains are being driven by many of the things the Health Foundation recommends: smarter use of technology, less reliance on agency staff, and leaner back-office operations. For patients, this means faster treatment, shorter waits, and an NHS that is more accessible in the evenings and at weekends.

“There is much more to do, but we will keep driving progress through our 10 Year Health Plan to deliver better care for patients and better value for taxpayers.”

Emmerdale is facing a "chilling shake-up" as actor James Chase prepares to reprise his role as Tom King.

In 2024, the ITV soap aired a narrative spanning several months that detailed the coercive control and domestic abuse endured by Belle King, played by Eden Taylor-Draper, at the hands of her manipulative husband, Tom.

Set in the Yorkshire Dales, the storyline concluded with Tom being convicted and imprisoned for his crimes.

Two years later, however, the character is due to return to screens.

Broadcaster ITV stated that audiences "previously watched in horror during a long-running domestic abuse storyline", which featured psychological abuse, cyber-stalking and harm to Piper, the family pet, leaving Belle "terrified and isolated".

Despite receiving a prison sentence for his actions, Tom is currently eligible for parole, with ITV saying his "unexpected return in Belle’s life threatens to reopen old wounds and inflict fresh trauma" on her.

“Can the Dingles find a way to keep Belle’s abuser behind bars and will Belle find the strength to keep free from Tom’s psychological grip or will he succeed in manipulating those around her once again?” ITV has teased.

Tom King is now up for parole, with ITV saying his “unexpected return in Belle King’s life threatens to reopen old wounds and inflict fresh trauma” on her ( PA )

Chase will appear on screen later this year.

He said: “Stepping back into Tom’s shoes is a responsibility I don’t take lightly. He is a character driven by obsession and a desperate need for control, and it is both fascinating and challenging to step back into that mindset.

“The audience knows exactly who he is and what he is capable of, so the challenge now is to show the lengths he is willing to go to in order to get what he wants, even if it means dismantling Belle’s life all over again. It’s a dark path, and I’m ready to see how far Tom will push it.”

Emmerdale producer Laura Shaw said: “James’s return isn’t just about bringing back a familiar face, it’s about reigniting a complex and challenging story. When Belle gets the news that Tom is up for parole, she’s forced to confront a trauma she battled hard to overcome.

“With her family and new partner Kammy by her side, we explore the lasting impact of Tom’s abusive actions on Belle as she fights to keep Tom away from the village.”

In 2024, vet Tom used a syringe to poison his wife’s dog, Piper, in an effort to see her after she went to a mental health facility.

Before administering it, Tom said: “Don’t worry, this is going to hurt me more than it hurts you. Actually, maybe not.”

The scene sparked hundreds of Ofcom complaints – including 513 in one day and a further 363 the following day.

In a post on X, the soap reassured viewers that the dog was perfectly fine and there was no harm done to the animal while filming.

“These scenes can be distressing to watch, but we want to remind you that Minnie (aka Piper) is a very good actor and is always living her best life on set! We can confirm that no harm has come to her whatsoever,” a statement said.

At the 2024 National Television Awards, Emmerdale scooped the best soap prize, and Taylor-Draper was also recognised with a nomination.

Emmerdale airs weeknights at 8pm on ITV1 and STV.

Nightclubs and bars have returned to growth for the first time in more than a year, but a trade body said early signs of stability come after the late-night industry has shrunk by more than a quarter since the pandemic.

The Night Time Industries Association (NTIA) called on Chancellor John Healey to use his autumn Budget statement to help set the industry on the path of recovery.

Its data, produced with market analysts NielsenIQ, showed the number of venues operating in the late-night economy increased by 0.4% between March and June, net of closures.

The figure incorporates bars, nightclubs and casinos that are open late into the night.

This marks the first time that the sector has grown in size since March 2025, which the trade body said reflected a small but significant reversal after years of the industry shrinking in size.

Compared with June last year, there are 3.1% fewer venues, according to the research.

Its analysis also unveils a steep decline since the Covid-19 pandemic, with nearly 29% of Britain’s late-night economy disappearing since March 2020.

This has been driven by a 36% decline in the number of nightclubs, which have been hit the hardest by the post-pandemic recovery and a broader shift in consumers’ going-out habits.

In contrast, the total number of bars has increased by 3.1% since pre-Covid, marking the only major sub-sector to have grown in size in the past six years, according to the report.

Michael Kill, NTIA’s chief executive, said: “Britain’s nightlife has spent six years taking hit after hit, and these figures show just how much we have lost.

“Almost three in 10 late-night venues have disappeared since Covid and more than a third of our nightclubs have gone.

open image in gallery The NTIA’s Michael Kill said businesses in the industry ‘need meaningful action on taxation and the cost of operating’ (Alamy/PA)

“For the first time in a long time, however, we can see the beginnings of something different.

“Venue numbers have edged upwards, entrepreneurs are investing and consumers are still demanding new experiences.

“There is a recovery waiting to happen, but the Government now has to decide whether it wants to accelerate it or tax and cost it out of existence.”

Mr Kill said businesses in the industry “need meaningful action on taxation and the cost of operating, alongside serious investment in transport, safety and late-night infrastructure”.

Nightclubs and bars have been among businesses in the hospitality industry calling for more support on costs such as business rates – a tax on the value of properties – and employers’ national insurance contributions.

It also comes amid changing consumer habits, with NIQ’s data showing that share of sales made in the late evening and into the night have dropped as consumers shift to going out and returning home earlier in the day.

Across the wider night-time industry, encompassing all licensed premises in Britain, the total number of venues was more or less flat in the three months to June, the report showed.

News.title: ‘42 surgeries in 48 hours’: Doctors face extreme pressure in South Sudan
News.content:
Dr Mathiang Agany had no idea what was coming.

On a humid morning in April, scores of patients were rushed into his basic hospital in rural South Sudan after a shoot out between rival gangs. As the most senior doctor, Dr Agany, a maternal health specialist, had to perform 42 surgeries in just 48 hours.

Working alongside a second surgeon, a nurse and an anaesthetist, Dr Agany, 44, carefully extracted bullets from the vital organs of nine patients.

In 22 cases, he glued together fractured bones; and in four others he clamped damaged tissues shut and repaired torn organs.

Over the same 48 hour period, he also delivered seven babies through emergency c-sections.

“You are tired... but you can relax later,” he told The Telegraph over a video call.

“My job [was] to keep people alive”.

Separate to the ruinous four-year civil war in neighbouring Sudan, the violence plaguing South Sudan is inter-communal, a self-perpetuating cycle of cattle raiding, territorial disputes and revenge attacks carried out by armed youth militias from pastoral communities known as Titweng (“cattle guard”).

Young children were among the victims, including a four-year-old boy, whose leg was fractured by a gunshot, and a nine-month-old baby girl whose chest was grazed by the same bullet that killed her father.

News.title: Afghan medical students face expulsion from Pakistan
News.content:
An educational lifeline for young Afghan women banned by the Taliban from training as doctors in their homeland is in jeopardy after Pakistan’s medical authorities tried to have them expelled.

Several hundred Afghan female students studying across the border in Pakistan have been threatened with removal, amid rising tensions and tit-for-tat exchanges between the neighbours.

The Pakistan Medical and Dental Council (PMDC) which regulates medical education earlier this month ordered medical and dental colleges with Afghan students to kick them out.

Within days, major institutions including King Edward Medical University (KEMU), Shaikh Khalifa Bin Zayed Al Nahyan Medical and Dental College, and the Services Institute of Medical Sciences, had ordered Afghan students to leave.

The nationwide order was estimated to have affected around 1,000 Afghan students, with 35 per cent of those thought to be female students.

Provincial high courts have now temporarily halted the expulsion pending further hearings, but Afghan students told The Telegraph they were terrified their careers would be ended.

“The government’s decision aimed to send us to the Stone Age because the Taliban in Afghanistan have banned female education,” said Sabiha Daftani, one of the 22 Afghan students given orders on September 7 by KEMU in Lahore on to leave within 24 hours.

“The fear is constant and haunting us,” she said.

News.title: Michael Carrick will not survive unless Manchester United change
News.content:
But so passive was their football that is the way he felt in the moment. For a club with United’s “attack, attack, attack” tradition – becoming something of a distant memory as seasons pass – that is a damning as it gets.

Neville’s Sky paymasters will be delighted by his emotive, insulting, headline-grabbing language. But he of course exaggerated a point to make a point. United, and Carrick, were, indeed, far too passive, lacking aggression, urgency and belief. They just do not press. United did, for too long, play like a team of dummies.

Against Fulham they almost played walking football until they conceded, desperation kicked in and they chased the game to salvage a late draw.

It begs the question: what is Carrick doing with this team? Yes, he may have been let down by no defensive signings in the summer – even if he must have bought into the plan to prioritise a midfield rebuild – but he is far from absolved from blame.

He will cling to the response to Lisandro Martínez’s own goal, to striking a post twice in the first half from Matheus Cunha and Bruno Fernandes, to managing to avoid a third successive defeat in a week, which would have led to the crisis klaxon being sounded. Carrick can talk about how ridiculous it would be to question his position as head coach. But is it?

We now go into a three-week international break and the Premier League vacuum would have been filled by a debate over Carrick’s future, whether he is up to the job and another existential examination as to where United are heading. And who is to blame.

That still might happen. United did not lose. But they were not remotely good enough, as has been the case for most of the season. Their only league win in five was against newly promoted Ipswich Town, having lost to newly promoted Hull City. They have also drawn at Everton and now at Fulham, who started the day bottom of the table and remain winless. Apart from facing Manchester City, it has hardly been the most taxing of starts. Except they are down in 12th and have not played well at all.

News.title: Alisson’s brilliance takes the breath away to show way forward for Liverpool
News.content:
It proved to be the foundation stone from which Liverpool were able to build and inflict Bournemouth’s first home defeat since January. There are plenty of [valid] questions to ask of Liverpool’s attack at present but, defensively, it is starting to come together.

“It was a really good fight,” Alisson said, in that self-effacing way of his. “But we have to improve a lot – on the ball and sometimes off the ball as well but we improved in the second half. We adapted to the opponent and that’s what we are doing.”

Any manager with a well-drilled defence stands a chance of improving and that is what Liverpool are doing. Only four weeks ago the discussion was about how easy it was for teams to play through their middle – remember that chaotic afternoon at Newcastle to start? – but that is changing swiftly.

Since Iraola replaced Jeremie Frimpong with Araújo at right-back, three consecutive Premier League clean sheets have followed. Araújo, the Uruguayan on loan from Barcelona, revels in doing the dirty work while Jacquet, the £60m signing from Rennes, oozes quality.

“He’s [Jacquet] very young and adapted really well to the Premier League,” Iraola said. “The first games, he was physically feeling the change of rhythm and I had to sub him. This was a step forward. He looked solid until the end. He’s in a good place physically and I hope he can continue his development.”

News.title: All that money spent and Spurs do not have a proper striker or goalkeeper
News.content:
It was an excellent goal, but Kinsky got a good hand to it and a top goalkeeper would have pushed it around the post. On the evidence of the first half, when he made four saves, Suzuki would have also stopped the ball creeping into the net.

Suzuki cost Villa in the region of £30m and he looks a more than able replacement for Emiliano Martínez. Spurs, on the other hand, have not had a top-class goalkeeper since Hugo Lloris and it is a puzzle that so much faith has been placed in Kinsky.

Spurs spent most of the summer firmly denying any links to Jackson before Villa signed him from Chelsea for an initial £47.5m that could rise to £65m. Given the London club paid an initial £75m for Sávio and committed to a £60m obligation to make Omar Marmoush’s season-long loan permanent, Jackson might have been a relative bargain for them.

Asked if Tottenham had made a big mistake by failing to sign a proper number nine, head coach Robert De Zerbi said: “The transfer market was long. The situation changed many times. There was also the financial rules, at the end of the transfer market. And we had to respect the rules.

“We didn’t sell the players who we thought, in the beginning, there was the possibility, the chance to sell. There are a lot of reasons. I think the club and the coach, we are not sleeping, we know the characteristics of the players, we know everything. And if we didn’t make any different decisions, it was because we couldn’t.”

News.title: An A to Z guide to what’s in your laundry detergent
News.content:
Laundry is one of those jobs that most of us do on autopilot. Throw a load of washing and your favourite detergent into the drum and wait for the machine to work its magic. Perhaps you’ve never even thought to ask yourself what chemicals you’re putting in with your clothes.

In the UK, detergent brands are legally required to state the use of surfactants and enzymes (the main ingredients for stain removal) in a way that is easy to understand, but you may see additional compounds that leave you scratching your head.

Here, I break down the words on the back of the bottle to help you understand exactly what you’re putting in your washing. Given that I’ve just tested 26 laundry detergents and developed an app to help you clean your clothes better, I’m the best woman for the job.

Below, you’ll find the most common detergent ingredients listed A to Z. If you’ve got a burning question about a laundry buzzword, I should be able to help. Add any in the comments section below.

Anionic

There are two main types of surfactants: anionic and non-ionic. A surfactant has a hydrophilic head that loves water and a hydrophobic tail that hates it. Anionic surfactants have a negative charge on their head, which is what helps lift soils and stains from the fabric, though they’re not so good at getting rid of oils. They create a lot of foam but their effectiveness can be limited by minerals found in hard water, which is why they are paired with non-ionic surfactants.

Bio

Short for biological, this label means that a detergent contains enzymes. These are proteins that break down fats, starches and grease, so use bio formulations when you need to tackle stubborn food stains. They are effective at lower temperatures but they can be abrasive on sensitive skin. If your skin is easily irritated, opt for non-bio, instead.

News.title: Spitting row mars feisty Millwall-West Ham clash
News.content:
Millwall manager Alex Neil said after the game that fourth official Lewis Smith had confirmed a spitting accusation had been made.

Asked if he had spoken to Marschall about the claim, Neil replied: “I haven’t asked him about it. But it’s like anything else; I’m sure there’ll be footage of it, or not of it, if it didn’t happen.

“I’d be extremely surprised if Fil’s made an accusation and nothing’s happened. But that’s not really for me to deal with; I’m sure the authorities will deal with that.”

West Ham manager Nuno Espírito Santo said: “I’m aware of the allegation. I didn’t see the image; I didn’t speak with Taty. I cannot go much further on that.”

He added: “I’m going to try to look at the images.”

There were also ugly scenes at full time when players had to be separated at the end of a derby that had been at the centre of an unprecedented police operation.

There were six arrests as of 4pm on Saturday for offences including tailgating, assault on a police officer and entering or attempting to enter a stadium while intoxicated.

News.title: Bloodthirsty Brighton feast on rattled Arsenal
News.content:
Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of today’s Premier League 3pm kick-offs, with Brighton vs Arsenal the pick of the three matches.

Brighton are the league’s top goalscorers so far this season and have amassed the most expected goals, but the champions have the league’s best defence and are seeking five wins from five to start their title defence. There is some welcome needle between Fabian Hurzeler and Mikel Arteta, dating back to Declan Rice’s contentious second yellow for delaying the restart two years ago, as well as the Brighton manager’s comments about Arsenal’s style of play in March.

That 1-0 Arsenal victory at the Amex coincided with Man City dropping points at home to Nottingham Forest on a pivotal night in the title race. Bukayo Saka scored a deflected shot in the ninth minute, and Arsenal held on from there in an ugly but resolute display.

With Saka, Martin Odegaard and Kai Havertz fit and firing, as well as the introduction of Myles Lewis-Skelly and Bruno Guimaraes to Arteta’s midfield stable, Arsenal’s football has been more technical and enterprising so far this season. Brighton are one of the few teams who will back themselves to play through Arsenal’s press, which should make for an absorbing game.

Elsewhere, Newcastle are looking to bounce back from their shellacking at Leeds at home to surprise package Hull City. Mattias Jaissle’s team took four points from Liverpool and Spurs but there is concern about how many shots they are conceding. Hull remain unbeaten and continue to confound the odds and underlying data, but that surely cannot last forever.

Everton are also one of the division’s unbeaten teams, but will be targeting three points from a home game against Ipswich after three consecutive draws. Ipswich are sitting comfortably on six points after their win at Crystal Palace, though they did have the extra man for the majority at Selhurst Park.

Full team news on the way shortly.

Sports.title: McLaren predict four-way battle for Baku win after confirming more upgrades
Sports.content:
McLaren have confirmed they will bring more upgrades to this weekend's Azerbaijan Grand Prix, where they are expecting a four-way battle for victory with Mercedes, Ferrari and Red Bull.

After failing to claim a victory in the first 10 grands prix of the season, the reigning constructors' champions have come into form, with Lando Norris claiming three pole positions at the last four races and only being denied a third win by the unfortunate timing of a virtual safety car last time out in Madrid.

McLaren have once more exhibited strength in development, with regular upgrades brought to the MCL40 having played a significant part in catapulting them back into contention for victories.

The team's official preview for this weekend's race in Baku, which takes place on Saturday rather than the usual Sunday slot, revealed there will be new parts, and that their rotating 'H-Wing' will return to the car after not being used in Madrid.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Norris lost the lead of the Spanish GP after an unlucky sequence of events which saw a missed a pit-stop opportunity under a VSC, followed by a very slow stop

"As part of the team's continued journey throughout the 2026 season, the team will bring to Baku a set of upgrades aimed to improve the aerodynamic performance of the MCL40," the team said.

"Additionally the H-Wing, that debuted in Monza, will be back in action on a track where the drag reduction can be a factor.

"As has been the approach in previous races this season, all new parts will be evaluated throughout practice before the team makes final decisions regarding the MCL40's Qualifying and Grand Prix setup for the weekend."

McLaren chief technical officer and chief designer Rob Marshall explained the team are keen to continue their development push despite their title hopes being extremely thin, with Kimi Antonelli dominating the Drivers' Championship and his Mercedes team well clear in the constructors' standings.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Watch the moment Norris thought he messed up his lap, which turned out to put him on the pole for the Spanish Grand Prix

"With regulatory continuity into next season and the competition at the front so close, our motivation to keep developing the car remains high," Marshall said.

"We must balance that with work on next year's car, but our immediate focus is on delivering more performance and fighting for more victories in 2026, while carrying forward everything we learn."

The Baku circuit, which features the longest straight on the F1 calendar alongside several slow corners, creates a challenge that Marshall expects to create entertaining competition between the top teams.

"Baku will provide another valuable test of the MCL40 across a very different range of characteristics," Marshall added.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Norris reacts to the news that the Monaco Grand Prix will be a Sprint race in 2027

"Energy management and deployment will be particularly important, as will tyre and brake management with the cars arriving at Turn 1 after the long straight with these areas relatively cold.

"Operationally, there is very little margin for error on a tight street circuit. A small mistake can lead to significant repairs, lost track time and resources being diverted away from performance, so confidence, precision and disciplined execution will be essential throughout the weekend.

"We expect any of the top four teams to be capable of winning in Baku, with the chasing pack also getting closer, and we hope to be firmly in the fight at the front."

Sports.title: F1 race distances set to be reduced for 2027 season
Sports.content:
There is set to be a slight reduction in the length of Formula 1 races for the 2027 season, the FIA has confirmed.

At a meeting of the F1 Commission in London on Monday, the sport's decision makers agreed to reduce Grand Prix distances from 305km to 290km, which corresponds to a reduction of two to three laps depending on the circuit.

The change is being made because fuel flow rates are being increased next season as part of measures the FIA are introducing to optimise the all-new regulations brought in at the start of 2026.

The FIA said: "In line with the refinements to the Power Unit regulations to be introduced in 2027 on fuel flow, a reduction in the total race distance from 305km to 290km was approved, corresponding to a reduction of two or three laps."

The decision must be approved by the World Motor Sport Council, but that is expected to be a formality.

The FIA also announced slight changes to protocols around races disrupted by rain or other factors, with a three-hour limit (including interruptions) from race to start to finish removed, but a "hard stop" time for the end of any racing activity to be introduced.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights from the 2026 Spanish Grand Prix.

A limit of two hours of actual racing remains, with those decisions taken "to ensure that the spectators have the best possible chance to enjoy a full race if disruptions occur."

It was also confirmed that there will be "greater flexibility to extend Free Practice sessions should they be interrupted."

The current rules only allow for practice sessions to be extended on Sprint weekends, but such measures may now also be available on a regular schedule.

Sports.title: Wakefield's Guler set to miss rest of play-offs with ban for punching
Sports.content:
Wakefield prop Emre Guler is set to miss the rest of the Super League play-offs after being handed a two-match ban for punching.

The forward was sent off following a clash with Leigh's Owen Trout during Trinity's 26-16 victory over the Leopards in their eliminator last Friday.

The punishment was confirmed following a meeting of the Rugby Football League's match review panel on Monday.

Barring a successful appeal against the grade E offence, Guler will now miss Wakefield's semi-final against Wigan on Saturday and the Grand Final, if Trinity reach it.

Guler only joined Wakefield last month having brought forward his planned arrival from St George Illawarra Dragons from the start of the 2027 season.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of the Super League semi-final match between Wakefield Trinity and Leigh Leopards.

Team-mate Mike McMeeken will be free to play after being fined following a grade B charge of dangerous contact against Leigh's David Armstrong in the same game.

Warrington's James Harrison was also fined following a grade C charge of head contact in the Wolves' win over Hull KR, which set up a semi-final at Leeds. Team-mate Luke Yates will face no further action over a grade A dangerous throw.

Hull KR centre Peta Hiku has also been banned for two matches for punching Warrington's George Williams but, with Rovers now out of the play-offs, his suspension will be served next season.

Sports.title: Atletico hit back at Mourinho for ref criticism after derby defeat
Sports.content:
Atletico Madrid have hit back at Real Madrid's criticism of the referring decisions during the derby on Sunday.

Jose Mourinho arrived at the post-match press conference with printouts displaying two incidents he believed should have resulted in red cards to Atletico players.

The former Chelsea manager accused officials of making key errors in the match, which Real lost 2-1.

On Monday, Atletico put two posts on their X account, the first a video showing a sheet of paper being printed with the words '#StopAcosoArbitalYA,' which means "stop referee harassment now".

A second post showed an image of Mourinho at the news conference with the same message.
