World.title: Africa: World Recognizing Africa as a 'Gamechanger for Global Business' - UN Chief
World.content:
Geneva — United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres has told the Global Africa Business Initiative that Africa represents a $3 trillion market opportunity and the world is finally recognizing it as a “gamechanger for global business”.

He addressed the 5th initiative titled Unstoppable Africa on Sept. 20, saying, “We come together inspired by a simple truth: that Africa’s future must be shaped by Africans, for Africans. That vision is rapidly gaining momentum.”

Guterres noted in his address to the African Union chairperson that Africa has the world’s fastest-growing labour force, holds 30 percent of global mineral resources and 60 percent of the solar potential.

Financial markets are taking notice, and Africa’s fintech sector is now the continent’s largest draw for investment capital, he noted.



‘No more plundering’

Still, he said the world must ensure that Africa’s vast natural resources – particularly critical minerals – create local value and decent jobs, rather than simply being shipped overseas, and he said there should be “no more plundering”.

“In short, the shift you long envisioned is taking place: from doing business in Africa, to doing business with Africa.”

Africa is “home to a growing cohort of thought leaders and youth entrepreneurs,” said the UN chief at the New York event according to a release made in Geneva.

“We are here to deepen investments, empower dealmakers, and build genuine partnerships. And the signals of growth are strong.”

Africa booming in renewable energy field

In the essential field of renewable energy, Africa is booming, said Guterres.

He noted that Kenya now generates more than 90 percent of its electricity from renewable sources, while Morocco is developing plans for the Pont de la Méditerranée, a submarine cable to supply green electricity to Europe.

In the technology arena, Tunisia is competing globally in AI and computer vision software, and Rwanda is pioneering nationwide drone delivery.

“Africa’s star is also rising in the entertainment sector,” observed Guterres, with Nigeria, South Africa, and Senegal creating music and film for audiences across the globe.

Close 

“All this has financial markets taking notice,” the UN chief extolled. “Africa’s fintech sector is now the continent’s largest draw for investment capital.”

Trade under the African Continental Free Trade Area is on track to reach $230 billion in 2026.

Despite global turbulence, all the wars and problems facing the world, Africa’s economy grew 4.4 percent in 2025.

Headwinds intensifying

“But the headwinds are intensifying,” noted Guterres.

Without referring to U.S. President Donald Trump specifically, he said tariffs are less predictable.

“Competition over critical minerals is rising. And the conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East are reverberating through supply chains for fertilizers, food, and fuel,” he said, while costs are increasing along with interest rates.

“Yet these disruptions also create an opportunity: to move from economies that depend on exports, to value that stays and grows at home,” said the UN chief.

Guterres also observed that in the continent’s conflicts, it is vital that Africa takes ownership and bring local mediation to bear, as it has in Ethiopia and the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

“And Africa also needs permanent seats on the United Nations Security Council, where it can contribute to dialogue and action for the whole globe,” he said.

World.title: Malawi: Malawi's Climate Fight 'Strangled' By Crushing Debt Burden, Actionaid Warns
World.content:
Malawi is being denied the chance to fight back against climate change because a staggering 24 percent of the national budget is being swallowed up by debt repayments, campaigners have warned.

ActionAid Malawi (AAM) Climate Justice Focal Chairperson Jimmy Chimalizeni made the explosive claim during an aerobics event the organisation jointly staged with fellow NGOs to rally young people ahead of the Global Week for Climate Justice.

Chimalizeni didn't mince his words, insisting Malawi simply cannot achieve climate justice while its finances remain shackled by debt.

He said the country's spiralling public debt is directly sabotaging the fight against climate change, with scarce cash that should be going towards climate action, health, education and agriculture instead being siphoned off to service loans.



"This year during the Global Week for mobilisation for climate justice, the young people have been mobilised. Mostly, we are talking about the issues of debt cancellation," he said.

"We have calculated a very huge amount of public debt, and at this stage, its repayment has affected the allocation of other resources into other essential public services like health, education, and agriculture."

For ActionAid, the message is stark: climate justice and debt justice are two sides of the same coin.

According to the organisation's own figures, more than 24 percent of the national budget -- recorded in government books as public debt charges -- is now being funnelled into debt servicing, leaving climate financing scraping the barrel.

"The funds that are required to be channeled towards climate action now have been redirected to debt servicing. This has left other sectors like climate financing with very little resources," he said.

It's why, Chimalizeni explained, this year's youth-driven campaign is demanding not just climate action but outright debt cancellation and a shake-up of the global debt system.

Youth demand a seat at the table

Campaigners are also pushing back against the idea that young people are merely helpless bystanders in the climate crisis.

ActionAid wants them recognised as "agents of change" with a genuine say in decisions on climate policy.

"We are seeing young people not just as victims of climate change... but we are also seeing them as agents of change, so we want them to have a seat at the table, even on questions of climate and climate justice," Chimalizeni said.

Mining cash 'must reach communities'

With mining activity booming across Malawi, ActionAid is also demanding that proceeds from extraction be transparently redirected into climate financing -- and that communities living alongside mining operations actually see the benefit.

Chimalizeni said the timing couldn't be more critical, with world leaders set to gather for the UN General Assembly in October and COP30 in November, where Malawi's negotiators must make the case for debt-distressed, climate-vulnerable nations like itself.

'People know the answers -- they just need the money'

Pressed on what government and NGOs should actually do to tackle the root causes of climate vulnerability, from farming to energy poverty, Chimalizeni insisted the solutions already exist at grassroots level -- they're just starved of cash.

"Most of our interventions, they simply need funding. This is right from the communities where we work, where a lot of people are saying we believe that the solutions are just there. They just need funding," he said.

He singled out energy as an urgent priority, accusing authorities of telling Malawians to abandon firewood without giving them anything affordable to replace it with.

Close 

"We are telling people not to use firewood, but we are not giving them the other alternatives. Most of these energy sources are expensive," he said, calling for government subsidies on solar, gas and other clean energy sources.

He also warned that Malawi's heavy dependence on hydropower -- vulnerable to both drought and flooding -- leaves the country dangerously exposed, and renewed calls for a genuine, "just" transition to diversified energy sources.

"We need a proper transition. We need a just transition to other sources of energy. If we can allocate more resources towards these investments, I'm sure we can deal with the climate crisis," he said.

ActionAid's verdict is blunt: unless Malawi frees up fiscal space from crippling debt, empowers its youth, and ensures mining wealth actually funds climate resilience, the country will keep paying the price for a crisis it did almost nothing to cause.

World.title: Uganda: Alarm Bells for Kasese As Rivers Swell
World.content:
Heavy overnight rainfall has caused major rivers in Kasese District to swell, with River Nyamwamba bursting its banks and flooding communities in parts of Kasese Municipality.

The flooding has renewed concerns about the district's preparedness for heavier rainfall during the ongoing rainy season, particularly in communities along river channels, low-lying areas and other flood-prone locations.

Kasese lies at the foot of the Rwenzori Mountains, where heavy rainfall in the highlands can quickly increase water volumes flowing downstream through the district's major rivers.

Rivers Nyamwamba, Nyamugasani and Mubuku all recorded significant rises following the rains, with Nyamwamba overflowing its channel and affecting homes and property in several communities.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Kasese Municipality Deputy Town Clerk Zedekiah Kayiri said some sections of Nyamwamba have weak points where water can easily escape its channel and reach nearby communities.

Kayiri called for accelerated intervention by the Ministry of Water and Environment to find a permanent solution to the recurring flooding along the river.

"The river has known weak points where water can break out of its channel and disrupt communities within the municipality, and therefore we ask the relevant Ministry to act swiftly towards River Nyamwamba," Kayiri said.

More than 80 houses were reportedly affected by the latest flooding, while at least 20 households were displaced.

Kasese District Disaster Focal Person Joseph Isingoma said the impact should serve as a warning to communities in vulnerable areas as more rainfall is expected.

"The latest rains left more than 80 houses affected while 20 households were displaced. This is a serious warning while more rains are still expected," Isingoma said.

Local leaders have urged residents living in high-risk areas to consider temporary relocation to safer places for the remainder of the rainy season.

Nyamwamba Division LCIII Chairperson Brian Kauntura asked residents in the most vulnerable areas to take precautionary measures rather than wait for floodwaters to reach their homes.

"I want to urge those living in areas of vulnerability to consider immediate relocation as we monitor the situation," Kauntura said.

The recurring floods have left communities along the river facing repeated threats to homes and property, while local authorities continue to rely largely on emergency measures when water levels rise.

Municipal authorities say a lasting solution will require addressing the points where Nyamwamba regularly breaks its banks and reducing the exposure of communities living in flood-prone areas.

Close 

With the rainy season continuing, residents have been urged to remain vigilant, monitor weather and disaster warnings and move to safer locations whenever advised.

The latest flooding has once again highlighted Kasese's exposure to extreme weather and the need for both immediate preparedness and longer-term measures to protect communities from rising flood risks.

World.title: Trumpeter Dr Jesse McGuire belts national anthem after instrument malfunctions in unforgettable MLB moment
World.content:
After being the Arizona Diamondbacks’ good-luck charm during their 2001 World Series run, trumpeter Dr. Jesse McGuire played the national anthem for the MLB franchise once more to commemorate 25 years since that last Fall Classic victory.

McGuire was known to perform the national anthem during that postseason, which included a decisive World Series Game 7 walk-off victory over the New York Yankees, whom the Diamondbacks just so happened to schedule their 25-year World Series anniversary for during their weekend series.

In fact, McGuire’s lore in Arizona led to him getting his own World Series ring.

But during his rendition on Saturday, with a sell-out crowd at Chase Field to celebrate and watch the D-Backs face off against the Yankees, McGuire’s trumpet began to malfunction.

It wasn’t the smooth song that McGuire was known for, but it was the equipment that was giving him a hard time. McGuire tried to correct it, but after realizing in the beginning of The Star-Spangled Banner that it wouldn’t cut it, he reacted in the best way possible.

McGuire sang the rest of the way.

The 68-year-old, who once served as the lead trumpeter for the Lincoln Center Jazz Orchestra in New York City, while also performing his trumpeted anthem for three U.S. presidents, took the microphone and started to belt the words right where he left off.

The crowd gave him a quick cheer before going silent again to honor the Stars and Stripes, as McGuire continued to show his vocal range in front of the mass crowd.

As McGuire reached the climax of the anthem, the large American flag began to wave in the outfield, bringing together a beautiful scene before first pitch that almost went totally awry.

McGuire didn’t seem too happy at the end of the anthem because his trumpet wouldn’t work properly, but he can’t be mad at all after showcasing his vocal range in front of a crowd that gave him a standing ovation at the end.

Even Diamondbacks manager Torey Lovullo was quick to show his respect to McGuire as he was leaving the field, commending him on the quick and patriotic act.

And if that wasn’t enough, McGuire was back in the seventh inning to perform "God Bless America," and yes, he sang this one as well.

World.title: National Park Service director calls Yellowstone's wild bison recovery an 'incredible conservation story'
World.content:
A little more than a century ago, Yellowstone's bison were hanging on by a thread.

Today, thousands of them roam the park. And the conservation challenge has shifted from simply saving the herd to figuring out how to manage a thriving one.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS

During an interview with OutKick OutDoors, Jessica Bowron, acting director of the National Park Service, called the recovery an "incredible conservation story."

After millions of bison once roamed the Great Plains, the animals were nearly wiped out across their historic range. Rebuilding those populations, Bowron said, has taken decades of careful scientific work and cooperation among the Park Service and its Tribal, state, local and federal partners.

"To show up at Yellowstone today and have the experience as a visitor of seeing a wild bison in a functioning ecosystem, I don't know that we could have predicted that 100 years ago," Bowron said.

That's a pretty remarkable turnaround.

And now, Yellowstone's bison are helping build conservation herds far beyond the park itself.

Yellowstone bison are finding new homes

Through the Bison Conservation Transfer Program, Yellowstone works with Tribal partners to relocate live bison that have completed the necessary quarantine process.

Since 2019, more than 600 bison have been transferred to 29 tribes across 13 states, according to Bowron. More than 200 were transferred in 2026 alone.

"This is one of the coolest parts of this entire conservation effort," Bowron said.

Once the animals are transferred, she explained, each tribe can manage its herd according to its own priorities and sovereignty.

"It's a great example of how we're able to establish and expand conservation herds through that kind of partnership," Bowron said.

But conservation success doesn't mean the work is finished.

In some places, rebuilding the population remains the goal. At Yellowstone, Bowron said the challenge now is largely about managing the healthy herd that's already there.

"I think at Yellowstone, we're in the latter — figuring out how to successfully manage the herd that we have with all of our partners," she said.

At the same time, the Park Service continues to pursue live-transfer opportunities with tribes interested in establishing or expanding conservation herds.

A conservation problem you want to have

The Yellowstone story is also a reminder that conservation wins don't happen overnight.

Bowron said rebuilding bison populations has taken decades of scientific monitoring and cooperation among Tribal, state, local and federal partners.

WHY TED TURNER'S APPROACH TO CONSERVATION IS THE MINDSET AMERICA DESPERATELY NEEDS RIGHT NOW

And even after a species rebounds, the work changes rather than disappears.

For generations, the question was whether wild bison could survive at all in places like Yellowstone.

Now, wildlife managers are dealing with a very different question: What do you do when the comeback works?

Bison don't care where Yellowstone's boundary lines are drawn. They move across a massive landscape, meaning managing a successful herd requires cooperation among the Park Service and the many communities and agencies surrounding it.

But the fact that there is a healthy herd to manage — and enough animals to help establish conservation herds elsewhere — would have been difficult to imagine a century ago.

For anyone who's ever sat in Yellowstone traffic because a bison decided the middle of the road belonged to him, it might be easy to forget just how close America came to losing that experience entirely.



Today, seeing those animals wander through the park feels almost inevitable.

It wasn't always.

So yeah, you can definitely call it a comeback.

World.title: Chiefs coach suggests Taylor Swift has sparked Travis Kelce's performance in first two weeks of season
World.content:
Travis Kelce had a vintage game in the Kansas City Chiefs’ overtime win against the Indianapolis Colts on Sunday night.

He had nine catches on 11 targets for 101 yards and a touchdown. It was the first time he had gone over 100 yards receiving in a regular-season game since Nov. 4, 2024, against the Houston Texans. He also had 117 yards against the Texans in the playoffs back on Jan. 18, 2025.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Kelce might be the first one to tell you that at 36 he can’t move the way he could at 26. However, Chiefs head coach Andy Reid suggested on Monday there may be a little added motivation given who he’s married to.

"Trav worked his tail off," Reid told reporters. "That's the bottom line, and I think he probably said it after the game somewhere there that the amount of work he put in. He likes his surrounding cast, that’s around him too, which sure helps as just an extra challenge there to make sure that you're up there and competing and doing your part with that other group.

"So, he takes a lot of pride in that, but I know … everybody questioned with the wedding and all that. Would he be out of shape and honeymooning the whole time and all that? But he works his rear end off and I think Taylor (Swift), you're putting on four-hour shows, you've got to work hard, too. So, I'm sure she kicks him in the butt a little bit there, too."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Swift has been at both Chiefs games so far this year. Against the Colts, she flashed her wedding ring to the crowd when Kelce scored a touchdown. She let out a jubilant, "That’s my husband," when he scored.

Reid said Kelce’s focus on physical well-being was something that the tight end targeted in the offseason.

"He's really focused in on his body strength and his glutes and everything where you develop all the power and speed and maintain it and he's done a good job in those areas, where he's been able to maintain good explosiveness," Reid said.

World.title: Fury erupts over Mamdani parade invite as old Columbus insult resurfaces: ‘Are you kidding me?’
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A decision to invite New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani to Manhattan’s annual Columbus Day Parade has sparked backlash among some Italian-American leaders.

The Columbus Citizens Foundation, which is responsible for holding the parade, invited Mamdani in the hopes of fostering a better relationship between City Hall and the Italian-American community, the New York Post reported. Mamdani’s past criticism of Italian explorer Christopher Columbus, however, has sparked backlash among Italians who feel inviting the mayor is in poor taste.

"Are you kidding me? This is a WEAK and FECKLESS move by the organizers," Italian American Civil Rights League president Mike Crispi wrote on X. "Zohran has showed contempt for our people and kissing a** won’t change his true feelings. Italian Americans need to wake up and get tough. It’s the only way to preserve our culture."

Crispi’s criticism was a reference to a 2020 social media post where Mamdani posted a photo of himself brandishing his middle finger at a statue of Columbus with the caption "take it down." Columbus holds a near-legendary status among Italian Americans, with the 15th-century explorer viewed by many as a historic link between their heritage and the United States.

'DIE HARD' ACTOR ROBERT DAVI BLASTS MAMDANI AFTER NYC MAP OMITS LITTLE ITALY

"We feel cooperating is always the better path . . . and we hope to create a good relationship with his office," Columbus Citizens Foundation president Christopher Loiacono told the New York Post when asked about his decision to invite Mamdani. "We hope he will be more open to [working] with the Italian community."

It is unclear if Mamdani has accepted the invitation to the parade. Columbus Day falls on Monday, Oct. 12, with New York City’s annual Columbus Day Parade set for Manhattan.

"This is a man who has made it clear that he doesn’t respect Christopher Columbus, and he doesn’t even think us enough of a group to put on his immigrant enclave map," New York City Councilwoman Joann Ariola, a Republican from Queens, wrote in response. "Why would he want to be there? To get pictures and pretend he’s a paisan now? He should sit this one out."

MAMDANI WON'T ATTEND ISRAEL DAY PARADE, BREAKING DECADES-LONG MAYORAL TRADITION AMID ANTISEMITISM SURGE

Ariola’s comment was an apparent reference to a map of ethnic enclaves published by the city earlier this year that excluded Little Italy, which also sparked backlash from Italians. The map was initially created by the previous administration in 2023, and Mamdani said his administration added several neighborhoods before releasing the 2026 version.

Nonetheless, Mamdani has moved to update the map to include Little Italy.

A Columbus Day parade wouldn’t be the first public event Mamdani has attended this year to draw organized opposition to his presence. The mayor’s presence at the annual memorial service at Ground Zero on Sept. 11 spurred some family members of victims to circulate a petition demanding that he stay home.

"Just as Mamdani's presence at the 9/11 Ceremony was inappropriate, we Italian/Americans don't want him on Columbus Day either," right-wing political operative Roger Stone wrote on X.

Some non-Italians are offended on behalf of the community.

FAMILIES OF 9/11 VICTIMS' MESSAGE TO MAMDANI: 'PLEASE DO NOT COME' TO MEMORIAL CEREMONY

"I’m not Italian but I’ve been an honorary dignitary for 5 years running at the Columbus Day Parade thanks to my friend Angelo Vivolo," Jewish radio host Sid Rosenberg wrote on X. "The organizers of the parade invited [Mamdani] to attend? What? This Radical Islam mother f*cker gave the finger to a Columbus statue and left Little Italy/Arthur Avenue OFF his bullsh*t immigrant map … When did my Italian brothers and sisters become so soft! … I will NOT attend this year if he is there."

"The Italians need to step up and stop this!" he added.

Crispi has threatened to hold a competing Columbus Day parade next year if the Columbus Citizens Foundation does not revoke its invitation to the mayor.

The Mayor’s office and the Columbus Citizens Foundation did not respond to a request for comment when reached by Fox News Digital on Monday.

World.title: 'The View' host Sunny Hostin claims her children experienced racism at private schools
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

"The View" co-host Sunny Hostin suggested Monday that her children faced racism while attending "predominantly White" private schools.

Hostin brought up the topic while discussing 1619 Project founder and The New York Times Magazine reporter Nikole Hannah-Jones, who recently admitted she regretted aspects of her decision to send her daughter to predominantly Black, high-poverty public schools in Brooklyn in an effort to challenge educational inequality.

Hostin empathized with Hannah-Jones' situation but suggested there were additional problems with sending Black children to "predominantly White" private schools.

KETANJI BROWN JACKSON AGREES WITH MICHELLE OBAMA’S CRITICISM OF ‘PLUCKING’ KIDS OF COLOR INTO ELITE SCHOOLS

"I think that this is a decision broadly that all parents make when it comes to educating their kids, but ... this is a very difficult decision for Black parents, in particular, because I made a very different decision," Hostin said. "I sent my children to private schools, a predominantly White private school. So, while they didn't suffer academically, they excelled, but it was a well-funded school, a private school, well-resourced school, they suffered a different type of pain."

"There was psychological trauma, there was racism that they experienced," she added. "They were bullied. There was, you know, trauma around their identity. My daughter wears a big afro, kids were trying to stick pencils in her hair. Boys were calling her butter face, meaning she looked good, but her face, and she is a beautiful girl."

While Hostin conceded that her children "did not struggle academically" like Hannah-Jones' daughter reported, she expressed concerns about the "systemic problem" affecting predominantly non-White school districts.

'THE VIEW' HOST SUNNY HOSTIN FUMES OVER BEING CALLED RACIST ON SOCIAL MEDIA

"So I think the real question here is, nationally, schools in predominantly non-White districts receive $23 billion less in annual funding than their White counterparts. Underfunded schools versus well-funded schools. So public schools are funded from property taxes. So we need to look at the systemic problem that's happening in this country around public education," Hostin said.

Fox News Digital reached out to ABC and Ethical Culture Fieldston School, where Hostin previously sent her children, for comment but did not immediately receive a response.

In a comment to Fox News Digital, Hannah-Jones said that the broader focus should remain on families who lack the resources to pursue better educational options for their children, rather than her decisions for her children.

STEVE MOORE, ED POZZUOLI: STOP FUNDING SCHOOL SYSTEMS. LET THE MONEY FOLLOW THE CHILD

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"I hope people concerned about the choice my husband and I made for our daughter will have equal or more outrage for the thousands of Black children whose parents don’t have the resources to send them to better schools," she said. "As I write in the piece, there is no absolution to be had for any of us."

Fox News' CJ Womack contributed to this report.

World.title: Rep Eric Burlison: 'Most of my colleagues' are 'drunk on spending other people's money, even Republicans'
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Facing a national debt that has exploded past $40 trillion, Missouri Rep. Eric Burlison isn't holding back on his own colleagues — accusing Washington lawmakers on both sides of the aisle of being "drunk on spending" while working-class families pay the price.

Burlison recently sat down for an exclusive interview with Fox News Digital to discuss fiscal prudence, healthcare, inflation, and how Republicans can lift their fortunes ahead of midterm elections just six weeks away.

CONGRESSMAN ERIC BURLISON: IN THE BIDEN ADMINISTRATION, 'THE INMATES ARE RUNNING THE PRISON'

"Most of my colleagues like to spend money…they like to spend other people's money. They're drunk on spending other people's money, even Republicans, unfortunately, and there's few people up here like myself who were willing to make significant spending reductions.

"And so we had to fight tooth and nail to get any spending reductions in the Big, Beautiful Bill. And we were demonized by the left, obviously, but we had to fight members even on our own side of the aisle to make those spending reductions.

"But, look, at some point, the party is going to be over, and we are all gonna wake up in a drunken stupor with a hangover, and it's going to be painful, and we're going to have to figure out how to get our way out of that.

"All of these sins of overspending are haunting us. And now we're seeing…inflation that we can't control. We're seeing the interest rates go through the roof. At some point, you can't keep borrowing money…Sadly, my colleagues that weren't willing to cut spending are going to be forced to cut spending."

Despite seeking to portray themselves as the party of affordability, the GOP seems to have a major messaging problem as it heads into the tumultuous midterm elections.

Burlison points to healthcare as the main problem:

"I mean, again, it's really sad. This office has been broadcasting to the leadership every chance that we can that the American people are feeling the crunch, they're feeling the affordability crunch. We put together a solution that we call the Great American healthcare plan. We also have another bill that addresses the housing affordability issue.

"This office has been doing everything we can to try to fix the affordability issue and have been putting these ideas and solutions in the faces of leadership for at least two years. It's just unfortunate that we can't get people to do the difficult things. And sadly that's because Washington DC doesn't like to do difficult things and fixing healthcare is the number one thing that we should be looking to do.

WE'RE MEMBERS OF THE HOUSE FREEDOM CAUCUS. THE US MUST CHOOSE: EITHER $20 TRILLION IN DEBT OR MEDICAID REFORM

"Healthcare cost is eating away everyone's discretionary dollars…In the year 2000, the average American family was paying $6,000 a year for insurance premiums for a family of four. Today, that's $27,000 a year. If that had followed normal inflation, that would only be $11,000 per year.

"So if you ask the average family of four, would you like to be paying health insurance premiums at $11,000 a year, they would say, heck, yeah, that sounds like a great deal. That is not what they're paying today. They're paying $27,000. So if you think about that, just that alone, that is crowding out everything else that the average American family has to pay. You have to come up with another $16,000 that you didn't have to come up with before, in order to pay for a healthcare system that has exceeded inflation by three-fold.

"So three times normal inflation for the healthcare premiums, health insurance premiums. It's not sustainable, and it's crowded out everything else, and it is the reason why young people cannot afford to buy a home. It's the reason why people have a hard time going out to eat. It's a reason why people aren't going on vacation as much. People are having to make very difficult choices, and it's not the same choices that people had to make 20 years ago."

As Elon Musk and DOGE-fervor swept across the nation's capital at the beginning of 2025, Burlison's initial enthusiasm soon turned to disappointment as he saw colleagues avoid much-needed spending cuts:

"DOGE was the most exciting thing I've ever seen in politics. And I was super excited about it. But I also was skeptical. I watched Elon come give speeches to my colleagues. And what was ironic is that some of the most swampy members of Congress were rushing to the microphones to embrace Elon to talk to him to tell him where he should go to look for spending reductions.

"And yet those very people were the ones that were voting against every spending reduction that you would ever bring to the floor. We've had hundreds and hundreds of opportunities to cut spending… We submitted hundreds of amendments to the appropriations committees to cut spending and yet each and every time, anytime there's ever a vote to cut spending, they fail.

"So, look. All we have to do as Republicans is look in the mirror and say where's the problem? It's me, it's us…I'm one of these almost going extinct members of the Republican Party that still believes in fiscal prudence, still believes and in cutting spendings this small government free market conservative. But unfortunately, that's not how all of my colleagues feel."

Burlison argues that the GOP has a fundamental messaging problem and has urged his colleagues to zero in on their economic pitch to the American public, with a particular focus on the healthcare crisis:

"So, in my opinion, it's not enough to run against a platform. If you have to provide a vision to the American people, and if you ask the American voter today, what will the Republican Party do if they're reelected…I don't think that they would know. And so to me, the vision that I would provide is to say, 'we're going to fix healthcare. We're going to make healthcare affordable. We're gonna to make it a free market. The prices are going to be transparent, and you're going to know exactly what you're buying'."

Finally, Burlison has a quick prescription for bringing down pain at the pump tied to the engagement in Iran:

"Well, conservatives, we love cutting taxes and I think that we should be cutting the fuel taxes during this period of time. I would love to eliminate the taxes altogether, but at least it would make sense that during this conflict that we should cut taxes on both gas and diesel until this war is resolved.

"I think that that would have a pretty good impact on people's pocketbooks. I mean you're talking for diesel that would be 40 cents a gallon. That's, that's pretty significant."

World.title: Italian PM pushes foreign student cap in classrooms, burqa, niqab ban in schools
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni announced plans Sept. 20 to introduce legislation capping the number of foreign students in Italian classrooms and banning face-covering garments, including burqas and niqabs, in schools.

The conservative leader said her proposed measures aim to foster integration, preserve Italian cultural identity and ensure that native children do not feel sidelined in the classroom.

"There’s no way that in an Italian classroom, the ones who feel marginalized are Italian children because they have become a minority," Meloni said during a speech to Gioventù Nazionale, the youth wing of her conservative Brothers of Italy party, in Rome, according to reports.

SWEDEN VOTES AS MIGRATION, CRIME AND ECONOMY DOMINATE HIGH-STAKES ELECTION

Under the proposal, individual classrooms would have limits on non-Italian students to prevent heavy concentrations in specific districts.

Meloni did not specify the exact cap but said the government would also require mandatory Italian-language lessons for parents of foreign pupils who struggle to integrate.

"For us, anyone who comes to Italy and wants to build their future here must learn our language, understand our culture, and respect our rules," Meloni said, The Associated Press reported.

"It is the only serious way to welcome them."

Students who don't hold Italian citizenship account for around 11.6% of school enrollment nationwide, according to Italy’s Education Ministry cited by the ISMU ETS Foundation.

Under Italian law, children born to foreign parents also do not automatically gain citizenship at birth and must wait until age 18 before they can apply.

RUBIO MEETS MELONI AS TRUMP–POPE CLASH CLASH ESCALATES US STRAINS WITH KEY EUROPEAN ALLY

Meloni argued that high concentrations of non-native speakers impact the learning process for everyone involved.

"If in a classroom there is only one child who doesn’t understand Italian, it is possible that that child will manage, with the help of his peers and teachers, to learn the language and integrate fast," she said.

"But if these children are many, or even the majority, that’s not integration anymore, that’s abandonment."

The proposed package also targets religious face coverings, explicitly prohibiting burqas and niqabs in educational institutions while permitting other forms of Islamic dress, such as the hijab.

In a series of posts on X on Monday, the Brothers of Italy party reinforced the prime minister’s message:

"Those who choose to build their future in Italy must learn our language, know our culture, and respect our rules.

"School is attended with one's face uncovered. No tradition can impose on a young woman the obligation to hide herself."

TRUMP SAYS MELONI 'WANTS TO BE FRIENDS AGAIN' AFTER ITALY REFUSED TO HELP US AMID IRAN WAR

A subsequent post added: "Limit on the number of foreign students in classrooms, obligation for parents of pupils with serious integration difficulties to learn Italian, and ban on burqas and niqabs in educational institutions.

"Integration comes through knowledge of our language, respect for our rules, and protection of our cultural identity."

Several European neighbors, including France and Belgium, have previously imposed bans on face-coverings in public places, though enforcement and legal frameworks differ.

The proposed Italian legislation is expected to be considered by Italy’s Council of Ministers before being sent to Parliament for consideration.

Meloni, who has led Brothers of Italy since 2014 and served as president of the European Conservatives and Reformists Party from 2020 to 2025, has governed Italy since 2022.

Her administration recently surpassed previous records set by Silvio Berlusconi to become the longest-serving uninterrupted government in modern Italian history.

World.title: Michael Penix Jr. officially named Falcons starter for a short-week trial by fire against Packers
World.content:
The mercifully short Cooper Rush era in Atlanta is officially dead, even if unwatchable Falcons football is still alive and well. Head coach Kevin Stefanski officially named Michael Penix Jr. QB1 for Thursday night’s clash against the Packers, desperately seeking any sign of life from an offense that hit absolute rock bottom during an atrocious 0-2 start.

Penix has been sidelined since November 2025 after suffering his third career ACL tear in a Week 11 loss to Carolina. After playing it cautious all summer and splitting first-team reps last week, Penix finally gave his reconstructed left knee the green light.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

The change became an absolute necessity after Sunday's brutal 34-3 beatdown. Through two weeks, Atlanta's offense has limped to just 16 total points and hasn't snapped the ball a single time inside the red zone.

ATLANTA FALCONS ARE DEALING WITH THE WORST QUARTERBACK SITUATION IN THE NFL AND IT ISN'T EVEN CLOSE

Rush was handed the Week 2 start after putting up a dismal 2.6 QBR in the opener, and the sequel was even uglier. He coughed up three turnovers against Carolina with two picks and a lost fumble before getting benched in the third quarter. Undrafted rookie Jack Strand entered in relief and immediately tossed a pick-six, capping off a complete disaster for Atlanta's passing game.

Atlanta ended up in this spot after offseason signee Tua Tagovailoa suffered an oblique injury during a Thursday practice right before Week 1. Tagovailoa had won the starting job in training camp, leaving Rush to take over by default.

FALCONS NAME SIXTH DIFFERENT WEEK 1 STARTING QUARTERBACK IN SIX YEARS

Stefanski held off on making the announcement official until addressing the locker room on Monday afternoon.

"I will give you an update when I've been able to talk to the players and work through it," Stefanski shared. "So, I don't have an update right this minute. But again, constant communication with Mike, with all of our guys, so we'll work through it this week."

Penix is getting thrown straight into the fire on a short week at Lambeau Field.

Facing Green Bay's pass rush on limited practice reps is a heavy ask, but Penix's arm strength gives Atlanta its best shot at backing defenses off, opening lanes for Bijan Robinson and perhaps getting Drake London and Kyle Pitts involved.

World.title: U.S. military leaders divided over action against the Houthis
World.content:
WASHINGTON — U.S. military leaders are divided on whether President Donald Trump should get involved with the conflict between Saudi Arabia and Iranian-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen, according to two U.S. officials.

The Saudis have been asking Trump for the U.S. military to take action against the Houthis, a request that grew more urgent in recent days as the rebels claimed they shot down a Saudi F-15 fighter jet and were quickly advancing on Marib province, which is home to Yemen’s largest oil and gas fields.

Some military leaders are making the case within the Pentagon and to Trump administration officials that opening another military front in the region is a bad idea amid concerns about the Pentagon’s dwindling supply of defensive and long-range weaponry, while noting that the Houthis are not striking U.S. ships, the U.S. officials said.

Yet other military leaders are arguing in favor of strikes, saying the U.S. should help Riyadh retaliate for Houthi strikes in Saudi Arabia and the claim of downing of the F-15 — a challenge to Saudi air superiority over Yemen, the officials said. They said these military leaders are privately expressing concern that for the U.S. not to act more forcefully is a betrayal of an important regional ally.

Trump had ordered strikes against the Houthis to begin around 5 p.m. Eastern Standard Time on Sunday, but the military was notified shortly after 2 p.m. on Sunday that the order was canceled, the two U.S. officials said. One of the officials said Trump has not taken military action off the table in the future.

One senior U.S. military leader in the region specifically warned that action against the Houthis could create unmitigated risk to U.S. troops in Middle East and the Iran war mission, including a U.S. naval blockade and security operations in the Strait of Hormuz, the two U.S. officials said. They said the military leader also made clear that U.S. forces could carry out the Iran mission and strikes against the Houthis and mitigate some of the risks, the officials said.

The internal divide underscores the bind the president is increasingly in as the U.S. remains locked in a war with Iran that he began but has struggled to end, and faces a shortage of key weaponry. The Saudis have been a critical U.S. ally in the Middle East, including throughout the war with Iran. Trump told Fox News over the weekend that he’s deciding whether to escalate the war with Iran, a position he has articulated on and off over the past few months.

The White House and a spokesperson for the Saudi Embassy in Washington, D.C., did not respond to a request for comment. The Pentagon declined to comment.

There has already been tension between the U.S. and its Middle East allies over the war. In May, Saudi Arabia was surprised by an announcement by Trump to help ships through the Strait of Hormuz and suspended the U.S. military’s ability to use its bases and airspace. Trump abruptly reversed his decision.

The U.S. has already been supporting the Saudis by sharing intelligence, helping with planning, sending military advisers forward with the Saudi forces and even providing some logistical support, NBC News has reported. But the Saudis have repeatedly asked the U.S. to do more, including help with strikes against the Houthis.

A satellite view shows the aftermath of the recent drone attack on the East-West pipeline in Saudi Arabia. The attack and the resulting fires, which occurred on Sept. 11, caused significant damage to the pumping station along the pipeline. Vantor

Trump had not shown interest in acting until Thursday, when Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman told him in a phone call that the kingdom cannot succeed alone and after a series of developments — including the Houthis targeting Saudi infrastructure, downing the F-15 and threatening to take control of Yemen’s oil industry, according to one of the U.S. officials.

After the call, Trump ordered the military to provide him with fresh options for strikes against the Houthis, the official said. Chairman of the Joint Chiefs Dan Caine called a 6 p.m. emergency meeting in The Tank, the top-security conference room in the Pentagon, to discuss options, the official said, canceling a trip to Copenhagen to meet with NATO chiefs of defense.

U.S. military officials have presented Trump with options for degrading Houthi military capabilities and stopping the rebels’ recent advances several times since Thursday, the official said, adding that the Pentagon has enough assets in the region to be ready to act if ordered to do so.

Saudi Arabia has closed the East-West pipeline while Houthi fighters captured key locations at the Bab el Mandeb strait Javier Zarracina and Jiachuan Wu / NBC News / ISW; Natural Earth

The New York Times reported some details of Trump’s decision-making process.

Violence escalated over the weekend, as the Houthis said they’d used missiles and drones on Saturday to attack “sensitive” sites in ‌Riyadh and an Aramco facility in the Red Sea city of Yanbu, a key oil export hub.

The spokesperson for the coalition forces issued a statement on Saturday saying Saudi Arabia had successfully intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched toward Riyadh and that the Houthis “target civilians and civilian infrastructure in the capital.”

The militant group also made a rapid advance to control the Bab el Mandeb Strait on the Red Sea, yet another oil chokepoint. The advance has posed a major challenge for the Saudis, who rely on that shipping route particularly since the Strait of Hormuz has been largely shuttered during the Iran war.

The Houthis took control of Yemen in a bloody civil war in 2014 against a Saudi-backed coalition. A fragile truce between the Houthis and the Yemeni government backed by the U.N. was reached in 2022.

Trump announced a ceasefire with the Houthis last year after weeks of punishing strikes against the militant group. Under the deal, the U.S. suspended military action and the Houthis stopped attacking U.S. ships.

Trump recently has said his administration has had discussions with the Houthis but has not offered details. “The Houthis called us, and they don’t want to fight with us,” he said earlier this month. “They would much prefer not having us involved.”

World.title: Flights resume after air traffic equipment failure snarls traffic in Newark, Philadelphia
World.content:
A major circuit blew at the Philadelphia facility that controls air traffic to Newark Liberty International, Teterboro and Philadelphia airports Monday — causing widespread delays and cancellations to thousands of flyers on the East Coast.

Dozens of planes were left idling for hours on runways across the region while the FAA scrambled to repair the issue affecting Philadelphia’s Terminal Radar Approach Control, or TRACON, facility that houses both a radar approach control room and an air traffic control tower.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said shortly after 5 p.m., some seven hours after the circuit blew, that the telecom lines had been repaired and all flights were resuming in the Northeast.

Delays would take time to clear, he said.

Federal Aviation Administrator Bryan Bedford said after the malfunction at TRACON that they tried to get the backup system up and discovered the backup line had been cut at a New Jersey construction site.

“That fiber break is probably 13 hours to repair,” Bedford warned. “It’s massive, I’m told. Meanwhile, we’ve got the new circuit ready to install now.”

Duffy said an Amtrak construction crew accidentally severed a fiber line in New Jersey, which caused a telecom outage and forced the FAA to pause Northeast flights.

“This incident underscores the need for additional funding to modernize aging infrastructure and prevent disruptions like this in the future,” Duffy wrote.

An Amtrak spokesperson told NBC that it was a New Jersey Transit contractor who accidentally cut the cable.

NJT said in a statement that a construction crew working between New Brunswick and North Brunswick “accidentally severed a fiber-optic cable” at 9:45 a.m. but indicated that it was working to determine if a Verizon crew might be at fault.

Verizon denied being at fault and placed blame with the NJT crew.

“Earlier today, construction crews for New Jersey Transit cut a Verizon fiber cable running adjacent to a rail line in New Jersey,” the company said in a statement. “Verizon’s facilities were fully functional up to that point.”

Initially, the FAA ordered ground stops at Newark Liberty International, Teterboro and Philadelphia airports.

Later, the ground stops were expanded to both LaGuardia and John F. Kennedy International airports in New York City, causing delays to hundreds of flights as many foreign leaders were flying in for the United Nations General Assembly.

The ground stop at Newark began around 10 a.m. after the stops at Teterboro and Philadelphia went into effect.

The result was departure delays of up to 150 minutes out of Newark and Philadelphia, according to the FAA’s website.

As of 6 p.m. ET, there were nearly 619 flights canceled at Newark airport and 197 flights canceled at Philadelphia, according to data from flightaware.com. Hundreds of additional flights were delayed at both airports.

One pilot appeared to be in the dark about what was causing the delays, according to an audio obtained by NBC News from ATC.com.

“What’s with the ungodly takeoff lines,” a pilot asked the air traffic control tower in Philadelphia at 11:45 a.m., according to the ATC.com audio.

“Equipment issues,” a controller replied.

“Is that expected to continue?” the pilot asked.

“No clue,” the controller said.

This is one of the heaviest air travel corridors in the country, and last year an equipment malfunction left about a dozen planes flying blind for 90 seconds in the crowded skies over New Jersey.

Duffy insisted at the time that there was never any danger of planes colliding during that brief communications breakdown.

World.title: Appeals court seeks to revive GOP congressional map in Missouri
World.content:
A federal appeals court on Monday introduced a new wrinkle into the convoluted fight over whether Republicans can use a new congressional map in November’s election, as the GOP tries to eliminate one of the state’s two Democratic House districts.

The St. Louis-based 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ordered that the new map drawn last year should be used this fall, even though the Supreme Court has already twice rejected Republicans on the issue in recent weeks and had apparently put the issue to bed.

“This Court holds that Missouri’s current plan to use the 2022 map in the November 2026 general election violates the Constitution. Only use of the 2025 map complies with the Constitution and federal law,” the appeals court said in an unsigned ruling.

The decision has no immediate effect and faces long odds to be implemented ahead of the election based on the Supreme Court’s previous action.

The three-judge appeals court panel was comprised of Republican-appointed judges, including two picked by President Donald Trump.

The appeals court put its ruling on hold for a week, giving the challengers time to seek Supreme Court intervention again.

“Ballots have been printed, and Missourians have already voted. Thousands more will vote before this order seeks to take effect. Officials should stop wasting taxpayers’ money on pointless legal action and instead focus on administering our elections,” Richard von Glahn, the executive director of People Not Politicians, the group challenging the map, said in a statement.

Monday’s decision upheld a decision by Missouri-based U.S. District Judge Stephen Clark, who had that the new map must be used, notwithstanding the Missouri Supreme Court having previously reached the opposite conclusion.

The U.S. Supreme Court put Clark’s ruling on hold on Sept. 10 in a decision that seemed to end the dispute, with the state set to use the previous map from 2022, which includes six seats held by Republicans and two held by Democrats. Missouri was one of several states where the Legislature drew a new map last year, seeking to draw out Democratic Rep. Emanuel Cleaver and create a 7-1 GOP map.

Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins, a Republican, had after a significant delay ordered election officials to use the 2022 map.

That followed an unusual proceeding in which the Missouri Supreme Court held him in contempt for failing to comply with its ruling that said the 2025 map had to be put on hold under state law while a voter referendum takes place.

The legal fight began when opponents of the new map gathered sufficient signatures to put the new map before voters in November as a ballot referendum.

But Hoskins delayed a decision about whether to include the measure on the ballot, waiting until the last minute before rejecting the plan, arguing that redistricting plans are not subject to voters’ approval.

World.title: CDC’s teen behavior report focuses on nutrition, downplays sex and drug use
World.content:
A biennial report on teen health from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention focused this year on high schoolers playing sports and making healthier food choices — priority areas for Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

The CDC on Monday published the results of its latest Youth Risk Behavior Survey, which queried high school students nationwide in 2025. The survey offers the most robust snapshot of teen health in the U.S., including their mental health, social media and substance use, physical activity, sleep behaviors and dietary habits.

Past reports noted a rise in sexual violence against teen girls and a high share of opioid use among high schoolers. Under Kennedy’s leadership, the new report emphasized that more high schoolers in 2025 ate fruits and vegetables daily and drank water at least three times per day compared with 2023.

Fifty-eight percent of students also played on a sports team in 2025, up from 52% two years prior.

Dr. Jennifer Shuford, CDC’s chief medical officer, said the findings “align with the Make America Healthy Again initiative led by President Trump and Secretary Kennedy,” which has emphasized the link between chronic disease in children and poor diet and sedentary lifestyles. Kennedy this year restored the presidential fitness test in public schools and released new dietary guidelines that limit ultraprocessed food consumption.

During the Biden administration, the same report underscored a worrisome trend of persistent sadness or hopelessness among high school girls. The share peaked at 57% in 2021, during the Covid pandemic, then fell to 53% in 2023. The 2025 report shows a steeper decline, down to 43%.

In the new report, the CDC highlighted overall improvements in mental health among high schoolers rather than sex-specific trends.

Compared with 2023, fewer students in 2025 reported persistent feelings of sadness or hopelessness, poor mental health or suicidal thoughts, the report found.

The report did not mention LGBTQ youth, who are more likely to experience poor mental health and suicidal thoughts than their peers, and were among the surveyed populations.

“The intent of this report was to provide a high-level snapshot of youth health behaviors for all youth and be applicable to communities and schools across the country,” Mike Underwood, acting director for the CDC’s Division of Adolescent and School Health, said on a press call.

Ariel Beccia, a research scientist at Boston Children’s Hospital, said mental health trends aren’t the same for every demographic group, and one of the strengths of the CDC survey is that it includes data for different races, ethnicities and sexual orientations.

“Overall, we see things are getting better, but for who? Oftentimes, it’s the more advantaged groups,” Beccia said.

In 2023, the survey asked students for the first time if they identified as transgender. According to a guide to the data published Monday, the 2025 survey also included a question about transgender identity. The Trump administration last year scrubbed references to that portion of the survey from a CDC webpage, after Trump instructed federal agencies to remove language that promoted “gender ideology.” A federal judge quickly ordered the administration to restore the webpage, along with others that had been similarly altered.

Beccia said several other items seemed missing from the new report. For instance, she expected it to mention social and economic factors that dictate whether teens can eat healthy foods, such as proximity to grocery stores.

But Dr. Aaron Reliford, clinical director of the Child Study Center at NYU Langone, said he appreciated the focus on physical health and nutrition. The report also highlighted that social media use among teens has stayed consistent in the last few years: around 1 in 3 students say they use social media at least every hour.

“The more that we can get kids off of their phones, the more that we can get them out and more active,” Reliford said. “And that, combined with ongoing nutrition, certainly can benefit mental health overall.”

World.title: Flights to resume at NYC-area airports following equipment outage, FAA says
World.content:
Flights into and out of Newark Liberty International, John F. Kennedy International and LaGuardia airports are expected to resume shortly following an earlier equipment outage, according to the Federal Aviation Administration.

The outage had and will continue to have a ripple effect on air traffic throughout the country.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Monday evening the telecom lines that had been damaged in an earlier incident on NJ Transit property have since been repaired. However, delays are expected to persist at the New York City-area airports for some time.

A ground delay at Newark Liberty is expected to last until 8:59 p.m., while ground delays at JFK and LaGuardia are expected to expire at 10:59 p.m. and 9:59 p.m., respectively, the FAA said.

Ground stops and delays had been issued at Newark Liberty, JFK and LaGuardia earlier in the day. Included in the stops were flights to the two New York City airports from more than a dozen regions across the U.S. and Canada, including Chicago, Atlanta, Boston, Cleveland, Miami, Toronto and Montreal.

Duffy said an Amtrak crew accidentally cut into a Verizon fiber line in New Jersey, causing the outage, according to a social media post. CBS News New York reached out to Amtrak, which said the incident happened on NJ Transit property.

NJ Transit then released the following statement:

"At approximately 9:45 a.m. today, a construction crew working on the Delco Lead project between New Brunswick and North Brunswick accidentally severed a fiber-optic cable while working at the site. We've been made aware that this cable served as a back-up to a primary circuit system that failed," NJ Transit said.

"Preliminary information indicates the crew was operating approximately 10 feet from the utility markings. NJ TRANSIT staff is currently on site working to determine the status of the repairs, while also determining whether it was Verizon or the contractor who made the utility markings at the site.

"We will continue to work closely with Verizon and the contractor as the circumstances surrounding the incident are being investigated. We will provide additional updates as information becomes available."

FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said the primary circuit in Philadelphia TRACON failed. The backup line also had a break, he said.

Bedford said the cut was somewhere between New Brunswick and Newark.

Some flights that were already in the air when the ground stops went into effect were sent to other airports. A spokesperson for Boston's Logan Airport confirmed they were "getting a lot of diversions from impacted airports."

Travelers are encouraged to check with their airlines for the latest information about individual flights.

World.title: Man shot by ICE being detained with bullet still in his back, lawyer says
World.content:
A Venezuelan man who was shot by an immigration officer while delivering a DoorDash order in Austin, Texas, was transferred from the hospital to a detention center with a bullet still in his back, his lawyer said Monday.

Wilber Rafael Garces Perez was shot in the back by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer after the officer sideswiped the 28-year-old's car early Sunday afternoon, attorney Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch told reporters at a Monday news conference. Garces Perez was then taken to the hospital, and his family was notified four hours later that he had been taken to the South Texas Processing Center in Pearsall, Texas, approximately a two-hour drive away from Austin, Lincoln-Goldfinch said.

Garces Perez spoke by phone during the news conference, saying in Spanish that he was in a lot of pain. He explained that the bullet wasn't removed because it was lodged close to his spine.

"I am not doing well, and I am not receiving the medical attention that I require," Garces Perez said, adding that he's being held in a cold room with no bed.

Lincoln-Goldfinch said her client also doesn't have access to pain medication at the detention center.

Multiple law enforcement sources told CBS News the ICE officer who allegedly opened fire at Garces Perez has been placed on administrative leave, which is standard for officers involved in pending investigations.

A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson said in a statement late Sunday that Homeland Security Investigations, which is a part of ICE, is leading the investigation into the shooting with the assistance of the FBI. The spokesperson said Garces Perez illegally entered the United States under the Biden administration and had a final order of removal.

"This is a developing situation, and we will update the public when more information becomes available," the spokesperson said.

Lincoln-Goldfinch said Monday that Garces Perez entered the U.S. from Venezuela in 2024 using the Biden-era CBP One app, which allowed more than 900,000 migrants from countries across the globe who were seeking asylum to enter the U.S. at official ports along the southern border after booking appointments.

Garces Perez had a work permit and was seeking asylum, but he had received a deportation order in absentia after missing a court hearing because the notice was sent to his old address, his lawyer said.

DHS has also terminated the parole status of those processed under the CBP One app last year and urged them to leave "immediately." In April, a federal judge in Boston ordered the Trump administration to restore their legal status, but DHS argued the president has the authority "to determine who remains in this country."

U.S. Rep. Greg Casar, a Democrat who represents parts of Austin, said Garces Perez has no criminal record and condemned ICE's presence in the city. Immigration arrests of those without criminal records reached a record high in July, according to federal data.

"The vast majority of people being pulled over have zero criminal records," Casar said Monday at the news conference. "ICE has not made us more safe by arresting 5-year-olds, by shooting delivery drivers, by raiding construction sites. We will all be more safe when ICE gets the hell out of Austin, Texas."

Lincoln-Goldfinch, Casar and other local officials have called for transparency and demanded that ICE release any body camera footage of the incident.

"The public deserves more than an agency's account of a shooting or killing. We deserve to see the evidence," Lincoln-Goldfinch said in a social media post. "ICE traffic stops also need to end. Too many of these encounters have resulted in violence, shootings, detention, and families desperately searching for loved ones who have been taken away."

Garces Perez's shooting comes a few months after an ICE officer shot and killed 52-year-old Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, of Houston, in July after federal agents driving unmarked vehicles pursued him while he was taking his construction crew to a job site. Lorenzo Salgado Jr. said his father had lived in the U.S. for over three decades.

Also in July, 25-year-old Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, a Colombian man, was shot by an ICE officer in Maine. Independent Sen. Angus King of Maine said Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin told him the man wasn't the target of the ICE operation.

And in Evanston, Illinois, on Sunday, federal immigration officers allegedly tried to arrest a man who turned out to be a U.S. citizen. The man reported injuries to his head, neck and teeth, local police said.

World.title: What the equinox 'henge' effect tells us about U.S. cities
World.content:
What the equinox 'henge' effect tells us about U.S. cities

toggle caption Bilgin S. Sasmaz/Anadolu Agency/Getty Images

The fall equinox brings shorter days, and the change of seasons. In some U.S. cities, it's also a chance to witness the striking alignment between the sun and Earth, as sunrises and sunsets align with city streets running east and west. It's a modern version of ancient observances of a celestial shift, like sunrise at Stonehenge.

"Humans still connect with how special it feels," says Geoff Boeing, who studies city design as the chair of the Department of Urban Planning and Spatial Analysis at the University of Southern California.

"The things we built helped us to frame the universe in a certain way," Boeing adds.

Sponsor Message

In this case, that framing is literal. Take Chicago, for instance.

"In Chicago's canyon of tall buildings, especially in the downtown area, the sun will be framed by the rising sun, and the setting sun will be framed by those tall buildings," says Michelle Nichols, senior director of public programs at the Adler Planetarium in Chicago. "The effect itself is accentuated by the height of the buildings and the width of the streets."

Fans of the phenomenon call it "Chicagohenge," after England's famously solar-aligned Stonehenge. It occurs thanks to Chicago's street design that follows the cardinal points of the compass: north, east, west and south. All you need to see it, Nichols says, is a wide street running east and west. A bit of elevation might also help.

The 2026 fall equinox arrives on Sept. 22 in the U.S., with the precise time falling in the evening, according to the U.S. Naval Observatory. It means roughly equal hours of day and night, as autumn begins in the Northern Hemisphere and spring starts in the Southern Hemisphere.

Other cities that are laid out on a grid, such as Washington, D.C. and Phoenix can also offer good chances to spot a "henge" moment.

Sponsor Message

A new twist on an ancient tradition

Humans have long laid out cities in ways that correspond to the skies, and cardinal points of the compass.

"It's interesting because this is a very old phenomenon," Boeing says. "Especially thousands of years ago, a lot of early cities would be developed with these almost cosmic urban plans."

Marking celestial change was a deeply religious and spiritual experience for people, he says, "and their cities would be designed almost like cosmological maps to follow it, where you could have points in the city that corresponded to certain stars in the night sky."

For example, Tenochtitlan, the Aztec precursor of today's Mexico City, was "carefully planned with astronomical knowledge," as a 2021 academic paper noted.

toggle caption Scott Olson/Getty Images

In modern cities, such points are often towers of steel and concrete, and asphalt streets. And their alignment with celestial features is more a byproduct of a grid layout than a cosmological goal. But, Boeing says, that hardly matters.

"Even if we didn't do it intentionally, we're still getting the same side effects at least once or twice a year."

As Nichols puts it, "We don't rely on these alignments to tell us things, but they are really great reminders that, hey, the sky really is still up there."

Does your city have a "henge" alignment?

toggle caption Courtesy Geoff Boeing

Cities like Chicago and Denver are good candidates for viewing an equinox because of their faithfulness to the compass, according to Boeing, who has published a comparative analysis of cities' street grids.

He says the cities "are really good examples of this kind of 19th century urban planning, spatial logic that spread across the Midwest and the Great Plains during the Great Westward expansion in the U.S. in the 19th century, that was really aligned with orthogonal grids."

Grids made it easier to buy and sell land, Boeing says. It also made it easier to map out infrastructure like railroads.

Some cities use a grid that's aligned not with the compass but with local geography, like waterways or mountains. That's why another famous "henge"— "Manhattanhenge" — doesn't occur on the equinox dates; neither does San Francisco's stunning "California Henge."

Even if your local streets "are all sort of wonky with the directions that they go," Nichols says, you might spot an interesting alignment.

Sponsor Message

"You just have to pay attention," she says.

Take your photos, but not in the street

Instagram and other photo-sharing apps have made the equinox something of a media darling, the Adler Planetarium's Nichols says, because of the dramatic scenes it can create. During pandemic lockdowns, she adds, the equinox gained popularity for another reason.

"The opportunity to experience an effect together while still being apart," she says. "That was extraordinarily important to people."

But Nichols says people should also be careful for their own safety, as they seek to create dramatic images and memories.

"Just be mindful," she says. "Don't walk out in the middle of the street to be able to take the perfect photo. You can do this from the sidewalks, on the side. It's totally fine."

And if you're driving in the morning or afternoon around the time of the equinox, it's good to remember that on east-west streets, you're likely to get a blast of sunshine directly in your face, with glare that makes it hard to see other cars, pedestrians and traffic signals

"You do see traffic buildups and backups because of the location of the sun in the sky," Nichols says.

World.title: Aviation regulators turn to AI to help manage the nation's airspace
World.content:
Aviation regulators turn to AI to help manage the nation's airspace

toggle caption Mario Tama/Getty Images

WASHINGTON — The federal agency in charge of air traffic control is turning to artificial intelligence to help manage the nation's airspace.

The Federal Aviation Administration officially launched its ambitious $875-million-dollar software overhaul on Monday, announcing the rollout would begin at three major airports that serve the Washington, D.C. region.

The new system is known as Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories, or SMART for short.

"By fundamentally reshaping how we manage our airspace and preventing problems before they happen, SMART will slash those frustrating delays, reduce stress on air traffic controllers, and lower travel prices," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in a statement .

Sponsor Message

The long-awaited rollout, however, was upstaged by an equipment outage that snarled air traffic at major airports on the East Coast.

The FAA said the problems began with a blown circuit at its air traffic control facility in Philadelphia, which also handles traffic at Newark Liberty International Airport. Aviation officials tried to switch to a backup line, but found it had been accidentally cut by an Amtrak construction crew in New Jersey, Duffy said in a social media post.

The cut fiber optic line caused a telecom outage and forced the FAA to pause flights in the Northeast, including at John F. Kennedy and LaGuardia Airports in New York City.

FAA administrator Bryan Bedford told reporters the equipment failure underscored the need to replace outdated infrastructure. The new software is part of a broader $12.5 billion push to modernize the nation's air traffic control system .

Regulators and airlines hope the AI-enhanced tool will make flying more efficient, though critics warn that it won't solve bigger problems with the air traffic control system.

FAA and DOT leaders emphasize that the new technology is not intended as a replacement for human air traffic controllers. They describe it as a tool that's supposed to make controllers' jobs easier by reducing congestion and conflicts in the air before they happen.

Sponsor Message

"The way we manage traffic today is chaotic and we can do better," said FAA administrator Bryan Bedford during a Senate hearing earlier this year. "We need to manage that at the FAA, rather than rely on commercial airlines to simply schedule however they want."

FAA leaders say the SMART system will help optimize the nation's airspace by considering all planned airline flights, as well as weather, wind, and other variables, and tweaking those flight schedules to reduce congestion.

The FAA tapped a relatively small company called Air Space Intelligence to build the system. The company has previously made AI-enhanced software for dispatchers at Alaska Airlines and other carriers, but this project presents a significantly bigger and higher-profile test.

Skeptics question whether the SMART system will be the game-changer FAA leaders have promised.

"It won't replace humans. It'll be another tool in the toolbox," said Dave Riley, a former air traffic controller who retired in 2020 after more than 20 years at the FAA. "But of course, when you call it AI, it gets a lot of attention."

Riley downplayed concerns of the AI tool going rogue because human air traffic controllers will still be in charge of keeping planes safely separated.

"The fears of AI killing us all in the next 10 years, I don't think this platform is going to be about that," he said.

But Riley doubts the tool will do much to solve the bigger problems in the air traffic control system — particularly the staffing shortage. The FAA is still thousands of certified air traffic controllers short of full staffing, forcing many controllers to work mandatory overtime and grueling schedules.

The National Air Traffic Controllers Association, the union that represents controllers, distanced itself from the new system.

"NATCA has not been involved in the design, testing, or implementation of SMART and therefore cannot speak to its effect on the air traffic control workforce at this time," the union said in a statement.

Sponsor Message

Airlines for America, the trade association that represents the major airlines in Washington, praised the FAA's push to modernize the nation's flight management tools.

"Its potential to strengthen safety, increase capacity and improve efficiency will have a direct positive effect on American travelers," the group said in a statement. "We're just in the initial stages, but it's one of the most exciting and bold initiatives taken on by the FAA in decades."

World.title: Paramount makes concessions to salvage $111 billion Warner Bros. Discovery deal
World.content:
Paramount makes concessions to salvage $111 billion Warner Bros. Discovery deal

toggle caption Noam Galai/Getty Images for Paramount/Getty Images North America



Paramount's owners have made a series of concessions to a coalition of 12 Democratic state attorneys general to resolve a lawsuit that endangered the media company's $111 billion takeover bid of its larger Hollywood rival, Warner Bros. Discovery.

"The settlement is not a vote of support for this merger," said California Attorney General Rob Bonta at a press conference Monday, adding he didn't think the two companies should merge. But, he said, the settlement is a "strong solution that protects competition and consumers."

Sponsor Message

The agreement, which still must be approved by a judge, will bind Paramount to operate Warner Bros. Studios and Paramount Pictures separately — at least for now. Together, they will release at least 30 films a year for two years, and 32 movies a year for the next three, or risk a financial penalty. They will also spend $300 million more annually to make movies in the U.S.

"More production means more work here at home," Bonta said.

And the deal will also create a board intended to insulate the combined company's tv news giants, CBS and CNN, from corporate intervention in newsroom decisions, a demand from several of the attorneys general.

A trustee will monitor Paramount's compliance with the terms, Bonta said. If the company fails, he said the states intend to take it to court.

The states' lawsuit and a similar one from the Writers Guild of America were the remaining hurdles in Paramount's path to take over Warner.

"Our goal has always been to build a stronger Hollywood — one with more stories told, greater choice for consumers and stronger competition," said Paramount CEO and Chairman David Ellison. "That vision was validated by unanimous approval from competition authorities in nearly 70 jurisdictions worldwide, who agreed this deal is pro-competitive, pro-consumer and pro-worker. Having now addressed the State AGs' and WGA's concerns, we have complete clearance for this merger and look forward to putting these commitments into action."

Sponsor Message

Close ties to Trump

The Ellison family has developed close ties with President Trump.

David Ellison bought Paramount just over a year ago. He took certain steps to win the approval of Federal Communications Commission Chair Brendan Carr for that deal. He went on to hire Bari Weiss as editor in chief of CBS News. The founder of the center-right views and news site The Free Press, Weiss has argued the mainstream press is too reflexively critical of the president. She has fired several CBS veterans – others have chosen to leave – and appointed her own picks.

Both the purchase of Paramount and the deal to buy Warner rely on the fortunes of Ellison's father, Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison, a Trump financial backer and adviser. Trump arranged for him to have a controlling stake of TikTok in the U.S. when it was spun off from its Chinese owner.

Given both the state of CBS News and the Ellison's ties to Trump, the attorneys general expressed concern about how that could affect the integrity of CNN's news coverage. Trump has long accused CNN of being "fake news" and recently barred its journalists from the White House. On Monday, the network joined MS NOW and Politico in suing the administration for infringing on their First Amendment rights.

Connecticut Attorney General William Tong said in a statement that Paramount resisted the creation of an independent editorial board until last week.

"Connecticut wanted and demanded full divestiture of CNN and CBS News," he said. "We wanted to save ethical and independent journalism and news. We fought aggressively for that remedy. I am deeply disappointed that we could not do more."

A Hollywood force laden with debt
