Paramount's acquisition of Warner will bring together the two iconic movie houses, CBS and CNN, a plethora of cable channels, the Paramount Plus and HBOMax streaming platforms, and such major franchises as DC Comics, Harry Potter and Star Trek.

Sponsor Message

Ellison argues Paramount needs to bulk up to compete against digital titans Netflix, Amazon and Apple, as well as Disney.

The attorneys general stepped in and filed their antitrust lawsuit, citing fears that the consolidation of such similar competitors could lead to mass layoffs in the entertainment industry, fewer films being made, higher charges to movie theaters, and higher ticket prices for moviegoers.

David Ellison — who helped to finance Tom Cruise's Mission Impossible franchise and the Top Gun sequel — is by all accounts enamoured of the film-making industry. But keeping his promise to make 30 films a year will be financially difficult. Paramount borrowed more than $54 billion to construct a bid for Warner that that company couldn't refuse, even though it had agreed to a competing bid from Netflix. Warner has its own debt, meaning the combined company will owe up to $87 billion.

As a result, unions at various divisions of the two companies are predicting significant layoffs. Bonta tried on Monday to reassure entertainment workers that would not happen.

On September 18, the FCC approved an enormous infusion of foreign cash to finance the deal. The merged company will be 49.5% owned by foreign interests, including the sovereign wealth funds of Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and Abu Dhabi. And the agency ruled that it could go up to 100%. Paramount has promised their stakes would be made up of silent, non-voting shares.

The idea that a major U.S. broadcast company or TV news outlet could have such a degree of foreign ownership was unthinkable in an earlier age, according to industry executives, outside analysts and former federal officials. Australian-born Rupert Murdoch famously became a U.S. citizen so that he could take over U.S. television properties in the 1980s.

Eager to avert hefty fee

The antitrust trial was to start in March. And the judge had ordered mediation to occur in mid-October. But dragging out the legal battle would have been costly to Paramount. In wooing Warner shareholders, Paramount had pledged $7 million every day past October first that it failed to wrap up the deal.

Sponsor Message

Bonta faced pressure too. Paramount let it be known it was hunting for vast new properties in Nashville, Tennessee and Austin, Texas to house its headquarters and studios. Such prominent California Democrats as Gov. Gavin Newsom, former state attorney general and U.S. Secretary of Health and Human Services Xavier Becerra — who is running to succeed Newsom — and Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass urged a compromise to keep Paramount in Hollywood.

Additionally, Paramount asked the court to require the states put up a bond to cover the money it would have to pay Warner shareholders because the trial would imperil, or at least significantly delay, the deal. Though the judge had not yet ruled, no state wanted to have to fork over money for that privilege — especially considering Paramount had voluntarily offered that fee to Warner as a sweetener to accept the deal.

World.title: World leaders convene for UNGA. And, Trump says D.C. arch will be a 'military complex'
World.content:
World leaders convene for UNGA. And, Trump says D.C. arch will be a 'military complex'

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Today's top stories

World leaders convene this week in New York for the United Nations General Assembly. It will be U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres' last General Assembly before his term ends in December. He will open the event on Tuesday morning, followed by Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and then President Trump. Here's what NPR will be watching throughout the high-level event, which runs through Sept. 28.

toggle caption Zhang Fengguo/Xinhua via Getty Images

🎧 Trump has tried to position himself as a peacemaker , but his war against Iran looms over the gathering, NPR's Michele Kelemen tells Up First. Iran's president will speak at the event the day after Trump, though interaction between U.S. and Iranian officials remains uncertain. The U.N. has been somewhat sidelined in the conflict with Iran, but it has offered to monitor civilian shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Kelemen says those efforts haven't gained much traction. Despite Trump's downplaying of artificial intelligence and climate change, these topics are expected to be big topics of discussion at the event.

, but his war against Iran looms over the gathering, NPR's Michele Kelemen tells Up First. Iran's president will speak at the event the day after Trump, though interaction between U.S. and Iranian officials remains uncertain. The U.N. has been somewhat sidelined in the conflict with Iran, but it has offered to monitor civilian shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Kelemen says those efforts haven't gained much traction. Despite Trump's downplaying of artificial intelligence and climate change, these topics are expected to be big topics of discussion at the event. ➡️ Trump has a busy week ahead, including a meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Washington, D.C., on Wednesday. The leaders meet as their two countries face fierce competition and mistrust over artificial intelligence.

Sponsor Message

Trump has announced that he wants his proposed 250-foot arch in Washington, D.C., to function as a military complex that features areas for snipers and weaponry. The president says these military operations are needed to enhance national security. The arch, which would be twice as tall as the Lincoln Memorial, has faced pushback even before the president posted his latest plans on Truth Social. People submitted more than 100,000 comments to the National Park Service, and the arch has also faced legal challenges.



🎧 NPR's Franco Ordoñez says that the president's plan reflects his push for increased executive power. Trump is bypassing traditional processes and Congress to establish a major national monument by broadly interpreting his executive authority, challenging opponents to stop him, Ordoñez adds. Many people fear he will act swiftly on this plan, outpacing any court responses and making it challenging to reverse the project. Some are also concerned that the president's proposal for the arch, along with other projects like the ballroom and threats to demolish the Kennedy Center, could significantly alter Washington's landscape.

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) is preparing to launch an $875 million AI-powered software overhaul to improve air traffic control efficiency. While regulators and airlines are optimistic about the potential of Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories (SMART), critics question its effectiveness.



Sponsor Message

🎧 FAA leaders say that the new tool is not meant to replace human controllers. It aims to help employees by minimizing congestion and potential conflicts in the air before they occur, NPR's Joel Rose says. SMART is supposed to analyze airline schedules, weather patterns, and other factors to optimize flight plans. Rose spoke to former air traffic controller Dave Riley, who wasn't worried that the AI tool would lead to problems because humans would still oversee safety. But Riley says the tool won't address larger issues like the staffing shortage. The FAA still lacks thousands of controllers, leading to mandatory overtime and demanding schedules for those on duty.

The Department of Homeland Security said today that it is investigating a shooting involving a federal immigration agent who shot and injured 28-year-old Wilber Rafael Garces Perez from Venezuela. DHS says that the shooting of "an illegal alien" happened during an Austin operation on Sunday. The circumstances leading to the shooting remain unclear. DHS says that Rafael Garces Perez is in stable condition and in federal custody pending removal. His attorney, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, said that Rafael Garces Perez called his wife to say he had been shot while sitting in his car and was yelling in pain. His wife has legal status to be in the U.S.

Today's listen

toggle caption Dimitrios Kambouris/Getty Images

You'd be hard-pressed to find a young child (or parent of one) who hasn't heard of Ms. Rachel. She and her husband, Mr. Aron, started their YouTube channel, Songs for Littles, in 2019. Since then, her signature pink headband and engaging singsong voice have amassed more than 17.2 billion views, making her one of the most recognizable figures in children's entertainment. Now, she is releasing her first album. I'm So Happy is a 23-song compilation filled with original tunes and beloved nursery rhymes, reimagining their successful YouTube magic for her youngest fans. In an interview with Morning Edition's Leila Fadel, Ms. Rachel discusses her new music and why she uses her platform to advocate for children affected by war and humanitarian crises. Listen to snippets of her songs before the album's release on Sept. 25, and read more about this new era in Ms. Rachel's career.

Sponsor Message

Picture show

toggle caption Viraj Nayar

In the heart of Chennai, India, the Kasimedu Fishing Harbour serves as a makeshift market where residents battle the sea for survival and a wage. Basket men, carrying around 35 pounds of fish on their heads, make 40 to 50 trips to the daily auction during long shifts. They're joined by fishermen, auctioneers, fish hawkers and wholesalers, transport workers and ice suppliers. The harbor, originally built for fewer than 600 boats, now serves more than 1,000. Bhagat Singh, a researcher and social worker, says that members of the fishing community understand the risks of the business. Fishermen there earn about $200 a month if they have good catches, but one bad season could potentially plunge them into poverty. This precariousness of the career path is driving younger generations to seek more reliable employment. Check out these photos of the lives of these fisherfolk.

3 things to know before you go

toggle caption Beth Novey/NPR

Rose Friedman, an influential editor and reporter at NPR for 15 years, has died from cancer at the age of 38. She co-created the popular annual Books We Love reading guide. A judge has ordered Fox Corp. to hand over hundreds of documents that could reveal how founder Rupert Murdoch managed some of his media companies' most significant scandals over the past two decades. Florida citrus growers are planting trees with gene-editing technology to combat the deadly citrus greening disease that has devastated many of their crops.

This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

World.title: Many GOP candidates still echo Trump's 2020 claims. Lots of voters want to move on
World.content:
Many GOP candidates still echo Trump's 2020 claims. Lots of voters want to move on

toggle caption Colin Hubbard/AP

President Trump is still talking about the 2020 election — even as early voting is underway in this midterm cycle and the Republican majorities in Congress are at risk.

And while many Republican candidates, even in some critical tossup races, still back the president's baseless claims about election integrity, some GOP voters say they are ready to move on.

In Georgia, Rep. Mike Collins, the Republican nominee for Senate, launched his first congressional campaign a few months after Trump pressed Georgia's secretary of state to find enough votes to reverse his 2020 loss.

In one campaign ad from that race, Collins falsely claimed that Trump won Georgia and said, "Georgians are tired of weak-kneed, spineless politicians who won't fight for Trump, get to the bottom of 2020 and fix our elections." The spot ended with Collins firing a long gun into a bin with a "voting machine" label.

Sponsor Message

Now as Collins runs for Senate, he has reiterated his position that the 2020 election was stolen from Trump. He has also expressed support for compensating some people prosecuted for storming the Capitol on Jan. 6 to disrupt the certification of the 2020 election.

"It bothers me a lot," said Lynn, a lifelong Republican voter in Georgia, who asked NPR to publish only her first name for fear of being ostracized by friends and family for her views. "It worries me for him to get elected. It concerns me any time someone gets pulled into those ridiculous looking-back discussions."

At a farmers market in Alpharetta, a tony suburb outside of Atlanta, Lynn said she could have easily voted for the other two Republicans who ran in the primary. Now she has not ruled out voting for Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff, in part because of Collins' positions on the 2020 election.

The Collins campaign did not respond to NPR's request for comment.

Finishing a plate of grits at the farmers market, voter Austin Sapp said he regularly votes for Republican candidates, believes election fraud does happen, and supports Trump's push to pass a strict voter ID law through Congress. He also wishes the president would move on from relitigating 2020.

Sponsor Message

"It is what it is," Sapp said. "He lost, then he won [in 2024]. Beating a dead horse serves no purpose. What is your platform? What are you going to do for me?"

"Regular humans have given this up"

Just 1% of voters in a September New York Times-Siena College poll said election integrity is the top issue deciding their vote this November.

"It's really big with the media and the far edges of both parties," said Gabe Sterling, a veteran official with the Georgia secretary of state's office. "Regular humans have given this up a long time ago."

After the 2020 election, Sterling was one of the most visible officials disputing Trump's false claims. Weeks before Jan. 6, he presciently warned people could get hurt. He says that feels far from the climate now.

Sterling says while resurfacing claims about fraud can still be an effective fundraising tool, the 2020 obsession is mostly alive among die-hard activists only.

That is not insignificant though. Some of those activists now hold influential positions on state and local election boards. They also vote reliably in Republican primaries.

Sterling spoke with hundreds of GOP primary voters as he ran for secretary of state this year. He stood firm in his defense of Georgia's elections and felt like he did sway people. It was not enough to win a primary.

"I would say things like, 'Georgia has the cleanest voter list in America,'" Sterling said. "We would get some boos and hisses, but I would just keep pounding away, explaining the data and explaining what happened."

Why some candidates still back Trump's claims

In primaries elsewhere, some onetime critics of Trump's claims have come to embrace them.

In Michigan, GOP Senate nominee Mike Rogers, a former congressman who chaired the House Intelligence Committee, once called Trump's Georgia pressure campaign "more gangster than presidential," and said Trump deserved blame for the violence on Jan. 6.

toggle caption Paul Sancya/AP

But while making an unsuccessful 2024 Senate bid, in an interview with the Detroit Free Press editorial board, Rogers refused to answer who won the presidential contest in 2020. Then at a local Republican meeting last fall, Rogers claimed the Senate seat was stolen from him, according to a video of the meeting obtained by NPR.

Sponsor Message

"Now there were some ballots that showed up at 5:30, I wish I were kidding, in a van, and that swung the election on us, and it happened to be here in Detroit," Rogers said at the time.

And after Trump gave a primetime Oval Office address this summer resurrecting debunked claims about election vulnerabilities, Rogers thanked him on social media.

Rogers' 2026 Senate campaign did not respond to a request for comment.

Michigan Republican strategist Jason Roe, a former executive director of the Michigan Republican Party, says many candidates still see echoing Trump's claims as a condition for his support.

"Frankly, I think most of the elected officials that still talk about it, it's not necessarily a sincerely held belief," Roe said. "It's usually at a Republican central committee meeting, throwing red meat to the base."

Throwing red meat is likely not a strategy to win a tossup state in November, however.

"I can't imagine any Republican in a general election spending any money talking about election integrity or what happened in 2020," Roe said.

How the 2020 fixation could still shape the midterms

And yet Trump is still talking about it, potentially to the detriment of his own party's bid to keep their majorities.

In Georgia, Trump declined to endorse a Republican alternative to Collins preferred by popular GOP Gov. Brian Kemp. One reason Trump cited was that candidate correctly saying Trump lost Georgia in 2020.

A similar scenario played out in the Texas primary, where Trump endorsed the controversial state attorney general, who backed his 2020 claims. That candidate ousted Republican Sen. John Cornyn, who was seen as more formidable in the general election.

"I think we should talk about 2026 and not 2020," Cornyn told reporters this summer.

The president said this year he will do "anything necessary" to ensure the U.S. has "honest" elections.

Sponsor Message

He nearly brought legislating in Congress to a standstill earlier this year over his demands for more voting restrictions through the SAVE America Act, as Republicans tried to reopen the Department of Homeland Security. Trump has also attempted to take unprecedented control of the voting process.

Georgia's Sterling sees one motivation behind Trump's continued focus on elections.

"It distracts from the Iran war, it distracts from the Epstein files," he said. "And this is the ground on which they want to fight."

A September poll by the University of California San Diego found that only 49% of Americans expect that the upcoming midterm elections will be free and fair — lower than before the 2024 election.

Sterling says Trump seems to be laying groundwork to deflect blame if Republicans lose. If that happens, claims about rigged elections could find an audience once again.

World.title: This farm raised thousands of pigs for slaughter. Now it's growing mushrooms instead
World.content:
This farm raised thousands of pigs for slaughter. Now it's growing mushrooms instead

toggle caption Madeleine Charis King/Iowa Public Radio

Inside a long, dimly lit building, Tyler Faaborg slipped into a "fruiting room" cordoned off by what looked like plastic curtains.

Fog rolled over shelves of sprouting mushrooms. A bulbous fungi called lion's mane still had another week before harvest, he explained.

"You can see they're sort of, a little bit pinkish," Faaborg said. "When they get mature, they're going to be almost all the way white."

Faaborg, along with his parents and brother, grows specialty mushrooms on their family farm in central Iowa and sells them as tinctures, coffee blends and flavored salt.

They call their operation 1100 Farm, which is a nod to the number of hogs this building and the one beside it each held for decades. The Faaborg family recently transitioned from pigs to mushrooms with technical and financial support from The Transfarmation Project, an initiative of the charitable organization, Mercy for Animals.

Sponsor Message

"We primarily work with industrial animal farmers to help them transition out of that way of farming and into sustainable practices, and that can be growing mushrooms, growing diversified vegetables, incorporating trees and agroecology," said Katherine Jernigan, who directs the project.

In addition to resources online and a network of experts to help farmers grow new crops and start small businesses, Transfarmation provides open-source blueprints for converting industrial pig, poultry and dairy barns.

"That's really what makes Transfarmation unique," Jernigan said. "We're finding ways to repurpose the infrastructure that the farmers already have."

toggle caption Madeleine Charis King/Iowa Public Radio

toggle caption Madeleine Charis King/Iowa Public Radio

The Faaborgs just finished converting half of one 200-foot-long hog barn this summer. They say the retrofitted space will allow them to scale up their mushroom production after a successful pilot project.

The new mushroom operation is also designed to be a resource for other farmers as Transfarmation's second demonstration hub in the U.S. The first is a former chicken farm in North Carolina.

"The reason we established this as a demonstration hub is very much so the doors can be opened, so people can come and see firsthand," Jernigan said. "They can ask questions, and also, importantly, we're collecting data from this hub with the whole transition, as well as their production."

Sponsor Message

That data includes the Faaborgs' costs, hours of labor and product margins, along with lessons learned along the way. A Transfarmation spokesperson said the Faaborgs are being compensated $216,000 through a four-year contract for tracking and sharing their information with other farmers in the Transfarmation program.

Jernigan said other farms enrolled in the program have shown it's possible to be profitable switching from industrial-scale farms — known as concentrated animal feeding operations, or CAFOs — to specialty crops. Transfarmation's website includes estimated budgets for farms that grow strawberries, tomatoes and microgreens.

Having more test cases and being transparent about both the challenges and opportunities could help other farmers make the leap, she said.

toggle caption Madeleine Charis King/Iowa Public Radio

Tanner Faaborg, who brought the vision of 1100 Farm to the family several years ago, wants their mushroom operation to be another "proof of concept."

"It just takes someone doing something a little different to help folks realize that it is possible," he said.

His parents, Rand and Tammy, bought their 25-acre farm in the 1980s with the dream of a homesteading lifestyle, he said. The family of seven harvested and preserved produce from their garden and fruit trees. They had a wood-burning stove and raised chickens for eggs.

Rand Faaborg said they started out by raising a few market hogs for "pocket money" to supplement his income as a welder. But it didn't work out.

"I lost money," Faaborg said. "And then I saw in the paper this  of contract feeding."

Becoming a CAFO

Under contract feeding, a company provides the animals and pays for the feed while the farmer contributes the labor and covers the costs of the infrastructure.

This legal arrangement is a key component of CAFOs, which the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency defines as operations that meet certain animal number thresholds and confine them in an area without vegetation for at least 45 days out of the year.

Sponsor Message

Large CAFOs in Iowa increased from 789 in 1990 to 4,444 in 2025, according to an analysis by the Environmental Working Group, an organization that advocates for greater regulation of CAFOs. Together with small- and medium-sized operations, EWG estimates 66% of all the CAFOs in the state housed a total of 33.4 million hogs.

Rand Faaborg said contract feeding seemed like a good opportunity at the time.

The family did not put up new buildings for the enterprise at first. They retrofitted existing buildings on the farm to raise 2,000 hogs at a time.

Faaborg said once the farm scaled up and became a CAFO, it was "very profitable" but required more work than he expected on top of his day job.

"I was working 16-hour days, sometimes 24-hour days, going to work without even sleeping," he said.

toggle caption Madeleine Charis King/Iowa Public Radio

After a few years, Faaborg said they borrowed $400,000 to build two new hog barns designed to improve efficiency. They had automatic feeder lines and systems to move the manure out to an open-air holding pit.

"Fortunately, we could make cash flow until we got the buildings paid off," Faaborg said, explaining it took 12 years to get out of debt.

But raising hogs was physically demanding work and became less profitable for the family over time, Faaborg said.

"In my day job, my pay over 35 years increased tenfold, and my pay raising hogs dropped by two-thirds," he said. He believes the decrease in profits was due to the proliferation of CAFOs across the state.

A new chapter for the Faaborgs

Rand and Tammy Faaborg decided several years ago they were ready to exit the hog business. Rand said they didn't have a deep love for raising pigs, but they'd poured so much money and time into the buildings that he didn't want to see them fall into disrepair or be bulldozed.

Sponsor Message

They asked their family if they had ideas to use the buildings for something else. That's when their son Tanner Faaborg began to lay out his vision.

"We have this infrastructure," he said. "We could retrofit it, change it, and do something that is a lot healthier on us, healthier for the planet, and actually is profitable, that'll be a job creator for the family, but for the community, as well."

toggle caption Madeleine Charis King/Iowa Public Radio

Tanner Faaborg said he developed a passion for sustainability and climate change mitigation in college. He joined Urban Ambassadors, a volunteer-driven nonprofit that promotes sustainability in the Des Moines area, and was part of the steering committee for the city's climate action and adaptation plan.

But his work in Iowa's capital felt out of line with other parts of his life.

"I would come back [to the farm] and help out with pig chores and kind of living a double life that I felt terrible about," Tanner Faaborg said.

The Faaborgs raised around 8,000 hogs each year, producing roughly a million gallons of liquid manure. They stored it in an open pit until Rand Faaborg could find row-crop farmers to haul it off to spread on their fields during tight windows in the spring and fall.

While manure can provide essential crop nutrients, it's a major contributor to climate change. Manure pits and lagoons release methane, which is "28 times as potent as carbon dioxide at trapping heat in the atmosphere," according to the EPA. Excess manure in fields can also increase nitrous oxide emissions and pollute nearby bodies of water when it rains.

Tanner Faaborg said he was also bothered by the reshaping of rural Iowa by industrial animal agriculture. Near his childhood home, he pointed to long buildings surrounded by cornfields down the road.

"There used to be a house over there. Now, instead, there's turkey barns," he said. "There used to be a house over there, and now it's hog barns."

Sponsor Message

These local changes have a ripple effect, he said. The small school he attended no longer exists.

"There's just not enough people," Faaborg said. "There are small towns and rural communities that are losing population every single year, and it's really devastating."

Where Tanner Faaborg saw an opportunity for change, his brother Tyler said he needed more convincing.

Tyler Faaborg said he raised and sold around 200,000 hogs a year across three counties. But when his parents announced to the family that they were done, he said it took about a week to decide he was ready to try something different.

"I had a good job. I got paid well," he said. "But I did it for 25 years. It's really hard on your body, and Tanner just kept talking to me about it."

toggle caption Madeleine Charis King/Iowa Public Radio

The Faaborgs began working with Transfarmation in 2021, sold the last herd of hogs a year later and received a $15,000 grant from the program in 2023 to start growing mushrooms and sell products as a yearlong pilot project. The Faaborgs reported that site preparations in one of their outbuildings, supplies, branding and website development cost roughly $35,000.

As the business grows and expands with the new demonstration hub, Tyler Faaborg said they'd like to sell fresh mushrooms to a few companies. Eventually, 1100 Farm could also convert the second hog barn. But Tanner Faaborg said it would be used for something else, possibly microgreens.

Rewilding the farm

The Faaborgs said the transition from CAFO to specialty mushrooms has not always been easy, and they have a long road ahead. But there have been rewards along the way, like the conversion of a manure pit into a freshwater pond.

A Natural Resources Conservation Service grant program, part of the U.S. Department of Agriculture, partially funded the remediation, Tanner Faaborg said. Instead of being an eyesore, he said it's become a haven for frogs, ducks and other wildlife.

Sponsor Message

"It just shows that if you create the right environment, that rewilding can happen faster than you think," Faaborg said.

Rand Faaborg said the manure pit was a significant source of anxiety when he raised hogs. Sometimes he'd make contact with people who said they would take the manure but not show up, he said.

"That part of my life is gone and in exchange is just this little pond. My grandkids catch frogs," he said. "That's probably been my favorite part of it all."

toggle caption Madeleine Charis King/Iowa Public Radio

The Faaborgs also have planted native grasses and flowers to support pollinators. They're expanding their orchard and adding hundreds of trees and shrubs next to the creek that cuts across the farm to support better water quality and wildlife habitat.

Standing next to an empty grain silo that once held pig feed, Tanner Faaborg said he'd like to turn it into a space for visitors to stay overnight and wake up the next morning to sip lion's mane coffee while looking out at the farm.

The list of projects is long enough that they could take the rest of his life to complete. But he hopes the impact of 1100 Farm extends well beyond that.

World.title: Germany's leader stands his ground after his party loses in state elections
World.content:
Germany's leader stands his ground after his party loses in state elections

toggle caption Michele Tantussi/Getty Images

BERLIN — On Sunday night, Friedrich Merz should have been on his way to New York to attend the United Nations General Assembly. Instead he was at his Christian Democratic Union (CDU) party's headquarters in Berlin from where he broke the stunned silence as exit polls for two state elections showed its worst result since World War II.

State elections for parliament seats, which in turn elect a government and a governor, were held in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and in the city of Berlin. In both places, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) made significant gains since the last state elections in 2021 and 2023, receiving 38.2% in the rural northeastern state and 16.3 % in the capital. In Berlin, the far-left Die Linke came in first with 25.7% of the vote, seven percentage points ahead of the CDU.

Receiving just 4.9% of the vote in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, the CDU hasn't even cleared the threshold meant to keep fringe parties out of parliament. Merz quashed talk within the press and his own party about his possible resignation despite Sunday's losses for his party just two weeks after a crushing defeat in the state of Saxony-Anhalt.

Sponsor Message

Usually, the German federal chancellor does not comment so promptly on state election results, especially for two states with relatively small electorates. But his party's crushing defeat in both states is starting to reflect poorly on Merz.

Merz conceded that the night spells "disaster" for the political center, but assured the public he'd push ahead with his federal agenda of tax and welfare reforms, describing them as "the antidote to the poison of authoritarianism."

He stressed that implementing these reforms "require backbone, steadfastness and patience" and that he will "demonstrate this" as "chancellor of our country."

toggle caption Ralf Hirschberger/AFP via Getty Images

Speaking to public broadcaster ARD, federal leader of the far-right Alternative for Germany — or AfD — Alice Weidel said the more Merz digs in his heels, the more her party benefits.

"Friedrich Merz is the wrong chancellor for the CDU," Weidel said, "and he is dragging the party down with him."

The far-right AfD also beat Merz's coalition partner, the Social Democrats (SPD), in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.

But the AfD is unlikely to find coalition partners willing to form a government so the incumbent SPD state governor, Manuela Schwesig — who came in second with 35% of the vote — is expected to find the allies she needs to remain in office.

Sponsor Message

In Berlin — which is both a city and a state whose mayor also serves as state governor — the far-left party, Die Linke, brought home its best ever result with a 25.7% share of the vote.

Its leader, Elif Eralp, pledged to make Berlin affordable again, drawing comparisons with New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani.

Taking to the stage as the results came in, Eralp said that Berliners will not tolerate the AfD's policies, adding "in our city, love and justice have triumphed over hate."

Eralp — whose parents fled Turkey after the coup d'etat in 1980 — pledges to introduce a rent cap and seize apartments owned by large corporate real estate developers.

But this second policy could prove contentious, even make-or-break as she enters into coalition negotiations this week.

Germany's electoral model is a combination of winner-take-all and proportional representation, meaning that parties need partners to form the parliamentary majority needed to govern.

For Eralp to take office as mayor, she needs to form a government with at least two other parties.

On a federal level, Merz — whose party co-governs with the Social Democrats — is finding that kind of consensus difficult with just one coalition partner.

Sudha David-Wilp of the think tank German Marshall Fund told NPR that despite talk of replacing him, Merz will counter any political reckoning by standing his ground.

"Merz himself has wanted to be chancellor for so long that he is probably loath to throw in the towel," David-Wilp said, "and he also knows the bar is very high to oust a chancellor in Germany."

But as an increasingly fragmented political landscape makes for unstable coalitions with parties blocking each other from implementing policy, the AfD tells the mainstream parties it's just waiting in the wings for the next federal election.

World.title: What to know as world leaders converge at the United Nations this week
World.content:
What to know as world leaders converge at the United Nations this week

toggle caption Zhang Fengguo/Xinhua via Getty Images

World leaders are gathering at the United Nations headquarters in New York this week "in an era of deep uncertainty," says U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres.

This is Guterres' final General Assembly high-level week, as his term ends at the end of the year.

He'll give opening remarks to start the event Tuesday morning, followed by Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva — as Brazil speaks first by tradition — and then President Trump. The packed schedule of other leaders and top officials runs through Sept. 28.

Guterres told reporters last week that he will use his meetings with world leaders to push for de-escalation in the Middle East and freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb waterway. He's also pushing for a ceasefire in Ukraine, well into the fifth year of Russia's full-scale invasion.

Sponsor Message

U.N. watchers, however, are not expecting major breakthroughs on these topics. Here's what we will be watching.

Iran

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian is expected to address the world body on Wednesday, a day after President Trump's speech — and nearly seven months after the U.S. and Israel launched their war on Iran in late February. The U.S. State Department says the Iranian delegation will be smaller than last year. The U.S. did not give everyone visas. Iranian officials will have strict limits on where they can go and what they can buy, enforced by diplomatic security agents. It is not clear if any will meet with Trump administration officials. The U.N. secretary-general has been trying to negotiate an opening of the Strait of Hormuz for fertilizer, though those efforts have not gained traction.

Ukraine and Russia

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is on the speakers list for Wednesday, too, and his European allies are trying to rally support as the country heads into another winter of war. Russia uses its veto power on the U.N. Security Council to block any meaningful role for the U.N.

Russian President Vladimir Putin, who launched the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, has not attended the General Assembly for over a decade. Instead, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov is expected to give an address on Sept. 26 — and meet Secretary of State Marco Rubio on the sidelines of the event earlier in the week.

Sponsor Message

Israel and the Palestinians

For a second year in a row, the Trump administration denied a visa for Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas and his delegation. The U.N. General Assembly voted overwhelmingly to criticize that move and to allow Abbas, again, to deliver his statement via video. His prerecorded speech is scheduled to be delivered Thursday morning.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who is in the midst of an election campaign, will take advantage of his 15 minutes on the world stage — later Thursday — to defend his record on Iran and Gaza. Israel's Ambassador to the U.N. Danny Danon said Netanyahu will "proudly address the General Assembly," despite planned protests. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani says he has no plans to attend those protests, though he had earlier suggested that Netanyahu should be arrested for an International Criminal Court warrant. The Trump administration dismissed that and is promising to continue its campaign to undermine the court in the Hague.

Split-screen diplomacy

About 120 leaders and senior representatives are gathering at the United Nations this week, but there will be some key players missing. The leaders of India, Germany and South Africa are expected to skip and send other senior representatives in their place. China's Xi Jinping, who only attended in 2015 and spoke via video during the COVID pandemic-era UNGA in 2020, will do the same, even though he's expected at the White House on Thursday.

"There's going to be a bit of a split-screen moment," says Richard Gowan, director for global issues and institutions at the International Crisis Group, a think tank focused on conflict prevention. "You're going to have the leaders of China in the U.S. meeting in Washington and then, on the other hand, you're going to have leaders of smaller countries continuing to give speeches in a pretty empty General Assembly hall. And I think that in itself could actually send a bit of a message about where power really lies," Gowan told NPR.

Sponsor Message

Venezuela

Just 8 1/2 months since the U.S. military swept into Caracas to oust and arrest Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro, his then vice president and now interim leader, Delcy Rodríguez, will make her U.N. debut Thursday afternoon. As Rodríguez addresses the U.N., Maduro remains in U.S. custody, just a few miles from U.N. headquarters. President Trump plans to meet with Rodríguez on the sidelines of the General Assembly on Tuesday, U.S. Ambassador to the U.N. Mike Waltz told reporters. Rodríguez recently announced a major oil deal with the Trump administration, giving the Pentagon a stake in Venezuelan oil fields. Secretary of State Rubio called it a unique opportunity that will benefit the U.S. and "produce royalties and revenue that will ultimately go into the hands of Venezuelan authorities, but a democratically elected Venezuela in the future." President Trump has said Venezuela is not ready for elections.

Race for U.N. secretary-general

The U.N. Security Council has held three straw polls on the candidates in the running to replace Secretary-General Guterres. So far, there has been no consensus, though Costa Rica's former Vice President Rebeca Grynspan and Guyana's former Foreign Minister Carolyn Rodrigues Birkett are among the front-runners.

The U.S. State Department will only say that the next secretary-general "must get the U.N. back to basics and publicly commit to the changes we require." As a veto holder, the U.S. can block candidates. It could take time for the divided Security Council to agree on a candidate that would be sent for a vote in the General Assembly. The deadline is the end of the year, which is the end of Guterres' term, and more candidates could still enter the race.

World.title: A consequential fall begins with familiar concerns and a new test for the Carney government
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

On the eve of Parliament's return to business, Mark Carney sought to manage expectations.

"We are meeting at a decisive moment for our country," the prime minister told a room full of Liberal MPs on Friday.

Near the end of his remarks, Carney told his caucus that this would be "a crucial session of the House of Commons."

"We are going to introduce some of the most consequential legislation, not just of this government, but in decades," he said.

Consequence can generally only be measured after the fact. But the prime minister's stark, ambitious foreshadowing and its promise of things to come seemed to at least meet this particular moment.

The broader moment that Canada now finds itself in has been apparent for something like 20 months — since the president of the United States started talking about Canada as the 51st state or since the president ruptured the Canadian-American relationship with the first of a series of unwarranted tariffs. But over the course of a few weeks this summer — from the collapse of trade talks with the United States in late August to last week's investment summit and Carney's address to the European Parliament — the moment has seemed to gain new urgency and momentum.

And with the political winds at his back, Carney is now touting a legislative agenda that befits the moment.

The Building Canada Strong Act, tabled on Monday, might be the new centrepiece of that agenda, but it will likely not be the end of it. New social media regulations, tabled last spring, are awaiting debate. The operations of Canada's biggest airports might be turned over to private investors. And the Carney government's second budget — and its first with a majority in the House — will land sometime later this fall.

Beyond Parliament Hill, potentially consequential events are scattered far and wide: a Quebec election on Oct. 3, a referendum in Alberta on Oct. 19, a Canada-European Union summit in Montreal on Oct. 29. The Supreme Court should deliver a ruling on the notwithstanding clause, a provincial election in British Columbia could yet be triggered and as many as six federal byelections might be called.

But on the first day of the fall sitting, the Official Opposition attempted to focus on matters most immediate.

The Conservatives want to save you money

"To the Canadian people," Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said, speaking directly to the television camera across from him, "the message of Conservatives is that we will fight to save you money."

A month ago, Poilievre had asked the prime minister to immediately reconvene Parliament so that MPs could discuss the worsening trade war with the United States. But at question period on Monday it took several rounds before Conservative MPs got to questions about the Carney government's handling of counter-tariffs.

Poilievre challenged Carney to acknowledge that the cost of living — specifically, the prices being paid for things like housing, gas and groceries — was still unacceptably high. Carney pointed to measures his government had taken to address affordability concerns — an income tax cut, a tax break for first-time home buyers, an enhanced GST credit.

WATCH | At Issue panel looks at Carney's EU pivot: At Issue | Is Carney’s Europe pivot in Canada’s best interest? | Duration closed caption 24:08 At Issue this week: Prime Minister Mark Carney moves to deepen ties with the European Union, but is it in Canada’s best interest? The Liberals try to lure foreign investment. And Stephen Harper stands behind the decision to walk away from U.S. trade talks.

Poilievre was unimpressed — all Canadians have received from the prime minister, he said, "is "big talk around the world and big bills here at home." Carney countered that Canadians knew it was the war in Ukraine, the war in Iran and a trade war that was increasing costs for Canadians.

Poilievre said it was federal policy that was to blame for consumer prices. Carney begged to differ.

It is hard to argue with the general relevance of such questions, both practically and politically. And "affordability" might yet grind away at the Carney government the way it undid Justin Trudeau's government — it might yet somehow revive Poilievre's political fortunes.

But if the history books remember the fall of 2026, it is likely to be for more dramatic matters.

A 'consequential' legislative agenda takes shape

It was not until the last intervention of Monday's question period — the lone opportunity provided to an NDP MP — that the government was asked something specific about that consequential legislative agenda.

"Well, Mr. Speaker, the real nature of this government is starting to appear," said the NDP's Don Davies, alleging that the Liberals were about to trample on the right to strike with the Building Canada Strong Act.

Patty Hajdu, the jobs minister, dismissed Davies's concerns and shortly thereafter her colleague, Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon, tabled Bill C-39, a 243-page piece of legislation that makes changes to environmental regulation, impact assessment and labour laws.

Speaking to reporters outside the House, McKinnon called it the government's "most significant piece of economic legislation yet."

Hajdu said the government was "responding to a crisis" and "doing exactly what Canadians have asked us to."

WATCH | Hajdu says C-39 will put 'guardrail' around Labour Code: Building Canada Strong Act will 'put a guardrail' around Labour Code provisions, says Hajdu | Duration 1:28 In response to a reporter who suggested that changes to the Canada Labour Code in the omnibus bill tabled by the government Monday will weaken the right to strike, Jobs and Families Minister Patty Hajdu says the bill will 'raise the bar around accountability' on both sides of negotiations.

If question period was any indication, the loudest opposition to C-39 may come from outside the House of Commons — in this case from environmental groups and organized labour.

Carney has built up an immense store of political capital over the last year and a half. And political capital exists to be spent. Carney's government has also not been particularly cautious before now.

But C-39 — and whatever else of consequence could follow this fall — might newly test how and how well this prime minister and his government respond to criticism and objections — and how well the prime minister can bring Canadians along with an agenda that won't always be easy or unanimously applauded. Not even a wartime prime minister can take the public's support for granted.

Probably no one would dispute that this is — one way or another — a consequential moment for the country. The extent of those changes remains to be debated. And the consequences for the Carney government itself remain to be seen.

World.title: U.S. shouldn't buy 'blood potash' from Belarus, Sask. premier says
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe defended the province's potash industry as ethically and economically superior to other international exporters after U.S. President Donald Trump threatened to source more of his country's fertilizer from Belarus.

"Buying blood potash from Belarus is supporting Russian aggression," Moe said in a post on social media. "It’s wrong and it doesn’t make sense."

Moe's post on Monday afternoon was a response to a Trump social media post from earlier that day.

"The United States is working on ​a massive Deal with respect to the purchase of Potash ​from Belarus," Trump said on Truth Social. "The pricing would be for substantially less than we are currently paying to Canada, very good news for ​our Farmers and Ranchers."

Potash is mainly used in fertilizers. In 2024, almost a third of the world's potash production came from Canada and all of the country's 10 active potash mines are in Saskatchewan, according to Natural Resources Canada.

"More than 40 countries — Canada and its allies — have sanctions against Belarus for supporting war criminal Putin’s invasion of Ukraine," Moe said in his social media post.

"Does anyone believe Belarusian blood potash shipped through Russia is going to be more affordable, more sustainable or more ethical than potash shipped from Saskatchewan — right here in North America?"

Nutrien Ltd., The Mosaic Company, Compass Minerals, and K+S Potash Canada are responsible for all of Canada's potash production. BHP is building the Jansen potash mine in Saskatchewan and expects to start commercial production in mid-2027.

Nutrien is the largest potash fertilizer producer in Canada and one of the largest in the world. The Saskatoon-based company referred CBC to Fertilizer Canada when asked to comment on Trump's post.

U.S. farmers have used Canadian potash for decades, said Fertilizer Canada, an industry trade group, in an emailed statement to CBC News.

"Reliability, proximity, transportation infrastructure, product availability and the ability to deliver during critical application windows all matter," the statement said.

"A strong and integrated North American fertilizer supply chain helps support farm productivity, affordability and food security on both sides of the border.”

Last year, Nutrien announced plans to build a potash export terminal at the Port of Longview, Wash., to handle expected growth in international demand for its fertilizer products.

The opposition NDP called Trump's social media post "infuriating" in a statement on Monday.

"He is looking at signing a deal with an authoritarian Russian satellite state that is supporting Putin’s brutal war against the people of Ukraine," the NDP statement said.

"This is a bad idea that will only hurt families and communities on both sides of the border."

World.title: 3 MLAs, including former leader, returning to B.C. Conservative caucus as prospect of election looms
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Interim B.C. Conservative leader Lorne Doerkson is moving to repair ruptures in the Opposition that saw 13 legislators quit caucus or be expelled by former leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay, who stepped down on Sunday.

Former leader John Rustad, former interim leader Trevor Halford and MLA Scott McInnis all say they've accepted invitations from Doerkson to rejoin the troubled caucus.

Rustad says in a statement that his "time as leader is over" but not his service to the province.

The Nechako Lakes MLA also says "high level" unity talks are underway between the Conservatives and the breakaway CentreBC party, and rated the chance of success at 95 per cent.

The developments come after the caucus of B.C.'s governing NDP met Sunday night to discuss a potential early election in light of Findlay's resignation, raising the prospect of voters going to the polls while the Opposition has no fixed candidate to become premier.

An interim leader is prohibited by the Conservative constitution from seeking the party leadership on a permanent basis, but Rustad says there is a way for Doerkson to become premier.

Rustad told a news conference at the legislature that there were "obviously lots of people" in B.C. who don't know the Cariboo-Chilcotin legislator, but he called Doerkson a "quality individual" and said he would be happy to have him lead the party into an election if he wanted.

WATCH | CBC's Justin McElroy looks at B.C. election speculation: Why David Eby is considering a snap election | Duration closed caption 2:37 B.C. Premier David Eby isn’t ruling out a snap election, but why is this suddenly being discussed? And what impact could it have on local elections underway across the province? The CBC's Justin McElroy takes a closer look at how speculation could turn into reality.

Rustad said of speculation about the future of the Conservatives that people like former premiers Christy Clark and Gordon Campbell needed to "let politics go."

He said Clark and Campbell were among the "players" trying now to manoeuvre what he called the centre right, and they should realize that "their time is over."

"That may mean time is over for me, too. I don't know," said Rustad. "But I'm not going to be trying to force my will or my vision in terms of what our party was … onto whoever the new leaders are going to be," he said.

"If they want me to be part of that in terms of supporting and building, I will do that. But it is time for that older generation of politicians to step aside."

WATCH | Findlay resigns as leader of Conservatives: Kerry-Lynne Findlay resigns as leader of the B.C. Conservative Party | Duration closed caption 4:57

Rustad provides timeline

In a statement later Monday that confirmed he had accepted Doerkson's invitation, Rustad said talks between CentreBC and the Conservatives should succeed and the province "cannot afford two opposition parties" with an election looming.

Findlay's resignation followed weeks of upheaval in the Conservative caucus, including the ejection of Rustad and two others on Friday.

He provided a timeline of the chaos the preceded that moment.

Rustad said he asked Findlay to step down last Wednesday at a caucus meeting, where there was "emotion and frustration around the table."

The next day he got a text from Findlay expelling him. Fifteen minutes later that was rescinded.

But on Friday he was told he was out.

Speculation about a snap election being called, less than two years since the 2024 election, intensified Monday when the NDP announced that cabinet minister Lana Popham won't be running for a sixth term.

B.C. NDP cabinet minister Lana Popham has announced she will not be seeking re-election in the riding of Saanich South. (CBC)

"After 17 years as the MLA for Saanich South, I have made the difficult decision not to seek re-election,” she said in a statement.

The minister of agriculture said her decision not to run again was difficult and sad.

Popham's statement came after NDP MLAs met Sunday night to discuss Findlay's departure, according to an email from party staff that was inadvertently sent to all legislators, instead of just those on the government benches.

"I’m sure you’ve seen by now, but KLF has resigned as leader of the B.C. Conservatives," the email obtained by The Canadian Press said.

It went on to say the meeting was to "to discuss and hear from Cheryl and her team," an apparent reference to Cheryl Oates, Premier David Eby's former chief of staff, who has been appointed to manage the NDP campaign for the next election, whenever it is held.

The Canadian Press briefly attended the meeting, along with at least two Conservative legislators, before being asked to leave.

Eby said last week that he told his legislators they need to be "election ready."

McInnis releases statement

McInnis, who represents Columbia River-Revelstoke, had quit the Conservative caucus on Sept. 2, saying he did not agree with the direction of Findlay's leadership.

Unlike other colleagues dissatisfied with Findlay, McInnis did not join CentreBC under their leader Peter Milobar.

McInnis said in a statement on Monday that the opportunity to return "home" came at a critical time for the province.

He rejected the need for "ideological purity tests" and said the prospect of a provincial election made a united opposition more important than ever.

Scott McInnis, the MLA for Columbia River-Revelstoke, is seen in the Legislature building. (Michael McArthur/CBC)

No party had ever defeated the B.C. NDP without being a "big tent party," he said.

McInnis said he never lost respect for his Conservative caucus colleagues, with whom he shared a "common belief that British Columbians deserve practical solutions, fiscal resposiblity, and a government focused on delivering results."

Turmoil in the Conservative ranks, who have been divided over ideology and direction, birthed the CentreBC party which picked up eight legislators last week, including Milobar.

All are former Conservatives, including seven who quit that party's caucus in recent weeks, while Eleanor Sturko was ejected by Rustad last year.

The legislature still says the party standings are 47 for the NDP — giving them a one-seat majority — with 24 Conservatives, two Greens, two vacancies, and 18 Independents, including those joining CentreBC, Rustad and McInnis. Those numbers have not been updated since Sunday.

Doerkson was first elected in the riding of Cariboo-Chilcotin in 2020 as a member of the B.C. Liberal party, which rebranded as B.C. United, before crossing the floor to join the Conservatives and being reelected in 2024.

World.title: Norway PM 'prepared, but not afraid' of Russian incursion
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The prime minister of Norway says threats from Russia are part of the modern security picture and should be taken seriously.

In an interview with the CBC's Power & Politics, Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre told host David Cochrane "we are prepared, but not afraid" of a Russian incursion.

He said the threat is "real" and should be followed "very carefully," especially by countries closer to the Russian border — including Canada.

"Intelligence services of NATO countries are pointing to that threat. It is real. It's happening," Støre said.

The threat conversation came to the surface this week following a warning from Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk that Russia is planning hybrid strikes on NATO territory.

Under this threat environment the Norwegian PM says regional groups must come together, welcoming Canada's recent move to seek membership in the U.K.-led Joint Expeditionary Force (JEF), a collection of a few NATO nations whose mandate is to respond more quickly in a crisis.

The JEF was initially formed by the U.K., Netherlands, Nordic and Baltic countries, but Støre says it's now important to talk more closely with countries that he says, "share challenges and security risks," including Poland, Germany, Belgium and Canada.

Støre says the JEF is helpful in cases when issues may be too big for a country on its own or it's not up to the scale of Article 5 — the NATO clause that requires alliance members to defend any other member that's been attacked — telling Power & Politics that NATO allies are engaged in "sophisticated debate" over the threshold for Article 5 to be triggered.

With Russia struggling to reach its strategic objectives in Ukraine, it could be wanting to test Ukraine's partners, says Støre.

Incidents in Europe this summer have raised those alarm bells for NATO partners.

German authorities blamed Russia for a drone attack at an airport in central Germany in August while last week, Bulgarian authorities announced they're investigating a fire at a munitions storage facility operated by arms maker EMCO — whose weapons are used in Ukraine.

Støre, right, greets Carney as he arrives at the Canada-Nordic Summit at Government House in Oslo, Norway, in March. Both countries signed a strategic partnership after the visit, broadly expanding areas of co-operation. (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)

Norway looks to Canada as an Arctic partner

Following Prime Minister Mark Carney's visit to Norway in March, both countries signed a strategic partnership committing to broadly expanding areas of co-operation — notably in the Arctic where both countries share a coastline with Russia.

"We see Canada very much part of the Northern sphere. We have the Atlantic between us, but we are Arctic states," Støre said.

With Russia not an ally in the Arctic, Canada and Norway must stay "very, very closely connected" to maintain order in the North.

In July, Carney chose to buy a dozen submarines from a European shipbuilder instead of a Korean firm, after a months-long, hotly contested bidding process. The chosen partnership involves a German company but partners with Norway, with the three nations collaborating to produce and maintain the submarines.

Inter-operability across submarines is a "major step" to increase Arctic security, Støre says, but also for industrial co-operation on Arctic research.

"That's why we need to work on our coast guards, that's why we need to work on our space ability to do surveillance. This is a very exciting theme between Norway and Canada."

Carney courts Europe

The Norwegian delegation's visit comes on the heels of Carney's address to the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France, a meeting with the new U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham in Liverpool, England, and a meeting with French President Emmanuel Macron on Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon, a French territory 20 kilometres off the southern coast of Newfoundland.

As for EU "associate membership"?

Støre says he welcomes "deeper ties," with Canada but on a basis that's "real," and with "meaning."

As Europe's most integrated non-EU country, Støre says Canada, the U.K. and Norway should work more closely together with the EU on new areas that require co-operation such as space, critical minerals, energy and artificial intelligence.

"We can all benefit and not let that sink into bureaucracy and regulations that sometimes complicate things."

World.title: Investigators identify police officer and suspect wounded in shooting near Belleville, Ont., synagogue
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results. Police have identified the suspect in a shooting outside a synagogue Sunday night that left a police officer injured. Police said Sean Ward, 29, was armed with a shotgun and fired at an officer before a second officer arrived and returned fire. The shooting comes as members of the Jewish community gather to mark Yom Kippur. Ward is in the hospital in life-threatening condition. Investigators have identified the wounded suspect in the shooting incident that unfolded near a Belleville, Ont., synagogue Sunday night, and the local police officer who was also wounded. The suspect has been named as Sean Ward, 29, of neighbouring Quinte West. The officer, who remains in hospital in critical but stable condition, is Const. Jeff Smith. The Belleville Police Service confirmed their identities Monday in a noon-hour news conference held just outside the taped-off scene. Sons of Jacob Synagogue is located at the corner of Bleeker and Victoria avenues. Yom Kippur services were underway inside when the suspect allegedly opened fire on Smith with a shotgun while the officer was stationed outside the building, Belleville Deputy Police Chief Sheri Meeks and Kristy Denette, a spokesperson for Ontario's Special Investigations Unit (SIU), said during the news conference. Another Belleville police officer also fired their weapon. Smith had been parked outside Sons of Jacob at the request of the synagogue, its president told CBC News. "We always have police protection," Norm Weddum said of large gatherings at the synagogue, adding that the pre-emptive police protection put in place for Sunday evening had been requested as a matter of routine a week earlier. "Thank God that person was there," Weddum said of the officer. PHOTOS | The unfolding scene in Belleville: Smith, who has been with Belleville's police service since 2013, suffered serious injuries during the shootout and is recovering in an intensive care unit where he remains in critical but stable condition. "While he continues to face a significant road to recovery, his condition has stabilized and we remain hopeful and encouraged by his progress," Meeks said. The shooting is a reminder that "every day [officers] leave their homes and loved ones not knowing what they may encounter," she added. Ward is in life-threatening condition. "It's my understanding that he was very critical and but was sort of brought back to life, so to speak," Denette said. Police on Monday were at the Quinte West home Ward shares with his mother. They have not yet announced any charges against him. A former employer and neighbours tell CBC that Ward was formerly in the Canadian military in Alberta. A Special Investigations Unit van is parked at the scene. (Radio-Canada) Questions remain Whether Ward was specifically targeting Smith, Sons of Jacob or the city's Jewish community is unclear. Meeks said Belleville police won't be providing any more updates on their own investigation of the incident while the SIU performs a parallel, narrowly focused investigation into the circumstances that prompted Smith and the other unnamed officer to fire their weapons. "We are in the process of securing body-worn camera footage from the officers involved and also in-car camera [footage]," Denette of the SIU said. "So until such time as we are able to review that, it's difficult for me to give you a sequence of events. "It's believed that [Ward] came in a truck and he had a shotgun and he discharged his firearm at a police officer and then that police officer returned fire and then there was a second officer who arrived and then also discharged [their] firearm. That's what we can tell you is our preliminary kind of findings." Asked about the timing of the incident during Yom Kippur and whether the evidence so far suggests it was an attack aimed at the Jewish community, Denette replied, "I'd be speculating, but ... I think that common sense would say that probably was the case." The Sons of Jacob Synagogue is shown in Belleville on Monday. (Sharif Hassan/The Canadian Press) 'Literally everyone went down' Weddum said the synagogue was ushering people inside when Yom Kippur services began at around 7 p.m. "It was boom, boom, boom," Weddum told CBC News Network of the gunshhots he heard outside. Weddum said he went to the lobby where he could hear more defined shots. "I could say, 'Oh, this is definitely … someone is shooting here,'" he said. "So that's when we ran back into the auditorium of the synagogue, closed the doors behind us so as to not leave a visible target and we hit the floor." "Literally everyone went down," he said. "I yelled for everyone to get on to the floor and the shots continued for a few more seconds, and then it was basically over." Weddum said an officer had been stationed outside the building in an unmarked car. WATCH | The synagogue president describes what he heard and saw: Member of Belleville, Ont., synagogue describes hearing shots that left 2 wounded | Duration closed caption 5:47 A police officer and a man were wounded in an exchange of gunfire Sunday near a synagogue in Belleville, Ont. Norm Weddum, president of Sons of Jacob Synagogue, was ushering in members for Yom Kippur when he heard shots and secured the building. Meeks, the deputy police chief, said that while there is no ongoing threat to public safety, the police service is increasing patrols and "maintaining a heightened police presence" throughout the city, including at places of worship. "Let me be very clear: Antisemitism, hate and violence have no place in our community," she said. "Every person deserves to feel safe when attending a place of worship, gathering with loved ones, or participating in community life. Denette said the SIU has sent four investigators and two forensic investigators to the scene, which she described as "complex." "There are dozens of bullet holes in the street behind me and some homes have been hit and there are some vehicles with shot out windows, that sort of thing. So it would have been quite the scene," she said. The scene will likely be blocked off for a couple more days, she added. Police and Ontario's Special Investigations Unit are shown Monday at the scene of the shooting that took place a half a block away from the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville, Ont., on Sunday evening. A suspected and a police officer are both wounded and in the hospital. (Ian MacAlpine/The Canadian Press) Carney, Ford release statements Yom Kippur, one of the most sacred days of the Jewish calendar, began at sundown on Sunday. Prime Minister Mark Carney and Ontario Premier Doug Ford were among the public figures to release statements after the shooting. "Jewish people must be able to worship safely. To live free, open, proud Jewish lives. Canada’s government will do everything in our power to support law enforcement in ensuring that the perpetrator is held accountable to the fullest extent of the law," Carney said on social media. WATCH | Carney comments on the shooting: Carney calls shooting outside Belleville, Ont., synagogue 'deeply distressing' | Duration closed caption 0:30 Prime Minister Mark Carney appealed for anyone with knowledge of a shooting near a Belleville, Ont., synagogue to speak to law enforcement, saying 'hearts go out to the community' after two people, including a police officer, were injured. Sunday's shooting comes months after Carney warned that Canada was failing its Jewish community amid a surge in antisemitism. "I'm disgusted by the shooting that took place outside the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville earlier this evening as Jewish community members gathered to mark Yom Kippur," Ford said in a post. "We owe an immense debt of gratitude to this brave officer and to all the first responders who acted so quickly to keep the community safe." I’m disgusted by the shooting that took place outside the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville earlier this evening as Jewish community members gathered to mark Yom Kippur.

My thoughts are with the Jewish community in Belleville and across Ontario, who have every right to… —fordnation Belleville Mayor Neil Ellis told the CBC's Ontario Morning he was shocked by the news of the incident and commended the injured officer. "We've been rocked by this … stuff like this doesn't happen in Belleville," he said. "We are a community that's strong, and we are a community that's vibrant, and we will get through this together." "The City of Belleville is behind the Jewish community," Ellis told CBC Ottawa later Monday morning, adding that he was brought to tears when he first heard about the shooting Sunday evening. 'It's just devastating that this happened to Belleville,' Mayor Neil Ellis says. (Christian Lachance/CBC) Hopefully the SIU investigation will get to "the root cause" of the incident, the mayor added. Belleville had about 55,100 people as of the 2021 census. The broader area has about 111,200 people. The city is a hub for Hastings County and eastern Ontario’s third-biggest city, about 175 kilometres east of Toronto and 190 kilometres southwest of downtown Ottawa. Witness counts over 20 shots Chris Masterson, who lives nearby, said he was watching TV on Sunday evening when he heard three "loud pops." "There was a little bit of a pause and then I heard more shots," he said. "It was very clear it was gunshots." Masterson said he estimates there were around 25 shots back and forth before he heard a siren and someone clearly yell: "Police, stop." "I've been living here for over 10 years and nothing like this has ever happened," said another resident, Cody Bain. "It kind of makes you nervous. Makes you wonder about the future." WATCH | Neighbour says he heard shots while out for a walk: Neighbour describes hearing shots near Belleville, Ont., synagogue | Duration 1:41 Scott Granville, who lives near the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville, Ont., says he was out for a walk Sunday night when he heard gunshots. 'It sounded almost like an explosion,' he said, adding that things unfolded in a matter of minutes. 'We will carry on': synagogue leader When asked what he thought the man involved in the shooting was trying to do, synagogue leader Weddum said he thought "his intentions were pretty clear." "Well, he was coming down the street with some type of a firearm, and he was headed toward a synagogue where Jewish people were having service. So I think his intentions were pretty clear," said Weddum. "It's rough. And unfortunately we can't have our services again today to complete the Yom Kippur holiday, because the building is under a lockdown right now for the investigation," he said. "But, you know, once the building is released we'll get back to having services. "We will carry on."

World.title: Converse apologizes, pulls ad that critics say evokes KKK and lynching imagery
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

It's been called disgusting, harrowing and racist.

Now, after intense backlash that included a U.S. congressman, several celebrities, marketing experts and a wide swath of the internet, Converse has pulled the sneaker ad critics have accused of evoking Ku Klux Klan imagery, and apologized.

"We're sorry," Converse, which is owned by Nike, said in a statement to CBC News Monday.

"We understand why this image is deeply upsetting and recognize that we got this wrong," Converse continued in the statement that was first released Friday.

"We removed it from our channels and are working to remove it everywhere it appeared. This should not have happened and we will do better."

The ad, posted on social media Sept. 3, showed a model — KPop singer Karina — holding a pair of Chuck 70 X high top sneakers. Many people have pointed out online that the lighting on Karina's skirt, which created a white triangle, resembles a KKK hood. And the placement of the sneakers made them look like dangling feet, evoking for many a lynching victim.

In this screengrab of a Threads post from Sept. 17, actor Yvette Nicole Brown criticizes an ad by shoe company Converse. (yvettenicolebrown/Threads)

"That's a lynching, yes?" actor Yvette Nicole Brown wrote on Threads Thursday.

U.S. Rep. Troy Carter, in a lengthy statement Friday, called the ad " racist, reckless and deeply offensive."

"Nike and Converse, what the hell were you thinking?" he said.

Carter called on the companies to explain how the ad was approved, adding that an apology isn't enough. In doing so, he joined the chorus of other critics who allege that the imagery was obvious and wouldn't simply get missed without several levels of corporate failures.

"Do not insult our intellig ence by dismissing this as an unfortunate misunderstanding. An advertising campaign does not just appear," he said.

"It is conceived, photographed, reviewed, approved and distributed. At every stage, someone had the opportunity — and the responsibility — to say no."

Hanging deaths evoke lynching history

Converse's ad comes as the Southern U.S. grapples with several recent deaths involving Black people found hanging from trees.

Over the past two years, about a half-dozen Black women and men have been found hanged across the South. Police in some of those cases quickly deemed them suicides — often eliciting historically grounded skepticism when investigators provided limited evidence ruling out foul play.

As the Associated Press points out, for many Black people, the imagery of a rope and noose evokes the legacy of lynching and vigilante violence against Black people in the U.S. and brings with it deep pain and trauma.

Converse's "apology doesn't undo what got past legal, marketing, and leadership at every step," Lee Merritt, a civil rights attorney based in Texas, posted on Instagram Friday.

"This wasn't hidden. It was styled, lit, and approved by a creative team. Someone signed off on this ."

Several media outlets have reported that a second Converse ad posted by the brand's Malaysia Instagram account earlier this month depicted a man climbing a wooden ladder to reach a pair of shoes seen dangling from a tree, which critics have also said evoke lynching imagery.

CBC News has seen copies of images of the ad shared on social media, but not the original, so can't yet confirm. CBC has reached out to Converse for clarity on the second ad and not yet heard back.

Civil rights lawyer Lee Merritt criticized the ad in an Instagram post on Sept. 18. (@leemerittesq/Instagram)

Racially insensitive ads in the spotlight

Several companies and brands have come under fire lately for racially insensitive products and campaigns.

Last month, for instance, retailer Target pulled a children's Halloween costume from its shelves after widespread social media backlash, apologizing for selling a garment that critics said evoked racist minstrel caricatures.

Last year, American Eagle and actor Sydney Sweeney faced backlash for an ad campaign that was criticized for promoting white standards of beauty at best, and eugenics at worst. In the ad, Sweeney makes a play on words between jeans (the clothing item) and genes (the genetic material).

Gucci apologized in 2019 for a sweater accused of resembling blackface. In 2018, H&M apologized for its image of a Black boy in a sweatshirt that said "coolest monkey in the jungle." The year before, Dove said it "missed the mark" for a body wash commercial in which a Black woman lifts her shirt to reveal a white woman underneath.

World.title: Carney government dealt an early blow in climate litigation
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

In an early loss for the Carney government, a federal court refused to strike down a climate lawsuit brought by Canadian youth.

Justice Patrick Gleeson sided with the young people and the environmental advocates who are asking the court to hear what could be a landmark case on the federal government's climate accountability legislation.

The ruling means the environmentalists will likely get their day in court where both they and the government will get an opportunity to argue whether the Carney government must update its climate plan, formally known as the Canadian Net-Zero Emissions Accountability Act.

Back in June, three young people and two environmental groups launched a lawsuit asking the Federal Court to order Ottawa to amend its climate plan.

Since the plan was first launched in 2022, the Liberal government under Prime Minister Mark Carney has eliminated key measures needed for Canada to achieve the 2030 target.
