Playa Escobilla is among the world’s leading nesting sites for the olive ridley, or Lepidochelys olivacea.

The species is listed as endangered in Mexico and faces risks from egg poaching, fishing, destruction of nesting habitat and climate-related events. Conservation efforts are abundant all over Mexico, and volunteer opportunities are many, as detailed this month in Mexico News Daily.

Despite the current large Escobilla tally, Rafael Villanueva Alcázar of the National Commission of Natural Protected Areas (Conanp) cautions that nesting totals do not guarantee a comparable increase in hatchlings.

“It sounds like a lot,” he said, “but it’s actually very low compared to other beaches that have a higher rate of hatchling production.”

Only about 30% to 40% of Escobilla nests hatch, Villanueva said. By comparison, Playa Ceuta in Sinaloa estimates an 85% hatch rate, but it has only about 500 olive ridley nests per season.

No global hatching rate for sea turtle nests could be found, but one widely cited statistic is that roughly one in every 1,000 sea turtle hatchlings worldwide survives to adulthood.

Rising sand temperatures, changes in sand composition, erosion, strong swells and low humidity are among the factors reducing hatching success. Egg theft and other human-caused damage also take a toll.

Conditions can vary sharply between seasons and sanctuaries.

At Morro Ayuta, another major olive ridley refuge on Oaxaca’s coast, a record 1.9 million olive ridley nests were protected and more than 34 million hatchlings were released into the sea during the 2025-26 season.

Guillermo González Padilla, the head of that turtle camp, said those numbers were “unprecedented” thanks to “the rains, the wetter beaches and the fact that the summer’s temperature [in 2025] was ideal for egg incubation.”

(For this season, Morro Ayuta had counted about 135,000 turtles through the start of its third arribada earlier this month, according to Conanp.)

Meanwhile, at Escobilla, conservation work over the past 35 years has helped. Officials set aside a 5-kilometer protected area for nesting during last week’s arribada, and Conanp is monitoring the nesting grounds along with other federal agencies and local communities.

Local participation is critical because available park rangers alone cannot protect the beach from poachers and other threats. Also, according to EDUCA, a Oaxacan community development NGO, locals help strategically relocate eggs — which average 100 per nest — after arribadas.

With reports from El Universal Oaxaca and MeganoticiasMx

World.title: Aeroméxico investigates possible leak of 15 million passenger records
World.content:
Aeroméxico is investigating a possible leak of customer information after the federal Ministry of Anti-Corruption and Good Governance (SABG) identified an online user offering to sell a trove of over 15 million passenger records.

However, Aeroméxico said Sunday that it hadn’t identified any compromise of its customers’ financial information.

🚨Detectan posible exposición de datos personales vinculada a Aeroméxico La Secretaría Anticorrupción y Buen Gobierno identificó indicios de una posible filtración de datos personales en un sistema que podría estar relacionado con Aeroméxico. El hallazgo surgió tras detectar,… pic.twitter.com/iSFbFpKhkx — Azucena Uresti (@azucenau) September 20, 2026

In a statement, Aeroméxico said that “based on the information available,” it hadn’t identified any “exposure” of its customers’ “financial information,” including details of cards used to purchase flights.

The airline also said it hadn’t detected any compromise of customers’ Aeroméxico account passwords, including those used to access the Aeroméxico rewards program.

“Furthermore, this situation has not created any impact on our operations,” Aeroméxico said.

The airline released its statement after SABG said it had detected that a user of the social media and instant messaging platform Telegram was attempting to sell a 1.1 gigabyte database “supposedly attributable” to Aeroméxico and containing more than 15 million passenger records.

“Within the framework of active forensic monitoring of possible security incidents, the Ministry of Anti-Corruption and Good Governance identified signs of a possible exposure of personal data in a system that could be related to Aeroméxico,” the SABG said in a statement.

The ministry said that its monitoring allowed it to locate a Sept. 18 post on Telegram in which “a user offers a database supposedly attributable to Aeroméxico with more than 15 million records,” including — allegedly — the full names of customers of the airline, their e-mail addresses, their telephone numbers and their dates of birth.

The SABG said that it “obtained a sample of 100,092 records” and subsequently identified the names of various people, including those of public servants and public figures.

The ministry said it would “analyze the data obtained” and begin an investigation aimed at determining “the alleged responsibility for the compromised databases.”

Aeroméxico said it would cooperate with federal authorities and report on any relevant developments in a timely manner.

The airline also said it had begun its own “exhaustive investigation” in order to “verify the authenticity and veracity” of the information being offered to “third parties,” determine “its origin” and “establish the reach of any possible impact.”

While the airline said it hadn’t identified any compromise of its customers’ financial information, it advised its customers to stay alert to “unusual e-mails, messages or calls that seek personal or financial information.”

Aeroméxico didn’t say that its systems or databases had been targeted in a cyberattack.

However, hackers have previously targeted both companies and federal and state governments in Mexico. Among the victims of previous cyberattacks are the Ministry of National Defense and state oil company Pemex.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: Sheinbaum pledges continued military support as Sinaloa’s cartel turf war shifts to Mazatlán
World.content:
A day after pledging Sunday to keep federal security forces in Sinaloa “as long as necessary,” President Sheinbaum on Monday repeated her conviction that U.S. interference precipitated the cartel turf war plaguing the troubled state. The violence, previously centered in Culiacán and rural areas, has spread south in recent months to the resort city of Mazatlán.

While in Culiacán, the Sinaloa state capital, on Sunday, Sheinbaum said Governor Graciela Domínguez can count on the complete support of the federal government.

Domínguez has been in office for less than a month after being appointed on Aug. 25 to replace Rubén Rocha, who was indicted by U.S. federal prosecutors for alleged links to drug trafficking.

“First and foremost, all federal forces … will remain here for as long as necessary,” she said. “We will not withdraw any element of the Army, the National Guard or the Navy; they will continue to support the governor and, above all, the people of Sinaloa.”

The state has been embroiled in a civil war between factions of the Sinaloa Cartel for two years, becoming what El País newspaper has described as “the biggest political crisis of Sheinbaum’s term.”

As the turf war spread to Mazatlán this summer, the government has deployed thousands of federal troops to the resort city, including 1,000 marines and over 800 Public Security Ministry agents last week. Despite an increase in military presence, homicides in Mazatlán outpaced killings in the larger city of Culiacán in August.

Sinaloa’s economy is facing a historic downturn, driven by severe security challenges and cartel-related violence, leading to a contraction of 4.5% in this year’s first quarter.

On Sunday, Sheinbaum blamed foreign interference for the current situation and then doubled down on that claim during her daily press conference on Monday.

“We don’t want interference from any foreign government in our territory,” she said on Sunday. “Interference generates violence, whereas cooperation for development generates peace.”

Sheinbaum said that before the U.S. “extraction” of drug kingpin Ismael Zambada, the murder rate in Sinaloa was low (“less than one homicide per day,” she claimed). Since then, violence has escalated, producing significant crime rates.

Sunday’s visit was Sheinbaum’s first to the state since the indictments against Rocha and nine other government and law enforcement officials from the state were made public in April.

To address the challenges, Sheinbaum said federal officials would travel in stages to Sinaloa; Security Cabinet officials will visit this week, followed by officials from the Agriculture Ministry.

“There will be no shortage of money to support farmers,” she said, acknowledging that agriculture is the backbone of the state’s economy.

With reports from N+, La Jornada and El País

World.title: After a shootout, authorities rescue 3 kidnapping victims and arrest 7 suspects in Puerto Peñasco
World.content:
Security forces arrested seven people and freed three kidnapping victims during an operation Friday afternoon in Puerto Peñasco, Sonora, a popular seaside resort city also known as Rocky Point.

Authorities also seized an arsenal that included more than 40 long guns, approximately 4,000 rounds of ammunition, two Minimi machine guns and a Browning M2 .50 caliber gun, the federal Security Cabinet announced on Monday.

En Puerto Peñasco, Sonora, trabajos de investigación de @fgjesonora, con información del Centro Nacional de Inteligencia de @SSPCMexico @Defensamx1, @SEMAR_mx y @Amicsonora.

En una operación encabezada por @Defensamx1 y @Amicsonora permitieron ubicar un inmueble relacionado con… pic.twitter.com/dtwS2fGtft — Omar H Garcia Harfuch (@OHarfuch) September 21, 2026

Security Minister Omar García Harfuch said that three federal agencies and the military joined an investigation by the Sonora Attorney General’s Office (FGJES), supplying intelligence that allowed state officials to identify a property linked to the kidnappings.

As state police and soldiers approached the premises, armed civilians opened fire. The authorities returned fire, eventually outflanking the suspects and containing them.

Three Sonora Investigative Police agents were wounded in the confrontation, none seriously, and three kidnapping victims were freed. Authorities captured seven suspects, including one minor.

The suspects will face charges for attempted aggravated homicide, crimes against public servants, aggravated vehicle theft, criminal association and kidnapping.

After the shootout, the authorities obtained a search warrant and re-entered the property, confiscating the weapons. The search also turned up evidence that was sufficient to merit another warrant that led to two weekend raids on additional properties in downtown Puerto Peñasco.

The sweep of those locations resulted in the seizure of heroin, methamphetamine, loaded magazines, bullet-proof vests, tactical gear and three high-end vehicles which had been reported stolen in the United States.

“We extend special recognition to the three AMIC [the Criminal Investigation Agency] agents who were injured during the attack,” García Harfuch said in a social media post.

A FGJES press release indicated that one of its agents was shot in a lower extremity, while two female agents suffered shrapnel wounds. All three were reported to be in stable condition.

The skirmish came about after several miners reported to police that they had escaped a kidnapping attempt last week, but others hadn’t. State officials alerted federal agencies, who were able to follow the route of the captors and locate a white Chevrolet Suburban truck that had been described by the near-victims.

With reports from La Jornada, Sonora Presente and Eje Central

World.title: Hurricane Polo expected to reach Category 5 as it nears Mexico’s Pacific coast
World.content:
Listen to this article

Hurricane Polo is expected to quickly intensify after forming Monday morning in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of Guerrero, with Civil Protection encouraging residents of several states to remain vigilant and follow safety recommendations.

Polo could bring heavy rain, rough surf and tropical-storm-force winds to parts of Mexico this week as it intensifies into a Category 5 hurricane near the coast of Michoacán by Wednesday, the U.S. National Hurricane Center warned.

⚠️ #Polo ahora como #Huracán categoría 1 ⚠️ ◾️Se localiza a 305 km al sur-suroeste de Zihuatanejo, #Guerrero, y a 435 km al sur-sureste de Manzanillo, #Colima

◾️Su circulación refuerza la psibabilidad de #Lluvias de distintas intensidades en Jalisco, Colima, Michoacán, Guerrero… pic.twitter.com/3RRiy2j0PQ — Coordinación Nacional de Protección Civil (@CNPC_MX) September 21, 2026

It was centered about 410 kilometers south-southeast of Manzanillo, Mexico, and 322 kilometers southwest of Zihuatanejo at 9 a.m. CST on Monday. As of 12 p.m., it was a Category 1 storm with maximum sustained winds of 129 kph (80 mph).

Mexico’s National Meteorological Service (SMN) predicted Monday that Polo would bring heavy rainfall to Pacific coastal regions, potentially raising river and stream levels, triggering flooding and mudslides.

Intense rain is expected over the coming days in the states of Oaxaca and Guerrero (75 to 150 millimeters), very heavy rainfall (50 to 75 mm) in Michoacán, and heavy rainfall (25 to 50 mm) in coastal Jalisco and Colima.

Winds of 10 to 20 kph, with gusts of 30 to 50 kph, can also be expected along the coasts of Colima, Michoacán, Guerrero and Oaxaca. In addition, the storm will bring waves of 1 to 3 meters to Guerrero, Michoacán, Oaxaca, Jalisco and Colima.

Officials urged the public to remain attentive to the warnings issued by Mexico’s National Meteorological Service (SMN) and to follow the recommendations of Civil Protection.

The SMN and the U.S. National Hurricane Center established a watch zone from Tecpan de Galeana, Guerrero, to Punta San Telmo, Michoacán, warning that Polo’s trajectory will be “erratic.” It is expected to curve and move parallel to the coasts of Colima, Michoacán and Guerrero.

Farther west in the Pacific Ocean, Tropical Storm Odalys is forecast to become a hurricane by mid-week. It was located over 2,000 kilometers west-southwest of the southern tip of Mexico’s Baja California peninsula on Monday morning.

In September 2024, Hurricane John hit coastal Guerrero as a Category 3 storm, just one year after Category 5 Hurricane Otis devastated Acapulco, one of Mexico’s main tourist destinations with a population of over one million people, from which it is still recovering.

With reports from AP News

World.title: MND Local Guadalajara: Airport road update and Line 5’s environmental cost
World.content:
This week, we have an update on construction of the Guadalajara International Airport’s second entrance and how the buildout of bus rapid transit (Line 5) along the Chapala highway has affected the local environment.

Airport’s 2nd entrance road now expected to open by March 2027

The project to add a second airport entrance kicked off in earnest 13 months ago. It aimed to ease chronic traffic bottlenecks along the Chapala highway, where airport travelers, daily commuters and commercial trucks all battle for scarce road space.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Gobierno de Jalisco (@gobjalisco)

In summer 2025, public officials promised the work would be finished in time for the FIFA World Cup earlier this summer, but that deadline came and went. Then work was suspended to prevent construction delays around the airport during the tournament.

Now that work has resumed, we have an updated timeline for completion. Earlier this month, Jalisco Gov. Pablo Lemus Navarro declared the airport’s new 6-kilometer entrance road should be ready for its debut by March 2027.

“The Guadalajara Airport will have a second entrance; it will no longer only be possible to enter via the Chapala Highway,” he told local newspaper El Informador. “This is good news for connectivity and mobility from the airport.”

The new road will connect Adolf Horn Avenue with the airport’s south side. For southbound drivers coming from areas like Tlajomulco, Tlaquepaque and Zapopan, the road will allow them to bypass the initial segment of the Chapala highway. It will also alleviate northbound traffic congestion on the Chapala highway by diverting drivers to Adolfo Horn.

Additional airport upgrades

In addition to a second airport access road, the project includes an internal interchange and new roads to connect to the airport’s future Terminal 2.

But that is not all. The final phase of work to modernize the Chapala highway also got started this month. This project involves new pedestrian bridges, public transport stations, storm drainage, sidewalks, streetlights, bike lanes and replacement trees (more on that below).

These improvements are expected to take eight months to complete, with final delivery by May 2027.

Airport access improvements are being jointly funded by the Jalisco state government and airport operator Pacific Airport Group (GAP). Guadalajara International Airport is the third busiest in Mexico, with annual passenger traffic of nearly 18.8 million in 2025.

The high environmental cost of the city’s new Line 5 mass transit system

The extension of public transit to the Guadalajara airport was constructed in a rush ahead of the 2026 FIFA World Cup. This new link to Guadalajara’s mass transit system was dubbed Line 5, even though it’s not a light rail system like Lines 1 through 4.

The impetus behind the new Line 5 was not visionary public planning but a FIFA requirement for all host cities, which mandated that tournament visitors have a public transport option from the airport to the soccer stadium. Chronic traffic bottlenecks along the Chapala highway, the sole access point to Guadalajara airport, also threatened to embarrass public officials on the world stage, something they were desperate to avoid.

Line 5 was completed in time for June’s World Cup matches. While some lamented the lack of rail service on this congested route, the project was widely hailed as a success.

The part that’s received far less attention is the environmental cost of this new infrastructure. Below is a look at that scorecard.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Pablo Lemus Navarro (@pablolemusn)

Constructing six new BRT stations over a 22.5-kilometer stretch of the Chapala highway involved the elimination of 1,541 trees along the route, according to the Ministry of Environment and Territorial Development.

All the trees cut were located in the El Salto and Tlajomulco municipalities, with authorization granted by local officials.

Tree cover loss and its effects

An environmental impact assessment completed ahead of Line 5’s construction identified 32 tree species (97% of which were deemed healthy), 133 bird species and six reptile species inhabiting the wooded areas in its path. The trees were removed anyway, with subsequent plans to add 2,846 new trees.

How has the sudden removal of so much tree cover impacted the urban area?

Dr. Lucila Méndez Morán of the Department of Applied Ecology at Centro Universitario de Ciencias Biológicas y Agropecuarias (CUCBA) explained that deforestation on the city’s south side tied to Line 5 has intensified the “urban heat island” effect already afflicting this part of the metropolitan area.

The loss of vegetation and shade not only elevates local temperatures but also reduces the area’s ability to absorb water during the rainy season, dampen noise and flush air pollutants. The state has said that while the short-term environmental impact of Line 5 is negative, the landscape should improve over the medium term.

Despite more trees being replanted than removed, it’s not a net benefit, ecologically speaking. The amount of oxygen generated by small tree saplings is a fraction of what’s generated by mature trees. Until those trees grow to maturity over the coming decade or more, their loss will be acutely felt.

Line 5 construction compounds legacy environmental issues

Massive tree loss in Tlajomulco and El Salto is especially painful due to a well-documented environmental crisis that predates the construction of Line 5.

Uncontrolled real estate expansion on the city’s south side in recent decades has already stripped much of the forest cover, raising local temperatures by 2 degrees to 3 degrees Celsius relative to other parts of the Guadalajara Metropolitan Area (GMA). Besides Tlajomulco and El Salto, this area also includes popular tourist destinations Tlaquepaque and Tonalá.

In addition, this zone suffers severe air pollution tied to chronic heavy traffic, under-regulated industrial emissions and thermal inversions in wintertime.

Going forward, this poses a risk of worse public health outcomes due to poor air quality and even hotter temperatures.

MND writer Dawn Stoner is reporting from Guadalajara.

World.title: Mexico bans cell phone use in grade schools starting in October: Monday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Listen to this article

Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

📵 Cell phones and tablets to be banned in primary and secondary schools : Education Minister Mario Delgado said federal and state education authorities agreed Friday to ban the devices at both levels. High schools will set their own limits. Once Sheinbaum approves and promulgates the agreement, it will take effect after 30 days.

: Education Minister Mario Delgado said federal and state education authorities agreed Friday to ban the devices at both levels. High schools will set their own limits. Once Sheinbaum approves and promulgates the agreement, it will take effect after 30 days. 🔍 Sheinbaum, Chihuahua governor talk security : Sheinbaum said she met Gov. Maru Campos in Ciudad Juárez on Saturday and reminded her that the FGR is investigating the alleged CIA participation in a Chihuahua drug lab raid five months ago.

: Sheinbaum said she met Gov. Maru Campos in Ciudad Juárez on Saturday and reminded her that the FGR is investigating the alleged CIA participation in a Chihuahua drug lab raid five months ago. 🇺🇸 Sheinbaum blames US interference for Sinaloa violence: Sheinbaum said that Sinaloa — a state plagued by violence — is “proof that interference … caused the situation we have [in the state] today.” Like her predecessor AMLO, Sheinbaum believes that the U.S. was involved in the kidnapping of “El Mayo” Zambada, an event that led to an escalation in Sinaloa Cartel infighting.

Why today’s mañanera matters

At President Claudia Sheinbaum’s Monday morning press conference, Education Minister Mario Delgado announced that federal and state education authorities had reached an agreement to ban the use of cell phones and tablets in primary and secondary schools.

His announcement came three weeks after he reported that 81% of more than half a million surveyed teachers were in favor of there being “guidelines and rules to guarantee the safe use [of devices] for educational purposes.”

Cell phone use in classrooms is already banned in half of Mexico’s 32 federal entities. Now, a national ban is set to be enforced.

Also of note at today’s mañanera were Sheinbaum’s remarks about her meeting on Saturday with Chihuahua Governor Maru Campos. Their meeting came five months after U.S. Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) personnel allegedly participated in a drug lab raid in Chihuahua. Two CIA agents and two Chihuahua state police officials were killed in a car accident on the day the raid took place.

Sheinbaum says that the CIA personnel participated in the operation alongside state forces without the knowledge or authorization of her government, violating Mexico’s Constitution and National Security Law. Campos has claimed that she didn’t authorize or have knowledge of the presence of the CIA personnel in the drug lab raid.

Sheinbaum has characterized the CIA’s alleged involvement in the operation as an example of U.S. interference in Mexican affairs, a topic she also spoke about on Monday morning.

Cell phones and tablets to be banned in primary and secondary schools across Mexico

Delgado told reporters that Sheinbaum had “initiated an essential debate for our country — a debate about the impact of screens and social media on this generation of boys and girls, adolescents and young people.”

He subsequently noted that federal and state education authorities reached an agreement last Friday “to regulate cell phones and tablets in schools.”

“The proposal is to not allow them for primary and secondary schools, to restrict their use in these education levels,” Delgado said.

At the high school level, the education minister said it will be up to “each institution” to determine “limitations” that ensure the “responsible and safe use” of devices for “educational purposes.”

Delgado noted that the agreement reached on Friday is subject to approval by Sheinbaum. He said that once the agreement is approved — which is certain to happen — and promulgated, it will take effect after 30 days.

“It will be at the end of October that this regulation will enter into force,” Delgado said.

“This agreement is a fundamental step forward in order to guarantee the rights of children, adolescents and young people, taking care of their mental health, their learning and their comprehensive development while strengthening their attention span, human contact and community,” he said.

Sheinbaum reminds Campos of the FGR’s ‘CIA in Chihuahua’ probe

Sheinbaum told reporters that she and Gov. Campos spoke about security coordination between federal and Chihuahua authorities at their meeting in Ciudad Juárez on Saturday.

“It’s essential that [coordination] occurs,” she said.

Regarding “the presence of individuals from a U.S. agency,” Sheinbaum said she reminded Campos that the Federal Attorney General’s Office (FGR) is carrying out an investigation.

“That corresponds to the Attorney General’s Office. It’s not within our purview as the government of Mexico,” she said, noting that Campos acknowledged that the FGR is conducting a probe into the CIA’s alleged participation in the drug lab raid in Chihuahua.

Campos said in a video message on Saturday that she and Sheinbaum spoke “very frankly and firmly” to each other.

Hoy me reuní en privado con la presidenta de la República, Claudia Sheinbaum. Un encuentro que era necesario para ambos gobiernos, ante las diferencias de lo que estamos haciendo en materia de seguridad. Tuvimos un encuentro franco y con firmeza, en donde ambas reconocimos la… pic.twitter.com/obtO7o33yG — Maru Campos (@MaruCampos_G) September 19, 2026

“We both acknowledged that we must improve our channels of communication without renouncing our convictions and the positions we defend,” she said.

“I confirmed to her that my government will continue respecting the law while combating organized crime with complete force and all the capacities [we have],” Campos said.

Sheinbaum blames violence in Sinaloa on US interference

Sheinbaum told reporters that the northern state of Sinaloa was registering “less than one homicide per day” before the July 2024 arrest in the United States of Sinaloa Cartel kingpin Ismael “El Mayo” Zambada, who was kidnapped by Joaquín Guzmán López, a son of convicted drug lord Joaquín “El Chapo” Guzmán, and forced onto a private plane that flew him and Guzmán López to New Mexico.

The kidnapping of El Mayo and his subsequent arrest in the United States led to an escalation of a long-running conflict between two rival factions of the Sinaloa Cartel, Los Chapitos and Los Mayos. Thousands of homicides and abductions have been attributed to the factional fighting.

Sheinbaum, like her predecessor Andrés Manuel López Obrador, believes that the U.S. government was involved in the events that led to Zambada’s arrest in New Mexico on July 25, 2024. Consequently, she believes that the U.S. government is at least partially to blame for the ongoing violence in Sinaloa.

On Monday morning, the president said that “in Mexico and the whole world, it is proven that interference and intervention don’t strengthen national institutions.”

“… On the contrary, they weaken them,” she said.

Sheinbaum went on to say that “Sinaloa is proof that [U.S.] interference, with the rupture of a criminal group, caused the situation we have [in the state] today.”

World.title: It’s official: Mexico City’s traffic is the worst in the world
World.content:
As World Car-Free Day approaches (Sept. 22), Mexico City residents have more reason than most to consider alternative modes of transportation, after the capital has again been named the most congested city in the world.

According to the annual Traffic Index by navigation-device maker TomTom, Mexico City recorded an average congestion level of 75.9% in 2025. Even though the indicator fell by 3.6 percentage points compared to 2024, the city occupies the top overall position, dethroning Barranquilla, Colombia, which had in turn dethroned Mexico City for the top spot in the previous edition.

The seven most congested cities in the world

In this edition, Mexico City was closely followed by Bengaluru, India, which recorded an average congestion level of 74.4%, and Dublin, Ireland, at 72.9%.

The ranking is compiled using anonymous GPS data from up to one in three vehicles on the road from cities around the world, showing vehicle movement—or the lack thereof. TomTom then calculates a congestion level based on how much slower traffic is moving compared to when the roads are clear.

In Mexico City, the company estimated that traveling 10 kilometers took an average of 34 minutes and 29 seconds in 2025 — 58 seconds longer than the previous year. Overall, then, Mexico City drivers can expect to cover on average approximately 4.4 kilometers in a 15-minute span.

During peak hours, however, the average speed is reduced to 13.5 kilometers per hour.

The time cost for drivers was significant. TomTom calculated that each motorist lost 184 hours to congestion during peak periods over the course of a year, equivalent to a total of seven days and 16 hours.

Although the yearly lost-time figure was one hour and 16 minutes lower than that recorded in 2024, it reflects the persistence of traffic jams as one of the metropolitan area’s major daily mobility challenges.

The index also revealed that Wednesday, May 28, was the most congested day in 2025, with an average congestion level of 117%. On that day, the indicator peaked at 167% at 3:00 p.m., according to the report.

Mexico City’s traffic congestion is not an isolated phenomenon. TomTom’s report showed that major cities across the world experienced increased travel times, including London, Barcelona and Athens.

Overall, TomTom’s findings revealed that congestion worsened globally in 2025 compared to 2024, with congestion levels and travel times per kilometer increasing in the majority of the nearly 500 cities analyzed.

In Mexico, other cities that made the ranking included Guadalajara, Jalisco (No. 17), Monterrey, Nuevo León (No. 111), Tijuana, Baja California (No. 118), León, Guanajuato (No. 186), Ecatepec, Mexico state (No. 197), and Puebla city (No. 211).

Mexico News Daily

World.title: Sierra Leone Constitutional Reform Goes to Supreme Court as Bio Holds Off Signing
World.content:
Sierra Leone · Politics

Key Facts — What happened President Julius Maada Bio deferred signing a disputed constitutional amendment and referred a petition against it to the Supreme Court.

— Why it matters The bill rewrites the rules for the 2028 elections, including the vote share needed to win the presidency.

— The numbers Amendments need at least 100 of 149 MPs; the ruling party holds 81 seats and the 14 chiefs’ seats are non-partisan.

— The catch The opposition walked out before the bill was declared passed, and no final vote count has been published.

— What comes next Ecofin Agency reports the Supreme Court will rule on 7 October 2026, before Bio decides whether to sign.

Parliament declared the bill passed after the opposition walked out. Now the president wants judges to say whether the vote counted before he signs.

Freetown, the capital of Sierra Leone, seen from the air in a file photograph. (Photo: Rio Times media library)

Sierra Leone constitutional reform is on hold. President Julius Maada Bio has declined, for now, to sign an amendment that parliament declared passed after the opposition walked out.

Instead, he has asked the Supreme Court for a judicial opinion on whether the bill was lawfully adopted. The presidency announced the decision on Monday 14 September 2026.

At stake are the rules for the 2028 general elections in the West African country of about nine million people. Bio, first elected in 2018, won a second term in 2023.

What Bio asked the judges

The referral rests on Section 122(1) of the 1991 constitution. It lets the president seek the court’s judicial opinion on “any Petition in which he has to give a final decision”.

The petition in question came from the Institute for Governance Reform, a civil society research group. It reached the presidency on Friday 4 September 2026, Benin Web TV reported.

The group questions whether the parliamentary procedure that produced the bill was constitutional. Bio directed the Attorney-General and Minister of Justice to take the petition to the court.

Parliament had sent the bill to State House for signature on Thursday 10 September 2026. The government statement called the referral “unprecedented”.

It said a bill touching “the constitutional and democratic foundations of the Republic” needs broad national consensus. It must also be “underpinned by constitutional clarity,” the statement added.

A walkout and a disputed count

The fight dates to Monday 10 August 2026. That day, MPs voted 96 to 41 to keep the president’s power to appoint electoral commissioners after consulting parties.

The opposition All People’s Congress (APC) had backed an independent nominating committee instead. Its leader in parliament, Abdul Kargbo, then led 49 APC lawmakers out of the chamber.

Their complaint was procedural: Section 108 of the constitution sets the bar for an amendment’s second and third readings. It demands “not less than two-thirds of the Members of Parliament”.

Speaker Segepoh Solomon Thomas, who presides over parliament, ruled otherwise for votes on individual clauses. He said a simple majority of members present applied at that stage.

Parliament then declared the whole bill passed in the same sitting, AYV News and Benin Web TV reported. It adjourned until 29 October 2026.

No final tally for the second and third readings has been published. The opposition and several civil society groups have demanded one, Benin Web TV reported.

A street in Koidu, Kono District, eastern Sierra Leone, in an old file photograph. Source: Wikimedia Commons / Brian Harrington Spier (CC BY-SA 2.0)

The arithmetic behind the dispute

Parliament has 149 members: 81 from Bio’s Sierra Leone People’s Party (SLPP), 54 from the APC and 14 paramount chiefs. The chiefs are traditional rulers who sit without a party label.

Two-thirds of 149 is 99.3, so an amendment needs at least 100 votes. The SLPP and every chief together make only 95.

The government therefore needs at least five opposition votes to reach the threshold. The 96 votes on the electoral commission clause on 10 August would have fallen four short.

According to Ecofin Agency, the question before the court is how that two-thirds is counted. The choice is between all members, including those absent, and only those present and voting.

What the Sierra Leone constitutional reform would change

The biggest change concerns the presidency. A first-round win would need 50% of valid votes plus one, down from 55%, with a spread across districts still required.

The bill would also make proportional representation, in which seats follow party vote shares, permanent for parliamentary elections. Bio says it would give “women, young people, professionals, and minority groups a fairer opportunity to be represented”.

It would require that at least 30% of candidates in national and local elections be women. Dual nationals could also stand for parliament and hold certain public offices.

Bio urged MPs to back the package in a national address on Sunday 9 August 2026. Delay, he warned, meant elections under the existing rules.

The government, the opposition, civil society, citizens and several election observer missions had all “recognized” them “as requiring reform,” he said.

Why the opposition is suspicious

The APC rejected the lower presidential threshold during the debate. Critics argue the combined changes could help the SLPP in 2028.

Bio himself cannot run again, because the constitution limits presidents to two terms. The online Sierra Leone Telegraph reports that many critics still accuse him of trying to extend his stay in power.

The APC has filed two cases of its own at the Supreme Court. One asks judges to interpret the constitution’s amendment rules; another challenges the Speaker’s conduct, Sierraloaded reported.

What happens next

Ecofin Agency reports that the court will rule on Wednesday 7 October 2026. Bio has said he will decide on signing only after receiving the opinion.

Normally the constitution gives a president 14 days to sign a bill or return it with reasons. For this bill, that window closes on 24 September 2026.

State House told parliament that if the opinion arrives later, Bio will inform MPs as soon as he receives it. A Sierra Leone Telegraph opinion piece argues the constitution does not say a referral pauses that clock.

For foreign investors and donors, the case is a test of whether Sierra Leone’s 2028 election rules rest on broad agreement. The Sierra Leone constitutional reform now depends on the judges’ reading of one clause.

More: Africa coverage, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did President Bio ask the Supreme Court?

He referred a petition from the Institute for Governance Reform, a civil society group, for a judicial opinion under Section 122(1) of the 1991 constitution. The petition questions whether parliament followed the constitution when it adopted the amendment. Bio deferred signing until the court gives its view.

How many votes does a constitutional amendment need in Sierra Leone?

Section 108 requires two-thirds of the Members of Parliament at the second and third readings. With 149 members, that means at least 100 votes. The ruling SLPP holds 81 seats and there are 14 non-partisan paramount chiefs.

When was the bill passed and when was it referred?

Parliament declared the bill passed on Monday 10 August 2026, after the opposition walked out. It reached State House on 10 September 2026. The presidency announced the referral on 14 September 2026.

When will the court decide?

Ecofin Agency reports that the Supreme Court will rule on 7 October 2026. Bio has said he will announce his decision on signing after receiving the opinion.

Sources: Constitution of Sierra Leone, 1991 (sections 106, 108 and 122), Ecofin Agency on the referral and the 7 October ruling date, Voice of Nigeria on the State House announcement, Sierra Leone Telegraph on the government statement, Benin Web TV on the 10 August adoption, AYV News on the passage of the bill, Sierra Leone Telegraph on the 10 August walkout, Sierraloaded on the 96-41 vote, Sierraloaded on seat numbers and the committee debate, Sierraloaded on the opposition’s court cases

World.title: São Tomé Election on Sunday Tests a Ruling Party That Split in Two
World.content:
São Tomé and Príncipe · Elections

Key Facts — What happens Sunday São Tomé and Príncipe votes on Sunday 27 September 2026 for parliament, local councils and Príncipe’s regional government.

— What is at stake All 55 seats in the National Assembly; a majority needs 28. Six parties and one coalition are standing.

— Who votes 146,510 people are on the provisional electoral roll, according to the National Electoral Commission in August 2026.

— The catch Former prime minister Patrice Trovoada, ousted as leader of the biggest party, has urged its members to abstain.

— Why it matters The vote decides whether Prime Minister Américo Ramos wins his own mandate after being appointed by the president in 2025.

— What comes next The campaign opened on 12 September 2026. No date for provisional results has been reported.

The prime minister now controls the party that once fought his appointment. Its ousted leader is telling supporters to stay at home.

Houses and palm trees on the waterfront below forested hills in São Tomé and Príncipe, in a file photograph.

The São Tomé election on Sunday 27 September 2026 will choose a new parliament, local councils and the regional government of Príncipe. It follows a court ruling that handed the country’s biggest party to the prime minister.

São Tomé and Príncipe is a two-island republic in the Gulf of Guinea, off the coast of Central Africa. The legislative vote will show whether Prime Minister Américo Ramos can turn an appointment into a mandate.

What voters are choosing

The National Assembly, the single-chamber parliament, has 55 seats, and a party needs 28 to govern alone. Seats are shared out by proportional representation from party lists.

Fifty-three members come from seven home districts, including the capital district, Água Grande, and the island of Príncipe. Citizens living abroad elect two more members, one for Africa and one for Europe.

The same ballot day also renews local councils and the government of Príncipe, the smaller island, which has autonomous status.

The National Electoral Commission counted 146,510 voters on its provisional roll in early August, Lusa, the Portuguese news agency, reported. That was 4,319 more than for the presidential vote in July.

The official campaign opened on Saturday 12 September. Six parties and one coalition submitted lists before the deadline of 13 August, according to Lusa.

A party taken over by the prime minister

The Independent Democratic Action party, known by its Portuguese initials ADI, won 30 seats in the last legislative vote in September 2022. Its leader, Patrice Trovoada, became prime minister.

On 6 January 2025 President Carlos Vila Nova dismissed Trovoada, who called the decision unconstitutional. Vila Nova then appointed Ramos, a former ADI secretary-general, against the wishes of the party leadership.

The fight then moved inside the party. After a congress on 27 June 2026, the Constitutional Court recognised Ramos as ADI president.

Trovoada’s camp had challenged that congress as illegitimate, the Portuguese newspaper Observador reported on 29 July.

In a Facebook video, Trovoada said a stage of his own political journey might be ending. He would accept that “with perfect calm, serenity”, he said, because “no leader is irreplaceable”.

On 12 August he went further in another Facebook video, as reported by the Portuguese broadcaster RTP. He urged ADI members to protest by “not going to vote, not leaving home to vote in the legislative and municipal elections”.

He left supporters free to vote in the Príncipe regional contest. Ramos replied that a call to abstain “is not a good strategy for a politician”.

Voting, he added in remarks carried by Observador, “is a civic duty”.

Forest, coves and a small settlement on the coast of São Tomé and Príncipe, in a file photograph.

A president re-elected on low turnout

Vila Nova won a second five-year term on 19 July with 55.88% of the vote, the Constitutional Court confirmed. His rival, Nito d’Abreu, took 41.46% with the official backing of the ADI.

Only about four in ten registered voters cast a ballot in that contest. In the 2022 legislative vote, turnout was just over 65%.

Vila Nova was sworn in again on 3 September, and his own term runs to 2031. Whoever wins on Sunday will govern alongside him for a four-year legislature.

The other contenders

The main opposition is the Movement for the Liberation of São Tomé and Príncipe/Social Democratic Party, or MLSTP/PSD. It led the country to independence from Portugal in 1975.

The party won 18 seats in 2022 and is led by Américo Barros.

The party opened its campaign on 12 September. “Spending must be cut where it is unnecessary: travel, posts, fossil fuels,” Barros said.

He also pledged to court foreign direct investment, Téla Nón reported.

A new party, Nossa Terra, meaning Our Land, is led by Abnildo d’Oliveira, who presides over the National Assembly. He was elected to parliament for the ADI.

His party proposes opening EMAE, the state water and power company, to private capital. In August opposition deputies blocked a session to demand he step down as speaker.

The coalition of the Independent Citizens Movement, the Socialist Party and the National Unity Party won five seats in 2022. Its slate of candidates has since been cut back sharply.

The Constitutional Court rejected its lists in Mé-Zóchi, Lobata, Cantagalo, Lembá and the diaspora over forged signatures, Lusa reported on 12 September. The coalition’s leadership rejects the accusation, the Brazilian site Africas Play reported.

The court referred the case to the Public Ministry, the state prosecutor’s office. It noted that forging signatures is a crime under the penal code.

The coalition may still compete in Água Grande, Caué and Príncipe. The Basta movement, the Democratic Convergence Party and the Democratic Movement Force for Change complete the field.

What the winner inherits

Campaigning in Caué district, Ramos said the economy was growing by 1% to 2% a year. It has to grow by more than 3% or 4%, he told Lusa in a report published on 20 September.

He pointed to a solar park that, he said, would install 11 megawatts of panels by December. By his estimate it would cover about half of current electricity needs.

The São Tomé election will not settle everything on its own. If no party reaches 28 seats, coalition talks would follow before the president names a prime minister.

For Ramos, the test is simple. He must show that the ADI’s voters followed the party, not the man who led it for years.

Frequently Asked Questions

When is the São Tomé election?

Voting takes place on Sunday 27 September 2026. The president announced the date in January 2026, together with the presidential vote held on 19 July. The official campaign opened on 12 September.

What is being elected?

Voters choose all 55 members of the National Assembly, local councils and the regional government of Príncipe, the autonomous smaller island. Fifty-three members are elected in seven districts at home, and two represent citizens living in Africa and Europe.

Who leads the ADI now?

Prime Minister Américo Ramos. The Constitutional Court recognised him as party president after a congress on 27 June 2026. Former leader Patrice Trovoada has asked ADI members not to vote in the legislative and municipal contests.

Who is the president?

Carlos Vila Nova, re-elected on 19 July 2026 with 55.88% of the vote and sworn in for a second term on 3 September. He dismissed Trovoada as prime minister in January 2025 and appointed Ramos.

World.title: Enugu Air Douala Route: Nigerian State Airline Starts Cameroon Flights 23 September
World.content:
Nigeria · Aviation

Key Facts — What happened Enugu Air, owned by Nigeria’s Enugu State government, plans to open its first international route, to Douala in Cameroon.

— When it starts The first flight is scheduled for Wednesday 23 September 2026. Services then run on Mondays and Wednesdays.

— The schedule Flights leave Enugu at 12:45 p.m. West Africa time and land in Douala an hour later.

— The aircraft BusinessDay reports the airline will use a 76-seat Embraer E170 regional jet on the route.

— The catch No fares have been reported, and the news site Camer.be said Cameroon’s aviation regulator had not confirmed its approvals.

— Why it matters It would give southeastern Nigeria a direct air link to Douala, Cameroon’s commercial capital, without changing planes in Lagos.

A young airline owned by a Nigerian state government is about to fly abroad for the first time. Its target is Douala, the port city that drives Cameroon’s economy.

A JetBlue Embraer 190 takes off from Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport in July 2016. Enugu Air flies Embraer jets. File photograph. (Photo: PlanespotterA320, CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

The Enugu Air Douala service is due to take off on Wednesday 23 September 2026. It will be the first international route for Enugu Air, an airline owned by the government of Enugu State in southeastern Nigeria.

The flights will link Enugu with Douala, the port city that serves as Cameroon’s commercial capital. Nigerian outlets including BusinessDay, Premium Times and the Nigerian Tribune reported the plan on 20 and 21 September.

For a region whose travellers usually route through Lagos or Abuja, it means a one-hour hop to a neighbouring country. The first flight has not yet flown.

Two flights a week, one hour each way

The service will run twice a week, on Mondays and Wednesdays. After the opening Wednesday flight, the first Monday rotation falls on 28 September 2026.

Flights leave Akanu Ibiam International Airport in Enugu at 12:45 p.m. West Africa time. They reach Douala International Airport at 1:45 p.m., as both countries share that zone.

The Tribune and Premium Times carried the same timetable. The return leaves Douala at 2:30 p.m. and lands in Enugu at 3:30 p.m.

BusinessDay reports the airline will fly a 76-seat Embraer E170, a Brazilian-built regional jet. Aviation Metric, a trade site, and Camer.be, a Brussels-based Cameroonian diaspora news site, also name the E170.

From a virtual carrier to an international route

Enugu Air is barely 14 months old. It began flying on 7 July 2025, at first as a virtual carrier using the operating licence of another Nigerian airline, XEJet.

On 10 March 2026 the Nigeria Civil Aviation Authority, the national regulator, presented Enugu Air with its own air operator certificate. That document allows an airline to run scheduled flights in its own name.

The regulator’s director general, Captain Chris Najomo, noted the airline had started with six aircraft, Vanguard reported that day. Enugu State’s transport commissioner, Obi Ozor, promised regional flights before the end of 2026.

The African Airlines Association, the continent’s airline trade body, admitted Enugu Air as its 50th member. It announced the membership in Nairobi on Wednesday 19 August 2026.

Mount Cameroon at dusk, seen from Douala across a railway yard. File photograph. (Photo: Edouard Tamba, CC0 via Wikimedia Commons)

Why Douala

Douala is not Cameroon’s political capital; that is Yaoundé. It is, however, the country’s largest city and its main seaport and business centre.

Enugu is the main city of Nigeria’s southeast, a region with strong trading links to Cameroon. Until now, flying from there to Douala meant changing planes in Lagos or Abuja.

Ugonna Agubuokwu, Enugu Air’s chief operating officer, framed the route in those terms, as quoted by BusinessDay. “This is more than the introduction of a new route; it is about creating stronger connections between Nigeria and Cameroon …”

He went on to promise “making regional travel more accessible, convenient, and seamless for our passengers.”

The airline also expects passengers from Lagos and Abuja, Nigeria’s two busiest air markets, to connect through Enugu. Enugu Air already flies domestic routes that include Lagos, Abuja, Port Harcourt and Kano.

The competition in the air

Enugu Air will not be alone on the corridor. Air Peace, a privately owned Lagos airline, flew its first Lagos to Douala to Libreville service on 2 August 2026, BusinessDay reported.

“Previously, Air Peace was the only airline operating a direct route between Nigeria and Cameroon,” the Tribune wrote. Camer.be reports that another Nigerian carrier, NG Eagle, has also served Cameroon since late 2025.

The Tribune adds that United Nigeria Airlines, a private Nigerian carrier, plans to enter the Cameroon market. Douala and Libreville are among its intended destinations.

Camair-Co, Cameroon’s state airline, had planned to resume flights to Lagos after a three-year gap. Camer.be reported that the timetable has slipped.

What travellers should know

No fares for the Enugu Air Douala flights have been reported. The airline’s website lists Douala as a new, non-stop route and invites bookings.

Camer.be, writing on 15 September, said the Cameroon Civil Aviation Authority had not yet confirmed issuing the certificates Enugu Air needs. It said neither the airline nor the regulator had answered its questions by then.

Travellers also need the usual documents. Nigerians and Cameroonians should check visa and passport rules with the Cameroonian and Nigerian authorities before booking.

What comes next

In December 2025, presenting his 2026 budget, Enugu State’s governor Peter Mbah pledged 14 more aircraft for the airline. That would take the fleet to 20, Arise News reported.

The pace of that expansion will shape how quickly more foreign routes follow the Enugu Air Douala launch.

For now, the test is simpler. Filling a 76-seat jet twice a week will show whether the trading ties between southeastern Nigeria and Douala translate into paying passengers.

More: Africa coverage, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

When do Enugu Air Douala flights start?

The first flight is scheduled for Wednesday 23 September 2026, according to BusinessDay, Premium Times and the Nigerian Tribune. After that, the service runs twice a week, on Mondays and Wednesdays. The first Monday flight would be on 28 September 2026.

What are the flight times and how long is the trip?

Flights leave Enugu at 12:45 p.m. and arrive in Douala at 1:45 p.m. The return leaves Douala at 2:30 p.m. and reaches Enugu at 3:30 p.m. Nigeria and Cameroon are both on West Africa time, so each leg is scheduled at about one hour.

What aircraft will Enugu Air use?

BusinessDay reports a 76-seat Embraer E170, a regional jet made in Brazil. Enugu Air’s fleet is made up of Embraer E170, E190 and E195 jets, according to the Enugu State government.

Who owns Enugu Air?

The airline is owned by the government of Enugu State, one of Nigeria’s 36 states. It began flying in July 2025 and received its own air operator certificate from the Nigeria Civil Aviation Authority on 10 March 2026.

World.title: Novo Nordisk Shares Sink Nearly 8% After Wegovy Maker’s 2030 Plan Disappoints
World.content:
Denmark · Markets

Key Facts — What happened Novo Nordisk shares closed 7.7% lower in Copenhagen on 21 September 2026, after the company’s strategy day in London.

— What Novo promised More than five multi-blockbuster launches by 2030 and over 150 billion Danish kroner (about US$23.1 billion) of risk-adjusted pipeline sales in 2035.

— The catch Revenue growth to 2030 is pitched “in line with industry peers”, which one Danish strategist called well below market assumptions.

— The patent clock US protection for semaglutide, the ingredient in Ozempic and Wegovy, expires in 2032, according to Quartz.

— Who leads Novo Mike Doustdar, chief executive since 7 August 2025, previously ran the company’s business outside the United States.

The Danish maker of Ozempic and Wegovy promised a wave of new drugs but only average growth to 2030. Investors sold the stock hard.

A Novo Nordisk office building and company sign in Denmark. File photograph (Photo: Rio Times media library)

Novo Nordisk shares fell 7.7% in Copenhagen on Monday 21 September 2026, after the Danish drugmaker set out its 2030 plans. Investors had hoped for a bold growth story from the maker of Ozempic and Wegovy, and did not get one.

The company adopted “Novo” as its everyday brand name on 14 September 2026, STAT and UPI reported. Its legal name remains Novo Nordisk, according to UPI.

Novo made its pitch at a Capital Markets Day in London, a strategy briefing for investors and analysts. The headline promise was more than five new “multi-blockbusters” by 2030, meaning drugs with the potential for very large annual sales.

The problem lay elsewhere in the same announcement. Novo said its revenue should grow only in line with its large rivals until the end of the decade.

What Novo promised in London

The company said its drug pipeline should deliver more than 150 billion Danish kroner (about US$23.1 billion) of risk-adjusted sales in 2035. Risk-adjusted means each drug’s potential sales are discounted for the chance that it fails in trials.

It plans at least five final-stage, or Phase 3, trial programmes in obesity and diabetes, and at least five in other diseases. It also aims to reach more than 60 million patients worldwide by 2030.

On manufacturing, Novo wants enough capacity to serve ten times more people with obesity on GLP-1 pills. GLP-1 drugs mimic a gut hormone that curbs appetite and helps control blood sugar.

Why investors sold the stock

The sticking point was growth. Novo said revenue from 2026 to 2030 should grow at a compound annual rate “in line with industry peers”.

Its list of peers names 14 large drugmakers, including Eli Lilly, AstraZeneca, Pfizer, Novartis and Roche. It also promised a “broadly stable” operating margin and an “attractive” dividend per share.

For a company long priced as a growth leader, matching the average was a hard sell. Jacob Pedersen is an investment strategist at Middelfart Sparekasse, a Danish savings bank.

He told CNBC that benchmarking against a wide peer group signals ambition well below what the market long expected of Novo. “The investors, they are very particular in what they want from Novo, and this doesn’t add up to it,” he said.

Sydbank analyst Søren Løntoft Hansen called convincing the market “a very tough task”, the Invezz news site reported. He blamed the competition.

Pedersen also saw some comfort, the Danish news agency Ritzau reported. A broadly unchanged profit margin should dampen nervousness about significant earnings declines, he said.

How the trading session unfolded

Trade date: Monday 21 September 2026. Novo’s B shares closed at 260.00 kroner (about US$39.96) on Nasdaq Copenhagen, down 7.7% from Friday’s 281.55 kroner (about US$43.27).

They touched a low of 257.90 kroner (about US$39.64), 8.4% below Friday’s close, according to RT exchange data. Quartz had reported the fall pared to 5.4% by midday, so the selling deepened in the afternoon.

About 13.9 million shares changed hands, against 9.3 million on Friday. In New York, Novo’s dollar-denominated American depositary receipts closed 8.0% lower at US$39.80, per RT.

Conversions use a rate of 6.5061 Danish kroner to the US dollar, Danmarks Nationalbank’s reference rate for 21 September 2026.

Boxes of Novo Nordisk’s Ozempic (semaglutide) and Eli Lilly’s Mounjaro (tirzepatide), rival injections. File photograph

The patent clock behind the caution

Behind the caution sits semaglutide, the active ingredient in Ozempic for diabetes and Wegovy for weight loss. Novo’s US patent protection on the molecule expires in 2032, according to Quartz and Invezz.

Doustdar called the coming loss of exclusivity the “elephant in the room”, the business site Quartz reported. Novo plans to emerge from it “as a bigger company than we are today,” Doustdar told investors.

He added that it would be “a much more diversified version of it”. In other words, Novo wants far more of its income to come from drugs other than semaglutide.

Doustdar said “almost every other single pharma company” is trying to compete in the obesity market Novo created, according to Invezz. Generic makers are also circling.

In South Africa, India’s Sun Pharma won regulatory approval for a generic semaglutide in July 2026, Business Standard reported. The biggest rival remains Eli Lilly, the American maker of the Mounjaro and Zepbound injections.

In the second quarter, Lilly held about 61% of the obesity-drug market and Novo 39%, per CNBC figures cited by Quartz.

Who is running Novo Nordisk

Maziar Mike Doustdar has been president and chief executive since 7 August 2025. He previously ran International Operations, the division covering Novo’s sales outside the United States.

He succeeded Lars Fruergaard Jørgensen. Monday’s London briefing put his strategy in front of investors in full.

Where the stock stands now

Monday’s close left the B shares about 20% below their last close of 2025, on 30 December, according to RT prices. The stock sits roughly 75% below its record close, set on 25 June 2024.

Novo stressed that its 2030 ambitions start from a 2026 baseline. The release says they “are inherently uncertain and do not constitute Novo’s financial outlook or guidance”.

For now, the market has delivered its verdict on the London pitch. Novo Nordisk shares lost 7.7% in a single session.

More: Europe markets coverage, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did Novo Nordisk shares fall on 21 September 2026?

At its Capital Markets Day in London, Novo said revenue should grow from 2026 to 2030 only in line with 14 large drugmakers, including Eli Lilly and Pfizer. Danish analysts quoted by CNBC and Invezz said the plan fell short of what investors wanted. The B shares closed 7.7% lower in Copenhagen, according to RT exchange data.

What did Novo Nordisk promise?

More than five multi-blockbuster drug launches by 2030 and more than 150 billion Danish kroner (about US$23.1 billion) of risk-adjusted pipeline sales in 2035. It also targets more than 60 million patients by 2030, a stable operating margin and an attractive dividend. It said these ambitions are not financial guidance.

What is semaglutide and why does its patent matter?

Semaglutide is the active ingredient in Ozempic, a diabetes drug, and Wegovy, a weight-loss drug. It mimics a gut hormone that curbs appetite. Its US patent protection expires in 2032, according to Quartz. After that, cheaper generic copies can compete, so Novo needs new drugs to replace the income.

Sources: Novo Nordisk company announcement on its Capital Markets Day ambitions, Quartz, via Yahoo Finance, on the share reaction and Doustdar’s remarks, Invezz on analyst reaction, Investing.com on the peer group and guidance caveat, Novo Nordisk on Doustdar’s appointment, Business Standard on Sun Pharma’s South African approval, Danmarks Nationalbank exchange rates, RT end-of-day exchange data

World.title: Dangote Refinery IPO Not Filed in Kenya, Securities Regulator Warns Investors
World.content:
Kenya · Nigeria · Capital Markets

Key Facts — What happened Kenya’s Capital Markets Authority said on 21 September 2026 that the Nigerian refinery offer was never submitted for its approval.

— Why it matters Kenyans are being courted by apps and agents, and the Kenyan regulator has not vetted the prospectus.

— The offer 4.1 billion shares at 525 naira (about US$0.39) each, open from 14 September to 13 October 2026.

— The catch Nigeria’s regulator says only authorised channels may take money; the offer’s website lists them, including channels for international investors.

— Who is promoting it Some promoters belong to the offer’s own selling syndicate, such as the Lagos broker Meristem.

— What comes next Kenya’s notice names no firm, no charges have been reported, and the offer closes on 13 October 2026.

Africa’s largest share sale is being sold far beyond Nigeria. Kenya’s watchdog says the offer was never submitted to it and wants investors to check who is selling.

Nairobi, Kenya’s capital, in a file photograph. (Photo: Antony Trivet, CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

The Dangote refinery IPO, or initial public offering, is being pitched to Kenyans, but Kenya’s regulator has not vetted it. On Monday 21 September 2026, the Capital Markets Authority, Kenya’s securities regulator, said the Nigerian share sale was never filed with it.

The offer, it said, “is regulated in Nigeria and has not been submitted for consideration and approval by CMA” under Kenyan law. The Kenya Times and People Daily reported the wording.

The notice matters because the sale is being marketed across Africa, often through phone apps. Kenyans who want in are being told to check who they hand their money to.

What the Kenyan regulator said

The authority posted the notice on X, according to Kenyan outlets. It urged the public to check the authenticity and source of any prospectus or offering document before sending money, Pulse Kenya reported.

It also told investors to use licensed intermediaries only, and to check their status on its official licence register. The Star said the regulator cautioned against schemes purporting to offer Kenyans the shares.

The notice, as reported, names no firm or platform. No Kenyan authority has accused anyone of wrongdoing over the offer, and no charges have been reported.

The offer itself is legal in Nigeria

The company selling shares is Dangote Petroleum Refinery and Petrochemicals, which runs Africa’s largest oil refinery at Lekki, near Lagos. It is controlled by the Dangote Group, founded by the Nigerian industrialist Aliko Dangote.

Its official offer website lists 4.1 billion shares at 525 naira (about US$0.39) each. The offer opened on Monday 14 September 2026 and closes on 13 October 2026.

Reuters valued the whole sale at 2.15 trillion naira (about US$1.6 billion) if fully taken up. The minimum purchase is 10 shares, or 5,250 naira (about US$3.95).

Conversions here use a rate of 1,329.30 to the US dollar, the Central Bank of Nigeria’s central rate on 21 September 2026. Nigeria’s Securities and Exchange Commission approved the offer.

The Dangote refinery site at Lekki, Lagos State, Nigeria, during land reclamation work, in a file photograph. (Photo: GodwinPaya, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.)

Who is allowed to take the money

Nigeria’s Securities and Exchange Commission warned on the opening day that investors should use only approved channels. It said only entities specifically authorised to take part in the offer may receive applications or money from investors, Nairametrics reported.

The offer website lists those channels: banks, stockbrokers, fintech apps and a separate group for international investors. That group includes Stanbic IBTC, FSDH, Bamboo, Paga and Payaza.

Eligibility, the website says, is governed by the prospectus. Aliko Dangote made the pan-African pitch himself at the signing ceremony on 7 September 2026.

“There is no segregation on who can own these shares. We want every human being living on the continent to be part of this action,” he said, according to Premium Times.

The brokers doing the selling

A Techpoint Africa guide of 10 September 2026, with a section marked as promoted, recommends the Lagos group Meristem. Meristem is itself part of the selling syndicate.

The official website lists Meristem Capital among the 26 issuing houses that manage the sale. Its sister firm, Meristem Stockbrokers, is a receiving agent and runs the Meritrade subscription app.

The same broker is named as sponsor of two fintech channels, Cowrywise and Paystro. None of this is improper, but it makes Meristem a seller, not a neutral guide.

Kenya, Rwanda and the regional pull

Rwanda’s regulator is taking a different line. Its Capital Market Authority said on 17 September 2026 that it was helping Rwandan investors take part, TheCable reported.

It directed them to register interest through United Capital Financial Services Rwanda. It stressed that registering is not a subscription and does not guarantee shares.

In Nairobi, the chief executive of the Nairobi Securities Exchange, Frank Mwiti, wants East African investors in the offer, TechCabal reported. A later listing in Kenya is his longer goal.

Dangote’s Kenyan ties go beyond shares. President William Ruto met him in New York on 21 September 2026, on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly.

They discussed financing for a planned Dangote refinery at Lamu, on Kenya’s coast, Capital FM reported. Groundbreaking is scheduled for Wednesday 30 September 2026.

What investors should watch

For Kenyans, the practical question is the route, not the Dangote refinery IPO itself. Buying through an approved Nigerian channel is different from answering an advert or a WhatsApp message.

As reported, the Kenyan notice does not bar Kenyans from buying. It says the offer was not submitted in Kenya, so the Kenyan regulator has not reviewed its prospectus.

The subscription window closes on 13 October 2026. Shares are then allotted through the registrar, Coronation Registrars, which Nairametrics lists among the offer’s advisers.

More: Africa coverage, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can Kenyans buy shares in the Dangote refinery IPO?

The Kenyan notice, as reported, does not bar them. Kenya’s Capital Markets Authority said on 21 September 2026 that the offer is regulated in Nigeria and was never submitted to it for approval. The official offer website lists channels for international investors and says eligibility is set by the prospectus. Kenyans are urged to use licensed firms and verify any document.

How much does the minimum purchase cost?

The minimum is 10 shares at 525 naira each, or 5,250 naira (about US$3.95). The offer runs from 14 September 2026 to 13 October 2026, according to the company’s official offer website.

Who is Meristem?

Meristem is a Lagos financial group. Meristem Capital is one of the issuing houses managing the sale, and Meristem Stockbrokers is a receiving agent that runs the Meritrade app. That makes it part of the selling syndicate.

Has anyone been charged with fraud over the offer?

No charges have been reported. Regulators in Nigeria and Kenya have issued general warnings about unofficial sellers, but neither has publicly named a firm.

World.title: Namibia Roads Company Probes US$1.8 Million Fuel Payments After Deliveries Fell Short
World.content:
Namibia · Governance

Key Facts — What happened The board of the Roads Contractor Company, Namibia’s state road builder, announced an internal fuel-payments investigation on 18 September 2026.

— How much The company paid N$30 million (about US$1.8 million) for fuel; N$17 million (about US$1 million) of it never arrived, The Namibian reported.

— Who the suppliers are Oshali Fuel Centre CC, whose owner faces charges in another case, and Eco Fuel Investment CC, reportedly tied to fugitive Victor Malima.

— The catch The Anti-Corruption Commission says it is not investigating this matter, and nobody has been charged over the road company’s payments.

— What the chief executive says Interim chief executive Dasius Nelumbu told The Namibian the matter is before court; the company itself denied opening a case.

— What comes next The board has set no public deadline; Oshali’s owner is due back in court in the Namcor case on 28 October 2026.

Namibia’s state road builder paid two suppliers for fuel that mostly never arrived. One is owned by a man facing charges in a separate state fuel-graft case; the other is linked in press reports to a fugitive.

Central Windhoek, the Namibian capital, in a file photograph. (Photo: Rio Times media library)

A Namibia roads company owned by the state paid N$30 million (about US$1.8 million) for fuel between 2023 and 2025. Fuel worth N$17 million (about US$1 million) never arrived, according to documents reported by the Windhoek daily The Namibian.

The company is the Roads Contractor Company, or RCC, a government-owned builder that spent 2017 to 2023 facing liquidation. Its board said on Friday 18 September 2026 that it had opened an internal investigation.

Where the money went

Most of the money went to Oshali Fuel Centre CC, a fuel supplier. The RCC paid it N$27 million (about US$1.7 million) for deliveries to road sites around the country.

Conversions use a rate of about 16.26 Namibian dollars to the US dollar, from European Central Bank data on 21 September 2026. The Namibian dollar is pegged one-to-one to the South African rand.

An RCC reconciliation found fuel worth N$14 million (about US$860,000) was never delivered. The Namibian quoted a demand letter from the RCC chief executive to Oshali, dated 18 February.

The first payment, N$17.5 million (about US$1.1 million), went out on 21 September 2023 for the Engoyi project site. The last listed payment, N$2.7 million (about US$166,000), followed on 30 April 2025.

Oshali delivered 680,561 litres of the nearly 1.4 million litres ordered, the chief executive wrote. That is less than half.

The Namibian reported that some sites had not begun operating when the fuel was paid for. It also reported that one N$2.7 million payment in April 2024 produced no fuel at all.

The remaining N$3 million (about US$185,000) concerns a fuel tender won by Eco Fuel Investment CC. The Namibian reported that the company did not supply fuel for a road project near Henties Bay in 2023.

The names behind the suppliers

Oshali’s sole member is a businessman named Handjene. In April 2026 he and his company were added as accused in the Namcor case, a major fuel-fraud prosecution.

Namcor is the National Petroleum Corporation of Namibia, the state fuel company. The Namibian says the case involves more than N$380 million (about US$23 million) in unpaid debts.

Handjene faces charges of theft, money laundering and receiving gratification under the Anti-Corruption Act, the news site Informanté reported. He was released on bail of N$50,000 (about US$3,100).

His case returns to the Windhoek Magistrate’s Court on 28 October 2026. The court is awaiting a decision from the prosecutor-general, Namibia’s chief state prosecutor.

Those charges concern Namcor, not the RCC. The Namibian could not reach Handjene for comment, and emails to his company bounced back.

Eco Fuel Investment CC has been linked by The Namibian to Victor Malima, a businessman sought in the Namcor inquiry. A warrant for his arrest was issued in July 2025.

The Namibian Sun reported that he left Namibia through the Wenela border post at Katima Mulilo on 11 July 2025. He is believed to have gone to Angola.

No arrest has been reported, and no comment from Malima on the RCC payments has been reported.

In February 2025 an Eco Fuel spokesperson denied wrongdoing. She told The Namibian the company was not involved in its clients’ procurement.

Road crews resurfacing a highway, file photograph. (Photo: Grand Canyon NPS, CC BY 2.0, via Flickr)

What the chief executive and the board say

The Namibian reported that the payments were personally approved by interim chief executive Dasius Nelumbu. In March 2025 the board said he took office in March 2024, after the first payments had been made.

Asked about the payments on Wednesday 16 September 2026, Nelumbu pointed to the courts.

He told the newspaper the matter “is before court and is therefore subject to the principle of res sub judice”. Sub judice is the rule against discussing cases still before a judge.

The RCC, however, denied opening a case, and the newspaper’s sources said none had been registered. They said talks over repayment were continuing.

In a 3 March proposal, Handjene offered to set aside 20 cents for every litre ordered toward the balance. He would do so in partnership with another fuel company, Vanco Energy CC.

In his February letter, Nelumbu threatened to sue if Oshali did not pay. He wrote that “the RCC’s legal department has instructions to institute legal proceedings against your company”.

Board chairperson Lea Namoloh said the board was “fully seized with this matter”. The inquiry will examine the procurement processes followed and any legal proceedings already under way.

“Should the investigation confirm misconduct, the board will act firmly to hold those responsible accountable,” she said. The board has announced no timeline and has not named anyone under review.

No criminal inquiry into the RCC payments

The Anti-Corruption Commission, Namibia’s graft investigator, says it is not investigating. “The Anti-Corruption Commission is not investigating this matter,” spokesperson Marina Matundu told The Namibian last week.

Nobody has been charged over the RCC’s fuel payments. No authority has found that Nelumbu or anyone else at the company broke the law.

In February 2025 The Namibian reported an anti-corruption inquiry into Nelumbu over three tenders. One was a N$1.5 million (about US$92,000) fuel purchase from Eco Fuel.

Nelumbu denied wrongdoing at the time. The board publicly backed him and said it would await the outcome, which has not been reported.

Why it matters beyond Namibia

The Namibian reported in February 2025 that the RCC had relied heavily on government bailouts, including to pay salaries. Its debts reached about N$900 million (about US$55 million) before the liquidation threat lifted, The Namibian reported.

For a country courting investors for offshore energy and green hydrogen, repeated disputes over fuel payments at state firms carry a cost. The internal probe at this Namibia roads company is the next test of whether procurement controls hold.

More: Africa coverage, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Roads Contractor Company?

The Roads Contractor Company, or RCC, is a state-owned civil engineering company that builds and maintains roads in Namibia. It faced liquidation between 2017 and 2023 because of debts of about N$900 million (about US$55 million). The Namibian has reported that it relied heavily on government bailouts, including to pay salaries.

How much fuel did the RCC pay for and not receive?

The Namibian reported that the RCC paid N$30 million (about US$1.8 million) to two suppliers between 2023 and 2025. Fuel worth N$17 million (about US$1 million) was never delivered. Most of the shortfall, N$14 million (about US$860,000), involves Oshali Fuel Centre CC.

Has anyone been charged over the Namibia roads company fuel payments?

No. The Anti-Corruption Commission told The Namibian it is not investigating the matter, and the RCC board’s review is internal. Oshali’s owner faces separate charges in the Namcor fuel case, which awaits a prosecution decision. Victor Malima, linked to the second supplier, is sought on a July 2025 arrest warrant in the Namcor inquiry.

World.title: Chad Foreign Minister Replaced by Former Intelligence Chief Ahmat Kogri
World.content:
Chad · Politics

Key Facts — What happened A decree signed on 21 September 2026 named General Ahmat Kogri as Chad’s foreign minister, replacing Abdoulaye Sabre Fadoul.

— Who he is A former head of ANSE, Chad’s state security and intelligence agency, and a presidential adviser on foreign affairs since July 2025.

— His full title Minister of state, minister of foreign affairs, African integration and Chadians abroad, under decree No. 2201.

— The catch The decree gives no reason for Fadoul’s removal, Tchadinfos reported.

— The back story Fadoul told senators in June that diplomats’ living and pay conditions would change only when the budget law outweighed the finance minister.

— Why it matters A security insider takes over diplomacy as Chad rebuilds ties with France after ending their defence pact in 2024.

President Mahamat Idriss Déby Itno has handed his country’s diplomacy to a long-time security insider. The outgoing minister had openly criticised the finance minister in June.

Mahamat Idriss Déby Itno, now Chad’s president, casts a ballot in a file photograph.
