World.title: UN Chief Condemns Mladic Glorification in Meeting with Bosnian Leader
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Bos/Hrv/Srp

UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres on Monday condemned the ongoing glorification of the late convicted Bosnian Serb war criminal Ratko Mladic during a meeting in New York with Denis Becirovic, chair of Bosnia’s three-member state presidency.

The encounter took place at the UN’s New York headquarters to discuss international law, regional stability and Bosnia’s current challenges. Guterres targeted recent revisionist actions and the denial of genocide in Bosnia, describing them as direct violations of international legal and civilisational norms.

According to the statement released afterwards, the conversation focused on implementation of the UN General Assembly’s Srebrenica Genocide Resolution, adopted in 2024, and the need to combat historical revisionism in the region.

“The UN maintains an unyielding stance against historical revisionism and the glorification of war criminals, which continues to jeopardise reconciliation efforts,” Guterres stated. “International law and civilisational standards must be respected to maintain regional stability.”

Becirovic invited Guterres to visit Sarajevo and the Srebrenica Memorial Centre in the future. He emphasised the importance of establishing permanent international outreach educational programmes on the 1995 genocide to prevent future historical revisionism and protect the historical truth established by international courts.

Mladic’s funeral in Belgrade on September 7 was attended by ministers and high officials both from Serbia and Bosnia’s Serb-led entity, Republika Srpska and was organised with military honours.

EU officials have condemned the government of Serbia – an EU membership candidate state – over the glorification of Mladic, saying it was incompatible with the bloc’s values.

World.title: Across Croatia, Protesters Demand Tougher Response to Violence Against Women
World.content:
Women’s organisations staged symbolic public protests in 17 towns and cities across Croatia on Monday, titled “While the Minister Sheds Light, Women Remain in the Dark” – a slogan pouring scorn on a comment made by Family and Social Policy Minister Alen Ruzic after a woman’s murder.

The groups’ demands include moving violence against women from the realm of misdemeanours into the criminal justice sphere.

“We demand a specific law against all forms of gender-based violence,” the organisations and initiatives said ahead of the National Day Against Violence Against Women, observed on September 22.

They also called for a unified, mandatory and standardized assessment of the risk of recurring violence and femicide, as well as mandatory specialized training for everyone involved in risk assessment and decisions concerning the protection of women.

World.title: Serbia ‘Still Ignoring’ UN Court Monitor over Vojislav Seselj Case
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Bos/Hrv/Srp



Vojislav Seselj. Photo: EPA/KOCA SULEJMANOVIC.

Monitor Dagmara Albrecht told the UN’s International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals in her latest report that she has not received any new information from the Serbian authorities about the status of the contempt-of-court case against Serbian Radical Party leader Vojislav Seselj and four of his party members.

The International Residual Mechanism transferred the contempt-of-court case against Seselj and his followers to Serbia in 2024, saying that conditions were adequate for it to be processed there, and appointed Albrecht to monitor progress.

But since then, Serbia has been ignoring questions about the status of the case, according to Albrecht. In her latest report, she said that since her previous report in May, she had “received no response to my numerous inquiries addressed to the Ministry of Justice of Serbia”.

In the May report, she also said that although the Ministry of Justice had promised to provide her with information, her emails went unanswered.

Her latest report suggests the case may not have moved forward. “Based on information previously received, the Seselj et al. case is still awaiting a preliminary opinion of the Ministry of Justice,” she added.

The case against Seselj and his followers – Miljan Damjanovic, Miroljub Ignjatovic, Ljiljana Mihajlovic, and Ognjen Mihajlovic – relates to his 15-year trial in The Hague for wartime crimes.

The indictment charges them with having “knowingly and wilfully interfered with the administration of justice; disclosed information in violation of court orders, including orders for the protection of witnesses; and failed to comply, without just excuse, with court orders to cease and desist from the publication of confidential information”.

Seselj already has a conviction for inciting crimes with his wartime speeches. The UN war crimes tribunal sentenced him to ten years in prison in April 2018. He did not serve any jail time, however, because of the time he had spent in custody prior to the verdict.

The Serbian Radical Party leader has been charged with contempt of court several times by the Hague-based tribunal. In 2011, he was convicted of revealing information about witnesses in a book he authored.

In 2012, Seselj and Radical Party colleagues Vjerica Radeta and Petar Jojic were also charged with pressurising witnesses in his trial using threats, blackmail and bribes to change their statements or not testify. This case is still ongoing in The Hague after the tribunal declined to transfer these proceedings to Serbia.

World.title: Romania Probes Far-Right Former Presidential Candidate Georgescu for Fraud
World.content:
Calin Georgescu at the Municipal Court in Bucharest, December 2025. Photo: EPA/ROBERT GHEMENT.

Romanian police on Monday detained far-right politician Calin Georgescu and anti-fraud investigators searched his home and other locations as part of an investigation in which he faces charges of defrauding a Romanian businessman of more than 1 million euros, according to judicial authorities.

“We carried out five residential searches … in a case in which three people acted with the aim of obtaining undue financial benefits,” said Romania’s Directorate for Investigating Organised Crime and Terrorism, DIICOT.

Prosecutors allege that from September 2021, a group allegedly led by Georgescu convinced the businessman that he could obtain a loan of 6 million euros in exchange for providing a guarantee. The victim then allegedly transferred some 1 million euros.

Subsequently, the suspects allegedly told him that the loan could be increased to 15 million euro, but an additional guarantee was required, after which the businessman allegedly transferred another 100,000 euros. The promised loan never materialised.

Georgescu has not issued any statement on this issue but he has previously claimed he was being investigated by the authorities because of his political activities.

His political ally, George Simion, who heads the far-right Alliance for the Unity of Romanians, AUR, condemned the move. “Any of us could be next. Stop the abuses! Romania is a dictatorship!” he wrote on Facebook.

Hundreds of Georgescu’s supporters gathered outside DIICOT headquarters, where he and other people were to arrive for questioning. Authorities have installed protective barriers and deployed gendarmerie units in the area.

This would be the third criminal case against Georgescu. He is already under investigation for endorsing fascist ideas in interviews, online posts and public appearances and also faces trial for complicity to undermine the constitutional order, spreading false information and founding an anti-Semitic organisation.

He denies all the charges.

After he unexpectedly won the first round of the Romanian presidential elections in November 2024, the Constitutional Court ordered a rerun of the vote, citing alleged manipulation of public opinion by a “foreign state”, likely referring to Russia.

Georgescu was banned from participating in the re-run in May 2025, which was ultimately won by centrist Nicusor Dan.

World.title: In Montenegro, AI is Helping with Schoolwork, But What Are the Rules?
World.content:
The Ministry of Education, Science, and Innovation told BIRN that currently AI is primarily used as a supplementary tool for lesson planning, creating materials, and clarifying content.

“At the same time, organised activities are being carried out that demonstrate that its application is no longer solely the result of individual teacher initiatives,” the ministry said. “We anticipate the alignment and enrichment of the curriculum, the digitisation of teaching and learning processes and the development of procedures for using artificial intelligence in education.”

Sara Scepanovic, who teaches Montenegrin language and literature, said schoolchildren are relying more and more on AI, even if they do not fully understand how it works.

“They use AI in particular to create presentations that look very polished and professional at first glance. However, the information is often unverified or contains errors, and this is precisely where it becomes evident that the student blindly trusted what the AI ​​offered,” Scepanovic told BIRN.

She said she also recognises AI use based on the language used.

“Words that students of that age wouldn’t normally use will appear, complex expressions or Croatianisms that aren’t a part of their everyday speech,” Scepanovic said. “I believe teachers know their students the best – we know their way of thinking, their vocabulary, and their capabilities. That’s why we can quickly sense when a text didn’t originate from their own minds.”

Antunovic, however, said teachers struggle to detect when AI has been used.

“There are other AI tools capable of taking AI-generated text and making it appear as though it were written by a real person,” he said. “Most teachers have started using AI detectors on assignments, yet even when they do, they fail to detect the AI-generated text.”

In Podgorica, 15-year-old Hana told BIRN: “When I don’t understand something, it’s easier and faster to ask ChatGPT than to seek help from others. I’ve asked AI to summarise books from the curriculum a few times because I don’t like reading.”

“Most students in my class use AI for homework, for additional explanations, and even to draft essays for their native language class.”

Some EU countries have already introduced rules on AI to prevent cheating within the education system.

In France, using AI to complete a school assignment without the teacher’s permission is considered cheating, while Denmark has banned the use of AI during exams and is introducing partially analog exams to accurately assess what a student truly knows.

At the same time, both countries are developing models that utilise AI as an educational tool.

Controlled learning assistance

World.title: In Moldova’s Minority-Populated South, Redrawing Municipalities is a Tricky Task
World.content:
Gagauzia exists because Moldova once solved a much more serious dispute over territory through compromise.

During the collapse of the Soviet Union, fears over language policy, Moldovan nationalism and possible reunification with Romania contributed to a separatist movement among the Gagauz, a Turkic-speaking and predominantly Orthodox Christian people concentrated in the country’s south. Gagauz leaders proclaimed a republic in 1990.

Unlike the conflict in Transnistria, the confrontation did not turn into full-scale war. A political settlement followed, and in 1994 Moldova established Gagauzia as an autonomous territorial unit .

Gagauzia is part of Moldova but has its own assembly and executive institutions under the autonomy settlement. Thirty years later, those institutions are visible throughout Comrat. Gagauz and Moldovan flags fly together and the assembly identifies itself prominently in the Gagauz language, though Russian remains pervasive in shops, s and conversation.

But the region’s autonomous institutions now create obstacles to the ongoing administrative reform across the country.

In August, Secretary-General of the Government Alexei Buzu said amalgamation in Gagauzia was effectively blocked because changes there must pass through the assembly, whose mandate has expired amid an institutional and electoral dispute . Elsewhere in Moldova, completed amalgamation proposals can move on to the central authorities.

In Gagauzia, the assembly’s leadership has challenged Buzu’s account of the dispute, illustrating the extent to which an ostensibly technical reform has already become politically contested.

Though Gagauzia is often understood from the outside through the lens of Russian influence, this situation is a reminder that the region’s identity and relationship with Chisinau is also governed through institutions that were created to protect a minority whose language, territory and political representation became intertwined during Moldova’s transition to independence.

Twenty kilometres south of Comrat, the Gagauz village of Besalma provides some historical context. Its National Gagauz History and Ethnographic Museum, founded by writer, filmmaker and cultural figure Dmitrii Kara Coban, documents successive efforts to preserve Gagauz culture under different political systems; Soviet-era Gagauz publications in Cyrillic sit alongside more recent material in Latin script. The museum also features traditional clothing, photographs and records of village life.

The collection makes clear that Gagauzia’s institutions emerged from a history in which cultural survival and territorial representation became closely connected.

Southeast of Besalma in Ceadir-Lunga, Gagauzia’s second biggest city, different cultural layers remain visible in the streetscape. Orthodox churches coexist with Soviet memorials, while Russian, Romanian and Gagauz occupy different parts of public life. Yet beyond such symbols, the problems that prompted Moldova’s administrative reform process are looming: ageing infrastructure, small administrations and the high cost of providing services to shrinking communities.

The government says eight out of ten Moldovan households without access to water or sanitation are located in settlements administered by mayoralties serving fewer than 3,000 people.

That is the less ideological side of the debate. Administrative fragmentation affects whether a municipality can hire specialists, prepare investment projects, maintain infrastructure or manage a water system.

Bespoke solutions for Moldova’s Bulgarians

World.title: New Law for Foreign Workers in Croatia Faces Criticism
World.content:
September the 22nd, 2026 – A new law facing foreign workers in Croatia as of 2027 is already causing a stir and facing criticism from migration experts.

You go to another country, get a job, learn around thirty basic phrases of its language and that is, according to the law, enough to be considered “integrated.” Most would argue that this statement is so ridiculous that it’s difficult to quantify. Poslovni reports that the aforementioned notion is all that will be required of foreign workers in Croatia as of 2027. They will have to prove knowledge of the Croatian language at level A1.1 in order to extend their residence and work permit. Apparently, that’s “integration”.

Is basic knowledge of a few dozen words really the same as integration into society? According to Ivan Balabanić, senior research associate at the Institute for Migration Research, the answer is very clearly “no.” The data that his institute collects shows that Croatia is only beginning to scratch the surface of a problem that, as the number of foreign workers grows, will become ever more complex. Balabanić views the obligation to pass A1.1 Croatian simultaneously as an integration measure and as an administrative condition, but emphasises that its meaning should primarily be integrative.

“Knowledge of the language of the country in which a person lives and works is one of the first preconditions for beginning to feel part of society. Nevertheless, such a low level of language knowledge by itself does not resolve questions of the legal security of foreign workers nor their finding their way in Croatian administration. Integration does not begin with a language course, but at the moment when a foreign worker knows their rights and can actually exercise them,” Balabanić highlighted.

croatia’s responsibility as a state

Precisely for that reason, while the worker hasn’t mastered Croatian, information about residence, work, the healthcare system and the protection of rights must be available to them in a language they understand, and that, Balabanić emphasises, in one place, and not scattered across a series of different institutions. Alongside economic integration, which in Croatia today mainly comes down to the relationship between the worker and the employer, the social dimension is equally important, and that, according to his words, cannot be one-way. Foreign workers need to get to know the norms and values of the society they are coming into, but the domestic population must also accept that Croatia is becoming culturally more diverse.

How weak that readiness is at this moment is shown by a study by the Institute for Migration Research from November 2025, conducted on a sample of 1,000 respondents: only 2.4 percent of citizens would accept a foreign worker as a friend, 5.7 percent as a neighbour, and as a family member only a negligible number of respondents. “That’s why I would say that Croatia is still in an early phase of the integration of foreign workers. Language is an important first step, but without legal security, available information, social contacts and the readiness of the domestic population to accept new fellow citizens we cannot speak of a serious integration policy,” Balabanić said. When it comes to the financing of integration, Balabanić clearly emphasises that the largest part of the cost should be borne by the state.

“The logic is simple: foreign workers come to Croatia primarily because of the needs of the domestic labour market and the shortage of labour in certain sectors. If the state creates a system that encourages the arrival of foreign workers, then it must also take on the largest part of the responsibility for their integration,” he is clear.

That, he emphasises, does not mean that the responsibility must be exclusively state. Local self-government has an important role because integration takes place in concrete communities – the needs of workers in Istria are not the same as the needs of those in Lika or Zagreb. Employers bear their share of responsibility within the work environment, but Balabanić warns that it would be wrong to shift the entire burden onto them, since they already bear significant costs of employing foreign workers. The least burden, he believes, should be shifted onto the workers themselves, although they too have the obligation to actively participate in integration by learning the language and respecting the law.

the so-called information vacuum

Precisely there Balabanić sees the real danger that integration becomes something that the state formally requires of the foreign worker, while at the same time not providing them with the tools to fulfil that requirement.

“It wouldn’t be logical for Croatia to actively attract foreign workers because its economy needs them, and then declare their integration exclusively their personal problem,” he said. When it comes to the biggest obstacles in the everyday life of foreign workers, Balabanić avoids singling out only one. The language barrier, inadequate accommodation, violation of labour rights, difficult access to healthcare and social isolation, he says, are intertwined – but the common denominator of most of these problems is the chronic lack of available and reliable information.

Croatia, he admits, is gradually responding regulatorily to the new situation; amendments to laws and regulations are being adopted, but the open question remains how many of them the administration manages to implement in practice. Tightened criteria for employers, for example, were supposed to regulate the market, but at the same time increased the administrative burden, so some workers waited months for the extension of their permit. A particular problem is the healthcare system – according to another study by the Institute from November 2025, conducted on 429 foreign workers from Asia and Africa in Zagreb and Zagreb County, only 28.7 percent of respondents have a chosen general practitioner, which seriously complicates regular health care.

Language remains an obstacle even when workers themselves try to find information, because the official websites of institutions are very often available exclusively in Croatian. Because of that many find themselves in what Balabanić calls an information vacuum, in which the main, sometimes the only, source of information becomes the employer or the employment agency. “A series of entirely practical questions, from whether the employer can keep the passport, whether they have the right to unemployment benefit, whom to turn to if their rights are violated – for a large number of workers remain without a reliable answer. Croatia today does not primarily lack regulations. It lacks a system that will enable the foreign worker to actually exercise the rights they have,” Balabanić highlighted.

financial burden

Particularly vulnerable, he warns, are workers in whom several unfavourable circumstances overlap – those who went into debt in order to reach Croatia at all through long chains of intermediaries, and therefore more readily accept poor working conditions, as well as those employed by an employer on whom they depend for salary, accommodation and information about their own rights. The education of children is for now not among the most pronounced problems, since a large part of labour migrants still live in Croatia without family, but with the growth in the number of those who stay long-term and bring families, that topic, Balabanić estimates, will become increasingly important.

World.title: Croatia in Top 20 Countries With Highest Quality of Life – But It Doesn’t Mean What You Think
World.content:
September the 22nd, 2026 – Croatia has entered into the top 20 countries with the highest quality of life, but it certainly doesn’t mean what you think it means…

The new ranking by World Population Review brings quite a surprise, and that’s that Croatia has placed 20th among countries with the highest quality of life. However, what’s odd to note is that behind this attractive ranking lies a methodology that is important to explain. Poslovni reports that Croatia has surprisingly found itself among the 20 best-placed countries in the world according to the quality of life ranking published by World Population Review. With an index of 181.7 points Croatia occupies 20th place, immediately behind Slovenia, which is 19th with 182.4 points.

the ranking leaves you scratching your head…

Particularly interesting is the fact that according to this ranking numerous developed countries remain behind Croatia. Lithuania is 21st, the United Kingdom 22nd, Czechia 23rd, Belgium 26th, Canada 27th, Ireland 28th, France 29th, Portugal 31st, while Italy is only in 40th place.

At the very top is Luxembourg with 218.2 points. It is followed by the Netherlands (216.5), Denmark (215.1), and a major surprise is Oman, which with the same result as Denmark occupies fourth place. They are followed by Switzerland, Finland, Norway, Iceland, Austria and Germany. Australia is 11th, New Zealand 12th, Sweden 13th, the USA 14th, and among the top 20 are also Estonia, Qatar, Japan, Spain, Slovenia and Croatia.

this ranking isn’t what you might think it is

Nevertheless, it is necessary to emphasise that this is not an official international ranking of the “standard of living” in the classical economic sense. World Population Review for this ranking uses Numbeo’s Quality of Life Index, which attempts to encompass everyday quality of life through eight areas: purchasing power, safety, healthcare, cost of living, the ratio of property prices to income, time spent in traffic, pollution and climate conditions. It is precisely the last items that help explain why Croatia stands so high. For example, Numbeo’s data for Croatia show high scores for safety and very favourable climate conditions as well as a relatively low level of pollution.

World.title: Croatia Among EU Countries With Lowest Share of Insured Climate Losses
World.content:
September the 22nd, 2026 – Croatia is exceptionally vulnerable to climate events, yet it is remains among the EU countries with the lowest share of insured climate losses.

Even before the catastrophic fire in Omiš, Croatia already had a 75 percent larger burned area in 2026 than in the comparable period back in 2025. Poslovni reports that the European Commission estimates that today. only around 25 percent of catastrophic losses across Europe are covered by private insurance, which is why national budgets too often become the “insurer of last resort.”

the number of fires in croatia increased

The number of fires in Croatia rose by 7.62 percent, while the burned area rose by 75.06 percent compared to the same period last year. That difference says more about climate risk than any single image of a burning hill; an individual event today simply carries greater damage than a few years ago. Recent fires near Omiš, on Pelješac and Brač further confirmed this. The Omiš fire affected more than 1,000 hectares and led to the evacuation of around a thousand people. By mid-September, around 668,000 hectares had burned in fires across the European Union, almost twice the twenty-year average for the same part of the year, although less than the record 2025. The figures from across Europe warn that this season was not an exception but a continuation of a trend that Croatian companies, banks and insurers still need to take more seriously. Behind the scenes of burning hills lies the statistics about money, about premiums, damages and about who ultimately pays the bill when one decides to gamble with climate risk.

“Climate risk is increasingly becoming everyday life and the question is whether we have an idea of how much it can cost us. Companies that today assess their exposure only through last year’s damage are building a false sense of security,” believes Jasminka Horvat Martinović, President of the Management Board of Marsh Croatia, warning that this is a major trap of the moment in which a large part of the Croatian business sector finds itself.

A Reuters analysis, based on data from the European Environment Agency, shows the scale of the problem at the level of the entire Union: climate disasters and extreme weather conditions cost the European Union around €822 billion in the period from 1980 to 2024, and as much as a quarter of that amount occurred in the last four years. According to the latest EEA data, less than 20 percent of total losses in that period were covered by private insurance. For Croatia the gap is even larger: less than three percent of total economic losses linked to weather and climate extremes were insured.

unsurprisingly, croatia isn’t doing anywhere near enough

Croatia is thus among the European countries with the lowest share of insured climate losses. The floods in Spain in 2024 imply reconstruction costs of around 0.7 percent of GDP in the period 2024–2026, which is approximately €11 billion, while the German floods of 2021 cost the state treasury around €30 billion because insurance covered only a smaller part of the damage.

“The problem is no longer in the cost that disasters bring but in the fact that they are becoming regular. As long as they are treated as one-off budget burdens, the system does not adapt. The result is that an ever larger part of the bill ends up with taxpayers,” emphasises Horvat Martinović.

Some countries have already gone a step further than considering new models. Portugal in April, after major floods at the beginning of 2026, announced a fund for natural disasters and earthquakes and a system of compulsory insurance of housing and business infrastructure, with a public assistance mechanism for lower-income households. In Greece, from 1 June 2025, insurance against forest fire, flood and earthquake has been compulsory for companies with annual turnover greater than €500,000, with coverage of at least 70 percent of the value of the assets covered.

In the meantime a new step has also been taken at the level of the European Union. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on 16 September announced the establishment of the Climate Insurance Alliance with the aim of reducing the large gap in insurance against climate disasters. The Commission estimates that today only around 25 percent of catastrophic losses in Europe are covered by private insurance, which is why national budgets too often become the “insurer of last resort.” The new initiative should include insurers, investors, risk modelling experts, public institutions and policyholders and encourage solutions such as group and parametric insurance.

croatia’s fire risk is enormous

That European statistic primarily reflects floods and storms, but the same pattern of underinsurance also applies to fires, and the Croatian 2026 season shows this on its own local example.

According to data from the State Firefighting Operational Centre 193 of the Croatian Firefighting Association, in the period from 1 January to 10 August 2026, 29,358 firefighting interventions were recorded in Croatia, of which 8,832 were fires. Of that, 5,575 open-space fires and 3,897 vegetation fires were recorded, and 9,646 hectares were burned. Compared to the same period in 2025, the number of open-space fires rose by 12.99 percent, the number of vegetation fires by 23.40 percent, and the burned area by 75.06 percent. What makes that statistic particularly relevant for the business community is the relationship between the two figures. On the day of that cut-off the total number of fires rose by 7.62 percent, and the burned area by 75 percent. The risk, therefore, does not grow so much by frequency as by consequence. An individual event today carries a significantly greater loss than a few years ago. The Omiš fire shows this precisely; it was not the largest by area – the Split one from 2017 was four to five times larger. In addition, fires are no longer exclusively a coastal story. The risk, in other words, is moving from a seasonal to a permanent category.

The Croatian business sector mostly reacts to risk after it materialises, instead of structuring it in advance. “A strategic approach is important, and that means recognising the risk before it becomes damage,” emphasises Horvat Martinović, adding that companies should carry out in-depth analysis of exposure to climate risks, scenario models and adapted insurance solutions, from parametric covers, where the payout is activated automatically on the basis of pre-defined parameters such as the amount of precipitation or wind speed, to solutions for critical infrastructure and renewable energy sources. For example, in the energy sector, better mapping and prevention can reduce risk by 20 to 30 percent.

In the meantime newer data from the Croatian insurance market are also available. In the first seven months of 2026 the total collected premium rose by 6.9 percent to €1.3 billion, while the non-life insurance premium rose by 7.3 percent. Insurance against fire and elemental damage accounted for 9.5 percent of the non-life insurance premium. At the same time the amount of settled claims in non-life insurance rose by 15.9 percent, and 9.7 percent of that amount related to fires and elemental damage.

croatian companies need to ask themselves some serious questions

The growth in the number of policies on the Croatian market looks like a sign of maturity. But if a large part of property still remains uninsured or underinsured, that growth only means that the bills tomorrow will be larger than today. What distinguishes companies that survive a major loss is a pre-set risk management strategy, not the policy itself.

Croatian companies, Horvat Martinović believes, need to ask themselves the practical question of whether their risk assessment has been made on the basis of what happened last year, or on the basis of what is already now visible as coming. Climate risk is entering insurance prices, property values and public budgets ever more strongly; waiting for the next major event to show where the system is vulnerable, concludes Horvat Martinović, is becoming an ever more expensive strategy.

World.title: Dismissal of Plenković Sought Following Hazardous Waste Scandal
World.content:
September the 22nd, 2026 – SDP is seeking the dismissal of PM Andrej Plenković following the hazardous waste scandal in Lika.

By the end of this week, SDP will officially submit to parliamentary procedure a proposal for a vote of no confidence in the Government of Andrej Plenković. Index reports that it will do so over the case of illegally dumped hazardous waste in Gospić and other parts of Croatia. 55 signatures of MPs were already collected for the initiative a month ago, but SDP will submit only 30, the minimum required. The proposal has been signed by all opposition parties except DOMiNO and the Croatian Sovereignists.

The reason for submitting only part of the signatures is a provision of the parliamentary Rules of Procedure according to which an MP can support only one such proposal within a period of six months. SDP is thus leaving open the possibility that some MPs, before the expiry of that deadline, support a new request for the dismissal of the Government or one of its members, reports Novi list.

an october vote

After Speaker of Parliament Gordan Jandroković receives the proposal and places it on the agenda, the Government has eight days to respond, and the vote must be held within 30 days. This means that MPs should declare themselves on confidence in the Government during October. The parliamentary majority currently has 79 MPs, so according to the present balance of forces there are not enough votes to pass a vote of no confidence. In the proposal SDP explains in eight points why it considers Plenković’s government politically responsible for the illegal accumulation of 37,000 tonnes of waste in Gospić, but also for cases of environmental pollution in other parts of Croatia.

sdp: the government shaped this system for years

SDP’s fundamental thesis is that long-term changes to regulations and the weakening of control mechanisms opened the space for illegal waste dumping. SDP claims that responsibility reaches the Prime Minister because his Government “for years shaped the regulations, organised supervision and chose the people at the head of key institutions.”

They also state that part of the powers for acting in such cases belonged to the Government and its president. They particularly single out suspicions linked to former Chief State Inspector Andrija Mikulić, who was appointed by Plenković’s government. “Were individual failures of supervision the result of deliberate favouritism, did those who were supposed to prevent the illegalities by their actions enable their continuation,” SDP asks in the proposal.

the pm is being accused of downplaying the issue

In the request SDP also deals with what it calls the Prime Minister’s downplaying of the seriousness of the problem of illegally buried waste in Gospić. “A stronger reaction by the Government followed only with the growth of public pressure and protests,” they claim.

In the final part of the request they state that political responsibility must lead to a change in the waste management system and that citizens have the right to effective remediation and the accountability of those who managed the system for years. An additional political dimension is given to the case by the statement of Deputy Prime Minister and Defence Minister Ivan Anušić, who last weekend recalled that as early as 2023, after the fire at Drava International, he called out the State Inspectorate. Anušić said at the time that the Inspectorate had to control the quantities and type of waste and the method of its disposal. “Unfortunately, three years later we see where we are when it comes to those who ran the Inspectorate and when we talk about Gospić, but also about scandals linked to waste,” Anušić said.

Back in July 2024, the Croatian Government gave Mikulić a second term as Chief State Inspector. Anušić was already a member of the government at that time.

World.title: Slaven Bilić: “All Four Matches Are Massive”
World.content:
The Croatia national football team is gearing up for its upcoming fixtures in the new edition of the UEFA Nations League.

Ahead of today’s gathering, Croatia coach Slaven Bilić held a press conference, opening with comments on the fact that several national team players changed clubs this summer.

“Josip Šutalo? That’s good for him and for the national team. It’s a similar situation to Majer. He’s gone to a club and a league where proper defending is played, and things are going really well for him at Lazio. Of course he’s not yet at his top level, he’s played two matches, but I’m happy for him.

Luka Vušković? I can’t do anything but add to the praise. I’ve watched all of his matches, and you keep waiting for him to make a mistake, but it doesn’t come. He’s smart, brave, confident, and a real leader. He’s a young player, very young, and it’s normal for players like that to have ups and downs. He hasn’t shown any so far, but we have to keep an eye on him.

Ivor Pandur? He’s excellent. He was one of the key players in Hull’s promotion push toward the Premier League. Dominik Kotarski? He’s back at Dinamo, a club where you have to win and can’t afford to concede. All of that is good news. The same goes for Dominik Livaković. Flick didn’t put Livaković in goal because of Croatia — he did it because Livaković showed him in training that he deserves it. That’s grounds for optimism.

Franjo Ivanović? He changed clubs, and he didn’t play all that much last season. He’s made a really good start. I’ve already said he brings something different from our other forwards. I don’t doubt him,” Bilić said.

Four big matches lie ahead…

“All four matches are massive. We can’t overlook the Czech Republic, because everything is built around that match. It’s first up on the schedule, and the public expects a win. With all due respect to our opponents, we know it’s going to be tough. Our last match in Prague finished 0-0. These days it’s hard to play against Spain and England, but it’ll be hard for them against us too. We’ll need a lot of sacrifice, but also a lot of courage.”

On the option of playing with three or four defenders…

“I’d single out the Czech Republic match. We have players we expect a lot from, and I’m hoping some things become clearer to me as well. They also have every right to think about what awaits them when they play us. Four matches lie ahead of us, and football isn’t mathematics. We’ll need a lot of players, but our focus is on the Czech Republic for several reasons. Croatia has enough quality in defense and midfield to play with either three or four at the back. I prefer four, but we have the kind of players that let us defend with four and attack with three within the same match. We’ll certainly make use of some of that.”

On Modrić staying on…

“We’re all happy that he’s staying. His passion has never been in question. It’s been more of a media circus, because everyone kept asking him when he’d say goodbye to football. When I became coach, I noticed the national team means everything to him. He’s the last person who’d want to coast. Milan don’t look the same with him as without him. He’s great, and when he plays at that level, Milan are far more vertical with him on the pitch. As long as he keeps playing there, he’ll keep playing for us.”

On Ante Budimir…

“I congratulate him. Scoring a hundred goals in any league, let alone in Spain, is a huge achievement. I remember when Šuker put together a tape of his hundred goals, and back then that felt incredible. It still does today; it’s just that Ronaldo and Messi have spoiled that feeling a bit. He plays for Osasuna, who are fighting for a mid-table finish. Given the way Croatia play, he can be very useful to us, as he’s already shown many times.”

On the players joining up with the squad…

“Nobody’s getting a few days off, because we don’t have room for that. Some have played more, some less, some are in top form, and some have changed coaches. That’s part of what makes the national team special — the players arrive in all sorts of different mental states. We’ve already done a lot of the work before the camp. We’ll run a few training sessions, and there’ll certainly be one or two where everyone is out on the pitch together doing a proper session.”

On Ivan Perišić’s positions…

“Both positions. I spoke with him among the first after the season ended. He can play equally well in both roles. If we had two Perišićs, both would play — one at full-back, one on the wing. That’s the kind of player he is, and mentally he’s in the right place too.”

On the excitement of returning after 14 years…

“I’m excited, and I’m not hiding it. A lot of time has passed, and my last spell in charge now feels like ancient history.”

On the Vušković–Gvardiol center-back pairing…

“We’ll see, we’ll talk about it. Gvardiol is a versatile player. At City he plays at full-back. We also have other center-backs there — Šutalo, Pongračić… I see Gvardiol as a center-back, which doesn’t mean he won’t step into the full-back role. The two of them are young, but Gvardiol has been playing at the top level in one of the best leagues in the world for years now. Logically, they’re the center-back pairing of the future. They’ll have to fight for their place with players like Šutalo, Erlić and Pongračić, and that’s a privilege.”

On Modrić’s performances at Milan…

“Modrić’s strength lies in controlling the match. You saw it against Lecce. Once he came off, the opponent started to dominate and Milan lost their stability. Modrić has a huge influence on the rhythm of a game. Now someone will spin that as meaning it’s a static style of play. Capello says Milan play far more vertically with Modrić on the pitch.”

On Martin Baturina and Luka Sučić…

“Baturina has become a complete player. What every coach wants is for his players to be a goal threat. Both of them have scored three or four goals. And I see them both close to goal, playing as wingers or in that second-striker role.”

World.title: The Brewery That Survived When Zagreb Ran Out of Beer
World.content:
September the 21st, 2026 – There’s a brewery that survived the crash, WWII and privatisation, they even managed to continue when Zagreb ran out of beer.

Back at the end of the 19th century, when craftsmen could no longer produce enough beer for the thirsty Zagreb market, a large brewery was built in Črnomerec. Dubravko Grakalic reports for Index that Zagrebačka pivovara, known for its lagers, has since grown into a symbol of Zagreb and one of the best-known Croatian companies. “The idea of founding a large brewery in Zagreb arose in the circle of the Croatian Discount Bank when Gustav Pongratz entered its management board in 1890 and around the middle of 1892 Baron Petar Dragutin Turković,” historian Mila Kolar-Dimitrijević notes in the expert article “Zagrebačka pivovara until 1945” published in the Journal of Contemporary History in 1992.

“The bank’s director from its beginning, Franjo Šverljuga, convened the founding assembly of Zagrebačka pivovara in the bank’s premises on 19 May 1892, and already on 26 May the city authorities issued the permit, on the basis of which it was entered in the register of companies of the Court Table on 4 June of the same year, with a capital of 300,000 forints, or 1,500 issued shares of 200 forints each,” Kolar-Dimitrijević adds.

origins from the zagreb industrial zone

Beer production in Zagreb, which dates from the 14th century, before that major business decision was based on smaller breweries. The best-known one was opened in 1850 on the Upper Town, in today’s Gjure Basariček Street, which was called Pivarska Street. Later the plant moved to the corner of Gajeva and Teslina streets. Zagrebačka pivovara was built in the then industrial zone in the western part of the city, where several other significant factories were located. “There the concentration of industry was noticeable from the 1870s, and the intensity grew towards the end of the 19th century. North of the railway line, along the eastern side of the street that led from the City Waterworks plant (1878) towards Ilica (Vodovodna Street), there was a parquet and furniture factory (1873), and opposite it the coffee-substitute factory of Hinko Franck and Sons (1892) was built.

Not far from the intersection of Vodovodna Street with Ilica the Zagreb Joint-Stock Brewery and Malt Factory (1892) operated,” Goran Arčabić from the Zagreb City Museum tells Index.

back to november 1892…

Contemporary Zagreb newspapers wrote extensively about the construction and opening of the brewery in Črnomerec. Narodne novine in November 1892 announced the construction of a large brewery in Zagreb: “The street façade of the main building, which will stand on the corner, will be 100 metres long in both streets. It will contain the brewing plant, malt house, fermenting plant and various necessary rooms for preparation. In addition a special building for apartments and offices will be built. The main building for brewing beer will be connected by an underground corridor with a large cellar in which the beer will mature.”

“Next to the large building where the beer will be served there will be a large garden that will be able to hold up to 1,500 guests, and that garden will be expanded for large celebrations, concerts and entertainments so that up to 5,000 people will be able to find places. In the immediate vicinity of the large ice-houses a fishpond will be arranged, about one jutro in size, from which the brewery will obtain the necessary ice, and which will also be able to be used as a skating rink,” Narodne novine published.

the trams ran until 02:00!

The skating rink was never opened, but the Zagrebačka pivovara restaurant was for decades a cult place in that part of the city.

The daily Obzor on the 13th of July 1893 reported on the opening: “Yesterday afternoon the new brewery was opened in a solemn manner. All afternoon, and especially towards evening, countless tram cars carried the public to the new brewery. The spacious garden, one of the largest in Zagreb, was packed with citizens from all strata of the capital. Towards evening there was such a rush of the public that much effort was needed to get to a glass of beer, because dense crowds surrounded the places where the beer was being poured. In the evening there were thousands of people in the garden, and the total attendance from 2 p.m. to two o’clock at night is calculated at more than 8,000 people.”

the brewery was saved at the last minute

The business of Zagrebačka pivovara in the first years was not positive because of strong competition – at that time about fifteen breweries operated in Croatia along with imported Austrian products – so in 1910 it came to the brink of ruin. Nevertheless, the unification of capital with the breweries from Sisak and Nova Gradiška saved the business. Then the management-ownership structure also changed, in which the main role was taken by industrialist Samuel David Alexander, owner of an oil mill and grain trader. Alexander modernised the brewery, connected it by rail to today’s Western Station and cheapened production. After the First World War, the brewery continued to operate successfully, opened a plant in Sarajevo, took over the brewery in Karlovac and significantly expanded the market to Dalmatia after the opening of the new railway line to Split in 1925.

escape from the ustaše…

In the 1930s Zagrebačka pivovara barely survived by selling real estate because of the great economic crisis, but that was only a prelude to greater troubles. “The authorities of the Banovina of Croatia had a negative attitude towards Jews, and a regulation was passed that they could not engage in the production and sale of food. A commissioner of the Banovina authorities, Vladimir Božić, was appointed to Zagrebačka pivovara, and at the annual assembly on 13 December 1940 Dr Božidar Alexander also resigned from membership of the management board, while Samuel David Alexander, together with his wife Ema, daughter of the prominent businessman Neuman, tried by converting to the Catholic faith to save at least their lives if not already their property,” historian Mila Kolar-Dimitrijević writes.

After the establishment of the Independent State of Croatia, the family was stripped of all property; Alexander himself took refuge from Ustaša persecution in the sanatorium of Dr Đuro Vranešić on Zelengaj, where he died in March 1943, while part of his family was killed in Ustaša camps and part survived by fleeing to the Partisans and abroad. The Ustaša authorities privatised the factory. In 1944 it ceased operations because of a lack of raw materials, which lasted until the liberation of Zagreb in May 1945. Zagrebačka pivovara was then taken over by the National Administration of People’s Property, which appointed its commissioner with the task of putting the brewery back into operation.

from 1945 to the present day

From then on Zagrebačka pivovara developed strongly – production of 60,000 hectolitres in 1952 rose to a million hectolitres in 1969. Sales were increased by the merger of trading companies from Bjelovar, Koprivnica, Našice and Labin, and by the opening of representative offices throughout Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Lika Brewery Otočac was merged in 1971 and ceased operations in 1996. At that time the breweries in Daruvar and Karlovac also operated within Zagrebačke pivovare, and the company employed 1,600 workers. At that time, through the then model of socialist associated labour (SOUR), within the single enterprise “Zagrebačke pivovare” the plants in Zagreb, Karlovac, Daruvar and Otočac operated together, so today’s fierce market rivals were for years under the same roof.

they produced over half the beer in the former sr of croatia

Until 1970 Zagrebačka pivovara produced more than fifty percent of the beer in the territory of the then SR of Croatia, after which production fell to thirty percent by 1990. In 1993 the company was sold to the Belgian Interbrew. After a series of global ownership restructurings, Zagrebačka pivovara became part of the North American group Molson Coors in 2012, one of the largest brewing giants in the world. It produces 1,500,000 hectolitres of beer annually and employs around 650 workers. “Being one of the economic and industrial symbols of Zagreb is for us first of all a responsibility. We must preserve the best from the tradition we have inherited, but at the same time invest in people, technology and more sustainable production,” they say for Index from this important company whose products are advertised as “the law” for beer drinkers.

World.title: Lika Residents Ask One Thing After Waste Scandal: Are We Infected?
World.content:
September the 21st, 2026 – Furious and deeply concerned Lika residents have been asking one very valid question following the shameful hazardous waste scandal was uncovered: Are we infected?

In wells in the Gospić settlement of Krpani, downstream from the illegal waste dump in Bilajska Street, PFAS compounds, which are so-called forever chemicals, have unfortunately been found. One of the wells is about 600 metres from the dump, HRT reported. The latest findings have further alarmed residents who have for years been using local springs and wells and are engaged in livestock farming and agriculture. Index reports that the Croatian Institute of Public Health published the results of extraordinary sampling of 43 private water facilities in the Lika area – 38 wells, three cisterns and two springs. PFAS was found in two wells in the immediate vicinity and downstream from the illegal dump.

In one of them, the sum of PFAS compounds amounted to 0.3018 micrograms per litre, more than three times above the maximum permitted value of 0.1 micrograms. In the other 0.0265 micrograms per litre was measured, which is below that limit.

serious concerns about the water in lika

Residents of Krpani warn that the groundwater from their settlement does not remain only in the area of the wells. “This water that flows through here goes into the well, and that well now has PFAS, it now has those compounds,” said OPG owner Marko Štimac for HRT. Resident Mate Krpan claims that these are groundwaters that are connected to local watercourses and warns of the possibility of further spread of the pollution. The exact direction and extent of the movement of the pollution through the groundwater still needs to be professionally determined.

“are we infected?”

The wells were once an important source of water for residents, and the new findings have caused fear because of possible long-term exposure.

“Are we infected or not, we’ll see. Who knows, who knows,” said resident Božo Krpan. “Of course I’m afraid for the children, there’s always the thought whether this has already affected their health, and our health in general,” said Josipa Krpan. PFAS is a large group of very persistent chemical compounds that are difficult to break down in the environment, which is why they are often called forever chemicals.

family farms fear for their livestock and produce

Particularly concerned are local farmers whose livestock used water from that area. “The livestock may be infected, I don’t know, that needs to be tested. I won’t sell calves and think whether I’ll infect someone with that,” said Štimac. Tomislav Krpan fears that the findings could completely destroy the market for local producers from Lika. “What we’ve been raising will obviously all go to ruin, and we will no longer have a market, nor will we be able to sell our products, neither lambs, nor calves, nor kids, nor potatoes,” he said. Their fears so far do not mean that the livestock or food from their farms is indeed contaminated. Separate tests would be needed for such a conclusion.

HZJZ this week published the results of testing 32 samples of locally produced food from 13 locations up to a kilometre away from the dump. The Institute states that the findings so far do not show general contamination of local food, and in seven samples tested for PFAS the values were below the limit of quantification.

public health authorities say the water is safe…

It is important to emphasise that the disputed wells are not part of the public water supply system. HZJZ states that residents of that area are connected to the public water supply and that the water from the two wells in which PFAS was found is not used for drinking. The Institute concludes that the results so far point to pollution of a local character, in a narrower area downstream from the dump. Analyses of the public water supply so far have not shown PFAS above the limit of determination. By 16 September a total of 93 samples of water from the public system in the Lika-Senj County and Pag area were analysed, and all were health-safe.

Earlier expert examinations carried out for USKOK already established PFAS compounds in the waste and groundwater immediately next to the illegal dump. HZJZ published that the compounds established in the waste match those found in the groundwater in its immediate vicinity.

Biologist and ecotoxicologist Branimir K. Hackenberger warned for HRT that the findings from different polluted wells are not the same. “The chemical fingerprint is completely different in those wells, which means that the source of pollution is also not one, and we cannot link all three wells to that one nearest source of pollution that is located there,” he said. For that reason, he is calling for a detailed hydrogeological investigation.

“Experts from the Institute and other institutions must absolutely go out into the field as soon as possible, see what the traffic of that water is like, what the hydrodynamics are, what the directions are, etc., so that anything further can be responsibly claimed on the basis of such analyses,” said Hackenberger.

covering this waste up is nowhere near enough of a solution

The citizens’ initiative Gospić is Our Home considers that the planned temporary covering of the waste can no longer solve the groundwater problem.

“That solution made sense a year ago, but now, as we know, the influence of groundwater cannot be prevented,” said Darija Dođen from the initiative. In the area of the former PPK Velebit complex in Gospić around 37,000 tonnes of mixed waste were illegally dumped. USKOK is conducting an investigation against a larger number of persons on suspicion that they committed criminal offences against the environment and the economy as part of a criminal association. The latest findings from private wells now open the question of how far the pollution has spread through the underground karst system and what additional tests are needed to assess its actual reach.

World.title: Number of Foreign Tourists in Croatia Falls With More Growth Elsewhere in Mediterranean
World.content:
September the 21st, 2026 – The number of foreign tourists in Croatia has actually fallen, with much more growth seen elsewhere across the Mediterranean.

Croatia recorded only 0.5 percent more tourist overnight stays in the first six months of this year than in the same period last year, according to the latest comparable Eurostat data. Index reports that this is one of the weakest results among Mediterranean tourist countries and the lowest growth among those that finished the first half of the year in positive territory. Looking at tourist accommodation in Croatia from January to the end of June this year, just under 26 million overnight stays were recorded, about 120 thousand more than a year earlier. Index reports that by comparison, at the level of the entire European Union, the number of overnight stays across Croatia rose by 1.7 percent.

albania, malta and slovenia grew several times faster

Among Mediterranean competitors Portugal had growth of 0.9 percent, Greece 1.4 percent, Spain 1.5 percent, Montenegro also 1.5 percent, and Italy 3.1 percent. Significantly stronger results were achieved by Slovenia, with growth of 5.7 percent, Albania with 9.1 percent and Malta with 9.9 percent. Two countries from that group were in negative territory: Bulgaria with a fall of 1.7 percent and Cyprus with a fall of 7.7 percent. As such, Croatia was at the bottom among the Mediterranean countries that achieved growth.

fewer overnight stays from foreign visitors

Even more interesting is the structure of the Croatian result. The number of overnight stays by domestic guests in the first six months rose by as much as 7.7 percent, while foreign tourists recorded 0.6 percent fewer overnight stays than last year. In neighbouring Italy, overnight stays by foreign tourists simultaneously rose by 4.4 percent, in Slovenia by 6.9 percent, in Malta by 11.7 percent, in Albania by 8.7 percent, and in Greece and Spain by 1.7 and 1.4 percent respectively. Domestic guests thus practically pulled the Croatian first-half result out of the red.

DZS data also shows just how quickly the situation changed during the pre-season. After the first five months Croatia had as much as 8.6 percent more commercial overnight stays than last year. But in June the number of overnight stays fell by 6.1 percent, and overnight stays by foreign tourists by as much as 7.5 percent. This brought the cumulative growth by the end of June down to only 0.5 percent.

july and august improved things, but the overall growth is still small

July brought a recovery. DZS recorded 25.3 million commercial overnight stays, 1.2 percent more than in July last year. In the first seven months growth was thereby raised to 0.8 percent, while overnight stays by foreign guests were only 0.2 percent above last year’s. Data for August also doesn’t show a major acceleration. According to the eVisitor system, which has a broader coverage than Eurostat’s commercial accommodation statistics, Croatia had 17.5 million arrivals and 90.5 million overnight stays in the first eight months. Both arrivals and overnight stays rose by around one percent. On the Adriatic alone the growth in overnight stays was 0.5 percent.

In August itself, 31.4 million overnight stays were recorded, only 0.5 percent more than last year. HTZ data also show differences among types of accommodation. In commercial accommodation by the end of August 78.6 million overnight stays were recorded, about 0.5 percent more than last year. Hotels had around 20 million overnight stays and growth of 2.7 percent, while almost 34 million overnight stays in household facilities were approximately at last year’s level.

croatia still clings onto july and august

The figures are particularly interesting in the context of the multi-year goal of extending the Croatian tourist season beyond July and August. Eurostat published that Croatia is the most seasonal tourist country in the entire EU. As much as 54.5 percent of all Croatian tourist overnight stays in 2025 were recorded only during July and August. The EU average was 31.1 percent, in Greece 41.6 percent, and in Bulgaria 43.4 percent. The difference between the main season and the rest of the year in Croatia is also the largest: last August as many as 41 times more overnight stays were recorded than in January. This means that Croatia, despite years of announcements about strengthening the pre-season and post-season, still depends significantly more than its competitors on two summer months.

europe is growing faster, and tourists are paying more and more attention to value for money

The broader European trend also shows that the weaker Croatian growth cannot be explained only by a general slowdown in tourist demand. The European Travel Commission in its July report states that international tourist arrivals in Europe this year grew by around five percent, and the number of overnight stays by 4.8 percent. At the same time it warns that travellers, due to weaker consumer confidence, are increasingly choosing destinations according to the price-quality ratio and are showing greater interest in travel outside the main season.

Price competitiveness was precisely one of the main topics of Croatian tourism before and during this season. Tourism Minister Tonči Glavina already at the beginning of the year warned that guests on the key German market are extremely sensitive to the price-quality ratio. The overnight stays statistics themselves, however, do not show why Croatia is growing more slowly than its competitors, so it cannot be concluded from those figures that prices are the only or main cause.

higher invoice values

On the other hand, physical traffic is not the only measure of the tourist season. The Ministry of Tourism states that in the first eight months €7.41 billion was fiscalised, 17.6 percent more than in the same period last year, while the number of invoices rose by 5.7 percent. According to the latest published HNB data for the first quarter, revenues from foreign tourists amounted to €945.2 million, 9.2 percent more than one year earlier.

World.title: Opposition in a letter to Estonian PM: Documents prove lies in defense procurement
World.content:
Opposition parties have written an open letter to Prime Minister Kristen Michal, raising questions and requesting information regarding the country's recent ammunition procurement scandal. ERR is publishing the letter in full.

The ammunition procurement contracts scandal has raised fundamental questions about failures to exercise due diligence and the risks of corruption. Falsehoods and distortions of the truth concerning the case have emerged publicly, along with claims that key documentation relating to the transactions cannot be found. Existing documents confirm that the public was misled.

The media has clearly highlighted the conflict of interest, but a whole series of important questions remain unanswered. You have said that you have now spoken with senior officials and received answers from them. We would now like substantive answers from you.

We are submitting the following questions and request for information regarding the ammunition procurement contracts case and ask that you respond without delay.

1. When did the defense minister inform you of the problems involving Datasel? When were you briefed by prosecutors and police about the criminal proceedings that had been launched? Why did you decide to keep this from the public?

2. How did the defense minister present the idea of purchasing ammunition from the ARCA factory to the government in February 2025 and when did you learn that a company owned by Jaanus Rahumägi also had a financial interest in the transaction?

3. Have you communicated with Jaanus Rahumägi about defense procurement or are you aware of the defense minister having done so?

4. The defense minister has told the media that concluding €91 million worth of transactions helped present Estonia in a favorable light to ARCA with regard to building a factory. At the same time, Rheinmetall and BAE Systems are known to have abandoned plans to build factories because the state would not provide a purchase commitment. Why did the government not decide to similarly "present Estonia in a favorable light" to Rheinmetall or BAE Systems?

5. How is the construction of the factory in Kiviõli progressing? When can the promised €300 million investment and 1,000 jobs be expected to materialize? In light of the new details and information that have emerged, do you have reason to review the decision concerning the ammunition factory to be built in Kiviõli?

6. Could it turn out that, in the case of the government's ARCA decision, there was never any intention to build a factory at all and that it was merely administrative cover for carrying out ammunition transactions in which the defense minister had a clear conflict of interest?

7. An article published in the media revealed that the defense minister repeatedly said that the prime minister was demanding rapid deliveries from the ARCA factory. Was the defense minister acting under pressure from you or was he acting on his own initiative when he repeatedly said that the prime minister was applying pressure and that the ammunition procurements therefore had to be carried out quickly?

8. ARCA's owner has been convicted of corruption. As prime minister, what safeguards did you require the defense minister to put in place to reduce corruption and reputational risks? As an experienced politician, you are aware of the potential risks. How did it happen that Jaanus Rahumägi's involvement instead increased the corruption risk?

9. Jaanus Rahumägi is a longtime Reform Party member and supporter. The transactions have revealed a glaring conflict of interest. What specific steps did you take to prevent the defense minister from establishing these business ties?

10. Jaanus Rahumägi has a fairly direct role in the Reform Party's defense and security policy network. For example, during the 2025 government coalition consultations, he participated in discussions on internal security and public safety as a representative of ESC Global Security. What positions did he advocate?

11. How did the defense minister establish contact with Oculus Strategic Solutions, which sought to act as an intermediary for Datasel's ammunition offer? Can you state with confidence that this contact was not established through Jaanus Rahumägi?

12. Why did the defense minister insist that the Greek company Nordeto be brought in as an intermediary in the Datasel transactions and how did the defense minister establish contact with the company?

13. According to media reports, the defense minister was actively involved in directing the transactions through a Signal group and his personal email account. Will you use your authority to make the contents of those conversations available to parliamentary committees?

14. Why did payments to Datasel continue after the Estonian Center for Defense Investments (RKIK) proposed considering terminating the transactions because of the risks involved? Media reports have since revealed that RKIK made such a proposal in writing on at least two occasions.

15. RKIK's previous director left office in summer 2025. The top civil service appointments committee, which is overseen by the Government Office, took more than six months to appoint Elmar Vaher as the new director. Why did you decide to delay the process and why was appointing Elmar Vaher as RKIK director considered more important than the risk of slowing defense procurement?

We hope to receive answers from you in the near future, particularly since you have said that you have familiarized yourself with the matter.

We also call on you not to block the establishment of a parliamentary committee of inquiry into financial matters in the defense sector.

World.title: Starting kids' ADHD treatment to become easier in Estonia
World.content:
Estonia will ease prescribing rules for certain ADHD medications for children and young people from October 1, removing the requirement for psychiatrists to consult a treatment team before prescribing them.

Under a draft regulation prepared by the Ministry of Social Affairs, the prescribing conditions for certain ADHD medications containing specific active ingredients and reimbursed at a rate of 75 percent will change for children and young people aged 6-19.

Currently, prescribing such ADHD medications requires consultation with a psychiatric treatment team that includes, for example, a clinical speech therapist and two psychiatrists with additional qualifications in treating children. Under the change, these ADHD medications may be prescribed by either a psychiatrist or a psychiatrist with additional qualifications in child and adolescent psychiatry.

The requirement to consult a treatment team will be abolished, said Getter Hark, head of the Health Insurance Fund's medicines reimbursement service.

"This concerns two active ingredients used to treat ADHD: methylphenidate (sold under the brand names Ritalin, Concerta and others) and atomoxetine (Atominiex). These are first-line medications for children and young people aged 6-19. The change was developed in close cooperation with the Estonian Psychiatric Association and the aim is to bring prescribing conditions more closely in line with those for adults so that there are not such significant differences between age groups, as well as to bring treatment practices into line with the clinical guidelines," Hark said.

The change will take effect October 1 this year.

The Estonian Psychiatric Association said the existing requirement to consult a treatment team has been an unnecessary waste of time and is not in keeping with the logic of modern clinical practice.

Association Vice President Anne Kleinberg said excessive regulation of clinical practice is in the interests of neither patients nor doctors, as diagnosing ADHD and making treatment decisions are routine parts of a psychiatrist's work.

"There is no need to add a requirement to consult a treatment team, especially considering that the team may include, for example, a speech therapist and a psychologist or a mental health nurse, for whom prescribing medication is neither part of their work nor their responsibility," she said.

According to Health Insurance Fund statistics, both the number of prescriptions issued for ADHD medications containing methylphenidate and atomoxetine and the number of children and young people aged 6-19 receiving them have increased in recent years.

In 2021, for example, nearly 4,200 prescriptions were issued to around 950 children aged 6-10. So far this year, nearly 9,600 prescriptions have been issued to around 2,430 people in the same age group.

Experts stressed that changing the prescribing conditions will not alter the thorough decision-making process involved in diagnosis and treatment.

"We have certain rules for diagnosis that we have to follow and those rules are not imposed on us through medication-prescribing rules. We follow clinical guidelines, which set out the diagnostic criteria. That is what doctors use to make a diagnosis. It would be very strange to regulate that through a document governing the prescribing of medication," Kleinberg said.

World.title: Retailers: People are buying less fuel each time they fill up
World.content:
Fuel retailers' data shows that drivers are buying significantly smaller amounts of fuel at a time in the hope that prices will come back down. Fuel retailers, however, say prices are likely to remain high for some time.

High fuel prices have not yet prompted people to drive significantly less. However, drivers are buying less fuel each time they fill up and are therefore visiting gas stations more often, hoping prices will be slightly lower the next time around.

"Over the past couple of weeks, prices have been higher than they were in August. The biggest effect on ordinary consumers is that they are buying less at a time, which means they fill up more often during the month. For the most part, necessary trips are still being made," said Tarmo Kärsna, head of business development at Alexela.

"Spending on fuel has actually increased in monetary terms because fuel has become more expensive. Consumption in liters is broadly similar to last year — perhaps slightly lower overall — but people are filling up more frequently. People are certainly not keeping their tanks full either. Instead, they tend to drive with less fuel in the tank in the hope that fuel prices will fall again tomorrow," said Raimo Vahtrik, motor fuels sales director at Circle K.

Fuel retailers do not currently expect prices to fall quickly.

"We have to take into account that high prices will be with us for a longer period. The conflict is still ongoing and has, if anything, escalated, while inventories have declined at the same time and the heating season is approaching. In that sense, diesel in particular is currently the biggest concern both in Europe and globally. Inventories are low and that is certainly having the greatest impact on diesel prices," Kärsna said.

If high prices persist, their impact will no longer be limited to higher fuel bills for drivers. Rising diesel prices increase transportation costs, which then feed through into the prices of goods and services.

"Goods are generally transported by diesel-powered vehicles. There is a concern that high diesel prices could start spilling over into everything else. Estonia is one thing, but there is also the broader European picture. If we look at eurozone inflation, there is now speculation in the market that the central bank may be forced to raise interest rates again, perhaps even twice. That would feed through into borrowing costs. So there are more ways in which today's diesel prices could begin to affect people's lives than just what we see at the gas station," said Mihkel Nestor, an economic analyst at SEB.

"Average fuel purchases in liters have fallen slightly because people generally spend about €50 on a single fuel purchase. At today's prices, that buys around 22 to 23 liters of fuel, compared with almost 30 liters during the same period last year, when fuel was considerably cheaper," Vahtrik said.

According to the European Commission, a liter of gasoline cost an average of €2.063 across the EU on September 14, while diesel averaged €2.159 per liter. Based on the latest average prices, filling a 50-liter gasoline tank costs about €103, while filling a diesel tank costs €108.

Both figures were the highest since the European Commission began collecting data in 2005. The previous peak for gasoline was recorded in 2022, while diesel prices last approached their current level in April of this year.

Diesel fuel cost €2.3 per liter in some Estonian filling stations on Monday.
