This calculation covers income tax only. The final amount a worker receives after tax also depends on other mandatory deductions and the tax allowances that apply to them. The changes do not affect workers in all sectors.

If an employer does not increase the gross salary and other deductions remain unchanged, the higher tax will reduce the worker’s take-home pay. To keep take-home pay at the same level, an employer may need to increase its labour costs.

Will higher social payments offset the higher tax burden?

Vugar Bayramov, a member of the Milli Majlis Economic Policy Committee, views the expected increase in the share of non-oil revenues to more than 60% positively. He considers this important for budget sustainability. According to him, structural reforms and greater transparency in public procurement could allow the government to allocate additional funds to social needs.

Economist Natig Jafarli said on 8 September, before the publication of the preliminary budget figures, that he expected pensions and salaries for public-sector employees to rise by 8–10%. He stressed that higher social payments sometimes only offset rising prices. This is the economist’s expectation.

Even if such increases take place, it cannot be said that they will offset the additional tax burden on private-sector employees. Higher salaries, pensions and benefits affect different groups of the population.

The preliminary figures point to the following trend: as transfers from the State Oil Fund decline, the government plans to increase tax revenues. What this will mean for citizens will depend on which services receive the additional funding, as well as on how their incomes and everyday expenses change.

Azerbaijan’s 2027 budget

World.title: Azerbaijan security service terrorism case spans five countries – what  is known so far?
World.content:
Azerbaijan security service operation in five countries

Azerbaijan says money collected for religious ceremonies was transferred to terrorist organisations using cryptocurrency. In a statement issued on 18 September, the State Security Service (SSS) said the alleged financing scheme and preparations to assassinate public and religious figures were being investigated as part of the same criminal case.

However, the statement published by the media does not specify the amount of money involved, the organisations alleged to have received it, or the five countries where the operations were carried out.

Information available from open sources does not allow the scale of the case to be independently verified. Available reports largely repeat the account provided by the agency conducting the investigation.

Charges brought

The SSS named the defendants as Vugar Abdullayev, Jalal Hajiyev, Javid Aliyev, Nijat Ahmadov, Nazim Aliyev, Ilkin Hasanzade, Aykhan Huseynov, Elshan Asgarov, Fakhraddin Imanov, Nail Rasulov and Elgun Ismayilov. Although the statement says 10 people were detained, it lists 11 defendants. The reason for the discrepancy is not explained.

They have been charged under Criminal Code articles relating to financing terrorism, forming a criminal organisation, preparing an assassination attempt against a state or public figure, and other offences. According to the SSS, a court ordered the defendants to be remanded in custody.

Link between two strands of case

In the SSS account, Jalal Hajiyev’s name appears both in connection with the alleged assassination plot and the financing scheme. The agency says Vugar Abdullayev and other defendants gathered information about the movements and security arrangements of the alleged targets. Hajiyev, meanwhile, is alleged to have used his contacts abroad to arrange money transfers to people involved in armed conflicts, as well as to terrorist organisations.

Although the two strands are being investigated as part of the same case, the SSS does not specify how they are linked financially. Were the funds allegedly transferred abroad used to finance preparations for the assassination attempts in Azerbaijan? Although some of the same individuals feature in both strands of the case, no evidence has been presented to establish a link between the movement of funds and the planning of the alleged attacks.

How was money traced?

According to the SSS, the funds were collected through fake s posted on social media, purportedly seeking donations for religious ceremonies. The agency says investigators obtained evidence showing where the money came from and how it was transferred.

To independently assess these claims, key evidence would include an archive of the s, payment details, transaction dates and information about the recipients. It is also unclear whether those who transferred the money knew its alleged true purpose or were themselves deceived – a distinction that could imply different degrees of responsibility.

The reference to cryptocurrency alone does not explain how the alleged financing scheme worked. The SSS does not say which digital assets were used, who controlled the addresses involved in the transactions, or how investigators established links between the recipients and terrorist organisations.

A 2023 report by the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) describes the risks of social media fundraising and the use of virtual assets for terrorist financing. It also highlights the difficulty of proving that funds were intended for terrorist purposes and stresses the importance of protecting legitimate charitable activity.

International experience suggests that the mechanism described by the SSS is possible in principle. However, the allegations against specific individuals would need to be supported by evidence in the criminal case. So far, that evidence has not been made public.

World.title: Abkhaz punk rock: TOM SQUARE leader Salima Sagaria tells her story – VIDEO
World.content:
Punk rock in Abkhazia

This story is about a rare phenomenon: Abkhaz punk. Salima Sagaria and her band TOM SQUARE could be described as unique.

Salima began her career in pop music and turned to punk several years ago.

“People say different things to me. Many are supportive and say they are glad that this kind of music has finally appeared in Abkhazia. But there is also a lot of hate. At the beginning of the year, I posted a clip from my new song online. I wasn’t wearing any make-up, I was in ordinary clothes at home, just sitting there and shaking my hair around. For some reason, that really shocked a lot of people. I received threats and was even cursed.

“Our latest track is about exactly that: why so many people are afraid of change, and why our society does not want to move forward and change. This attachment to tradition also manifests itself in preventing creative people from expressing themselves,” Salima says.

“But I’m going to keep going, releasing new tracks and mixing different styles. I want to bring traditional instruments and choir into punk rock. I like introducing something new.”

World.title: Lindsay Clancy's lawyer asks judge to investigate lone holdout juror
World.content:
A lawyer for Lindsay Clancy has asked a judge to investigate the conduct of the lone juror who wanted to convict the Massachusetts woman of murder in the deaths of her three young children.

Warning: This story contains details that may be distressing for some readers.

In a motion filed Friday but made public Monday, local time, Ms Clancy's lawyer asked the court to question juror Michael Desronvil about his alleged use of a mobile phone during deliberations, along with his truthfulness on a questionnaire that prospective jurors filled out before the trial and when jurors were questioned by the judge a day before the trial ended.

Among other things, lawyer Kevin Reddington asked the court to obtain a record of any calls or texts Mr Desronvil made between 8am and 4:30pm on each day the jury deliberated. Phone use during deliberations is prohibited in the state.

Mr Reddington is calling for the motion to be heard at the next scheduled hearing on September 29.

Kevin Reddington has asked the court to investigate the lone juror's phone use and truthfulness when he was questioned by the judge. (AP: Charles Krupa)

The judge declared a mistrial earlier this month after the jury insisted it could not reach a unanimous verdict, despite days of trying.

Eleven of 12 jurors were ready to clear Ms Clancy of criminal responsibility, with the majority feeling that she was in the grip of a rare condition called postpartum psychosis when she killed her children.

Holdout juror in Lindsay Clancy trial speaks The lone juror who wanted to convict Lindsay Clancy of murder for killing her three children said he was certain of her guilt, but that other jurors would not listen to him.

But Mr Desronvil sided with the prosecutors, who had argued Ms Clancy knew what she was doing.

"I didn't have any doubts," Mr Desronvil said in a statement released on X by his lawyer, Edward Paltzik.

The jury's foreperson had claimed in an earlier media interview that Mr Desronvil had admitted having "reasonable doubt" about Ms Clancy's guilt but wanted to convict her anyway. Mr Desronvil said that was not true.

"As I tried to explain different possible theories during deliberation, I kept getting cut off as if I had doubts based on the evidence presented," he wrote.

" Based on all the physical evidence, key witnesses, and what the prosecution presented, I thought it was enough proof that [Ms Clancy] knew exactly what she was doing. "

Mr Desronvil has not been accused of any wrongdoing in connection with his service on the jury, though other jurors complained that he was inflexible in his opinion that Ms Clancy was guilty.

Since the trial ended, Mr Desronvil has been both publicly praised and scorned for his actions, and his personal life and past financial and legal problems have become the subject of scrutiny by the news media and amateur sleuths.

The public revelations include he had a restraining order against him at the time of jury selection and was facing eviction from his apartment due to over $US12,000 ($16,800) in unpaid rent. He also was accused of domestic violence in 2021, a charge that was later dismissed.

He also has been embraced by those who feel Ms Clancy should be found guilty. A fundraiser to cover what organisers say are costs of "security, lawyers, and lost work" for Mr Desronvil has raised nearly $US375,000 ($526,600).

Judge asked to dismiss case

Prosecutors have yet to say whether they plan on putting Ms Clancy on trial again. She remains charged with murder and is in a psychiatric hospital until her case is resolved.

In another motion on Monday, another lawyer for Ms Clancy, Martin Weinberg, asked the judge to take the unusual step of dismissing the criminal case, rather than putting on a new trial, on the grounds that a mistrial should not have been declared in the first place.

The jury's deadlock forced the judge to declare a mistrial on September 4, leaving the case unresolved. (AP: Greg Derr/The Patriot Ledger/Pool)

Mr Weinberg argued that the judge should have replaced the holdout juror with an alternate during the deliberations after a jury foreperson complained to the judge that one juror was refusing to listen to the law on reasonable doubt.

"Contrary to the court's stated believe [sic] at the time, it did have viable choices other than declaring a mistrial," Mr Weinberg wrote.

That follows an earlier motion filed by Ms Clancy's legal team arguing that she should not be tried a second time because prosecutors do not have enough evidence.

Under Massachusetts law, prosecutors had to prove either that Ms Clancy did not have a mental disease or defect or that, despite having one, she retained the capacity to know what she was doing when she killed her children.

Mr Reddington argued in Thursday's court filing that prosecutors proved neither.

A spokesperson for Plymouth County District Attorney Timothy Cruz would not comment on the motions.

AP

World.title: 13yo Mount Isa bull rider sets sights on Texas
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Inside the Kalkadoon Arena, in the heart of Queensland's wild north-west, courage can be measured in eight seconds.

The Mount Isa Rodeo is the biggest in the Southern Hemisphere and this year some of its youngest riders made the biggest impression.

Kalkadoon and Pitta Pitta cowgirl Lareece Daley-Kennedy, 13, is preparing to step onto the international stage after receiving invitations to two youth world finals in the United States.

Bull riding runs in the family for Lareece Daly-Kennedy, who took up the sport after hearing stories about her dad's rodeo days. (Supplied: Pete Wallis)

She has been invited to compete at the Professional Youth Roughstock Association World Finals in Oklahoma and the World Championship Mini Bulls World Finals in Texas.

The invitations follow a string of strong performances across the North West, including a second-place finish on her first steer ride earlier this year.

At this year's Mount Isa Rodeo she came just short of the buzzer in the Mount Isa round before returning to place third in the Indigenous mini bulls.

Lareece Daley-Kennedy prepares to ride at the Mount Isa Rodeo. (Supplied: Pete Wallis)

Now the Mount Isa Rodeo is putting real weight behind that next generation, committing $10,000 to help get Lareece to the United States.

It is the first time the incumbent board has directly backed a young rider in this way.

For Lareece, the secret to lasting eight seconds is simple.

"Just lock your knees in and your legs and just hold on," she said.

Lareece was not the only young rider to impress.

Cloncurry brothers Dallas and Ashley Murphy, aged 10 and 14, swept the mini bull titles.

Cloncurry brothers Dallas (10) and Ashley (14) Murphy won the mini bull titles. (Supplied: Pete Wallis)

Cade Ferguson, 19, was crowned the rodeo's all-round cowboy, just weeks after becoming world champion in bull riding and reserve world champion in saddle bronc at the Cinch World Championship Junior Rodeo in Oklahoma.

Cloncurry's Cade Ferguson (19) was crowned the Mount Isa Rodeo’s all-round cowboy. (Supplied: Pete Wallis)

In her father's footsteps

Lareece took up riding after hearing stories about her father Nathan Kennedy's own days in the sport.

"I just wanted to follow my dad's footsteps," she said.

Lareece Daley-Kennedy embraces her father Nathan Kennedy after coming third at the Mount Isa Rodeo. (Supplied: Mount Isa Mines Rodeo )

The sport has taught her how to take a hard landing and get back up.

Earlier this year she was winded on her first steer ride and last year at Cloncurry she was thrown and landed on her neck.

"I'd heard people say, 'Oh, she came second', and I just got up like nothing happened," she said.

Her family initially set out to raise about $15,000 to make the trip to the US possible, with supporters across the north-west chipping in through raffles and donations.

Then came the call from the Mount Isa Rodeo to the shock and delight of her family.

"Blew me away, made me cry actually," Mr Kennedy said.

"It's got us there. It's got us over the line."

Backing the young ones

The junior clinic teaches young riders safety, technique and competition skills. (Supplied: Pete Wallis)

The Mount Isa Rodeo has already had to fight for its own future.

The event fell into voluntary administration in September 2024, before a group of residents rallied to revive it for last year, bringing it back before a record crowd.

Now the board is turning its attention to the riders coming through.

Mount Isa Rodeo vice-chair Marcus Curr said developing young riders was becoming an important part of the organisation's future.

Marcus Curr says supporting young riders is an important part of the rodeo's future. (Supplied: Marcus Curr)

"A lot of kids in the bush … don't get to play cricket and football as much as city kids do," he said.

"So rodeo is a big part of their life and their culture."

The board runs an annual junior clinic where young people including children from remote communities learn about safety, technique and competition.

Young riders learn early that rodeo takes courage — and knowing how to get back up. (Supplied: Pete Wallis)

Mr Curr estimated about 50 children attended this year.

Smaller rodeos across the region also give young competitors somewhere to build their skills before stepping into the Kalkadoon Arena.

Mr Curr said the Murphy brothers and Cade Ferguson were examples of what can happen when talent was matched with family support and opportunities to compete.

"If there's talent around, we've got to support them and encourage them and give them opportunities," he said.

About 50 riders took part in this year’s junior clinic. (Supplied: Pete Wallis)

Beyond the Kalkadoon Arena

Mr Curr said he wanted the Mount Isa Rodeo to become "more than just running a rodeo for the weekend".

Young riders are being given opportunities to develop their skills. (Supplied: Pete Wallis)

"It's about investing in opportunities for kids and having Mount Isa Rodeo being a part of Australia developing some of the best cowboys and cowgirls in the world," he said.

For Lareece, one of those opportunities is already waiting in the United States, with plenty of pressure and expectation.

But ask what she loves most about bull riding and the answer is much simpler.

" Winning and holding on. "

World.title: Tarik had to break his favourite rare instrument to make another
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Tarik Hussein thinks there were only 10 kanuns in Australia when he began playing in 2006.

The Sydney musician and engineer says he grew up playing the piano and guitar, and discovered the kanun when he was 17 years old.

The kanun is a precursor to the piano, played by plucking 78 strings with the fingers while it lays across the player's lap.

The kanun is a centuries-old instrument from the Middle East. (ABC News: Declan Bowring)

Mr Hussein says it is impossible to find kanuns in Australia, so when he started teaching the instrument, he needed to get them imported from Türkiye.

He says because the instruments are generally quite old and rare, they would often get damaged in transit or wear out quickly.

"They would have a lot of issues with the skin tearing and the bridge collapsing," he says.

Tarik Hussein and his father-in-law learned how to build kanuns by pulling one apart. (ABC News: Declan Bowring)

To avoid this, Mr Hussein resolved to become the only maker of kanuns in Australia, enlisting the help of his father-in-law, who had a functioning home workshop and a passion for challenging craft projects.

"His woodworking skills helped me to maintain the instruments and repair the instruments," Mr Hussein says.

" And then I thought to challenge him and ask if he'd be willing to try to make one together. "

Having played the kanun since he was 17, Tarik Hussein now teaches it. (ABC News: Declan Bowring)

Mr Hussein said making a kanun was something of a close-guarded secret among the makers in Türkiye, so they reverse-engineered his favourite one.

"He pretty much pulled my favourite one completely apart. It was actually very heartbreaking to see," he said.

"We came up with something that I would say is quite unique. It's not the same as what you'd get overseas.

" It's more, it's more of an Australian version of the kanun. "

The kanun is seen as a forerunner to the piano. (ABC News: Declan Bowring)

Mr Hussein says as far as they can tell, they are the only kanun makers in Australia.

But they do this as a labour of love, not as a commercial outfit.

"We spend more than a year or two per instrument," Mr Hussein said.

"Then, seeing my students' face light up when I tell them that this is something that we built here, and they're going to learn on that. That really brings me joy."

Exceptional stories in items in the suburbs

Mr Hussein and his father-in-law's personal connection with kanuns features in a new film series launching with a festival marking the opening of Powerhouse Parramatta on November 7.

The series of short films, called Moments in Waiting, is by western Sydney artist Khaled Sabsabi and focuses on significant objects from the Islamic world found in Sydney's suburbs.

Western Sydney artist Khaled Sabsabi produced the film collection Moments in Waiting. (ABC News: Jade Barker)

Mr Sabsabi says he found the extraordinary in the ordinary after a series of public call-outs over the past few years.

"It is about not just the objects, but also the stories that are contained within those objects," he said.

" It's a way to bring out these stories and share them with broader Australian communities. "

Mr Sabsabi says Mr Hussein's story shaped up as a modern Australian experience of migration and cultural diversity.

"We come together and, from various places, we bring our technologies, our stories, our being, to shape a modern contemporary Australian identity," he said.

Mr Hussein will also perform on his kanun with the Three Rivers Ensemble during the opening festival.

The recently announced festival spans 179 events across four weekends in November, including a talk by veteran astronaut Charles F Bolden Jr, a major performance by a Torres Strait Island group for the first time outside of the islands, and a Diwali day party.

A collection that rivals a museum

Among the stories in Moments in Waiting is a decree from the Ottoman Empire written in four languages that found its way to Australia when the owner fled the early 1990s war in Bosnia.

The series also features an entire home in Bonyrigg in Sydney's south-west that at one point served as a mosque and produced the Australian Muslim Times.

Mohamad Ali has an extensive collection of calligraphic manuscipts. (Supplied: Powerhouse Parramatta)

There's also a collection of more than 100 calligraphic manuscripts of the Koran that rivals any Australian museum collection, owned by Sydney teacher Mohamad Ali.

Mr Ali said he had extensively collected vinyl, cassettes and T-shirts of artists such as Madonna, Prince and Eurythmics before finding an interest in Islam in his 20s, when he saw an exhibition by Persian-born collector Nasser David Khalili.

He became fascinated with the intricate work of calligraphers, who would likely have taken years to write a 600-page Koran.

"For them, it was a journey — a spiritual journey," Mr Ali said.

Some of the manuscripts in Mohamad Ali's collection go back 1,200 years. (Supplied: Powerhouse Parramatta)

"I just wanted to learn a little bit more about the scribing process … but then that led me to a greater understanding, or a deeper understanding, of what my own personal faith was about."

Mr Ali's extensive collection goes as far back as the 8th century, encompassing many Islamic empires and dynasties.

He hopes the story of his collection will go beyond the Islamic community and create a greater appreciation for the cultural impact of Islam on the world, in art and education.

"Islam's got a lot, and has always had a lot, to contribute to the world's existence," Mr Ali said.

World.title: Formula 1 agrees to shorter races in 2027
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Formula 1 has approved a 15 kilometre reduction in official race distances starting next season.

The change means the total distance will be cut from 305 to 290 kilometres.

The Formula 1 Commission finalised the decision in London.

"In line with the refinements to the power unit regulations to be introduced in 2027 on fuel flow, a reduction in the total race distance from 305km to 290km was approved, corresponding to a reduction of two or three laps," a statement read.

Aussie F1 GP loses season-opening honour Melbourne's Australian Grand Prix will not have the privilege of opening the 2027 Formula 1 season, but it will boast two races in its biggest weekend yet.

The power unit regulations favour increased engine power over hybrid electrical output.

To better handle rain delays and red flags, the commission has also abolished the strict three-hour overall event cap.

While the two-hour maximum of active racing time remains, the change gives organisers flexibility to complete full race distances.

Another objective ‌is to give spectators the best possible chance ‌to enjoy a full race when disruptions occur.

Practice sessions will also gain added flexibility to extend following stoppages.

AP/Reuters

World.title: Consumers duped by price comparison websites, ASIC warns
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Australians hunting bargains on comparison websites risk being duped by sites that only offer a selection of preferred providers.

The corporate watchdog has issued a warning after launching multiple court actions against websites for allegedly misleading consumers about the range of financial services and products on offer and, in some cases, promoting multiple leads from a single brand.

While comparison websites are a good place to start for prices and services information, consumers should conduct deeper research, Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) commissioner Alan Kirkland said.

"The products that are listed by many comparison sites are selected and ordered based on what the product providers pay to the comparison sites, and they may not give you a full view of the market," Mr Kirkland said.

" It's important to actually use a range of comparison sites in order to get a fuller view of the market. "

The Federal Court recently found comparison site Choosi — which offers life, funeral, income protection and health insurance products — misled consumers over four years from mid-2019 after claiming to compare a slew of funeral and life insurance policies, when Hannover Life Re issued all but one of the policies offered.

Every single policy in question was distributed by Greenstone Financial Services, a company linked with Choosi.

The court has not set a date to hand down Choosi's penalty, but an administrative hearing will be held later on Tuesday.

Warning shot fired

The watchdog launched a case on Friday against lead-generating business Clark Family Pty Ltd, which offers free online assessments for loans and insurance products.

The commission alleges up to 70 of its websites misled consumers by claiming to compare rates and options from multiple providers and providing consumers "tailored" recommendations.

Loading...

"In reality, consumers' inquiries were (allegedly) sold to the highest-bidding broker," Mr Kirkland said.

With Australians already struggling with cost-of-living pressures and stubborn inflation, the court actions are a warning shot across the bow to the price comparison platform market.

"We've got very strong laws in Australia against making false or misleading representations about the products that you provide to consumers," Mr Kirkland said.

" Where we find comparison sites misleading consumers, we will take action. "

Consumers must also be alert to service agreements to ensure they do not sign away their private data with a click.

"Your information may not be used solely for the purpose of the comparison that you're seeking," Mr Kirkland said.

"Your personal details may be sold to another business, and you may then find yourself the subject of telemarketing calls or marketing emails as a result of your information being sold on."

AAP

World.title: Half of 'ecologically thinned' trees from WA forests chipped or burned
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

More than half of the trees harvested through Western Australia's ecological thinning trial are being chipped or burned, according to new information tabled in state parliament.

Native logging was officially banned in WA in 2024, resulting in mill closures and job losses in historic timber communities.

Soon after that the Department of Biodiversity, Conservation and Attractions (DBCA) began the ecological thinning trial, which involves the strategic removal of trees to alleviate water stress and ecological imbalance in regrowing forests.

The practice has been criticised by an independent scientist and environmentalists, who argue the approach is driven by profit rather than environmental benefit.

Ecological thinning began in WA in 2024. (ABC South West WA: Neve Brissenden)

Commercial users revealed

The state-owned Forest Products Commission (FPC) did not answer repeated questions about the commercial buyers of timber harvested from the program.

The uses of ecologically thinned wood were revealed in WA's Legislative Council last week, in response to questions from Greens MLC Jess Beckerling.

Since the beginning of the program in 2024, 58.6 per cent of thinned wood is being chipped or burned.

Some 93,510 tonnes have gone to the Japanese-owned company Simcoa, which relies on the wood to manufacture silicon at the Kemerton industrial estate.

Perth-based laminated lumber manufacturer Wesbeam is the next-highest buyer, purchasing 41,670 tonnes.

Woodchips at WAPRES Preston milling facility in Bunbury. (ABC South West WA: Neve Brissenden)

Japanese-owned company WA Plantation Resources (WAPRES), previously known as WA Chip and Pulp, has purchased 22,688 tonnes.

The company exports 1 million tonnes of woodchips a year to Japan and China.

WAPRES chief executive Ian Telfer said no ecologically thinned wood had been chipped and exported overseas.

"It is a viable market, but certainly at the moment, despite any other hysteria there is, we're not receiving or exporting any fibre," he said.

" But we would hope to be doing so as ecological thinning increases in accordance with the forest management plan. "

Mr Telfer said a 28-tonne consignment of raw jarrah logs was exported to China as part of a trial this year.

Forestry Minister Jackie Jarvis said that trial was a "one-off".

"[This was] to inform the development of alternative local wood-processing opportunities that maximise the value of jarrah log typically too small for milling," she said.

Ms Jarvis said the government was working to ensure the wood harvested in ecological thinning was being put to "productive use".

Motives of thinning questioned

Ms Beckerling said the public was being deceived about the program.

"It absolutely should not be going overseas in whole log form and it should absolutely not be going to woodchip or charcoal unless that is genuinely the only possible use," she said.

Jess Beckerling says the government's lack of transparency is concerning. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

" The WA public has every reason to be really concerned about what's going on with thinning because there's been a significant lack of transparency. "

Jason Fowler says the stated approach of the strategy is being undermined. (ABC Great Southern: Mark Bennett)

West Australian Forest Alliance convenor Jason Fowler said the end uses of the wood were contributing to carbon emissions, negating any net environmental benefits of the trial.

"It is quite alarming because we can see that at least half of it or more is being burnt straight away," he said.

"That means that the carbon is released and it contributes to climate change, which speeds up the stress and pressure on those forests."

Scaling up the trial

The ecological thinning trial increased its output by more than 70 per cent in the past year.

In 2024/25 73,307 tonnes of ecologically thinned wood was harvested.

In 2025/2026 the amount increased to 124,922.

But Mr Telfer, who is also president of the Forest Industries Federation of WA, rejected suggestions from activists that the trial was being driven by an industry keen to replace native logging.

An ecologically thinned site near Pemberton in WA's South West. (ABC South West WA: Neve Brissenden)

"It's a coordinated operation but it's not driven by industry, it's not driven by commercial utilisation," he said.

"It's driven by the forest management and healthy forest objectives of the state government."

The ecological thinning trial is set to be reviewed over the next two years.

World.title: Teacher receives $1.3m payout over mob attack at Marist
World.content:
NationalQueenslandEducation Teacher receives $1.3m payout over mob attack at Marist Julius Dennis September 22, 2026 — 8:53am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A Brisbane teacher who says she suffered permanent injuries after she was allegedly attacked by a mob of food-throwing private school boys has received a $1.27 million payout. Victoria Sparrow took Marist College Ashgrove to the Supreme Court of Queensland over allegations she had been surrounded by up to 300 students in October 2023, leading to injuries she said doctors told her would stop her from working as teacher again. In a statement on Tuesday she said she had accepted the WorkCover compensation rather than fight the school’s national organisation Marist Schools Australia and their “unlimited resources”. The incident led to a cultural review at the school. Marist College Ashgrove “I have made that choice knowing that I need costly ongoing specialist treatment, both now and for many years ahead,” she said.



“I hope one day to return to some form of employment despite my permanent injuries preventing me from ever teaching again.” Sparrow’s case accused the school of fostering misogyny, and sparked a review of the all-boys school’s workplace culture. Sparrow’s barrister, Gerard Forde, said the drama teacher was supervising students on lunch when the alleged incident occurred. In her statement, Sparrow said she was “surrounded by young men, some standing on chairs and tables, inches above her, chanting and yelling loudly”. Forde told the Supreme Court Sparrow’s psychological injuries were due to both the incident itself and how the school treated her afterwards.



Rick Green, the barrister representing the school, argued the allegations about the culture of misogyny were irrelevant. In a letter sent to school staff on Monday, Acting Head of College Paul Blinkoff said the payout made no finding of wrongdoing by the school. Marist head of school Michael Newman allegedly said “boys will be boys” following the incident. Marist College Ashgrove “Throughout this process Marist College Ashgrove and Marist Schools Australia have engaged from a position of respect for Ms Sparrow and for what she said of her experience and the effect it had on her,” he wrote. “We apologise to Ms Sparrow for her experience and its impact, and we earnestly hope that the resolution of this matter today provides her a foundation for healing and assists her recovery.”



In her statement, Sparrow thanked Spillane and former Marist teacher Stan Kosiek, who previously took the school to the Fair Work Commission over an unfair dismissal claim. “I would like to thank two special people: Madonna Spillane, an incredibly brave co-worker who was prepared to stand right beside me ... and the inspirational Stan Kosiek … he is genuinely someone young men can look up to,” she said. Marist College Ashgrove has been contacted for comment. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Surprise! Putin just won the Russian elections. But his biggest win was elsewhere
World.content:
Analysis WorldEuropePutin's Russia Surprise! Putin just won the Russian elections. But his biggest win was elsewhere David Crowe September 22, 2026 — 8:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: There were no shocks in Moscow on Monday when Vladimir Putin’s allies declared victory in elections that gave them almost 80 per cent of the seats in the national parliament. All the political shocks are elsewhere in Europe. Right now, none are greater than the upheavals in Germany, where voters are deserting Chancellor Friedrich Merz and seeking salvation from the hard right. Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow on Monday. AP And there is a direct link from the ballot boxes to the bombs falling in Europe’s worst conflict since World War II. In Russia, the election result was predictable for a country ruled so long by an autocrat whose enemies have a habit of falling out of windows from great heights.



If anything, the minor surprise was that Putin’s party, United Russia, only gained 58 per cent of the vote. How could 42 per cent be allowed to choose anyone else? This helped prop up the democratic facade, of course. It did not have any broader meaning because United Russia gained overwhelming control of the parliament, the Duma, with 355 of the 450 seats. Related Article Russia-Ukraine war ‘Total war’: The human face of the assault on Ukraine Anyone who seriously challenged Putin, or opposed the war in Ukraine, was simply not on the ballot. Putin’s spokesman, Dmitry Peskov, took all this as proof the people backed their leader. “These indicators, of course, point to the highest level of consolidation within Russian society around the head of state,” Peskov told journalists in Moscow.



European leaders, however, called it out as a fraud. “The so-called Duma elections marked another major setback for Russian democracy. Their outcome was never in doubt,” said Kaja Kallas, the former Estonian prime minister and the European Union’s high representative for foreign affairs. “The Kremlin silenced dissent, barred the only registered party that opposed its war in Ukraine, and shut out international election monitors.” Ukraine has stepped up its long-range bombardment of the Moscow region and its oil refineries, like this one on Sunday. AP While the election is an unreliable guide to Russian sentiment, there are other ways to measure opinions about Putin. There was, for instance, the revolt led by former presidential favourite Yevgeny Prigozhin, with his Wagner Group mercenaries, three years ago.



Prigozhin failed in his attempt to march on Moscow, and he died in an aircraft explosion a few months later, but his uprising was a reminder of the constant threat to Putin. If the president were adored, he would not need to hide his physical location or send impersonators to act on his behalf at public events. Related Article Exclusive

Russia-Ukraine war ‘We are made of iron’: The workers who keep trains running under fire The election outcome does not change Putin’s long-term strategy of applying pressure on Europe in the hope he will one day absorb Ukraine into his concept of greater Russia. It is not just that he will approve civilian deaths from Russian drone and missile strikes on Kyiv and other cities. It is that he will intensify “hybrid” warfare on the West, such as a drone attack on a German airport, a cut to internet cables on the sea floor and a drone incursion into Lithuanian airspace. Putin not only gained strength in the Russian parliament on Monday. He also gained some more support in the American capital.



Donald Trump once again complained about Ukraine as if it were hurting global energy markets. The US president first said this a week ago when he publicly urged his Ukrainian counterpart, Volodymyr Zelensky, to stop attacking Russian oil refineries. “He’s causing a shortage of diesel,” Trump said during a visit to Ireland on September 14. Related Article Russia-Ukraine war The new terror stalking Kyiv day and night Trump put the complaint directly to Zelensky in a phone call, according to The Financial Times. Then he took to social media to express his exasperation. “Russia has unfortunately lost control of its Diesel Oil Industry due to its War with Ukraine,” Trump said. “A large number of their Diesel refineries have been blown up and are, at least temporarily, out of commission. This ridiculous and never ending War with Ukraine must be ended.” Never mind that Trump launched a war on Iran that sent oil prices soaring.



Trump has gained more power to halt the war in Ukraine if he chooses: the US Congress just passed the Lindsey Graham bill to allow tougher sanctions against Russia and the customers who buy its oil – including India and China. There are times when Trump talks tough about Putin. In most of his actions, however, he clearly seeks to trade away Ukrainian sovereignty in pursuit of a deal, even if that means emboldening Putin and heightening future risks to Western Europe. Putin will hope for help from the White House in forcing a peace deal in Ukraine on his terms. The question is whether he might one day gain the same help in the European capitals. For now, most European leaders display total unity against Putin. Leaders from Britain, France, Germany, Italy, Spain and Poland will not play nice with the Russian president. On Monday, the European Union disbursed another €3.3 billion ($5.3 billion) to Ukraine to fund military supplies under a €90 billion support loan. Europe faces electoral shift The electoral shocks in Germany, however, highlight how European leaders are trying to stand firm as the ground shifts beneath their feet.



German voters rallied to the hard right in state elections in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania on Sunday, following a similar shift in Saxony-Anhalt two weeks earlier. Voters are deserting Germany’s Chancellor Friedrich Merz. Bloomberg The biggest winner in both elections was the AfD, or Alternative for Germany. It got 37.9 per cent of the vote in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, a region east of Hamburg, and 43.8 per cent in Saxony-Anhalt, in the centre of the country. Even in Berlin, which held a regional election on Sunday, the AfD gained 16.2 per cent of the vote. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz rightly called this a “disaster” for his party, the Christian Democratic Union. He insists he will stay on, despite speculation about a party spill to install a more popular leader.



Related Article Analysis

World elections Election shockwave: Meet the smiling new leader set to bring hard-right upheaval to Germany But the political upheaval is not about whether Merz stands or falls. It is about the collapse of the old centre parties and the rush by voters to the political edges: to the right (mostly the AfD) and the far left (to Die Linke, which incorporates Communist factions). If the AfD continues its rise in national elections due by 2029, the result will be a dramatic change in policy on Russia. If this is the future, Putin may hold out hope he can one day negotiate with friendlier leaders in at least some parts of Western Europe. It is too early to make sweeping forecasts. It was only a few months ago that voters in Hungary swept away Viktor Orbán, one of Putin’s greatest friends in the EU. Last week, she blamed Moscow for trying to interfere in French politics.



“We will never tolerate a foreign power, in this case Russia, hoping to dictate our country’s policy directly or indirectly through intimidation, threats, destabilisation, or psychological pressure,” Le Pen said in a statement with her party president, Jordan Bardella. World.title: Gianni Infantino open to FIFA reform ahead of 2027 elections
World.content:
SportSoccerFIFA Gianni Infantino open to FIFA reform ahead of 2027 elections Jeremy Wilson September 22, 2026 — 8:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Gianni Infantino, the FIFA president, has suggested a review of the world governing body’s decision-making and governance as he tries to gather support ahead of next year’s election. In a letter addressed to the 211 member associations, Infantino acknowledged the backlash against the proposal to sell off stakes in FIFA competitions and set out a series of proposals that would formalise consultation with federations. FIFA boss Gianni Infantino. Getty Images Despite being under intense pressure to stand down after scrapping the so-called FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal, Infantino has confirmed that he will seek re-election next year. The leaders of UEFA, the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) and Concacaf, which represents North, Central America and Caribbean football, accused Infantino of “deception” in an open letter last month, but it is unclear how many of their individual federations will vote for an alternative. Infantino has now written directly to the heads of national associations to propose a series of reforms.



“First, I will ask the council whether it wishes to commission an independent external review of FIFA’s current governance framework for major strategic initiatives and recommend potential improvements,” he wrote, adding that he will also “propose that the [FIFA] Council establish a direct, structured and time-limited consultation with confederations, member associations and relevant stakeholders on how FIFA’s decision-making can be further strengthened. “The consultation would invite specific proposals on earlier institutional involvement, the respective roles of the President, the Bureau, the Council and the Congress, and practical ways to strengthen transparency, participation and accountability in major strategic initiatives.” FIFA president Gianni Infantino and US president Donald Trump at the FIFA World Cup final. Getty Images Infantino has asked for the initial proposals to be considered at the council meeting scheduled for October 15. Infantino replaced Sepp Blatter as president of FIFA in 2016 but has faced calls to resign after proposals to create a commercial subsidiary to run its biggest events, such as the World Cup and Club World Cup, were leaked in July.



Related Article Australian soccer Maty Ryan on outer as Socceroos call up seven uncapped players for Brazil series European football’s governing body UEFA responded by threatening to boycott FIFA competitions. It later suspended that threat, but has urged Infantino to resign and has taken legal action while calling for an investigation. In his letter to members, Infantino said that the idea to sell a stake in the World Cup was only ever a proposal. “I recognise that, without the full context, this caused concern and created the impression that decisions had already been taken. They had not,” he wrote. “It remained a proposal, not a decision, and was always subject to the necessary approvals of the council and the member associations. It has now been withdrawn and will not proceed.” Infantino is so far the only candidate to have put his name forward for the election next March. The Telegraph, London

World.title: The proposed fire team reshuffle set to trim a quarter of (vacant) roles
World.content:
NationalQueenslandPublic service The proposed fire team reshuffle set to trim a quarter of (vacant) roles Matt Dennien Updated September 22, 2026 — 8:27am ,first published 7:59pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Welcome to Brisbane Times’ Queensland public sector column, Public Circus. This week: a shake-up for some in the Fire Department, free-text feedback and child safety watchdog cash questions. The phrase “proposed organisational change” is enough to raise the hackles of most working in a place large enough to support such an occasional reshuffling. Particularly in an environment, across the Queensland public sector, with agencies scratching for all the cash they can. So spare a thought for some of the folks over in Commissioner Steve Smith’s Queensland Fire Department. Queensland Fire Department’s (for now) 47-role Asset Services team is responsible for things including the vehicle fleet, uniforms, logistics, capital works and building management. Queensland Fire Department / Facebook The change in question involves the Assets Services team within chief operating officer Dr Rebecca Denning’s Strategy and Corporate Services division, responsible for things including the vehicle fleet, uniforms, logistics, capital works and building management.



Not insignificant stuff to ensure those holding the literal hose can do the work they need to do when a house, business, or large swathe of the state is in flames. So what’s on the cards? An internal document outlining the proposal, which has found its way to the Circus tent, puts the headline at 13 vacant roles being “removed” from the 47-person organisational chart of the group under executive director Adam Green. Queensland Fire Department Commissioner Steve Smith during estimates in July. Queensland Parliament “It has been identified that these roles may no longer be required, and other identified roles have been varied to accommodate the duties and responsibilities of the 13 vacant positions,” the proposal states. A tale almost as old as time itself. The change is said to stem from a recently consulted Asset Operating Model shift, and will also result in some subsequent reshuffling of the team – including the relocation of multiple roles from Kedron, and even one from Caloundra, to the department’s shiny new Albion HQ.





“The QFD supports the Queensland government’s steadfast commitment of no cuts to public sector workforce,” a spokesperson said in a statement. There was no update on that executive review. Free-text feedback flows in Circus’ own Working for Queensland callout Public Circus’ inaugural Working for Queensland survey callout has yielded a number of responses already, so we figured we’d share some initial anonymous (free-text) feedback. The most curious being the word from one tipster that they had got to the end of a Department of Housing and Public Works survey to find … no free-text feedback sections.



A spokesperson for the department confirmed this to have been the case – and noted it had been so since 2024. “The department includes specific agency-related questions which are designed to gather information and feedback which aligns to the department’s strategic direction and to support us measuring performance,” the spinner said in a statement. Another wondered whether the public airing of pointed responses to such prompts, as part of CFMEU inquiry evidence from former Office of Industrial Relations boss Kym Bancroft, may have rattled some current agency chiefs likely to have them land in their inboxes. One former senior manager described the results of the trauma dump as “exactly that … for those who receive it”, suggesting a new section for anyone who answered yes to “are you willing to leave” with a spot to upload your CV and details for a recruiter. There was also the concern raised that the survey could be completed as many times (and under whatever persona) as desired by those with an axe to grind or too much time on their hands – claiming one colleague filled it in 23 times one year.



“Then the executive implement action plans to address low score areas (clue, no action plan will give the whingers a promotion they don’t deserve or a workload that is significantly lower than what a competent person can complete etc) and then wonder why most staff view the survey with complete derision with the lowest score (reliably every year) for, you guessed it, the executive,” a fourth respondent said. While the official surveys – and the reminders to fill them out – might end this week, Circus takes a rolling approach to anyone wishing to vent anonymously to us. So keep it coming below. Child safety ‘intelligence hub’ funding sits outside new watchdog budget Parliamentary consideration of the state’s proposed new child safety watchdog got under way last week, with a committee briefing from Department of Justice figures.



While they largely told us what we already knew about the merged mega commission set to replace the Queensland Family and Child Commission, there was a sliver of new detail. Beyond the fact that work is still very much ongoing to figure out how many folks from agencies beyond Luke Twyford’s QFCC will be seconded into its replacement next year, responses to two questions taken on notice get to some of the pointier questions remaining. The first was how much of the $255 million headline figure from Attorney-General Deb Frecklington’s (albeit qualified) announcement back in June is set to be allocated for staffing and resources. According to the department’s response, published on Monday, that entire figure and the $74 million recurring funding across this and each of the next three financial years will be “primarily” set aside for such purposes. Attorney-General Deb Frecklington and Queensland Family and Child Commissioner Luke Twyford. Courtney Kruk



“Additional resourcing for the new child safeguarding intelligence hub function is subject to further consideration by government and will be informed by the design work, which has commenced,” the department said. As you might imagine, we’ve sung out to Frecklington’s office for some clarification on this rather major detail, and will report back if and when we get it. Another response addressed the question of what other entities, if any, were subject to similar ministerial powers which will allow the dismissal of a new commissioner or their deputies for no reason. While noting it was a “policy decision made by government”, the department noted this reflected the “high level of public trust in these roles and their critical importance in delivering a robust child safeguarding system in Queensland”. And after scouring state laws for other examples, the department found six cohorts also facing no-cause dismissal: Safe Food board members, the Racing Queensland chair, deputy chair or chief executive, hospital and health board members, and the director of Forensic Science Queensland.



Sure. (And we’ll ignore another government bill this year which removed such powers over Stadium’s Queensland board members because the power “does not … align with fundamental legislative principles”.) But on Circus’ reading of the Forensic Science side of things, that power does not, in fact, exist there. While a director can be removed at any time on the minister’s recommendation, there are specific reasons such a call can be made – none of which include, well, “none”. Have a curiosity for the Circus tent? Email on m.dennien@nine.com.au. For more security, sing out with a non-work device and network via Signal (mattdennien.15 or here) and mattdennien@protonmail.com. World.content:
The defining moment of 2025’s gathering of world leaders at the UN may have been Donald Trump’s accusation of “sabotage” after his teleprompter blinked out and an escalator stalled while he was on it.

Now the world body is working overtime to make sure nothing similar happens again to distract from its focus on solving the world’s problems this week. Trump is set to deliver his speech at the UN’s iconic East River headquarters in New York City tonight.

Loading

“It has been checked and rechecked,” UN spokesman Stéphane Dujarric told reporters about the escalator at a briefing, ahead of the high-level General Assembly session.

The UN is anxious for everything to run smoothly a year after Trump called for the arrest of the person who purportedly triggered an escalator to shut down just as he and first lady Melania Trump stepped onto it. At the time, the UN said Trump’s videographer may have been to blame.

World.title: WA news LIVE: WA to ban smart glasses in classrooms
World.content:
Smart glasses will be banned from WA classrooms in an effort to protect teachers and students from being secretly recorded.

The ban will be announced by education minister Sabine Winton this morning, with the prohibition to come into place from the start of Term 4 for all public schools.

Smart glasses can record and even live-stream conversations, vision and images of people, without their knowledge or consent.

Winton said the crackdown was necessary as smart glasses become cheaper and more accessible.

World.title: Teacher receives $1.3m payout over mob attack at Marist
World.content:
NationalQueenslandEducation Teacher receives $1.3m payout over mob attack at Marist Julius Dennis September 22, 2026 — 8:53am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A Brisbane teacher who says she suffered permanent injuries after she was allegedly attacked by a mob of food-throwing private school boys has received a $1.27 million payout. Victoria Sparrow took Marist College Ashgrove to the Supreme Court of Queensland over allegations she had been surrounded by up to 300 students in October 2023, leading to injuries she said doctors told her would stop her from working as teacher again. In a statement on Tuesday she said she had accepted the WorkCover compensation rather than fight the school’s national organisation Marist Schools Australia and their “unlimited resources”. The incident led to a cultural review at the school. Marist College Ashgrove “I have made that choice knowing that I need costly ongoing specialist treatment, both now and for many years ahead,” she said.



“I hope one day to return to some form of employment despite my permanent injuries preventing me from ever teaching again.” Sparrow’s case accused the school of fostering misogyny, and sparked a review of the all-boys school’s workplace culture. Sparrow’s barrister, Gerard Forde, said the drama teacher was supervising students on lunch when the alleged incident occurred. In her statement, Sparrow said she was “surrounded by young men, some standing on chairs and tables, inches above her, chanting and yelling loudly”. Forde told the Supreme Court Sparrow’s psychological injuries were due to both the incident itself and how the school treated her afterwards.



Rick Green, the barrister representing the school, argued the allegations about the culture of misogyny were irrelevant. In a letter sent to school staff on Monday, Acting Head of College Paul Blinkoff said the payout made no finding of wrongdoing by the school. Marist head of school Michael Newman allegedly said “boys will be boys” following the incident. Marist College Ashgrove “Throughout this process Marist College Ashgrove and Marist Schools Australia have engaged from a position of respect for Ms Sparrow and for what she said of her experience and the effect it had on her,” he wrote. “We apologise to Ms Sparrow for her experience and its impact, and we earnestly hope that the resolution of this matter today provides her a foundation for healing and assists her recovery.”



In her statement, Sparrow thanked Spillane and former Marist teacher Stan Kosiek, who previously took the school to the Fair Work Commission over an unfair dismissal claim. “I would like to thank two special people: Madonna Spillane, an incredibly brave co-worker who was prepared to stand right beside me ... and the inspirational Stan Kosiek … he is genuinely someone young men can look up to,” she said. Marist College Ashgrove has been contacted for comment. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

The leaders of UEFA, the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) and Concacaf, which represents North, Central America and Caribbean football, accused Infantino of “deception” in an open letter last month, but it is unclear how many of their individual federations will vote for an alternative. Infantino has now written directly to the heads of national associations to propose a series of reforms.



“First, I will ask the council whether it wishes to commission an independent external review of FIFA’s current governance framework for major strategic initiatives and recommend potential improvements,” he wrote, adding that he will also “propose that the [FIFA] Council establish a direct, structured and time-limited consultation with confederations, member associations and relevant stakeholders on how FIFA’s decision-making can be further strengthened. “The consultation would invite specific proposals on earlier institutional involvement, the respective roles of the President, the Bureau, the Council and the Congress, and practical ways to strengthen transparency, participation and accountability in major strategic initiatives.” FIFA president Gianni Infantino and US president Donald Trump at the FIFA World Cup final. Getty Images Infantino has asked for the initial proposals to be considered at the council meeting scheduled for October 15. Infantino replaced Sepp Blatter as president of FIFA in 2016 but has faced calls to resign after proposals to create a commercial subsidiary to run its biggest events, such as the World Cup and Club World Cup, were leaked in July.



Related Article Australian soccer Maty Ryan on outer as Socceroos call up seven uncapped players for Brazil series European football’s governing body UEFA responded by threatening to boycott FIFA competitions. It later suspended that threat, but has urged Infantino to resign and has taken legal action while calling for an investigation. In his letter to members, Infantino said that the idea to sell a stake in the World Cup was only ever a proposal. “I recognise that, without the full context, this caused concern and created the impression that decisions had already been taken. They had not,” he wrote. “It remained a proposal, not a decision, and was always subject to the necessary approvals of the council and the member associations. It has now been withdrawn and will not proceed.” Infantino is so far the only candidate to have put his name forward for the election next March. The Telegraph, London

World.title: The proposed fire team reshuffle set to trim a quarter of (vacant) roles
World.content:
NationalQueenslandPublic service The proposed fire team reshuffle set to trim a quarter of (vacant) roles Matt Dennien Updated September 22, 2026 — 8:27am ,first published 7:59pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Welcome to Brisbane Times’ Queensland public sector column, Public Circus. This week: a shake-up for some in the Fire Department, free-text feedback and child safety watchdog cash questions. The phrase “proposed organisational change” is enough to raise the hackles of most working in a place large enough to support such an occasional reshuffling. Particularly in an environment, across the Queensland public sector, with agencies scratching for all the cash they can. So spare a thought for some of the folks over in Commissioner Steve Smith’s Queensland Fire Department. Queensland Fire Department’s (for now) 47-role Asset Services team is responsible for things including the vehicle fleet, uniforms, logistics, capital works and building management. Queensland Fire Department / Facebook The change in question involves the Assets Services team within chief operating officer Dr Rebecca Denning’s Strategy and Corporate Services division, responsible for things including the vehicle fleet, uniforms, logistics, capital works and building management.



Not insignificant stuff to ensure those holding the literal hose can do the work they need to do when a house, business, or large swathe of the state is in flames. So what’s on the cards? An internal document outlining the proposal, which has found its way to the Circus tent, puts the headline at 13 vacant roles being “removed” from the 47-person organisational chart of the group under executive director Adam Green. Queensland Fire Department Commissioner Steve Smith during estimates in July. Queensland Parliament “It has been identified that these roles may no longer be required, and other identified roles have been varied to accommodate the duties and responsibilities of the 13 vacant positions,” the proposal states. A tale almost as old as time itself. The change is said to stem from a recently consulted Asset Operating Model shift, and will also result in some subsequent reshuffling of the team – including the relocation of multiple roles from Kedron, and even one from Caloundra, to the department’s shiny new Albion HQ.





“The QFD supports the Queensland government’s steadfast commitment of no cuts to public sector workforce,” a spokesperson said in a statement. There was no update on that executive review. Free-text feedback flows in Circus’ own Working for Queensland callout Public Circus’ inaugural Working for Queensland survey callout has yielded a number of responses already, so we figured we’d share some initial anonymous (free-text) feedback. The most curious being the word from one tipster that they had got to the end of a Department of Housing and Public Works survey to find … no free-text feedback sections.



A spokesperson for the department confirmed this to have been the case – and noted it had been so since 2024. “The department includes specific agency-related questions which are designed to gather information and feedback which aligns to the department’s strategic direction and to support us measuring performance,” the spinner said in a statement. Another wondered whether the public airing of pointed responses to such prompts, as part of CFMEU inquiry evidence from former Office of Industrial Relations boss Kym Bancroft, may have rattled some current agency chiefs likely to have them land in their inboxes. One former senior manager described the results of the trauma dump as “exactly that … for those who receive it”, suggesting a new section for anyone who answered yes to “are you willing to leave” with a spot to upload your CV and details for a recruiter. There was also the concern raised that the survey could be completed as many times (and under whatever persona) as desired by those with an axe to grind or too much time on their hands – claiming one colleague filled it in 23 times one year.



“Then the executive implement action plans to address low score areas (clue, no action plan will give the whingers a promotion they don’t deserve or a workload that is significantly lower than what a competent person can complete etc) and then wonder why most staff view the survey with complete derision with the lowest score (reliably every year) for, you guessed it, the executive,” a fourth respondent said. While the official surveys – and the reminders to fill them out – might end this week, Circus takes a rolling approach to anyone wishing to vent anonymously to us. So keep it coming below. Child safety ‘intelligence hub’ funding sits outside new watchdog budget Parliamentary consideration of the state’s proposed new child safety watchdog got under way last week, with a committee briefing from Department of Justice figures.



While they largely told us what we already knew about the merged mega commission set to replace the Queensland Family and Child Commission, there was a sliver of new detail. Beyond the fact that work is still very much ongoing to figure out how many folks from agencies beyond Luke Twyford’s QFCC will be seconded into its replacement next year, responses to two questions taken on notice get to some of the pointier questions remaining. The first was how much of the $255 million headline figure from Attorney-General Deb Frecklington’s (albeit qualified) announcement back in June is set to be allocated for staffing and resources. According to the department’s response, published on Monday, that entire figure and the $74 million recurring funding across this and each of the next three financial years will be “primarily” set aside for such purposes. Attorney-General Deb Frecklington and Queensland Family and Child Commissioner Luke Twyford. Courtney Kruk



“Additional resourcing for the new child safeguarding intelligence hub function is subject to further consideration by government and will be informed by the design work, which has commenced,” the department said. As you might imagine, we’ve sung out to Frecklington’s office for some clarification on this rather major detail, and will report back if and when we get it. Another response addressed the question of what other entities, if any, were subject to similar ministerial powers which will allow the dismissal of a new commissioner or their deputies for no reason. While noting it was a “policy decision made by government”, the department noted this reflected the “high level of public trust in these roles and their critical importance in delivering a robust child safeguarding system in Queensland”. And after scouring state laws for other examples, the department found six cohorts also facing no-cause dismissal: Safe Food board members, the Racing Queensland chair, deputy chair or chief executive, hospital and health board members, and the director of Forensic Science Queensland.



Sure. (And we’ll ignore another government bill this year which removed such powers over Stadium’s Queensland board members because the power “does not … align with fundamental legislative principles”.) But on Circus’ reading of the Forensic Science side of things, that power does not, in fact, exist there. While a director can be removed at any time on the minister’s recommendation, there are specific reasons such a call can be made – none of which include, well, “none”. Have a curiosity for the Circus tent? Email on m.dennien@nine.com.au. For more security, sing out with a non-work device and network via Signal (mattdennien.15 or here) and mattdennien@protonmail.com. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

The defining moment of 2025’s gathering of world leaders at the UN may have been Donald Trump’s accusation of “sabotage” after his teleprompter blinked out and an escalator stalled while he was on it.

Now the world body is working overtime to make sure nothing similar happens again to distract from its focus on solving the world’s problems this week. Trump is set to deliver his speech at the UN’s iconic East River headquarters in New York City tonight.
