The UN is anxious for everything to run smoothly a year after Trump called for the arrest of the person who purportedly triggered an escalator to shut down just as he and first lady Melania Trump stepped onto it. At the time, the UN said Trump’s videographer may have been to blame.

World.title: Dunedin man loses $500,000 in 18-year romance scam
World.content:
A Dunedin man thought he was having a romantic online relationship with an Australian police recruit and sent her $500,000 over 18-years, in the hope they could one day be together.

But, in reality the woman was in Auckland, unemployed and living rent-free with her mother.

Instead of spending the cash on moving to Dunedin to be with the man - who eventually ran out of funds and developed cancer - she spent his money on food, shopping and paying off her personal debts.

Her offending only stopped when the man's daughter took over his finances, due to his declining health from cancer.

The 44-year-old, who has continued name suppression, pleaded guilty to a representative charge of obtaining by deception when she appeared in the Auckland District Court on Wednesday.

Prosecutors lay a representative charge when they allege the offending happened on more than one occasion.

The summary of facts, released to RNZ, shows the offending happened much more than once - it continued for years and involved elaborate back stories and even an invented health scare on her part.

The woman admitted obtaining over $525,000 between 2006 to 2024.

The court document shows the victim is a Dunedin man, aged in his late 60s.

The pair met online in 2006.

She told the man her name was Amy Skyers and that she was a police recruit living in the Gold Coast, Australia.

She sent him photos of an athletic model, implying they were her. The victim believed her, commenting on how great she looked.

They began an online relationship, with the victim depositing small amounts into the woman's accounts.

The couple would have intimate discussions either online or over the phone.

The man would physically deposit cash into an ASB bank account given to him by the woman, which appeared under her real name on the victim's bank statements.

When he asked who that was, she said it was her friend, who would then transfer the money through to her. She said it was necessary to avoid paying more into an Australian bank account.

Amy Skyers told the man she was planning on moving to Dunedin so she could be with him ... she just needed money for tickets and a shipping container.

She went so far as to send a blurred image of a fake travel itinerary she sourced from the internet.

As the move grew closer, the woman made up various excuses as to why she could not relocate to Dunedin.

These included needing to sell her belongings or requesting to be transferred by her work.

In reality, the woman was living rent-free in Auckland with her mother, and was unemployed.

She would make up situations, asking the victim to urgently send her money.

"Skyers" would tell the man she faced being kicked out of her rental, or would need to pay double the rent if it wasn't paid immediately. The man obliged and sent her the money.

In 2021, she told the man she was in hospital with a cyst on her vulva, spinning a yarn that she had been a foster child with a traumatic upbringing.

Court documents reveal this was all an attempt to convince the man to pay for her 'operation'.

While he empathised with her, the man said he could not pay because he was retiring in the near future and had cancer.

On one occasion, he told the woman he had no more money to share and was financially struggling.

The woman said she could not return the funds as she would be evicted from where she was staying.

She added that her friend, who she said was moving the cash, would be assaulted by her partner if the money was returned.

The woman continued to ask for money, telling the man it was for rent, flights, petrol, and other items.

The summary of facts said she actually spent the money on shopping, laybuy repayments, and food.

Some of the money was spent on petrol.

Between January 2006 and April 2024 the victim sent $525,537.10 to the woman's bank account.

That was made up of 1149 separate transactions from the man into her bank account.

In November 2021, the woman asked for $5000 to pay for a shipping container and flights so she could relocate from Australia to Dunedin and be with the man.

He was reluctant until the woman provided documents that she said showed she was in discussions with a shipping company.

The man paid a further $5000.

By December 2021, New Zealand was still in the grips of Covid-19 travel restrictions.

The woman told the man she was flying into New Zealand but her arrival would be delayed by two weeks, as she would need to spend time in a managed isolation facility.

She asked for more money to move to Dunedin and the man sent her a further $3050.

The offending only ended when the man's daughter took control over his financial affairs at the start of 2024, as his health deteriorated.

As well as his cancer, there were also concerns raised about dementia.

His daughter restricted his ability to pay the woman, and the payments stopped along with the communication between the two.

Court documents show the woman later admitted to deceiving the man and stated everything she said was a lie to trick him into believing they were in a relationship.

"She never intended to move to Dunedin," it said.

Explaining why she scammed the man, the woman said she was young when it first began and that she was financially motivated.

The police are asking a district court judge to order the woman to pay reparations.

In court, the woman's lawyer, Marek Hamlin, said she was doing what she could to find work, in order to pay back some of the money.

Judge Kathryn Maxwell remanded the woman on bail.

World.title: Thousands of children under 5 receive flu vaccine as sickness overwhelms health system
World.content:
Thousands of children under five have had a flu shot since it was made free for all of them.

On 1 September, Pharmac made vaccinations free for under fives after hospitals and clinics became overwhelmed with this season's very infectious strain of influenza A.

In figures provided on Tuesday, Health NZ said 3,843 under-fives had had their flu shots between then and 20 September.

Of these, 1723 were in the Northern region, with more than 800 each in the lower North Island and the South Island regions, and 435 in the Midland region which comprises Taranaki, Waikato and Bay of Plenty.

The number vaccinated in those 19 days was three and a half times the amount of the two weeks before the vaccination was free.

Auckland GP Mamaeroa David said a vaccination clinic at a Kōhanga Reo shortly after the change was one of the highlights of her career.

As well as under fives, the team immunised kuia and parents, including the whānau of a three-day-old baby. They also did catch-up vaccinations for a two-year-old who had never been vaccinated, she said.

"The whānau were really ready to engage because they had suffered a hard flu season this year - in fact there was still a third of that kōhanga reo roll not at kohanga on the day," she said.

"It was just amazing to be able to not have those whānau pay for those little kōhanga reo pēpē to have their flu vaccine."

It was heartening to know they were helping protect whole families, said David, who is also the senior Māori medical advisor for the Immunisation Advisory Centre.

In figures released last week, hospitalisations for children with flu-like illness had finally dropped, after spending weeks climbing.

But David warned there were still a lot of "snotty illnesses" circulating and there was often a sting in the tail of the winter season.

Health NZ was also encouraging parents to get their children immunised.

The flu vaccine was free for children from six months until their fifth birthday. Previously, it was only free for those at higher risk of serious disease.

The immunisation director of Health NZ's National Public Health Service, Nikki Canter-Burgoyne, said it was not too late for anyone to protect themselves.

"Vaccination remains important, even for people who have already had influenza this season, as it helps protect against influenza viruses they may not have previously encountered," she said.

This season's vaccination would be available into the new year, she said.

World.title: Group injecting of drugs creates risk to Fiji families - expert
World.content:
The chair of Fiji's National HIV outbreak and cluster response taskforce says group injecting of drugs in Fiji has significant potential to impact families.

Fiji last week declared a national HIV emergency.

Dr Jason Mitchell highlighted risky behaviour around injecting drugs, inconsistent condom use, and sharing equipment, known as Bluetoothing.

He told RNZ Morning Report that Bluetoothing is not as common as it has been made out to be, but it's still a concern.

Audio player for " Dr Jason Mitchell discusses HIV outbreak in Fiji " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/pacific/1516571%2Fgroup-injecting-of-drugs-creates-risk-to-fiji-families-expert

Dr Jason Mitchell discusses HIV outbreak in Fiji Morning Report Download MP3 5m

"What is unique about our injecting practices here in Fiji is the fact that we inject in groups," he said.

"And oftentimes you might have various family members in that same group, so the potential for it to impact the family is significant, especially if you take into consideration the ongoing risk factors that are associated with sexual transmission.

"Because then that's the mode in which it can transfer from, say, an injecting male parent to a female who then, if she becomes pregnant, then it's obviously at risk to her baby as well."

Dr Mitchell said pre-exposure prophylaxis - a preventative medication - has been made available in Fiji, but uptake has been slow.

"Despite the the knowledge that HIV is on the rise, and there's a lot of scare tactics going on, it hasn't resulted in an uptake in the use of pre-exposure prophylaxis," he said.

"So the onus is on us, as part of the task force and the government of Fiji, to really promote the availability of pre-exposure prophylaxis in the population. There's no limits to who can take it, unlike in some countries [where] it's only limited to certain population groups such as men who have sex with men or sex worker populations. In Fiji, we've made it available to everyone."

Dr Mitchell said new interventions take time to be accepted by the community.

But he added most resources in Fiji are free of cost.

"There's lots of reasons why people should engage in the services. It's widely available and it's free. And it's also protected through confidentiality and privacy laws that we have under the HIV Act."

Fiji's tourism minister said last week that Fiji remains open for tourism despite the outbreak.

World.title: British migrants take top spot in new citizen numbers
World.content:
British migrants have taken the top spot in new citizen numbers for the first time in five years.

India had been the top source country for residents becoming New Zealanders since 2022, when they accounted for one in five new citizens.

It is now in third place behind South Africa.

Overall citizen numbers climbed to 51,632 last year, a 12,000 jump on the previous 12 months and a record for recent figures.

UK residence-visa holders accounted for 12 percent of those numbers, with 5955 new citizens, followed closely by South Africa on 5939 and India with 5896.

Citizen growth is forecast to carry on climbing, as more than 200,000 people became residents in the Covid-era fast-track process, and they become eligible for citizenship after five years.

More than 54,000 became resident in late 2021 and early 2022.

Citizenship applicant numbers may also have been affected by people wanting to avoid needing to take a new test to become New Zealanders by grant, due to start late next year.

Those under 16 and over 65 are exempt.

Timeframes for citizenship decisions have improved in the last two years, after complaints from people who had waited between one and two years.

World.title: Explainer: What is a citizen's arrest and how do you make one?
World.content:
Explainer - Do you plan on making a citizen's arrest any time soon? There's some things you might want to know first.

Last month, Parliament passed an amendment bill updating the Crimes Act to include an expansion to citizen's arrest powers.

Members of the public can now detain others for Crimes Act offences including theft, assault or burglary.

The changes drew strong criticism from the police association, retailers and others, while Justice Minister Paul Goldsmith said it would help crack down on retail crime and allow security guards and others to legally detain thieves.

"Our government is committed to fixing the basics in law and order, and that means ensuring retailers are being effectively protected, are empowered to stop offending, and that offenders are caught and deterred from doing it again," Goldsmith said.

The changes took effect in early August, but last week saw a 19-year-old become the first person who was arrested over trying to do a citizen's arrest himself.

Police said the man detained an alleged shoplifter, but then assaulted them during the incident.

The Hamilton incident has fired up critics of the citizen's arrest laws.

So what exactly is a citizen's arrest, what are the rules and how can it go too far?

Who can make a citizen's arrest?

The idea of a citizen's arrest dates all the way back to English common law. It basically means anyone who's not a police officer making the claim to arrest someone for committing a crime, and then holding them for the authorities.

First off, you don't actually need to be a citizen, despite the name.

"Any person in New Zealand is able to make a citizen's arrest as per the provisions detailed under the relevant sections of the Crimes Act," a New Zealand Police spokesperson said.

There's also no requirement to be over 18 to make a citizen's arrest, police said.

Police do say would-be arresters should know "your safety comes first" and an arrest could "carry legal and personal risk".

"The risk of serious harm to yourself and others can be heightened if a situation escalates," their website states.

"In most situations, the safest action is to keep yourself and others safe, observe the crime, and call 111 and ask for police."

Auckland University of Technology law professor Kris Gledhill recently wrote about the new powers for RNZ.

"The amendments to the law relating to citizen's arrests have not reduced the complexity of the law to any significant extent; and there are no doubt false summaries circulating about what people can do, both about when you can arrest and what you can do on arrest," he said.

Changes to the Crimes Act have expanded powers to make a citizen's arrest - but there are many rules to follow. 123rf

What can and can't you do when making a citizen's arrest?

On their website, police say to make a citizen's arrest you must:

Believe, on reasonable and probable grounds, that an offence against the Crimes Act has been committed by the person;

Ask for the person's cooperation;

Clearly tell the person you are making a citizen's arrest and holding them until police arrive;

Call 111 and ask for police as soon as you can and follow all directions from them. This may include being told to release the arrested person;

Avoid using force. Only use force if it is necessary and proportionate and use the minimum required. What amounts to "reasonable force" will depend on the circumstances;

Do not question the person or search the person or their belongings

You also must keep the person detained safe, and are responsible for determining whether the person needs medical assistance and if they are vulnerable physically or mentally.

"Do not kneel or sit on the person, or apply pressure to the neck or head," police warn, and be aware of the risk of suffocation.

"Remember if you are found to have used excessive force, unlawfully arrested someone or failed to follow police directions without reasonable excuse, you may face criminal or civil legal action," the website warns.

Adults can also arrest youths and even children, the police spokesman confirmed - but there are rules in place about doing such things.

"There is no age-based restriction on arresting a child or young person," they said.

"While a member of the public may lawfully carry out a citizen's arrest where the criteria are met, the subsequent police response remains subject to the legislative framework that applies to children and young people in the Oranga Tamariki Act."

Gledhill said that the law remains complex and easily misunderstood, and even the police information on it may cause confusion in the courts.

He said, as an example, that while the police information says people should believe an offence against the Crimes Act "has been committed" by the person, Section 35 in the Crimes Act says the person should be found "committing any offence against this Act." (Italics added for emphasis.)

There is "a general principle that if you think you are acting within the law but you are not, you cannot rely on your mistaken belief about your powers - that is, if you have got the law wrong, you might end up committing a criminal offence," he said.

Retail crime was given as one reason for citizen's arrest changes. RNZ / YouTube

What is using 'reasonable force' to detain someone, anyway?

Well, that's where it gets tricky. One person's reasonable force may be another person's excessive force.

"It's important to always think what is 'reasonable and proportionate' in the circumstances," the police spokesperson said.

Section 39 of the Crimes Act allows "such force as may be necessary to overcome any" resistance when making arrests.

To get specific, it reads: "Justification or protection shall extend and apply to the use by him or her of such force (for example, the use of physical or mechanical restraints) as may be necessary to overcome any force used in resisting such execution or arrest, unless the sentence, warrant, or process can be executed or the arrest made by reasonable means in a less violent manner."

That could, in theory, include the use of cable ties to restrain someone, but that could also be done in a way that could be considered excessive force.

"If people exercise the citizen's arrest powers, the starting point is that an arrest can be made by words alone," Gledhill said. "Force can only be used if that is 'necessary' to overcome resistance or to prevent escape."

The New Zealand Police Association has been critical of the citizen's arrest changes, and its president Steve Watt said one of the concerns is around what reasonable force might be.

"Reasonable force is a widely misunderstood concept that can have serious consequences if applied incorrectly," Watt said.

"In its simplest form, it means you may use only the amount of force necessary to overcome the force being used against you. Permitting untrained members of the public to apply such a concept is an unjustifiable gamble."

It's too easy for people to assume they know how to make a citizen's arrest from what they see on TV, Gledhill said.

"This is language that risks being inflammatory because people watch too many TV programmes, particularly based in the US, where force is more or less always used on arrest and people are by default placed into handcuffs. That is simply not the law in New Zealand: restraints can still only be used if that is 'necessary'."

"Even police officers, despite their extensive training and experience, can sometimes face challenges when assessing and applying the concept of reasonable force," Watt said.

"This is where people can find themselves in trouble. What may seem reasonable to someone involved in a confrontation may not appear reasonable to an observer (the courts) taking a step back and reviewing the situation afterward."

So how is making citizen's arrests different now?

The Crimes Act Amendment Bill changed the rules so that people could intervene to stop any Crimes Act offence at any time of day.

Before that, people could make a citizen's arrest at night between 9pm and 6am where there were reasonable grounds for believing a person was committing a crime.

A citizen's arrest could also be carried out during daytime for an adult suspected of committing a crime punishable by more than three years' imprisonment.

There were also changes to certain sections of the Crimes Act to the protections an individual has when making a citizen's arrest, including being able to arrest a person without a warrant if they're committing a covered offence.

Paul Goldsmith. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Is expanding citizen's arrest powers a good idea?

The justice minister has stood by the policy. After the Hamilton arrest, Goldsmith told RNZ there were "clear directions" over what people should do.

"We passed a law and we expect people to follow that law. The clear directions in that is if the situation is appropriate, people can hang on to somebody and then call the police and follow the instructions of the police."

However, before its passage, groups including the New Zealand Police Association and Retail NZ opposed the changes.

Before they were finalised, Watt called the recommendations a "train wreck waiting to happen".

"In the association's submission on the legislation we noted 'A civilian attempting a citizen's arrest is at high risk of either using too much force and exposing themselves to an assault charge, or, using too little force and being injured themselves, and unable to safely detain the suspect'."

There are also many possible dangers for retail workers in confronting suspected shoplifters.

Auckland dairy worker Janak Patel was stabbed to death in 2022 when he chased after a shoplifter, while a teenager was jailed after killing a security guard who tried to stop him at a Papakura Countdown in 2019.

Gledhill described the changes as one that "could open a legal can of worms".

"The minister of justice is unhelpful in saying that there is a new law and people are expected to abide by it: the message should be this remains a quagmire that will trap some people."

Goldsmith has said the legislation will be tested over time.

"Whenever there's changes to legislation there will be instances that require the judgment of the court. There'll be a period of working our way through how that works in practice."

Goldsmith said he could not comment on the specifics of the Hamilton arrest, which is before the courts.

"We're trying to send a clear message that society doesn't tolerate shoplifting, it doesn't tolerate retail crime, so we're about giving the extra tools to retailers where appropriate. But of course, they've got to follow the law."

Gledhill said there still remains a risk of people getting the law wrong.

"Parliament regularly uses phrases like what is 'reasonable' or 'necessary' and then leaves it to the courts to work out how that applies on a case by case basis," he said.

World.title: Fijian chief calls for scrutiny of Fiji-Australia security treaties
World.content:
One of Fiji's most prominent traditional and political figures is warning the country's lawmakers "not to approve" two major bilateral agreements with Australia.

In early July, the Fijian and Australian prime ministers signed the Vuvale Union and the Ocean of Peace Alliance (Veitacini Treaty), marking a major upgrade to relations between the two nations.

The Vuvale Union is a broad political and economic framework, while the Veitacini Treaty is the specific defence and security pillar within that wider strategic partnership. Both governments have hailed the agreements as "significant" for future Fiji-Australia relations.

Australian PM Anthony Albanese said that signing the agreements was "one of the most significant endeavours" Australia had undertaken with any country.

Fiji and Australia say the agreements will strengthen cooperation on security, economic development, climate resilience and regional stability.

However, Ratu Tevita Mara, a paramount chief of Lau Province, is urging the Fiji parliament to withhold approval of both agreements "until the people of Fiji have been given a full, fearless and independent account of what these treaties commit our nation to".

"Both treaties were signed in Suva on 6 July 2026. Under our [2013] Constitution, neither binds Fiji until Parliament approves it, and both are now before Parliament's Standing Committee on Foreign Affairs and Defence," he said in a media statement.

"This is the moment - the last moment - for Fiji to examine them properly. Once ratified, they cannot easily be undone."

He said the examination of the agreements needed to be given sufficient time, independent advice and public participation.

"Let me be clear: this is not a rejection of Australia. It is a defence of Fiji," he said.

Ratu Tevita Mara Facebook / Ministry of Education FIJI

He described Australia as a "valued friend" but noted that an arrangement "presented in the language of family and cooperation" must still be read line by line.

"We must not accept terms whose deeper consequences become apparent only after Fiji is bound.

"Friendship must never require blindness. Cooperation must never become subordination. And no government has the right to gamble with the sovereignty of future generations."

World.title: Power companies warned to ensure customer apps functional as complaints surge
World.content:
Audio player for " Utilities Disputes sends app warning to power companies " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/personal-finance/1515863%2Fpower-companies-warned-to-ensure-customer-apps-functional-as-complaints-surge

Utilities Disputes sends app warning to power companies Nine To Noon Download MP3 13m

The Utilities Disputes commissioner is warning power companies to make sure apps they get consumers to use are functional, after a surge in customer service complaints.

Commissioner Neil Mallon said complaints about power companies' customer service are for the first time outpacing those about prices. That comes as Powershop consumers are reporting their frustration with high bills and not being able to get through to the company's customer service.

In Utilities Disputes' latest report, it shows Powershop as having 13 percent of all complaints that had to be resolved with the help of the Commissioner, well above its proportion of customers in the market.

A retiree couple in Auckland say they have had monthly power bills between $650 and $800 despite living in a warm, insulated house, but they have not been able to reach Powershop to try understand why their bills are so high.

A Facebook page for Powershop complaints now has 2000 members regularly posting their problems with the retailer.

Meridian Energy owns Powershop and its chief customer officer Lisa Hannifin said the company was aware of the app problems customers had had and was sorry for them.

Mallon said power retailers need to be clear with any changes to apps or websites that consumers are using and to avoid timing changes around winter and around April when prices are typically on the rise.

"We've seen at Utilities Dispute an increase of around 300 percent in the complaints we're getting about apps and what customers are telling us is delays getting through to the call centre, they're also telling us they've got disputed bills and they're having issues with using those apps to sort their way through."

There were also complaints about general communication and customer service issues with companies that are using apps, he said.

When a company moved to a new system such as an app there were generally some issues in terms of embedding that with customers, he said.

New technology could have a negative impact on customers and companies needed to be careful about how and when they rolled the new tech out, he said.

Mallon believed rolling out new technology in winter when it coincided with high bills was a bad idea.

"But also what's your customer base - are they the sort of customers that can readily pick up these apps and use that technology or do they need more support?"

There was a big spike in customer service complaints in 2025 which was where customers struggled to get through to their preferred method of speaking to their retailer and that had continued this year, he said.

"There are certainly some retailers that just specialise on those digital channels where customers don't have a call centre they can come through to, they use an app or they use the online channel.

"What I would say about those is they need to be really clear with customers before they sign up those are the only channels they can access because it's not for everyone and if you do have a complaint or an issue, that's where generally you want to speak to someone, you don't want to go through a digital channel."

Anyone who had an issue with the app or with contacting retailer could contact Utilities Dispute's industry ombudsman so they could look at the situation, he said.

Customers were able to switch power companies but it was not just information about prices that they needed, he said.

"They need to know how am I going to communicate, what access am I going to get to a real person or an app and how am I going to use this service."

Last year Utilities Disputes saw a 62 percent increase in the number of complaints, while over the last five years complaints had increased by more than 500 percent, he said.

That was likely due to a number of factors including an increasing awareness Utilities Disputes complaints service, the cost of living crisis and electricity price increases, he said.

Utilities Disputes received about 12,500 in 2025 and this year it was on track to get about 16,500 complaints, he said.

About 90 percent of those complaints could be resolved just by working with the company and the customer, he said.

World.title: Start-up Gigablue denied law change to push ahead with controversial marine carbon storage
World.content:
An international start-up wanting to carry out controversial carbon storage research in New Zealand waters has had its request for regulation changes turned down.

Gigablue warned it could be forced to stop operating in New Zealand if it did not get the changes it wanted, putting future economic investment here in jeopardy.

It wanted marine carbon research to be deemed a 'permitted activity' that could bypass the consent process, and consents for larger-scale, commercial activities to be non-notified.

But officials advised government ministers they had seen minimal evidence the company's idea worked or that it was environmentally safe.

Government ministers subsequently told the company they did not think that changes to New Zealand's exclusive economic zone rules were warranted.

They would need "robust evidence" to consider it again in future.

The decision leaves a question mark over Gigablue's future in New Zealand, with no applications for research or other activity lodged since March.

The company acknowledged questions from RNZ but did not provide a response prior to publication.

Co-founded by four Israeli entrepreneurs, Gigablue is one of a number of start-ups and research groups working in the growing field of marine carbon dioxide removal (mCDR).

Its business model relies on being able to sell credits on the voluntary carbon market. It has already pre-sold 200,000 credits to an aviation company.

If mCDR can be proven to work at scale, then it could be a vital tool to help cool the planet.

But experts in marine science and law say all mCDR technology is in its infancy, and is hard to prove, hard to measure, and - at worst - unsafe for the environment.

Gigablue's 'microalgae carbon fixation and sinking' method resembles an especially controversial method called ocean fertilisation, though the company contests this.

The company's method involves encouraging phytoplankton growth on particles, which store carbon in the deep ocean when they sink to the seafloor. RNZ

Ocean fertilisation involves adding iron or other nutrients to the water to encourage the growth of carbon dioxide-capturing phytoplankton, and is currently commercially prohibited under international protocols.

Gigablue says its method differs, because it encourages the phytoplankton to grow within proprietary particles that sink to the deep ocean.

Government advisers took a different view in a briefing to the climate and environment ministers in June, which was among documents released to RNZ under the Official Information Act.

"Officials consider MCFS is likely a form of ocean fertilisation," they concluded.

"Ocean fertilisation poses potentially long-term, severe, and widespread environmental risks."

Those included harmful algal blooms, oxygen depletion, altered food webs, and nutrient depletion.

"It remains unclear how these risks apply to Gigablue's MCFS technology."

This naturally-occurring phytoplankton bloom off the coast of New Zealand was captured by a NASA satellite. Gigablue says its method does not create uncontrolled blooms. NASA image by Jeff Schmaltz, MODIS Rapid Response Team

Regardless of the risk, the company had also provided limited evidence for its other claims, officials said.

"Officials have not seen any evidence that [Gigablue's technology] can sequester carbon dioxide from the atmosphere for any period of time."

Nor had they seen evidence that the technology could transport phytoplankton to the seabed, or that monitoring and verifying any carbon sequestration was even possible.

In late 2025, Gigablue published a 170-page methodology in collaboration with carbon removals monitoring, reporting and verification (MRV) company, Puro.Earth.

Other aspects of its work have been reviewed by Earth Sciences New Zealand, which has also carried out some desktop studies on the company's behalf.

Experts in marine science and law who spoke to RNZ earlier this year said those were good early steps, but insufficient evidence on their own.

They said there was extensive lab-based and controlled-environment research the company could do to help build its evidence base, before it resorted to large-scale field trials or commercial activities.

The Environmental Protection Authority (EPA) has allowed Gigablue to carry out three small sea trials since 2024 as marine scientific research, which is a permitted activity.

It turned down a much larger plan to deploy 1000 tonnes of the company's proprietary particles off the coast of Otago, judging that it amounted to marine dumping and was likely not legitimate scientific research.

The trials have so far been unable to track the particles into the deep ocean and the most recent trial in March this year ended early after storms damaged equipment.

Gigablue has previously chartered the Earth Sciences New Zealand vessel Kaharoa for its early field trials. Supplied / Eleanor Haigh

In a 'stakeholder document' it supplied to officials after the March trial, Gigablue said the current regulations were not fit for purpose and were causing "ongoing issues and delays".

It wanted marine carbon dioxide removal activities with "low/negligible impact" on the environment to be classified as a new permitted activity that would not require any consent.

Larger scale activities should be classified as a non-notified activity, with no public hearing required for a consent, the company said.

"The need is urgent," it wrote.

"If a workable permitted activity framework is not in place before the 2026/27 summer, Gigablue will not be able to proceed in New Zealand."

New Zealand was its preferred location, but it was "actively developing or evaluating operations in Australia, Canada, Alaska, and Chile".

New Zealand stood to lose out on "substantial" economic benefits if Gigablue left, it suggested.

An economic assessment it commissioned estimated the company's development phase could generate 5000 full-time years of work between now and 2029 and contribute $818 million to New Zealand's economy.

Once Gigablue's commercial activities were fully up and running, it could create 4000 ongoing jobs and $585 million in GDP a year.

The assessment itself cautioned that the benefits were likely overstated, a view shared by ministry officials.

The company has previously contracted scientific organisations in New Zealand to review its methods and conduct some desktop studies, and has also chartered local vessels to conduct its trials.

However, one OIA document refers to the particles themselves being produced in Australia, while its website states they are currently manufactured in France.

Despite the company's pitch to ministers - who it met with in March - they ultimately accepted officials' advice to keep a watching brief on Gigablue and international developments.

Climate Change Minister Simon Watts and Environment Minister Nicola Grigg wrote to Gigablue in July informing the company they did not think regulatory changes were needed. RNZ / Nate McKinnon

"Having considered the proposal, we do not consider legislative or regulatory amendments are warranted at this time," Environment Minister Nicola Grigg and Climate Change Minister Simon Watts wrote to Gigablue's chief operating officer.

"The EEZ Act already provides a framework for considering marine scientific research activities … consistent with New Zealand's international obligations."

The ministers encouraged the company to keep engaging with the EPA and the scientific community.

Publication of research would "assist in strengthening the evidence base for marine carbon dioxide removal technologies", they suggested.

Gigablue acknowledged RNZ's request for comment about its future plans in New Zealand but did not supply a substantive reply ahead of publication.

Its website still refers to New Zealand agencies, including Earth Sciences New Zealand and the EPA, but its plans here appear to have stalled.

The EPA said there was currently "no active communication" between itself and Gigablue and the company had not lodged any new permitted activity notifications or marine consents.

"The EPA is not currently aware of Gigablue's intentions regarding any future permitted activity notifications or marine consent applications."

James Kerry, chief scientist at European NGO OceanCare and adjunct research fellow at Australia's James Cook University, said turning down Gigablue's request was "the only responsible conclusion the government could have reached".

Kerry, whose organisation previously raised concerns about the company's approach at an intergovernmental marine law meeting in 2025, said it was not a case of regulation standing in the way of established science.

"Gigablue is pressing for regulatory changes to enable much larger deployments before the effectiveness, measurability and environmental safety of its approach have been adequately demonstrated," he said.

"Regulation should follow robust evidence, not be weakened in anticipation of it."

New Zealand had already played a constructive role by keeping its fellow signatories to the London Convention and Protocol - a key international marine law agreement - informed of its experience with Gigablue, he said.

World.title: Lions 'praying' Neale gets off but confident they will cope if ban stands
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Brisbane Lions players are confident they can cover the potential absence of Lachie Neale in the grand final, with the two-time Brownlow medallist facing a one-match ban.

Neale and the Lions will challenge the suspension at the AFL tribunal on Tuesday evening.

The 33-year-old has been charged with striking Hawthorn's Jack Ginnivan in last Saturday night's preliminary final.

Neale facing grand final ban The Lions will contest a one-match suspension handed to Lachie Neale, which would rule the two-time premiership captain out of the AFL grand final.

If the suspension is upheld, Neale will miss Saturday's grand final against Fremantle at the MCG.

Lions teammate Jarrod Berry said it would be a blow to lose Neale.

But he said the Lions were equipped to overcome any adversity.

"One of our best traits is being able to deal with that [adversity]," Berry said.

"We do it well and there's no point putting energy into it until we know the result.

"We'll be sitting tight and praying that he gets off. But if he doesn't, we'll face it when it comes."

Neale's gut punch on Ginnivan was graded as intentional conduct, medium impact and body contact by match review officer Michael Christian.

There is damning vision showing Neale guilty of the behind-play strike and numerous precedents this season of other players being banned for one match for similar incidents.

But the Lions are set to argue the suspension should be downgraded to a fine.

They will cite a fresh clause that allowed Collingwood great Scott Pendlebury to avoid a suspension in March.

Clause that could save Neale The Brisbane Lions will challenge Neale's one-game suspension for striking Hawthorn's Jack Ginnivan in last Saturday night's preliminary final.

Pendlebury was given a one-match ban for rough conduct for a bump on Adelaide's Josh Worrell.

He was found guilty by the tribunal but the sanction was downgraded to a $3,000 fine due to "compelling and exceptional circumstances", a clause open to the tribunal that will be central to Neale's case.

The relevant clause states: "Players will not automatically receive a reduced sanction for a good record.

"However, if a classifiable offence is contested or referred to the tribunal, a player with an exemplary record may argue that their good record constitutes exceptional and compelling circumstances."

The Magpies successfully argued the clause applied to Pendlebury, who had never previously faced the tribunal in his storied 21-year career.

Neale also has not previously appeared before the tribunal in his 320-match career.

He is also a dual Brownlow medallist and premiership captain, plus a four-time All Australian.

Geelong coach Chris Scott does not agree with the provision.

"Seriously, when we're starting to say, 'There's a rule for you because you've done good things for the game,' it's almost implying that other people haven't done a good job," Scott said on Fox Footy.

But Scott added: "I know his record is exceptional, but aside from that, I just like to see them play.

"I actually think that's going to be hard to defend personally, but my hope is that he does play."

AAP

World.title: Banned Swan falls well short in Brownlow Medal vote
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

The AFL has avoided the unwanted scenario of one of Sydney's suspended players winning the Brownlow Medal, with Isaac Heeney finishing outside the count's top five.

The league had a contingency plan in place if Heeney had won the game's highest individual honour.

But Nick Daicos's record-breaking number of votes, and prolific polling from Bailey Smith and Marcus Bontempelli, meant the plan never needed to come into play.

Daicos wins first Brownlow Nick Daicos breaks Patrick Cripps's record in the 3-2-1 voting era by winning the first Brownlow Medal of his career.

Heeney, and Swans teammates Chad Warner and Nick Blakey were among the notable absences from Monday night's awards ceremony.

Along with Riley Bice and James Jordon, they have been absent from Sydney's headquarters since being suspended by the club in August.

The five were stood down for breaching club standards following a post-match incident at the Pullman Hotel in East Melbourne.

Those suspensions are separate to a police investigation into sexual assault allegations, with Victoria Police flagging an update is not expected until late October.

No charges have been laid and the ABC is not suggesting any wrongdoing on the part of the five suspended players.

Daicos rewrites history with Brownlow win Nick Daicos's stardom has always had an inevitability to it, and his maiden Brownlow Medal triumph is the latest example of him fulfilling his immense promise.

The five players were ruled ineligible for All-Australian honours and were not invited to the Brownlow Medal function in Melbourne.

But they remained eligible for the award.

Brodie Grundy, Charlie Curnow, Dane Rampe, Logan McDonald and Tom McCartin were among those on hand for the Swans.

Once the count started, Heeney was the only player considered a genuine contender.

Heeney did not poll until round four, when he landed two votes, and claimed three votes against Gold Coast in Gather Round.

Warner polled for the first time in round four, while Blakey claimed three votes in round six.

Heeney claimed three consecutive three-vote performances to rise into the top four of the count at one point.

But his best performances were not enough to come close to Daicos's record-setting mark of 47 votes.

Heeney finished equal-eighth on 26 votes, ahead of teammate Errol Gulden (17), who ended the season with five consecutive best-afield performances.

AAP

World.title: Brownlow simply latest chapter as Daicos continues rewriting AFL history
World.content:
When Nathan Buckley's decade-long tenure as Collingwood coach came to an end midway through 2021, there was a silver lining for the club amid the painful exit of the club legend.

Buckley's tenure had seen the Pies flirt with winning a premiership in 2018 and 2019 before ultimately failing, but by the time he wrapped up, Collingwood seemed well out of the premiership window.

The silver lining came in the form of a player who was yet to set foot on an AFL field: Nick Daicos, then a teenager touted as a generational prospect years before he was eligible to be drafted.

Daicos wins first Brownlow Medal and sets new modern-day voting record Nick Daicos breaks Patrick Cripps's record in the 3-2-1 voting era by winning the first Brownlow Medal of his career.

The AFL world was no stranger to the Daicos surname due to the exploits of Nick's famous father, Peter, who was immortalised at Collingwood as a member of the club's 1990 premiership side.

You did not need to be a Collingwood fanatic to know about Nick Daicos. Everyone around the game knew the kid was on his way because of his prolific exploits at the junior levels.

The weight of expectation that comes with the level of hype Daicos had as a draft prospect can prove crippling. Unfortunately, years of evidence support this.

Sometimes even the most hyped prospects can take time to fit into the AFL system, and it makes sense. These are boys coming to a man's game.

The more rigorous training regimes, expanded playbooks, media commitments, dietary requirements, and everything else that comes with being an AFL player can be too much. That is even before we get to the pace of the game being completely different.

Nick Daicos with his parents. (Getty Images / AFL Photos: Michael Willson)

That hasn't been the case with Daicos, who, as an audacious Nike advert claimed on the morning of the Brownlow count, has proven it inevitable from day one.

From his first game, Daicos showed an ability to bend the game to his will in ways not seen in teenagers, and we have all been blessed to witness it.

Daicos's arrival helped catapult Collingwood from second-last in 2021 to fourth in his first season in the AFL.

Collingwood fell one point short of a grand final appearance in Daicos's debut season, but went all the way in his second.

After collecting boatloads of the football across halfback while occasionally dipping his toes in the midfield as a rookie, Daicos supercharged the Pies engine room in 2023, helping them claim the flag, and he has not looked back since.

Daicos helped propel Collingwood to a premiership in just his second season in the AFL. (AFL Photos via Getty Images: Dylan Burns)

From very early on in Daicos's career, the Brownlow win appeared to be a question of when rather than if, but it was the one accolade he was frustratingly made to wait on.

Daicos followed up his premiership by polling a ridiculous 38 votes in 2024, the most by any player in the league's history up until that point, only for that year's winner, Patrick Cripps, to poll 45.

Last year, he was again a seemingly unbackable favourite before being stunned by Gold Coast's Matt Rowell.

Missing out on a Brownlow after being among the favourites for a few years can be something that follows you.

Marcus Bontempelli, despite being widely considered the best player of his generation, has yet to win the prestigious medal.

Bulldogs star Marcus Bontempelli's career is an example of just how hard Brownlow Medals are to come by. (Getty Images: Michael Willson)

Buckley was famously made to wait year after year before eventually breaking through in 2003, his 11th season, while Gary Ablett Jr was even denied by his own teammate before his maiden Brownlow triumph. It is almost a rite of passage if you're an all-timer.

Despite Bontempelli, Zak Butters and Bailey Smith all challenging him at various points during the count, Daicos would not be denied this year.

Almost in revenge for the previous two seasons, this year, Daicos turned in an individual season that would ultimately prove impossible to ignore for the umpires.

Daicos broke Cripps's record with 47 votes and set a few more records along the way.

He is now the only player in league history to poll over 30 votes in three consecutive seasons, the only player to put together six straight three-vote games, and the only player to put together 13 three-vote games in a single season.

Daicos celebrates his Brownlow triumph with his parents after the count. (Getty Images: Morgan Hancock)

Given the ease with which Daicos has played from his first contest in the AFL four seasons ago, it was surprising to talk about the weight of expectation actually weighing on him after winning his elusive first Brownlow.

You get the sense that the weight of expectation might be the only thing that is capable of slowing him down, because efforts from his AFL counterparts to do so have so far proven futile.

For a player so metronomic and seemingly superhuman on the field, it was refreshing to hear Daicos admit he too deals with nerves and struggles with criticism, just like the rest of us.

Daicos admitted to the Brownlow win being a relief after being denied for so many years as a favourite, even saying he had given up trusting in betting markets.

Daicos is likely to put together more dominant seasons now that the weight of winning a Brownlow is no more. (Getty Images: Daniel Carson)

Now that the Brownlow box has been ticked off, it is frightening to think of what an unburdened Daicos could potentially achieve.

Still just 23 years of age, Daicos has gone from being the precocious youngster to one of Collingwood's veterans, and he will act as the bridge from one era of Collingwood premiership contention to the next, just as Scott Pendlebury did.

He seems good enough to single-handedly wrench Collingwood's premiership window open for as long as he wants.

Daicos has the chance to eclipse Scott Pendlebury (right) as Collingwood's greatest-ever player. (Getty Images: Morgan Hancock)

Adding premierships to his 2023 triumph will be at the top of Daicos's to-do list, and the hope will be that in the process of achieving that goal, his resume ultimately becomes undeniable.

The chance to be Collingwood's greatest player is in play. The chance to be the greatest player in league history is as well, as premature as that shout may seem.

The records Daicos set with his maiden Brownlow win will eventually be just another footnote for a player who is poised to rewrite the game's history books.

Like the commercial said: inevitable.

World.title: Thirteen-year-old surfer breaking records as first Indigenous world champ
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Leihani Zoric almost didn't compete in El Salvador, but now the 13-year-old is the youngest International Surfing Association (ISA) Under 18 World Junior Champion in history.

"When I went over there, I was extremely sick," Zoric told ABC Weekend Breakfast.

"I wasn't even going to go, my mum and dad were like, 'Leihani don't go, you're that sick'."

But the teenager was committed.

"I was like, 'no, I'm going to go. I believe that I can go all the way'," she told her parents.

And all the way she went, using visualisation to help her through.

"I wrote it down about 1,000 times [and] I said to myself, 'I'm going to become this year's Under 18 ISA gold medallist'," Zoric said.

"So, when it happened, I was like, oh my God, this is crazy."

Zoric, from Byron Bay in northern NSW, is the youngest ever surfer to win the ISA Under 18 World Championship. (Supplied: Surfing Australia)

Across more than a week of competition, Zoric was part of a 12-strong Australian team that went head-to-head with the world's best junior surfers.

She competed three age divisions above her own, to take out the title.

"It feels amazing," Zoric said.

"I'm really proud of myself for all my hard work and effort I've put in, and all the people that have helped me along the way."

It comes after a stand-out year so far, which includes winning the Junior Girls and Open Women's divisions at the 2026 Indigenous Surfing Titles.

She's now back home not only as a World Champion, but a history maker.

And she's taking it all in her stride, with a maturity that's beyond her years.

"I'm just so grateful to have been able to go to El Salvador and represent my culture and my country as best as I can," she said.

Loading Instagram content

Creating a proud history

Zoric, from Byron Bay in northern New South Wales, is also the first Indigenous world champion surfer at any level.

"I'm really proud to have represented my Yued mob over in Western Australia," she said.

"We have such important history in our culture and I feel like [that] has really shaped me as a person."

Zoric first got a feel for surfing at two days old, when her dad put her on a surfboard in the shallows at Broken Head.

From then on, she just loved the water.

Thirteen-year-old Zoric has had a stellar year, also winning the Open Women's division at the 2026 Indigenous Surfing Titles. (Supplied: Surfing Australia)

She takes inspiration from Soli Bailey, the first pro surfer to compete under the Aboriginal flag in the World Surfing League, and Cathy Freeman.

"Having those people inspire me has definitely made me want to be like them one day," she said.

Along with looking up to others, Zoric wants to be a positive role model herself.

When she's not in the water, she's busy creating connection, with things like Lei's Lu'au, a community day celebrating girls and women in surfing.

Loading Instagram content

"I hope that I inspire, not just as an athlete, but being a good person and always caring about others, being encouraging and just having a positive attitude all the time," she said.

"Bringing people up and lifting their spirits and attitudes and just [making] them feel like they belong here in this world.

"Because everybody is important and special in their own unique ways."

Locana Cullen (Under 16 men's) and Lucy Darragh (Under 16 women's) also claimed individual golds at the World Junior Championships, with Australia winning three out of the four divisions.

The Australians also won their third consecutive team gold at the event.

World.title: NRL set to axe ref Klein after controversial semifinal ending
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

The NRL is reportedly set to axe top referee Ashley Klein for the preliminary finals after admitting the Warriors were wrongly denied a crucial late penalty in their 12-10 semifinal loss to Newcastle.

NRL officials today confirmed the Warriors should have been awarded a penalty for an escort infringement by the Knights' Tyson Frizell with a minute left in yesterday's Eden Park thriller.

Had the penalty been awarded, the Warriors would have had the chance to level at 12-12 via a penalty goal from just to the side of the posts and send the match to extra time.

NRL investigating Eden Park incident The NRL is threatening to ban spectators who threw projectiles at referee Ashley Klein, with the league's integrity unit investigating the aftermath of Sunday's semifinal in Auckland.

But the call was instead missed on the field, with the bunker unable to review the play, despite a stoppage for an injury soon afterwards.

A comprehensive NRL review of Newcastle's 12-10 semifinal did, however, back the bunker over two other contentious calls.

First, it was deemed that bunker official Chris Butler was right to rule that Warriors centre Ali Leiataua got a thumb to a ball before it went to ground late in the match.

The NRL also supported the bunker's decision to stick with the on-field call of a strip against Warrior Te Maire Martin.

But it is the non-call on Frizell that will annoy the Warriors most.

The Newcastle veteran appeared to get in the way of Leka Halasima as he chased through on a kick in the Warriors' last attacking raid.

Given the seconds that would have come off the clock while the Warriors lined up the shot, there would probably not have been time for a restart.

"I thought they were trying to find ways to take it off us," Warriors coach Andrew Webster said after the game.

Projectiles thrown at ref as Knights win Projectiles have been thrown at the NRL refereeing crew following Newcastle's upset semifinal win over the New Zealand Warriors.

"The last one, two points would have drawn the game, he is going across Leka, pretending to try and catch the ball which they've told us you can't do."

AAP understands Klein will pay for the error by losing his spot in the preliminary finals, with Grant Atkins or Gerard Sutton likely to be called up.

Klein has overseen every game of the past five State of Origin series and two of the last four grand finals.

He had been expected to referee last year's decider, before losing out to Atkins following 18 penalties in a Melbourne-Cronulla preliminary final.

Meanwhile, the NRL have threatened bans for fans who threw projectiles at Klein as he walked off Eden Park on Sunday night.

Vision showed a mass of bottles and rubbish being thrown at the long-time official, with Warriors great Shaun Johnson labelling the fans' behaviour "embarrassing".

AAP

World.title: Daicos wins first Brownlow Medal and sets voting record
World.content:
Collingwood superstar Nick Daicos has finally claimed his first Brownlow Medal in a runaway victory with a record-breaking 47 votes.

The 23-year-old surged to a perfect nine votes from his first three games, led from round 11, then registered six consecutive best-on-ground performances between rounds 15 and 20 to seal victory by round 21.

Daicos won the AFL's greatest individual honour from Geelong star Bailey Smith (36) and Western Bulldogs champion Marcus Bontempelli (34).

The Magpie had 13 three-vote performances and beat the previous votes record of 45 set by Carlton champion Patrick Cripps in 2024.

Daicos, the son of Magpies great Peter Daicos, conceded he was relieved, having finally prevailed after runner-up finishes in the past two seasons, a third placing in 2023 and an eighth place in his debut year of 2022.

"I've just learned not to trust the the betting markets, to be honest," Daicos said at Monday night's vote count.

"But no, there is (relief).

"It's a massive award, and I'm so privileged to be up here. And yeah, I can't believe I'm a Brownlow medallist, to be honest."

The dynamic midfielder had already snared the AFL Players Association and AFL Coaches Association player-of-the-year awards this season.

It was the fourth consecutive year that Daicos was favourite, and with the umpires able to consult statistics for the first time, the star Magpie was irresistible.

Nick Daicos and partner Arlette Amor. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

Daicos averaged 34.9 disposals, 5.7 clearances, 6.7 inside-50s and 1.1 goals.

The brilliant playmaker was edged out by Gold Coast's Matt Rowell last year and Cripps the year before, when Daicos polled 38 votes.

Daicos, the Collingwood vice-captain who's widely expected to be named skipper next season, is the club's first Brownlow medallist since Dane Swan in 2011.

Bontempelli and Smith were the next best performers ahead of Melbourne skipper Max Gawn (28), Brisbane star Will Ashcroft (27), Carlton's two-time winner Patrick Cripps (27) and North Melbourne's Harry Sheezel (27).

Port Adelaide superstar Zak Butters, set to join Bontempelli at the Bulldogs next season, was among the contenders before his late-season ankle injury and finished on 26.

Sydney's Charlie Curnow, Collingwood's Nick Daicos, Geelong's Bailey Smith and Collingwood's Josh Daicos. (Getty Images: Michael Wilson/AFL Photos)

Banned Sydney stars Isaac Heeney and Chad Warner weren't in the room as they polled 26 and 12 votes respectively.

Brisbane's Conor McKenna won goal of the year while Hawthorn dynamo Nick Watson was awarded mark of the year.

World.title: How Freo's former number one ticket holder has helped Brisbane's dynasty
World.content:
If the Brisbane Lions win a third straight AFL premiership on Saturday, they will be thanking a former number one ticketholder for the Fremantle Dockers.

Luc Longley, a three-time NBA champion with the Michael Jordan-led Chicago Bulls, knows what it takes to reach the top and stay there.

Longley, a Fremantle native, was also the Dockers' number one ticketholder in 2006 and 2007.

But a meeting the Olympian had with the Lions in July may be the catalyst for Fremantle's downfall this Saturday.

The Lions are in their fourth consecutive AFL decider, and are trying to complete three premiership triumphs in a row and join the list of all-time great dynasties.

Despite finishing third on the ladder and making it to the final day in September, the Lions' 2026 season has not been smooth sailing.

Brisbane lost their opening two matches of the season, conceded a record 86 points in the third quarter of their loss to GWS, were hammered by 76 points against Carlton, and lost the qualifying final by 53 points to an understrength Sydney.

But they have overcome all obstacles to be in another grand final, with several players telling ABC Sport of a meeting with Longley in July which has spurred them on.

Former NBA champion Luc Longley is from Fremantle, and was once the Dockers' number one ticketholder. (Getty Images: James Worsfold)

"The ability he had to share some of that wisdom and talk to us about what he went through, it was awesome," Lions star Cam Rayner said.

"Just being able to compare and bounce ideas off him and learn things from him about the ability to keep turning up and find that motivation again has held us in good stead."

The Lions had six wins and six losses through 12 games, but were on a five-match winning streak before meeting Longley ahead of their round 18 clash against West Coast in July.

Rayner said Longley's discussions with the team about keeping the desire to win, despite already experiencing success, resonated with the team as they strived for a third consecutive flag.

"The hunger to want to win and to continue to have that success. At the start of the year there were times that wasn't really there in our performances," he said.

"We were dropping in and out of games and struggling to really perform to the level that we could.

"You can't really question the hunger after the game last week. It's back to a level that it needs to be and it's exciting to bring it to this week.

"That's one of the messages Luc Longley brought to us, he said, 'If the game's not going to get you up, you're probably playing it for the wrong reasons'. I feel like that really resonated with a lot of the boys."

Longley was an important part of the Bulls' 1996-1998 championship run, without being the star player.

Michael Jordan was the star of the NBA, while Scottie Pippen, Dennis Rodman and Steve Kerr also enjoyed big-name status.

For experienced Lions' midfielder Jarrod Berry, speaking to a champion who was known for his team-first work ethic was exactly what he believed Brisbane's dynasty has been built on.

"He [Longley] was never the big dog, the star, the whatever. He got more satisfaction out of seeing his teammates succeed," Berry told ABC Sport.

"Our squad is so talented and we've got so many stars and whatever, but it's not necessarily those guys that are making the club so special.

"It's the other guys that are doing all the tough work and hard work and selfless stuff.

"It was really nice to highlight that. It's all about being generous to your teammates and doing it for them."

The Lions are attempting to become the sixth team to win three consecutive V/AFL premierships, and the first since Hawthorn, who did it from 2013-15.

The Lions won three premierships on the bounce in 2001, 2002 and 2003, then lost the 2004 grand final.

The only club to have won three consecutive flags twice is Melbourne, which did it from 1939–1941 and 1955–1957.

ABC Sport will have a live blog of the AFL grand final between Fremantle and Brisbane from the MCG on Saturday.

Tech.title: California tightens rules on AI data center energy and water use
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom has signed seven bills designed to prevent AI data centers from passing utility costs onto residents, as reported earlier by the Los Angeles Times. The package of laws requires the California Public Utilities Commission to introduce a new rate classification for data centers, while forcing them to pay for upgrades to local power grids and water systems.

Other bills included in the package will require proposed data centers to disclose their estimated water use to local governments, along with information about energy efficiency and drought planning. They must also meet certain energy, water, and fuel consumption requirements before qualifying for a streamlined approval process. Last week, Newsom signed an executive order to speed up the creation of an AI “kill switch.”

Related Gavin Newsom is pushing for an AI kill switch

“While the Trump administration moves toward deregulation, communities are left to deal with the consequences — higher electricity demand, grid constraints, water use, and pollution,” Newsom says in the press release. “With these laws, we are ensuring that Californians remain in the driver’s seat — and that those profiting from data centers aren’t doing so at our expense.”

Tech.title: GM can’t ‘bring back’ Apple CarPlay because it never left
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

Last week, GM announced a new software experience for its upcoming Chevy Silverado and GMC Sierra trucks, including a new look for Apple CarPlay and Android Auto, the popular phone mirroring systems that the automaker made a big deal about removing from its electric vehicles in 2023.

Naturally, this led to some confusion about whether GM was “bringing back” CarPlay and Android Auto to its vehicles. Yahoo Finance reported it that way, calling it an “about-face” by the automaker, while Apple Insider’s headline boasted that GM “cave[d]” on its decision to remove the interface from its gas-powered vehicles. Even The Verge’s own commenters were a bit flummoxed about what was going on.

It’s certainly true that GM has not offered phone projection in any of its electric vehicles for the past three years. That means no CarPlay or Android Auto in the Chevy Equinox, Blazer, Bolt, and Silverado EVs; Cadillac Lyriq, Optiq, Vistiq, and Escalade IQ; or GMC Sierra and Hummer SUV and Truck EVs.

All of those vehicles have Google software products embedded in their systems, like Maps and Gemini. That’s because GM builds its operating system on top of Android Automotive, which is often called Google Automotive Services or GAS when bundled with the full suite of native apps. But if you’re hoping to plug in your phone, or connect wirelessly, and see the familiar app layout on the infotainment screen of a GM electric vehicle, you’ll be sorely disappointed.

The same can’t be said about GM’s many gas-powered trucks and SUVs. GM never disabled phone projection in its best-selling ICE models. Tens of thousands of owners of GM-branded vehicles regularly project their phones’ displays on their vehicles’ infotainment screens without any issue. And now CarPlay and Android Auto are both getting spiffy new picture-in-picture upgrades in the Chevy Silverado and GMC Sierra, a sign that perhaps GM is learning to co-exist with phone mirroring.

GM is partly responsible for the confusion. In an October 2025 appearance on Decoder, GM CEO Mary Barra defended the company’s decision to prohibit CarPlay in its electric vehicles and indicated that the policy would eventually extend to GM’s gasoline-powered lineup as well.

Everyone freaked out for a second time. Removing phone projection in EVs was one thing, but many truck and SUV owners were understandably incensed about the prospect of losing the capability in their beloved GM-branded vehicles. But a few days later, GM seemed to walk back that statement, clarifying to a number of outlets that Apple CarPlay and Android Auto would remain available in its gas-powered vehicles “for the foreseeable future.” Last week’s announcement of a new software experience in the Silverado and Sierra trucks would seem to be included in that “foreseeable future.”

Allow me to add some further reporting here. For the Silverado/Sierra announcement, I spoke to Colin McCormick, group product manager for Google built-in, projection, and profiles at GM. Here’s what he had to say about how GM’s position on phone projection has evolved over the years:

And so the way that I look at this is that we were one of the early adopters of CarPlay and Android Auto when it first came out. And we do have a small segment of EVs right now that don’t offer that, but there is a large majority of our vehicles that do offer that. And our big position on this is that it shouldn’t be two competing systems. So as we work together with Apple and Google to provide solutions that we think are best for the customer, this is what we’re representing in this new UI design. So I think we’re landing in a spot where … we don’t have a customer that has to decide, ‘Oh, I’m going to use projection,’ or, ‘Oh, I want to use the native system.’ That’s our sweet spot for us. And that’s where we want to live.

GM most likely realizes that its position on CarPlay and Android Auto isn’t popular. People really like mirroring their phones! It’s clean, it’s familiar, and it’s (mostly) dependable. The same can’t be said for most modern cars’ native software. Even the ones that are really well designed, like Rivian and Tesla, still struggle with some core functions like profile logins and messages. And you can find plenty of owners of both brands that would give their firstborn child for the ability to mirror their phone.

CarPlay and Android Auto aren’t perfect. They have dependability problems and connectivity problems aplenty. But they are worlds better than the majority of the native operating systems in cars today — most of which are just trash. Yes, they’re getting better. And GM is not wrong in thinking it can offer a better experience. But people get testy when you take away their choices.

So GM is finding ways to coexist with CarPlay and Android Auto. It doesn’t want to lose more customers over it, which is why we’re getting this most recent solution that includes picture-in-picture phone projection. GM thinks this solves the “two competing systems” problem, as mentioned by McCormick. But what it really does is get it out of the corner it backed itself into over phone mirroring.

Tech.title: Bungie says it’s ‘not done with Destiny’ and will bring back vaulted content
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Months after seemingly giving up on Destiny 2, Bungie now says it’s planning to restore vaulted content in the game like campaigns, destinations, and raids. The decision reverses the Destiny Content Vault that Bungie created six years ago, controversially removing older content from Destiny 2 that players had paid to access.

“We understand that removing these experiences had a lasting impact on player trust and enjoyment of Destiny,” admits Bungie. “We cannot change the decision we made, but we can acknowledge its impact and do the work to make it right by restoring these important parts of Destiny’s history.“

All Destiny 2 players will get access to the vaulted content, but it’s not a simple switch of a button for Bungie. The developer made big changes to Destiny 2 with the Beyond Light expansion, meaning it has to go back and update lighting, encounters, combatants, and other underlying systems for this older content. “That work will take time, but it is necessary to ensure returning content meets the stability and gameplay standards of Destiny 2 today,” says Bungie.

The decision to return this content to Destiny 2 comes just weeks after a “Sunrise” Destiny 2 offline preservation mod appeared. The mod lets players access older areas in Destiny 2 that had been vaulted, but not the exact campaigns and missions that players had experienced previously.

Bungie now says its own restoration project is the “first step to lay the foundation for how we reforge into new stories and games that you all deserve.” Could that be a Destiny 3 sequel? There’s no mention of such a project, despite fans desperately pleading for a successor to Destiny 2 in multiple high-profile Twitch streams in recent weeks. Bungie is only committing to building a “stronger long-term future for Destiny” right now.

Alongside the Destiny 2 efforts, Bungie is also admitting that Marathon, its extraction shooter, didn’t “reach as many players as we had hoped, and we also know and understand that the game needs to evolve.” That means Marathon will expand deeper into a survival experience. The changes are a little vague right now, but it sounds like Marathon really needs to change and attract more players if it’s to be a sustainable project for Bungie.
